language.summary:
STATE OF THE BOOK. Two books share one binding. The learn-to-program part (12 chapters) is the strongest writing in the repo. It is coherent, warm and precise, and every chapter is live with tests and Try-it exercises. It needs an edit pass, not a rewrite. The TJS-for-JS-developers part is uneven. The Basics/Patterns/Advanced example chapters mostly follow a good house pattern (live block, "What to notice", "Things that trip people up"). But the reference half under "The TJS Language" mixes reader-facing reference, maintainer design notes, implementation history and one chapter (CONTEXT.md) that belongs to the AJS book. All but a handful of chapters still carry `<!-- TODO review -->` markers. Strip them in the edit pass.

FLOW. Learn: the order mostly builds well. The one structural problem is that When Things Go Wrong (order 11) comes after the capstone, A Calculator (order 10). The calculator's exercises (make 1÷0 show an Error, ignore unknown keys) need what that chapter teaches, and the book ends on a debugging chapter instead of its project. Swap them. TJS part: the Basics section page promises an order (equality+footguns, then polymorphism/classes, then safety) that the `order` numbers do not produce. Current nav: Honest Equality 15, Polymorphic Functions 16, JS Footgun Fixes 17, Polymorphic Constructors 18, Safety 19, Better Classes 20, Local Extensions 21, Safer Code 22. Renumber to: honest-equality 15, js-footgun-fixes 16, polymorphic-functions 17, polymorphic-constructors 18, better-classes 19, local-extensions 20, safety-validation 21, safer-code 22 (or swap Better Classes in before Polymorphic Constructors, see briefs). The-tjs-language section puts eight maintainer design notes (type identity, runtime fusion, north star, FunctionPredicate design, parser primitives, ambient contracts, native engine, CONTEXT) in the same list as the reference. A reader cannot tell what is shipped, proposed or internal.

COVERAGE GAPS. (1) There is no chapter on where TJS runs: the CLI (check/run/emit/test, and the trap that `run` does not gate on tests), the Bun preload and Bun.build plugins, the browser bundle, what emitted .js looks like, .d.ts output. Pieces of this are scattered across inline-tests, local-module-imports and PRINCIPLES. (2) The book bans `Date` and says to use `Timestamp`/`LegalDate` in five places but never teaches them. Measured: `Timestamp` is NOT ambient in a .tjs file ("Timestamp is not defined"); imported from 'tjs-lang' it is an object with `now()`; an imported `LegalDate` has no `.check`. The built-in types (TEmail, TUrl, TUuid, TInteger, TPair, TRecord, Nullable, Optional) are not taught anywhere. (3) TJS-SYNTAX, billed as covering "everything else", has no `given`, no `test` blocks, no Enum/Union, no async, no imports/modules, no Timestamp, and no error-value API (`isMonadicError`, `.path/.expected/.actual`, `try` without `catch`). (4) Learn-to-program never covers waiting (timers, async/await, fetch), and it uses string methods (`split`, `slice`, `includes`, `repeat`) and `import` without ever treating text or modules as a topic.

OVERLAP (the same thing taught twice or more). Equality and the legacy-escape list appear in TJS-SYNTAX, honest-equality, js-footgun-fixes, why-tjs and PRINCIPLES. `const!` is taught in full in both const-and-bang and safer-code. Multiple constructors appear in both polymorphic-constructors and better-classes. Dictionary defaults appear in dictionary-defaults-example, docs/dictionary-defaults (a spike-history spec), TJS-SYNTAX and required-vs-optional. Error propagation is in safety-validation, error-handling and learn/when-things-go-wrong. Learn-to-program teaches 0.1+0.2 twice (values-and-names, checking-your-work), `? :` twice (decisions, when-things-go-wrong), and introduces off-by-one as new three times (repetition, lists, when-things-go-wrong).

CONTRADICTIONS AND STALE CLAIMS (verify-then-fix list):
- PRINCIPLES' ugliness table says `LegacyEquals(a, b)`. The real name is `DangerousLegacyEquals`.
- PRINCIPLES says AJS "bans `for`". AJS bans C-style `for(;;)` and allows `for…of`, which undercuts the Starlark comparison as written.
- PRINCIPLES says the AST is "unversioned today". `$ajs` v1/v2 exists (src/vm/ast-version.ts).
- PRINCIPLES describes "per-mode directives… one mode at a time". Abolished; TJS-SYNTAX says migration is per-construct.
- PRINCIPLES says "tracked in TODO.md". Work is on the Virta board.
- TJS-SYNTAX and PRINCIPLES say TjsCompat means "safety none". Measured: TjsCompat still validates parameters, as date-formatting says.
- TJS-SYNTAX says extend has a "runtime fallback via registerExtension". local-extensions (correctly) says a variable receiver throws TypeError, and north-star calls the runtime half dead code.
- TJS-SYNTAX's WASM section says "No imports/exports beyond the function itself", which contradicts `export wasm function` libraries.
- TJS-SYNTAX says FunctionPredicate `:!` "throws on mismatch". function-predicate-design says `:!` is "declared but not verified".
- function-predicate-design says untyped callbacks fail `fn: formatter` checks. declarations/higher-order say the runtime only checks callability.
- declarations says a regex makes a predicate unverifiable, while predicate-types says regex literals run on the linear engine. Both are true on different paths (emitVerifiedPredicate certifies no regex; compilePredicate does), and neither says which.
- given-dispatch cites "given 4/5 correct" as evidence. case-study-switch shows that exact number swung 1/5 to 4/5 on a re-run and was noise.
- runtime-fusion §8 is headed "planned" for a prelude that has shipped (`tjs-lang/prelude`).
- native-engine-integration's "current transpiler output" sample is out of date (no try/finally now, `__tv` unwrap).
- CONTEXT cites tosijs-schema 1.2.0 (the floor is ^1.12), its numbering jumps from §5 to §9, and its metadata says section "ajs".
- dictionary-defaults §5.4 still recommends stripping excess keys, the policy reversed in 0.13.0, and its header still calls it "a gated native-TJS mode".

IDIOM DRIFT. Error checks alternate between `instanceof Error` and `isMonadicError()` with no stated rule. Test syntax alternates between `test 'x' {}` and `test('x') {}` (lodash). Several Basics chapters lead with `tjs:static` blocks (hello-tjs, array-types, polymorphic-functions, polymorphic-constructors, local-extensions, js-footgun-fixes, error-handling, and every block in declarations), so the reader cannot run the chapter's main example.

BIGGEST PROBLEMS, in priority order: (1) The reference chapters (TJS-SYNTAX, PRINCIPLES, dictionary-defaults) carry stale or contradictory claims and history-as-documentation. (2) Design notes, a misplaced AJS doc and a user reference share one undifferentiated list. (3) Missing chapters: toolchain, built-in types/Timestamp, async for learners. (4) Duplicated equality/const!/constructor/error material in Basics. (5) Hello TJS and Declarations are static where they should be live.

New chapters are proposed below, all with integer `order` (no float orders exist in the repo) and basenames confirmed unique with find.

newChapters.brief: Running TJS: files, the CLI and bundlers. The book never says where a .tjs file runs. Cover: the .tjs/.js/.ts extension rule and dialectForFilename. The CLI: `tjs check` (type/signature/test gate, exit codes, --max-warnings), `tjs run`, and the trap that `run` exits 0 on a broken signature example; `tjs emit` (refuses on failing tests, --jfdi); `tjs test`; `tjs types`; `tjs convert`. Bun: the `tjs-lang/bun-plugin` preload in bunfig.toml and TJS_RUN_TESTS=1; Bun.build with `tjs-lang/bun-build-plugin` and sharedPrelude. Browser: `tjs-lang/browser` from any CDN. Programmatic: `tjs(src)` returns an object (use .code), plus the routing recipe currently buried in PRINCIPLES. What emitted .js looks like: the inline runtime, `__tjs` metadata, `prelude: 'import'`. .d.ts output. Installing the shared runtime (installRuntime) and why isMonadicError needs it across files. A two-file project (main.tjs importing mymath.tjs) run three ways. Absorb the CLI list from inline-tests and the project recipe from local-module-imports. Examples: one live tjs:inline showing `tjs(src).code` output, and static shell blocks for the CLI.

Dates, Timestamps and the built-in types. The book refuses `new Date` in .tjs and points to Timestamp/LegalDate in five chapters, but never teaches them. Measured: in a .tjs file `Timestamp` is not ambient ('Timestamp is not defined'); imported from 'tjs-lang' it is an object with `now()`; an imported `LegalDate` has no `.check`. So first establish the real public API with the maintainer: what is ambient, what must be imported, from which entry, and what each exposes. Then cover: Timestamp (epoch ms, now(), check), TimestampISO, LegalDate (calendar-valid date strings), LegacyDate as the escape, and why a raw Date is refused (mutable, timezone-dependent). Also the other shipped types: TEmail, TUrl, TUuid, TInteger, TPositiveInt, TNonEmptyString, TPair, TRecord, Nullable, Optional, with one live example each used as a parameter type. Close with a worked date pipeline without TjsCompat, which the Date Formatting chapter can then reuse. Follow the house pattern: live block with tests, What to notice, Things that trip people up.

For learners, placed after When Things Go Wrong (order 10) and before A Calculator (moved to 12). Programs that wait: a timer (setTimeout) driving a tosi model, a countdown, 'the handler runs later' (building on Responding to the Reader), then `async`/`await` with a small simulated delay, then one real fetch from a CORS-friendly public JSON endpoint the doc site allows (as the AJS API examples do). Show the common mistakes: using a value before it has arrived (printing a Promise), forgetting `await`, and a typed async function resolving to an error instead of throwing (tie to When Things Go Wrong). Tests: show how a test awaits a result (confirm the harness supports async tests first; if it does not, say so and test the pure parts, as the calculator does). Try it: a stopwatch with start/stop/reset, and a 'fetch a random fact' button that shows a friendly message on failure.

briefs.guides/sections/learn-to-program.md: Section page for the learn part. Keep the promise paragraph and 'How to read this part'. Fix: it says 'Along the way you build a working calculator', but the calculator is not the last chapter (When Things Go Wrong is). After the reorder (When Things Go Wrong 10, the proposed Things That Take Time 11, A Calculator 12), say the calculator is the closing project. Add one sentence naming what the reader will not have met by the end (classes, modules, servers) and where the book goes next: Basics, starting with Hello TJS. That bridges the learner into the JS-developer half, which currently starts cold. The 'quick start (/tjs/)' link points to another book; label it as such. Remove the TODO marker. Do not hand-edit the generated toc.
briefs.guides/learn/how-this-book-works.md: Strong opening chapter; light edit only. Must cover: what a program is, running/editing a live example, top-to-bottom order, the two kinds of mistake, the console, reading a test, chapter pattern, typing code exactly. Fix: the 'Breaking things on purpose' step 3 message wording ('Preview is not defined') varies by browser ('Can't find variable'); say so here once (When Things Go Wrong says it later). Exercise 2 promises 'the next two chapters explain' '7'+'6'. It is explained in Values and Names (chapter 2) only; say 'the next chapters'. The tosijs-ui link is fine. Strip the six TODO markers. No new examples needed.
briefs.guides/learn/hello-screen.md: Good. Covers strings, quotes, append order, comments, elements (h1/p/strong/em), + joining, templates. The `import { elements } from 'tosijs'` line is introduced as 'fetches the building blocks'. Add one sentence that this is an import, revisited later (and name where, once the book has a modules treatment), so it is not permanent magic. The 'Joining strings' section introduces `const` before Values and Names. Keep it, but the forward reference is fine as written. Consider moving 'Backticks, not quotes' to sit directly after the first template example; the two sections teach one idea. Strip TODO markers.
briefs.guides/learn/values-and-names.md: Covers numbers/strings/booleans, typeof, arithmetic order, string length/toUpperCase, const/let, naming, += , '5'+3, ==, undefined. Cut: the 0.1+0.2 paragraph. Checking Your Work teaches it again with the testing consequence, which is where it matters. Keep a one-line forward reference here. The `typeof` mention: TJS typeof differs from JS only on null; no change needed for beginners, but do not claim more. The '42' == 42 aside ('Some other languages quietly treat them as equal') is good; keep it. Add a short 'Try it' item using `typeof` on something surprising (typeof null gives 'null' in TJS) only if you want to seed later chapters; optional. Strip TODO markers.
briefs.guides/learn/functions.md: The best chapter in the book. Covers function/parameter/return/call, examples-as-types (0, 0.0, +0, '', true), required vs default, scope, signature examples as tests, :! for non-deterministic results. Verify in the live page that the repeatWord(3, 'ha') error names `word` and that the final 'swap price and quantity' exercise really refuses (quantity: 1 rejects 2.5): it does by the integer rule, so keep it. The table of examples duplicates the one in Hello TJS for the other audience; fine. One small fix: the first tips program writes `breakfast * 0.51` deliberately. Make sure the prose and the code agree (they do), and that the live result is visibly wrong. Strip TODO markers. No cuts.
briefs.guides/learn/checking-your-work.md: Covers test/expect, matchers, signature examples, edges, mutation testing by hand, fractions, errors as testable values, reading failures, test-first. Keep the 0.1+0.2 section here (it is the right home) and cut it from Values and Names. 'Mistakes are values' introduces `instanceof Error`; add one sentence that TJS also offers `isMonadicError(x)`, which later chapters for developers use. Then the two idioms do not look like contradictions when a learner moves on. The final exercise mentions `&&` 'from Decisions', which is the next chapter; reword as a forward reference. Strip TODO markers.
briefs.guides/learn/decisions.md: Covers comparisons, if/else/else if, a validated input meeting a decision, = vs ==, &&/||/!, ? :, given. This is the canonical home for `? :`; When Things Go Wrong re-explains it, so cut it there. The `given` section closes with '(Other languages have switch for this. It is easy to get wrong…)'. Keep it, but note for the developer half that `switch` still works in TJS with C semantics. Verify the `n % 2 = 0` claim (an error before anything runs) in the live example. Strip TODO markers.
briefs.guides/learn/repetition.md: Covers for, counting variants, off-by-one, running totals, block scope, tables with \n and pre, nested loops, drawing with div styles, while, break. This is the canonical home for 'off by one'. Lists and When Things Go Wrong should refer back to it, not reintroduce it as a new name. The 'change let to const in the loop' experiment depends on the first round running before the TypeError; verify on the page. Strip TODO markers.
briefs.guides/learn/lists.md: Covers arrays, indexing, length-1, for…of, typed list params [0.0] with per-item errors, push, toEqual vs toBe, includes/indexOf, map/filter with arrow functions, sort (including the numeric trap), spread copy, rendering lists. Arrow functions are introduced inside the map section; the sort section then uses `(a, b) => a - b` and says 'the map section explains the arrow'. Fine as ordered. 'When a list has the wrong thing in it' uses `bill.message`, good. Its last paragraph says changing 'four' to 4 makes 'the first two checks fail… that is right too'; that is confusing for a beginner, so rephrase or drop it. Remove the 'has a name' framing of off-by-one; point back to Repetition. Exercise 4 tells the reader to discover `slice` at a console; consider a two-line demo instead. Strip TODO markers.
briefs.guides/learn/things-with-parts.md: Covers objects, properties, typos-as-undefined, nesting, bracket access, Object.keys, lists of objects with reduce, returning objects, shorthand, == vs Is vs toEqual, object-shaped parameters, Type with description/example, Type with predicate. Good arc; the typo problem is set up and paid off. `reduce` arrives with one sentence; either slow it down (show the running value per step) or replace it with the for…of version the text says is equivalent. Beginners stall on reduce. The predicate section is the reader's first predicate; add one sentence that predicates should be plain checks (no loops, no fetch) because TJS can then prove them safe. That foreshadows Predicate Types without jargon. Strip TODO markers.
briefs.guides/learn/responding-to-the-reader.md: Covers events/handlers, onClick, calling too early, tosi models, bindValue, numbers from text boxes, keeping rules out of handlers. Strong. The 'In plain JavaScript the same slip…' aside is the only place the learn part addresses JS directly; keep it short. `event.target.value` appears without comment. Fine for learners; do not import the TS-pessimism discussion. Verify in the browser that `press`-style functions with object-shaped params accept tosi proxies (the calculator relies on it). Strip TODO markers. If the proposed Things That Take Time chapter is added, end with a one-line pointer: 'some events are not clicks: a timer, an answer from the network'.
briefs.guides/learn/when-things-go-wrong.md: Move to order 10, before the calculator, so the calculator's error exercises can use it. Covers two (three) kinds of wrong, errors as values with .message/.received, a field guide to messages, not-defined/not-a-function, propagation, checking with instanceof Error, making your own Error, the flight recorder (__tjs.errors()), console.log, a debugging method. Cut: the re-explanation of `? :` (Decisions owns it; one back-reference is enough). Cut: the 'off-by-one has a name' paragraph; refer back to Repetition. 'Errors pass along' says `toBe(first)`: same object, good. The claim that returning your own `Error('…')` does not propagate but is kept as `received` is subtle; keep it, but test it on the page. Strip TODO markers.
briefs.guides/learn/a-calculator.md: Move to the last order (12, after the proposed Things That Take Time) as the capstone. Covers planning state in prose, a pure press/calculate brain with tests, the tosi face, adding keys test-first, signature example on run, Infinity/NaN cases, exercises. The brain code is repeated three times in full (brain, face, workbench); that is ~250 duplicated lines. Consider showing the face with only the model and buttons and saying 'paste press and calculate from above', or keep one workbench and make the face import-free by repetition only once. 'The example on press' section is excellent; keep it. Exercises now can lean on When Things Go Wrong (make 1÷0 an Error). Strip TODO markers.
briefs.guides/sections/the-tjs-language.md: Rewrite the 'How to read this part' paragraph against what the chapters really contain. It claims TJS-SYNTAX covers 'everything else', which it does not (no given, test blocks, Enum/Union, async, imports, Timestamp). Split the list visibly into three tiers: Argument (why-tjs, PRINCIPLES), Reference (declarations, TJS-SYNTAX, dictionary defaults, plus the proposed running-tjs if parented here), and Design notes. Mark the design notes with status (shipped / decided / proposed / exploratory) in the section page itself, because the notes do not do it consistently. Remove CONTEXT.md from this book: it is the AJS VM's technical context. Remove or relabel the 'the TJS section is the practical half' line, since Basics/Patterns/Advanced hang off tjs-examples.md, not off this page. Strip the TODO.
briefs.guides/why-tjs.md: Polemic chapter; keep it as the opener of the reference half. Must cover: the history (Good Parts, JSLint, use strict, TS/Flow, ESM/.mjs), the gap table, the three commitments. Fix metadata: drop the legacy keys `section/group/navTitle` if unused by the doc site (check doc-site-structure.test.ts). The ESM section says 'abolished all nine of its mode directives'. Accurate, but readers of this book never saw them; say 'its earlier mode directives'. The typeof table uses an indented code block; convert it to a fenced js block with `<!-- prettier-ignore -->` if needed. The closing links point to TJS-FOR-JS/TJS-FOR-TS and the generated difference table (other books); keep them, labelled as other books. Tone check: 'TypeScript is the set of lies…' lives in PRINCIPLES, not here; keep this chapter's tone measured, as it is.
briefs.PRINCIPLES.md: Currently half reader-facing invariants and half maintainer rules. For this book keep: 'type system is not the source of truth', on-ramp/off-ramp and the named-confession tests, the subset invariants and 'more, never illegal', signature tests inconclusive vs failed, 'make stupid stuff stand out', the conversion contract (short). Move out: 'Routing all three dialects' (a recipe for tool authors; it belongs in the proposed running-tjs chapter or an integrations doc), 'the formal AST contract is AJS's' and the AJS loop rationale (AJS book), and the north-star section (duplicates docs/type-system-north-star; leave a two-line pointer). Fix stale items: the ugliness table says `LegacyEquals(a, b)`, but the real name is `DangerousLegacyEquals`. 'AJS bans for and keeps while' is wrong: AJS bans C-style for(;;) and keeps for…of, so the Starlark contrast must be restated (AJS keeps the bounded form AND an unbounded one, because fuel carries termination). 'Current node set (unversioned today…)' is stale: $ajs v1/v2 exists. 'Combined with per-mode directives (TjsCompat, then one mode at a time)' is stale: modes were abolished, and migration is per-construct (as TJS-SYNTAX says). 'TjsCompat… dialect' is fine, but TjsCompat does NOT imply safety none (measured: parameters still validated). 'tracked in TODO.md' should point to the Virta board. '~16 source-text transforms' should be '~30' or drop the count (CLAUDE says skip stale-prone counts). Add one runnable example to the 'You cannot lie to a worked example' paragraph (add(a: 2, b: 3): 0 failing), as tjs:inline expect-error if supported.
briefs.guides/examples/tjs/declarations.md: The right content, but every block is tjs:static. Make them tjs:inline, since each block is self-contained by design and has tests. Covers Type (simple, block, predicate block/function form), serialisation to facts, Enum, Union, Generic, FunctionPredicate, declarations in signatures, parameterised Type, what an example can say, inline vs library differences. Fix: the Generic section and the parameterised-Type section both define `Box`, and the reader cannot tell Generic Box<T> from Type Box<T>. Rename one, and add a sentence on when to use which (Type<T> when the example locates T; Generic when you need a predicate). `dist(a: Point, b: Point): 0`: the return example is an integer, but hypot returns floats. Use `: 0.0` or a worked pair (the signature test calls dist with two {0,0} points, so `: 0.0` passes). Clarify the regex paragraph: in a .tjs Type predicate, a regex literal is not certified (emitVerifiedPredicate cannot carry the linear engine), while compilePredicate/$predicate paths run regexes on the linear engine. Predicate Types states the second without the first. Mention built-in types (Timestamp, TEmail…) with a pointer to the proposed built-in-types chapter. Consider moving this chapter's file out of guides/examples/tjs/, since it is not a playground example (check that the docs builder does not treat it as one).
briefs.TJS-SYNTAX.md: The reference. Needs restructuring, accuracy fixes and gap-filling. Reorder to the order a reader looks things up: parameters, then return annotations, then safety markers, then the .tjs rules and named escapes, then declarations (short, pointing to Declarations), equality/typeof/truthiness, control flow (`given` is missing; add it, with a pointer to the case study), test blocks (missing; add `test 'x' { }`, the expect matchers, when they run, inconclusive), errors (missing: MonadicError, isMonadicError, .path/.expected/.actual, `try` without catch, bang access), classes, polymorphism, extend, const!, bare assignments, doc comments, modules/imports (missing), async (missing: params checked, return example not run), WASM (short; DOCS-WASM is canonical), and @tjs annotations. It currently opens with classes, written as a `typescript` fence using `constructor(public x: number…)`, TS parameter-property syntax in a TJS reference. Replace it with TJS. Fixes: 'For a guided introduction, start with DOCS-TJS.md' points to another book; point to Hello TJS. The TjsCompat line says 'JS semantics, safety none', but parameters are still validated (measured), so correct it. Local Class Extensions says 'Runtime fallback via registerExtension()/resolveExtension() for unknown types', which contradicts local-extensions (a variable receiver throws) and north-star (runtime half dead). WASM 'Current Limitations: No imports/exports beyond the function itself' contradicts `export wasm function` libraries. FunctionPredicate return-contract comments (':! assertReturns (throws on mismatch)') contradict function-predicate-design; settle it from the code and fix both. `@tjs-unsafe` 'becomes the unsafe marker' but `unsafe` is deprecated; say what conversion emits now. The 'Module Safety Directive' section should say plainly that `safety all` is a no-op in emitted code and `?` is ignored (safety-validation already admits it). Check whether `safety` directives survive the abolition of modes and, if so, say why they are not modes. Use one fence convention (`tjs` for TJS, not `typescript`). Make the Equality Operators inline example avoid `const same = a Is b` (the doc itself says to prefer `Is(a, b)`).
briefs.docs/dictionary-defaults.md: Currently a spec-plus-implementation-diary (spikes, stages, ns/op benchmarks, OQ resolutions), with stale passages: §5.4 still recommends 'strip always', reversed in 0.13.0; the header calls it 'a gated native-TJS mode' and 'Stage 4 dogfood remaining'; §2 'what current tjs actually does (measured 2026-07-18)' describes pre-feature behaviour. For this book, rewrite it as the normative reference: the rule (= object literal = per-member defaults), trigger conditions (absent/undefined fill, null is a value, example-null admits null), recursion, arrays as values, excess keys pass through (and the dict-default-excess-key lint), prototype keys rejected, purity restriction on default literals, complete-payload identity, : vs = vs `p: T = {…}` (atomic), LegacyDefault, dialect gating (off for .js/fromTS/TjsCompat; TjsStrict enables), the `!` interaction, and .d.ts deep-partial output. Keep the WebIDL divergence box. Move §7–§10 (runtime design, spikes, benchmarks, stages) to docs/reviews or an appendix file, linked. Add one live example per rule, or link to the Basics example and avoid duplicating its demos.
briefs.docs/type-identity.md: A maintainer note, accurate and recently measured ('Nowhere in the corpus'). Keep it in the design-notes tier, labelled 'internals'. Fix metadata: `section: internals`, `navTitle` are legacy keys; check what the site uses. Add a 3-sentence reader summary at the top for a TJS user: emitted code checks with the file's own inline stub; the library's Type gives the same verdicts; this page is for people changing the runtime. Links to src/*.test.ts are fine for maintainers, but they will 404 on the doc site. Render them as code, not links.
briefs.docs/runtime-fusion.md: Design note. Keep it in the design-notes tier. Stale: §8 is headed 'planned 2026-10-31' and has a 'Done when' list, but `tjs-lang/prelude` and `tjsPlugin({ sharedPrelude: true })` have shipped (CLAUDE.md). Retitle §8 as shipped, convert 'Done when' to 'What shipped / how it is tested', and keep 'Measured' and 'Self-critique'. Add a reader-facing first paragraph: when to use `prelude: 'import'` / `sharedPrelude` and why default output stays standalone. That user-facing guidance belongs in the proposed running-tjs chapter too; link both ways.
briefs.docs/type-system-north-star.md: Strategic note, 579 lines, mixing the principle, a design for `asCompared`, a registry-chain decision, an `extend` dead-code finding and a `Predicate` umbrella proposal. Label status per section (direction / decided / open). The 'Prerequisite: extend's runtime half is dead code' finding contradicts TJS-SYNTAX's claim of a runtime fallback; whichever is true, fix the other. Trim or split: the `asCompared` and `Predicate` umbrella material could be separate design notes, because readers come here for the lens and leave before reaching it. PRINCIPLES carries a duplicate summary; keep one pointer there and the substance here.
briefs.docs/function-predicate-design.md: Written as a proposal ('TJS has no way to express…', '() => void becomes undefined in fromTS output', 'Implementation Path'), but FunctionPredicate has shipped. Either convert it to 'design rationale + what shipped vs what did not', or mark it historical. Specifically: state that the runtime check is callability only (declarations.md and higher-order-functions say so), and that the `fn: formatter` function-as-type-example form with __tjs shape matching is not implemented (verify). ajs.summary:
STATE OF THE AJS BOOK (read in order, claims spot-checked against the tree at 47303274 by transpiling and running them on the current VM).

FLOW. The book has two halves that don't connect. (1) A teaching half (DOCS-AJS, the examples, patterns, safe-eval) that is mostly current and often very good. The 26 example pages and patterns.md had a recent careful pass. (2) Six docs/ design notes (ajs-native-vm, ajs-lean-spec, pattern, vm-budgets, universal-endpoint) plus two contributor setup docs (lm-studio-setup, mlx-setup), all attached as `parent: ajs.md`. They are internal design history or test-suite setup, and they're written for maintainers, not for this book's reader. The landing page (guides/ajs.md) is the weakest chapter: it's an older, parallel copy of DOCS-AJS, it uses the "Agent99" name, and it contradicts the current VM in several places. A reader meets two overlapping references before any example. Sibling `order` values collide: patterns=5 and universal-endpoint=5; lm-studio, ajs-lean-spec and vm-budgets are all 7; mlx and pattern are both 8. The committed `<!-- toc -->` in guides/ajs.md lists 8 of the 13 children; it's regenerated at build, but the collisions make the order unpredictable.

PROPOSED ORDER (children of ajs.md): 1 DOCS-AJS (the language), 2 AJS Examples, 3 patterns, 4 safe-eval (the two-line embedding), 5 NEW ajs-host (embedding AgentVM), 6 NEW ajs-capabilities (capabilities and custom atoms), 7 NEW ajs-atoms (atom reference), 8 ajs-llm-prompt, 9 universal-endpoint, 10 vm-budgets, 11 lm-studio-setup / 12 mlx-setup (local models), then design notes under one "Internals and roadmap" heading: 13 ajs-native-vm, 14 ajs-lean-spec, 15 pattern. Or move those three out of the book.

COVERAGE GAPS. (a) No chapter is the embedder's manual. Run options, the RunResult shape, AgentError's fields and the catchable vs run-ending refusal split are scattered across DOCS-AJS, safe-eval, patterns and the examples. The same goes for `context` keys (allowedFetchDomains, allowedFetchMethods, allowedRequestHeaders, requestDepth), the transpile/vm-ast split and the deprecation of vm.run(source). (b) No complete atom reference. The VM registers 60 atoms with batteries. DOCS-AJS tables list about 30 and omit template, regexMatch, runCode, transpileCode, jsonParse/jsonStringify, xmlParse, pick/omit/merge, consoleLog/Warn/Error, varAssign/constSet and callLocal, which examples and prompts already use. (c) Custom atoms and capability interfaces (the shape of fetch/store/llm/code/agent, storeOf, egressValue, effects, resolveInputs) get a few dense paragraphs at the end of DOCS-AJS.

OVERLAP. guides/ajs.md and DOCS-AJS teach the same material twice: types, builtins, Set/Date, errors, security, API. Fuel and quotas are explained in DOCS-AJS, safe-eval, fuel-limits, patterns and llm-chat. The fetch admission rules appear in DOCS-AJS, patterns and safe-eval. The uncatchable-refusal rule appears in DOCS-AJS, patterns, ajs-error-handling and safe-eval. Pick one home for each and link to it.

VERIFIED WRONG OR STALE ACROSS CHAPTERS:
- Default timeout. safe-eval.md and fuel-limits.md say "by default 10 ms per unit of fuel", and eval.ts's own JSDoc says `fuel * 10`. The code passes `timeoutMs` through undefined, so vm.run uses `defaultRunTimeout` = max(60 s, 2 × slowest atom), which is 240 s with batteries loaded. Fix the docs, or fix the code to match the promise; that's an owner decision.
- guides/ajs.md says a declared return type is not checked. That is false since #3834; DOCS-AJS documents the enforcement.
- The LLM prompt says `for...of` is NOT supported, forbids `console.log`, and forbids return types. In fact `for...of` works, `console.log` transpiles and runs, and return types are now an enforced contract.
- The prompt's rule 1, "positional params not supported", is contradicted by its own examples, and positional entry params do run (`function f(n: 5)`). DOCS-AJS's "Functions take a single destructured object parameter" is likewise a convention, not a rule.
- The prompt's examples use `search`/`summarize` atoms that don't exist and `llmPredict({ system, user })`, but llmPredict takes `prompt`.
- lm-studio-setup says the base URL is hardcoded with "no env override", but TJS_LLM_BASE_URL exists.
- The chained-callback error message reads "Unsupported expression type in condition: ArrowFunctionExpression". The docs teach the rule well, but this message is misleading; file it as a transpiler card. `break` gets no hint, while `switch` does.

BIGGEST PROBLEMS, in priority order: rewrite guides/ajs.md as a short landing page; write the embedder chapter (ajs-host); fix the LLM prompt (it's load-bearing for test:grok, so re-measure after changing it); de-book or regroup the design notes; fix the timeout claim. Most pages still carry `<!-- TODO review -->` markers from the last pass, so the edit pass should clear them as it goes.

newChapters.brief: Title: 'Embedding the AJS VM'. The embedder's manual, which no chapter is today. Its content is scattered across guides/ajs.md, DOCS-AJS (The VM, Capability Injection, membrane, heap, quotas, Fetching, Tracing, Performance), safe-eval, patterns and the examples' 'running it locally' snippets. COVER: (1) The two-step architecture: transpile where parsing is safe (`transpile(src, { atoms: vm.atoms, maxSourceBytes })`), store or ship the versioned JSON AST, and run it on `tjs-lang/vm-ast` (no parser). `vm.run(source)` is deprecated, and why. (2) Every RunOptions field, as a table with default and what it bounds: fuel, timeoutMs (the REAL default: max(60 s, 2 × slowest atom); verify), maxHeapBytes, membraneMaxBytes, argsMaxBytes, maxSourceBytes, quotas and quotaUsed (trusted host state; re-entrancy), costOverrides, timeoutOverrides, signal, trace, capabilities, context. (3) The `context` keys the VM reads: allowedFetchDomains, allowedFetchMethods, allowedRequestHeaders, requestDepth/X-Agent-Depth, plus Eval's fetchPolicy equivalent. (4) The RunResult shape: result, error (AgentError: message, op, cause), fuelUsed, trace; `$error` inside result; isAgentError. (5) Refusals: catchable (the world's) vs run-ending (the program's bug, or a host returning non-JSON), with the one-question test 'could plain JSON have done this?'. (6) Argument admission: args cross the membrane, class instances are refused, the input schema is checked before the run, and a declared result is checked after. (7) Signatures and tool definitions: createAgent, .signature, getToolDefinitions. (8) Tracing for audit. (9) Deployment shapes: in-process, worker, separate process (with safe-eval's out-of-scope list), and browser/server isomorphism (link universal-endpoint). EXAMPLES: one complete host (transpile in a 'trusted' function, run on vm-ast with fetch policy, an llm capability, quotas and trace, then branch on error kind); a quota held across a nested run with a shared quotaUsed; a run-ending refusal versus a catchable one, side by side. Link instead of restating: safe-eval's guarantees section, vm-budgets for the invariants.

Title: 'Capabilities and Custom Atoms'. How a host gives an agent power, and how to add atoms safely. Today this is a few dense paragraphs at the end of DOCS-AJS plus CLAUDE.md-only knowledge. COVER: (1) The Capabilities interface, each key with its exact signature and the atoms that use it: fetch(url, init) → body as data; store { get, set, query?, queryPredicate?, vector ops }; llm { predict(prompt, options), embed? } and how options/responseFormat arrive; llmBattery and vector (batteries; getBatteries; null when no server or under HTTPS); code { transpile } for runCode/transpileCode; agent { run } for agentRun. (2) What a capability may return: JSON data plus Date, no accessors, no spreading host objects, same-realm plain values, size under membraneMaxBytes; the Response → { ok, status, body } recipe. (3) defineAtom in full: opCode, input/output schemas (required for IO atoms, no pattern), the implementation, cost (static or a function of resolved input), timeoutMs, effects ('io' default; 'pure' only when deterministic and capability-free, and why predicate safety depends on it), resolveInputs (false for step-taking atoms), storeOf(ctx), egressValue, createChildScope/releaseScope, ctx.signal. (4) Registering atoms (`new AgentVM({ ... })`) and passing them to the transpiler so calls are checked. (5) Writing a safe fetch capability: allowlist, no redirects, no ambient credentials, depth header, rate limit, retry/backoff living here rather than in the agent. (6) Testing atoms and agents with fake capabilities (move patterns.md's 'Mock Capabilities' here, or link it). EXAMPLES: a pure atom; an IO atom wrapping a REST API with a cost function; a step-taking control atom with resolveInputs:false; a store capability backed by a Map; the wrong-then-right Response example.

Title: 'Atom Reference'. Every atom the VM registers, which is 60 with batteries (`Object.keys(new AgentVM(batteryAtoms).atoms)`). DOCS-AJS's tables list about half and omit atoms the book already uses: template, regexMatch, runCode, transpileCode, jsonParse, jsonStringify, xmlParse, pick, omit, merge, keys, len, split, join, consoleLog/Warn/Error, varAssign, constSet, callLocal, evaluate, storeQueryWhere, storeVectorSearch. One row per atom: name, named inputs (required/optional), output, base fuel cost (static or 'dynamic: …'), default timeout, effects ('io'/'pure'), the capability key it needs, and whether it's callable from AJS source or is v1/builder-only (data atoms like map/filter/push are v1 thin wrappers; v2 emits methodCall). Group them as flow control, state, data (v1), text/JSON/XML, store, network, AI core, AI battery, code and agents, procedures, utilities, console. GENERATE THE TABLE rather than hand-writing it: src/vm/core-atom-inputs.ts already holds the inputs and coreAtoms carries cost, timeoutMs, effects and docs, so build the page from data with a freshness test, the way docs/tjs-vs-typescript.md is built from differences.ts. A hand-copied table is exactly what drifted here. Short prose per group: when to use the atom versus the builtin method (llmPredict vs llmPredictBattery; template vs a template literal; regexMatch vs String methods; filter() schema projection vs Array filter). Move the Battery Atoms Reference detail sections from DOCS-AJS here.

ts.summary:
STATE: The TypeScript book has a strong core and a weak frame. The example chapters (14 ts-*.md) and the three practical chapters (ts-converting-a-project, ts-json-boundary, typescript-good-bad-ugly) are in good shape: consistent voice, each has a runnable `ts:inline`/`tjs:inline` example, a 'What to notice' section and a 'The gotcha' section, and they agree with each other on how conversion behaves (faithful by default, TjsStrict opts in, `:!` return types, MonadicError values). All of them still carry `<!-- TODO review -->` markers, so none has been signed off.

FLOW: The entry point is wrong. typescript-good-bad-ugly.md is the book's argument and its 'How this book is organized' map, but it has order 50 while TJS-FOR-TS.md has order 30 and is also pinned top. So a reader opens a 1,260-line reference first and only reaches the essay that motivates it afterwards. Suggested order: GBU (the why), then TJS-FOR-TS (the reference), then Converting, then JSON boundary, then the Examples, then the design notes. TJS-FOR-TS's checked-in toc lists only 'TypeScript Examples' even though Converting (order 2) and JSON boundary (order 3) are also its children. The site build regenerates that list; re-run it and confirm.

OVERLAP: TJS-FOR-TS.md duplicates most of the book. Its 'Automatic Conversion' and 'What to Watch For' sections repeat ts-converting-a-project. Its 'Runtime Validation' repeats ts-json-boundary and the GBU 'Bad' section. Its 'Return Types' and 'Inline Tests' sections repeat GBU 'Examples as contracts' and three example chapters. The worked-example/`:!` explanation appears at least six times in the book; teach it fully once (GBU or TJS-FOR-TS) and link to it everywhere else. The enum gotcha appears twice, and both copies are now WRONG.

STALE / WRONG (verified against the source):
(1) Commit 381a5948 (#3840) made enum members readable as properties: `Color.Red` works, and numeric members map back to names (`Dir[0]`). TJS-FOR-TS §Enums ('Color.Red on its own is undefined') and the ts-converting-a-project gotcha ('Code that reads Color.Red gets undefined') now teach the old behaviour.
(2) TJS-FOR-TS's equality block uses `{a: 1} Is {a: 1}` and `new Set(...) Is new Set(...)`. TJS-SYNTAX.md says infix `Is` with object/array-literal operands or spaced calls 'is misread or fails to parse', and recommends the call form `Is(a, b)`.
(3) TJS-FOR-TS says `safety all` means 'validate everything (debug)'. TJS-SYNTAX says it currently validates the same as `safety inputs`.
(4) TJS-FOR-TS says '=== unchanged'. TJS-SYNTAX's `LegacyExactly` row ('NaN is not itself; a boxed primitive is not its value') implies native `===` differs from JavaScript's. Verify, then state it accurately.
(5) generic-dts-design.md presents declaration blocks as the next step ('Now: any-based stubs'), while TJS-FOR-TS and dts.ts say declaration blocks already reach `.d.ts`. The design note is out of date.
(6) postmortem §8.3 and §9 ('compat-all cannot currently fail', the 89% corpus figure) predate the 2026-09-25 compat run in CLAUDE.md (zod 1959/1959, vitest harnesses now fail on a failed suite) and the compat-scan ratchet. It needs a dated 'since then' addendum.
(7) TJS-FOR-TS's Bun plugin snippet says 'bunfig.toml already preloads the TJS plugin'. That is only true inside this repo; a consumer needs `preload = ["tjs-lang/bun-plugin"]`, and `tjs-lang/bun-build-plugin` for Bun.build.
(8) The tooling table claims 'Transpiles in-browser, no build step'. That overclaims for a TS team, and the CLI, the plugins and the editors deserve accurate rows.

COVERAGE GAPS for a TS developer evaluating TJS:
- What a TypeScript consumer sees when it imports a TJS module: the `.d.ts`, how a `MonadicError` return is typed, `isMonadicError` from TS.
- Build and CI integration: bun-plugin, bun-build-plugin, `tjs check --max-warnings`, sharedPrelude, a mixed .ts/.tjs tree, editors.
- Replacing Zod/io-ts/Ajv: `Type.check`/`strip`/`toJSONSchema`, `functionMetaToJSONSchema`, `tjs-lang/schema`, predicates. Every chapter says TJS replaces 'the second type system', and none shows the replacement side by side.
- The `tjs-vs-typescript.md` page (generated, order 1 under GBU) is the book's evidence table, but it is missing from the chapter list given to editors. Confirm it renders in the ts book.

newChapters.brief: Publishing TJS to TypeScript consumers, and calling TJS from TypeScript. The gap: every chapter goes TS→TJS, and none shows what a TS codebase sees when it imports a TJS module. Cover: `tjs emit` producing .js + .d.ts; what each TJS construct becomes in .d.ts (Type → interface/guard, Union, Enum, Generic with a declaration block, functions, callable classes); how a validated function's possible MonadicError return is typed and how TS code should handle it (`isMonadicError` from `tjs-lang/runtime`, narrowing); `@tjs declaration`/`@tjs-skip`/`@tjs example` annotations for types with no runtime meaning (conditional, mapped); package exports and the `prelude: 'import'` / sharedPrelude option for one runtime per bundle. Examples: a small TJS module with its generated .d.ts shown side by side (static), and a `ts:inline` consumer handling an error result. Absorb the user-facing half of generic-dts-design.md.

Replacing Zod / io-ts / Ajv. Every chapter claims TJS removes 'the second type system', and none shows the replacement. A side-by-side table and runnable examples: `z.object` → `Type` example; `.optional()` → `| undefined`; `.nullable()` → `| null`; `z.enum` → `Union`/`Enum`; `.refine` → `predicate`; `z.infer` → not needed; `.parse` (throws) vs a gate function / `Type.check` (returns a value); `.strip()` → `Type.strip`; `zodToJsonSchema` → `Type.toJSONSchema()` and `functionMetaToJSONSchema(fn.__tjs)`; `tjs-lang/schema` (tosijs-schema with `$predicate`) for code that wants a schema-builder API. Include an honest 'what Zod still does better' list (transforms/coercion pipelines, error message customization, member-level error paths for named types) and a migration recipe for a typical API-handler module.

Fitting TJS into a TypeScript team's build and CI. Currently scattered (an inaccurate Bun-plugin snippet and an overclaiming tooling table in TJS-FOR-TS). Cover: a mixed .ts/.tjs tree; `preload = ["tjs-lang/bun-plugin"]` in a consumer's bunfig.toml; `tjsPlugin` from `tjs-lang/bun-build-plugin` for Bun.build; TJS_RUN_TESTS; the CLI (`tjs check` with `--max-warnings`, `tjs convert` exiting 0 on failed embedded tests, `tjs emit` for .d.ts); a CI recipe (convert to tjs/, check, run the project's own tests); editor support (Monaco/CodeMirror/Ace adapters, VSCode/Cursor grammars); the browser bundles (`tjs-lang/browser`, `/browser/from-ts` lazy-loading TypeScript from esm.sh); runtime configuration for debugging (`configure({ logTypeErrors, throwTypeErrors })`, the `__tjs.errors()` flight recorder in tests). Mostly static snippets; one `tjs:inline` showing `__tjs.errors()` after a bad call.

- Set navTitle to "The Language" and the H1 to "The AJS Language". The rest of the metadata line is unchanged, and `<!-- TODO review -->` is on line 2.

  - `String(n)` and `Number(s)` are not functions.

  - `:` means required.
  - `=` means optional with a default.

The `async`/`await` row now says what actually happens: `await` is refused, and an `async` marker is silently ignored. The old table called both forbidden.

  - Raising errors with `Error()`.

findings.where: What is AJS? — "every atom that touches the world needs a capability the host chose to grant"
findings.problem: 'host', 'capability' and 'fuel budget' (line 34) are used before they are defined, and the page never says how the pieces fit: source -> transpiler -> JSON AST -> VM run by the host. A reader embedding the VM has no picture of who transpiles, where that happens, and what the host gets back. No `vm.run` call shows up until the Builder API section near the end, and even there the result envelope is only `{ result }`, while Errors talks about a run's `error` and 'fuel spent'.
findings.fix: Right after the first example, add a 4-6 line host snippet (transpile, `new AgentVM()`, `vm.run(ast, args, { fuel, capabilities })`, the `{ result, error, fuelUsed }` that comes back) with a one-sentence definition each of host, capability and fuel, then link to Hosting the VM.

findings.where: Use cases / AI agents — "on this page the example stops with a message saying so"
findings.problem: This assumes the reader is on the live doc site with runnable examples. In print, in the repo, or for a model reading the markdown, the sentence makes no sense. It also never says what the run returns without an LLM: an error? a partial result?
findings.fix: Say what happens without the capability (e.g. 'llmPredict fails with a catchable error naming the missing capability') and mark the live-example behaviour as site-only.

findings.where: Use cases / Remote jobs — "Send the code to the data instead of the data to the code."
findings.problem: The example has nothing to do with sending code anywhere: it is a local map over [1,2,3]. It also brings in a helper with positional parameters (`applyTransform(item, transform)`) before the page has explained that helpers and the entry function follow different calling rules, so a reader who has just been told agents take one named-argument object is thrown.
findings.fix: Add one sentence on how this is remote (the AST is shipped to a service that holds `items`, e.g. via the store). Or move the example after Local helper functions, or note that helpers take ordinary positional arguments.

findings.where: What's Allowed tour — "const note = items[0]?.note ?? 'none'"
findings.problem: The example uses `?.`, yet a later section says every member access is already null-safe. A reader cannot tell whether `?.` is needed, redundant or different. The return description also leaves out `size`, `label`, `note` and `all`, so the reader cannot check the operators shown (what is `note`?).
findings.fix: Use `items[0].note ?? 'none'` with a comment pointing to Null-safe member access, or explain why `?.` is shown. Give the full returned object.

findings.where: What's Allowed tour — "// try / catch: the error is a string"
findings.problem: This is the first time error semantics come up, as a one-line comment inside a tour, with no context (why a string? what is in it?). The tour also shows `JSON.parse` failure being caught before the reader knows which failures are catchable.
findings.fix: Keep the comment but add 'see Errors', or drop try/catch from the tour and leave it to the Errors section.

findings.where: What's Allowed — "for...of and while (there is no C-style for)"
findings.problem: With no C-style for, no break and no continue, the obvious questions are how to loop over indices 0..n and how to stop a loop early without leaving the function. The page only gives fragments ('while with a counter', 'an if around the loop body, or a return') and never shows the idioms.
findings.fix: Add a short 'Loop idioms' block: an index loop with while + counter, early exit with a `done` flag in the while condition, and skipping an item with if.

findings.where: Calling atoms — "fails at transpile time and names what the atom takes: `storeSet('k', v)` (refused)."
findings.problem: The sentence ends on the refused example without showing the error message it promises. 'The transpiler' appears here as if already introduced. A reader handling untrusted code also wonders whether these checks matter for safety, since the Builder section later says the VM runs any AST as written.
findings.fix: Show the actual message (e.g. `storeSet takes { key, value }`). State plainly that transpile-time checks are a convenience for authors, not a safety boundary: the VM is the boundary.

findings.where: Calling atoms table — "httpFetch({ url, method?, headers?, body? }) | an HTTP request"
findings.problem: The table gives no return shapes. The first example reads `r.full_name` directly, which suggests httpFetch returns the parsed JSON body, but nothing says so (or what happens with non-JSON, or how to read status). `agentRun`'s `agentId` (where does an id come from?) and `hash`'s algorithm are unexplained, and `regexMatch` sits in the 'most used' list even though regex is deprecated on the same page.
findings.fix: Add a 'Returns' column (parsed body or text? string; value; boolean; the agent's result object) and one line on where agent ids come from.

findings.where: Calling atoms — "builtins (`Math.max(a, b)`, `Error('message')`, `encodeURIComponent(s)`) take positional arguments"
findings.problem: `Error('message')` is listed beside pure functions, but it is the raise mechanism with control-flow effects. Here it reads as just another builtin.
findings.fix: Remove Error from this list, or add '(Error raises, see Errors)'.

findings.where: Local helper functions — "Call them at statement level. A helper call cannot sit inside a larger expression"
findings.problem: 'Statement level' is ambiguous: `const d = double(n)` is a declaration, so are `if (double(n) > 1)`, `return double(n)` or a helper inside a `map` arrow allowed? The counterexample is fenced as ```javascript, not ajs, which hints it is not AJS. It is also unexplained why helpers cannot see the caller's locals while arrow callbacks may read outer variables (Forbidden table).
findings.fix: List the allowed positions exactly (`let/const x = helper(...)`, `x = helper(...)`, a bare call statement) and say whether `return helper(x)` and calls inside arrows work. Add one sentence contrasting helper scope with arrow-callback scope.

findings.where: Local helper functions — "Only the entry function is held to the object-return contract."
findings.problem: This forward-references a contract defined about 150 lines later, under Input/Output Contract. On a first read 'the object-return contract' is undefined.
findings.fix: Inline it: '(the entry function must return an object; see Input/Output Contract)'.

findings.where: What's Forbidden — `throw` | `Error('message')`
findings.problem: Telling readers to use `Error('message')` instead of `throw` suggests the two are equivalent, but the semantics (an 'error state' that skips steps until a catch) are not explained until much later. The table is also wide and wraps badly (the 'Functions as values' row runs to about 150 characters).
findings.fix: Shorten the cells and link each one to the section that explains it. Keep the long explanations in prose below the table.

findings.where: Differences from JavaScript — "Agents should not crash on missing data. Returns `{ missing: true }`."
findings.problem: The motivation sentence sits awkwardly between the code and its result. More importantly, the trade-off is never stated: a typo like `user.nmae` silently becomes undefined instead of failing, which matters to someone writing or debugging an agent.
findings.fix: Put the motivation before the example and add a sentence on the cost (typos read as undefined; a declared result type or input contract catches some of it).

findings.where: Equality — "They unwrap boxed primitives and treat `null` and `undefined` (and `NaN`) as equal."
findings.problem: This reads as if null, undefined and NaN are all equal to each other. 'Unwrap boxed primitives' is meaningless in AJS, which has no `new` and so no way to make a boxed primitive. 'Footgun-free `===`' is jargon.
findings.fix: Write: '`null == undefined` is true; `NaN == NaN` is true; otherwise `==` is `===`.' Drop the boxed-primitive clause, or explain where a boxed value could come from.

findings.where: There is no `Is` — "TJS's structural comparison (`a Is b`) is not available in AJS."
findings.problem: The AJS reader is told what a different language has. The infix `Is` syntax means nothing to them.
findings.fix: Lead with the AJS answer ('== on objects compares identity; to compare contents, ...') and mention TJS in a parenthesis, if at all.

findings.where: Functions and namespaces are not values — "A `Set` is an array of its items, and a `Date` is a plain object of its fields; the VM supplies their methods"
findings.problem: This is a big conceptual leap with no explanation. If a set is just an array, how does the VM know to give it `.add`, and why is `push` refused on it (Set section)? Does an array that comes back from a store or capability regain set methods? Is any object with a `timestamp` a date? The reader cannot form a model.
findings.fix: Add a short paragraph: a set or date is tagged or tracked by the VM (say how), what survives JSON and store round trips, and what does not (e.g. 'call `Set(x)` again after reading from the store').

findings.where: Operators — "'tags: ' + tags would end the run: '+' needs a string, not an array."
findings.problem: 'End the run' has a specific meaning (not catchable) that is only defined later, in Catchable, and run-ending, and that list does not include operator type errors. The reader cannot tell whether this is a transpile error, a catchable runtime error or a run-ending one. Mixed primitives (`'a' + 1`, `'a' < 'b'`) are not covered either.
findings.fix: State the category explicitly (and list it under run-ending if that is what it is). Add one line on string + number and string comparison.

findings.where: Methods — "Exactly the documented arguments" / "A method the VM does not list is not callable"
findings.problem: 'Documented' and 'list' point to nothing on this page or in the links: docs/vm-budgets.md explains why the list is closed, not which methods are on it. Someone writing an agent cannot find out whether `padStart`, `flatMap` or `toUpperCase` exist. `Object.keys(obj)` is given as an example of a method argument, but it is a static function. Leaving out `some`/`every`/`findIndex`/`sort` comparators gets no reason.
findings.fix: Add or link a per-receiver method list (string, array, object statics) with signatures. Give the one-line reason callbacks are limited to four methods.

findings.where: Regular expressions — "Regex is deprecated in AJS 0.14 in favour of `Pattern` ... ([`docs/pattern.md`])"
findings.problem: The reader cannot tell whether Pattern exists yet. If it does not, 'deprecated in favour of' a nonexistent feature leaves them stuck. The section then spends three paragraphs teaching regex in detail, which sends mixed signals. Limits like '20,000 instructions' and 'about four instructions per count' cannot be used by an author.
findings.fix: Say whether Pattern is available today and what to use now. Trim the limits to rules of thumb (e.g. 'bounded repeats up to about {2000}').

findings.where: Input/Output Contract — "Positional parameters, `function add(a: 2, b: 3)`, compile to the same contract and read the same named arguments"
findings.problem: This contradicts the reader's intuition: a positional signature that the caller still invokes with `{ a, b }`. Meanwhile helpers with positional parameters ARE called positionally. The colon-example syntax `a: 2` also appears here for the first time and is never contrasted with JavaScript destructuring, where `{ a: 0 }` means 'rename a to 0' (a syntax error). A JS reader will stumble on `function f({ a: 0, b = 'x' })`.
findings.fix: Add an explicit callout: 'In AJS, `{ a: 0 }` in a parameter means required `a`, example 0 (an integer), not JS renaming.' Say once, clearly: entry parameters are always named arguments; helper parameters are positional.

findings.where: Parameters are the input contract — "`{ n: 5 }` requires an integer `n`"
findings.problem: The page never says what an example can express: is `5.0` a float, `+0` non-negative, `[0]` an array of integers, a nested object a nested shape? The refusal message 'args do not match expected schema' names no field, and the page does not say who sees it (host or agent).
findings.fix: Add a small table of example -> accepted type (0, 0.0, '', true, [''], { x: 0 }, null). Say where the validation error surfaces.

findings.where: A declared result — "function score({ n = 12 }): { score: 0, label: 'low' | 'high' }"
findings.problem: The union `'low' | 'high'` is new syntax and evidently EXACT (`'mid'` is refused), while the page just taught that a colon value is an example that widens to a type. The reader cannot reconcile 'example' with 'exact literal union'. The failure examples also mix two faults: `{ score: 1.5 }` is wrong both because 1.5 is not an integer and because label is missing. 'A failed run reports its own error, not the contract's' is cryptic.
findings.fix: Explain that in a union string literals are exact values (an enum), while a lone example widens. Give each failure example a single fault. Rephrase: 'If the agent fails before returning, you get that failure, not a contract error.'

findings.where: Set — `tags.remove('a')`, `tags.diff(['b'])`
findings.problem: These differ from JavaScript's Set (`delete`, `difference`), but the page does not flag it, and someone who knows JS (or a model) will write `delete`/`difference`. 'Data that JSON and the capability boundary keep as it is' uses 'capability boundary', which is undefined.
findings.fix: Add 'Unlike JavaScript: remove, not delete; diff, not difference; size is the length'. Replace 'capability boundary' with plain words or define it once near the top.

findings.where: Date — "`month` (1–12)" / "a frozen data object"
findings.problem: 1-based months are a deliberate break from JS's 0-11 and deserve a visible warning, not an inline parenthesis. 'Frozen': what happens on `d.year = 2025`? An error, catchable? The `format` tokens beyond 'YYYY-MM-DD' are not listed.
findings.fix: Add a callout: 'month is 1-12, unlike JavaScript'. Say what assigning to a date field does. List the format tokens or link to them.

findings.where: Schema — `Schema.response('person', { name: '', age: 0 })` vs `Schema.response('user', Schema.object({...}))`
findings.problem: The same argument position takes an example object in one call and a schema in the other; the page never says how it tells them apart (what if an example has a `type` key?). `person` is built and returned but never used. `Schema.isValid(input, user.json_schema.schema)`, reaching inside the response wrapper, is unexplained. 'A nullable field is optional' is a surprising rule buried in a comment. `responseFormat` belongs to an atom option not shown in the atom table.
findings.fix: Explain the example-vs-schema rule, validate against a plain `Schema.object` instead of digging into the wrapper, promote the nullable-means-optional rule to prose, and show `llmPredict({ prompt, options: { responseFormat: user } })`.

findings.where: Schema — "A guest schema is a closed dialect. It may use `type`, `properties`, ..."
findings.problem: This is one roughly 90-word sentence listing more than 25 keywords plus limits. It is a wall of text, and the reason given for refusing `pattern` (the host's regex engine) is an implementation detail. 'Match inside the program with regexMatch' does not show how to apply that to a schema field.
findings.fix: Turn it into a bulleted list or table (structure / bounds / formats / annotations / limits). Show a two-line example of checking a field with regexMatch after Schema.isValid.

findings.where: Errors / Raising and catching — "puts the program into its error state"
findings.problem: Never answered: can you `return Error(...)`? Can a catch block re-raise (call Error again)? Is there `finally`? What happens to an `Error(...)` at top level outside any try (the run's error, presumably)? The parseAll example also has no 'Returns' line, unlike every other example.
findings.fix: Add bullets on re-raising, finally (supported or not) and top-level errors. Add `Returns { results: [1, 3, { a: 4 }], errors: [{ item: 'x', error: '...' }], ok: false }`.

findings.where: Catchable, and run-ending — "a capability's answer that is too large" (catchable) vs "a value that cannot be copied out to a capability (too large...)" (run-ending)
findings.problem: 'Too large' is catchable in one direction and run-ending in the other. The rule behind this (the world's fault vs the program's fault) is only implied. 'Fetch blocked: domain not in allowlist' brings in an allowlist the page never mentions.
findings.fix: State the rule up front in one sentence ('if the world did it, you can catch it; if your program or the host broke the contract, the run ends'), then the two lists. Add one line on the fetch allowlist (set by the host) with a link.

findings.where: badInput example — `httpFetch({ url: 5 }) // url must be a string` / "The transpiler reports the ones it can see before the program runs."
findings.problem: A literal `url: 5` is exactly what a transpiler can see, so a reader suspects this example would never transpile and so never reaches the runtime behaviour it demonstrates. The agentRun parenthetical ('served by the host is a separate run') is opaque.
findings.fix: Use an input the transpiler cannot see (e.g. `url: data.port` from an argument), or say explicitly that this would be caught at transpile time and the runtime rule covers ASTs built otherwise. Rewrite the agentRun note in plain terms.

findings.where: What a run costs — fuel table
findings.problem: The costs mean nothing without a scale: what is a typical or default budget, and how many llmPredict calls does fuel 1000 buy? The table also sits under 'Errors', and lists `seq`, which is not defined until the AST section.
findings.fix: Give the default fuel (or a typical value) and one worked example ('this agent costs about 7 fuel'). Consider moving costs to their own top-level section. Replace 'seq' with 'block'.

findings.where: JSON AST Format — opening
findings.problem: The page's audience is agent authors, but this section offers no motivation for why they need the AST (auditing? debugging? hand-building?). The Sequence example has no parameters, so `varsImport` and a non-empty `inputSchema`, which the prose then describes, are not shown. Values appear as bare `10` in Sequence but as `{ "$expr": "literal", "value": 42 }` in Expressions, and the inconsistency is not explained. Most important, the AST of an atom call (httpFetch), for...of and try/catch is never shown, though these are the most audit-relevant nodes.
findings.fix: Open with one sentence on who reads ASTs and why. Use an example with a parameter and an atom call. Explain when a literal is bare vs wrapped. Add atom-call, for...of and try nodes.

findings.where: Builder API — `.return({ properties: { total: {} } })` / "The builder writes a version-1 AST."
findings.problem: The argument to `.return` is a schema fragment with no explanation. The page has just taught v2, then shows a tool that writes the legacy format without saying why or whether that matters. For someone embedding the VM for untrusted code, 'nothing checks atom calls or parameters' raises a safety question the page does not answer: is the VM still safe?
findings.fix: Explain the `.return` argument, say why the builder is v1 (persisted format, compatibility), and add 'the VM's safety guarantees do not depend on the transpiler's checks'.

findings.where: Limitations — "What AJS doesn't do" / "What AJS intentionally avoids"
findings.problem: The first list repeats the Forbidden table almost word for word. The second list is too vague to act on. 'Slower than native JavaScript' gives no magnitude.
findings.fix: Cut the repeated list or replace it with a link. Make the 'avoids' list concrete, or merge it into the intro. Give a rough slowdown figure or link to benchmarks.

findings.where: Learn more — mixed link styles (`/ajs-host/` vs `guides/patterns.md` vs `docs/vm-budgets.md`)
findings.problem: Site-style and repo-relative links are mixed throughout (also the Methods and Regex sections). The repo-relative ones will likely break on the doc site, or on the npm/GitHub view if the site ones are used.
findings.fix: Use one link convention that resolves in every place the page is read.

findings.where: Line 2 — `<!-- TODO review -->`
findings.problem: A leftover working note at the top of a published page.
findings.fix: Remove it once the review is done.

findings.where: Syntax intro — "small enough for a 4B-parameter model to write correctly"
findings.problem: A strong claim with no evidence or link, and the reader cannot tell whether it is measured or aspirational.
findings.fix: Link to the grokkability measurement, or soften the wording.

findings.where: Operators example: "// 'tags: ' + tags would end the run: '+' needs a string, not an array."
findings.problem: The chapter's Errors section gives 'end the run' a precise meaning: not catchable, even inside try. This operator error is an ordinary catchable error. Calling it 'run-ending' teaches the wrong distinction.
findings.evidence: probe `function f({tags=['a']}){ try { let x = 'tags: ' + tags; return {x} } catch (e) { return {caught: e} } }` → result {"caught":"'+' needs a string, number, boolean or null, not an array — convert it explicitly (e.g. arr.join(','), JSON.stringify(obj))"}
findings.fix: Say 'would be an error' (or 'would fail the run unless caught'), not 'would end the run'.

findings.where: Catchable, and run-ending: "The transpiler reports the ones it can see before the program runs." (after the `httpFetch({ url: 5 })` example)
findings.problem: The example right above it is one the transpiler could see (a literal number for url), and it is not reported. It transpiles cleanly and ends the run only at run time. The transpiler checks input NAMES (missing, undeclared, positional, spread), not value types.
findings.evidence: transpile(`function badInput() { try { httpFetch({ url: 5 }) } catch (err) { return { caught: err } } return { after: true } }`) succeeds with no warnings; the run returns error "'httpFetch': its input does not have the shape the atom declares"
findings.fix: Say exactly what the transpiler checks: 'The transpiler catches a missing or undeclared input name before the run; a value of the wrong type is caught only when the call runs.'

findings.where: What's Forbidden: "Each of these is a transpile error that says what to write instead."
findings.problem: Several rows are not transpile errors, and several transpile errors do not suggest a fix. `o.__proto__` / `o.constructor` reads are RUNTIME errors. Holding a builtin as a value (`const m = Math`, `const f = parseInt`, `Object.values(Math)`, `const g = s.trim`) is a runtime error. Holding a helper as a value (`let g = h`) is not refused at all: g is silently undefined. `break`, `continue`, `class`, `this` and destructuring declarations fail with bare messages ('Unsupported statement type: BreakStatement', 'Only simple variable names are supported') that suggest nothing.
findings.evidence: probes: `let x = o.__proto__` → run error "Security Error: Access to '__proto__' is forbidden"; `const m = Math` → run error 'A function or builtin namespace is not a value in AsyncJS…'; `function h(x){return x}\nfunction f(){ let g = h; return {g, t: typeof g} }` → result {"t":"undefined"}, no error; `break` → TRANSPILE-ERR 'Unsupported statement type: BreakStatement at <source>:1:37'
findings.fix: Change it to 'Each of these is refused, most at transpile time.' Mark the runtime rows. Separately, file a card: `let g = helper` should be a transpile error, not silently undefined.

findings.where: Syntax / What's Forbidden (no row)
findings.problem: Assigning to a member or index (`o.a = 1`, `o['a'] = 1`, `a[0] = 1`) is a transpile error, and the chapter never says so. A JS writer hits this almost at once. The message ('Only simple variable assignment is supported') does not suggest the fix either.
findings.evidence: `function f() { let o = {}; o.a = 1; return {o} }` → TRANSPILE-ERR Only simple variable assignment is supported at <source>:1:27 (same for o['a'] = 1 and a[0] = 1)
findings.fix: Add a row to the Forbidden table: 'Writing a member or index (`o.a = 1`, `xs[0] = v`). Instead: rebuild the value, `o = { ...o, a: 1 }`, or `push` onto an array.' Show it in the What's Allowed tour too.

findings.where: Methods: "Callbacks only where they are listed. map, filter, find and reduce take an arrow function."
findings.problem: Callbacks take ONE simple parameter (reduce takes accumulator and item), and the chapter does not say so. Anything else misbehaves, often silently: an index parameter is undefined, a destructured parameter is undefined, a three-parameter reduce fails with an unrelated message, and reduce without an initial value is reported as 'reduce is not available'. `items.map(parseInt)` is also reported as 'map is not available'.
findings.evidence: `['a','b'].map((x, i) => i)` → [null,null]; `[1,2].filter((x, i) => i > 0)` → []; `[{a:1}].map(({a}) => a)` → [null]; `[1,2].reduce((s, x, i) => s + i, 0)` → "Output validation failed for 'reduce'"; `[1,2].reduce((s, x) => s + x)` → TRANSPILE-ERR Method 'reduce' is not available in AsyncJS; `['1'].map(parseInt)` → TRANSPILE-ERR Method 'map' is not available in AsyncJS
findings.fix: Document it: 'map/filter/find take `(item) => …`; reduce takes `(acc, item) => …` and an initial value. There is no index argument: use for...of with a counter.' Raise a card: extra or destructured callback parameters should be transpile errors, not silent undefined values.

findings.where: Expression Builtins > JSON, Array, Object…: `assigned: Object.assign({}, { a: 1 }, { b: 2 })`; Set section: "push and Object.assign are refused on a set"
findings.problem: In AJS, Object.assign returns a new merged object and does NOT change its first argument. That is a silent difference from JavaScript. The Set sentence suggests that Object.assign writes into ordinary objects.
findings.evidence: `let o = {}; let r = Object.assign(o, { a: 1 }); return {o, r}` → {"o":{},"r":{"a":1}}
findings.fix: Add to Differences from JavaScript: 'Object.assign returns a new object; it never changes its target. Write `o = Object.assign(o, extra)` or `o = { ...o, ...extra }`.'

findings.where: Parameters are the input contract: "An argument the agent does not declare is refused."
findings.problem: This holds only when the agent declares at least one parameter. A parameterless entry compiles to `inputSchema: { type: 'object', properties: {} }` with no `additionalProperties: false`, so it accepts any arguments. The chapter's own JSON AST sample shows this schema.
findings.evidence: `function f() { return { ok: 1 } }` run with args {z: 1} → result {"ok":1}, no error; its AST inputSchema is {"type":"object","properties":{}}
findings.fix: Either qualify the sentence ('…when the agent declares parameters; an agent with none accepts any arguments'), or file a card to make the transpiler emit additionalProperties:false for an empty parameter list. If you choose the card, the JSON AST sample changes too.

findings.where: Local helper functions
findings.problem: Two related behaviours are undocumented. A top-level `const`/`let` outside the functions is silently dropped, so the entry reads undefined. A function declared inside another function is a transpile error ('Unsupported statement type: FunctionDeclaration').
findings.evidence: `const k = 1\nfunction f() { return {k} }` → result {} (no error); `function f() { function g() { return 1 } let x = g(); return {x} }` → TRANSPILE-ERR Unsupported statement type: FunctionDeclaration
findings.fix: Add: 'A source file contains only function declarations. Top-level variables are ignored (put constants inside the entry, or pass them as arguments), and functions cannot nest.' Consider a card to make a top-level statement a transpile error.

findings.where: Calling atoms: "…an input the atom does not declare, or a missing required input fails at transpile time and names what the atom takes"
findings.problem: A call to a name that is not a known atom passes transpile and fails only at run time with 'Unknown Atom: fooAtom' (unless the host passed its atoms to the transpiler). The positional-call message also does not name the atom's inputs, as the prose claims: it says `write storeSet({ name: value, … })`. Builtins that do not exist hit the same path: `String(5)` / `Number('5')` / `Is(a, b)` report "'String' takes named arguments", which tells the reader nothing.
findings.evidence: `let x = fooAtom({ a: 1 })` → run error 'Unknown Atom: fooAtom'; `storeSet('k', 1)` → "'storeSet' takes named arguments: write storeSet({ name: value, … }), not storeSet(a, b)"; `String(5)` → "'String' takes named arguments: write String({ name: value, … })…"
findings.fix: Say that an unknown atom name is caught only at run time. Soften 'names what the atom takes' for positional calls. Under String/Number, quote the confusing message readers will actually see, or file a transpiler card to say 'String is not available; use a template'.

findings.where: Operators: "Arithmetic, comparison and string operators (`+`, `-`, `*`, `<`, …) … take primitives"
findings.problem: 'Comparison' includes `==`, but the Equality section right above it compares arrays with `==` (identity), and that works. Readers cannot tell which comparison operators refuse objects.
findings.evidence: `[1] == 1` → false (no error); `a == b` on objects → identity; `[1] < 5` → error "'<' needs a string, number, boolean or null, not an array"
findings.fix: Say 'Arithmetic, ordering (`<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`) and string operators'. Add that `==`/`===` accept any value and compare objects by identity.

findings.where: ## Errors > ### What a run costs (fuel table)
findings.problem: The fuel table sits under the Errors H2, where nobody looks for costs. The table also lists `storeVectorize` and `llmVision` without saying they are battery atoms, which exist only when the host registers them.
findings.evidence: costs verified against source: seq/if/while 0.1, varSet/varGet 0.1, httpFetch 5, llmPredict 100 (src/vm/runtime.ts:7476), storeVectorize 20 and llmVision 150 in src/vm/atoms/batteries.ts:66,417
