examplesFailing: Not a failing fence, but a language bug the chapter now warns about: Error() with a computed message loses it. Error('bad ' + x), Error(m) and Error(`bad ${x}`) all arrive as '[object Object]', whether caught or not. That includes re-raising with Error('re: ' + err). Only a literal message works. The Errors section now says to give Error a literal message 'for now'.

Not a failing fence, but a bug the chapter now warns about: `try { … } finally { … }` transpiles, but the finally block never runs, even when nothing throws (probe: ran stays false). The page tells readers not to rely on finally.

Atom calls inside a larger expression (`return { id: uuid() }`, `{ h: hash({ value }) }`) pass transpile and fail only at run time with 'Atom calls in expressions not yet supported'. A helper call in the same position is refused at transpile time. The chapter now documents the run-time behaviour.

researchAgent needs an LLM capability, so it can't be checked end to end here. Its transpile and fetch work, and it ends with the catchable 'Capability 'llm.predict' missing', which is what the prose now says.
questions: Should the transpiler refuse `finally`? Today it is accepted and silently dropped. Should it also refuse an atom call inside an expression? Today that fails only at run time, while the same position for a helper is a transpile error.

Should `let g = helper` (silently undefined) and extra or destructured callback parameters (`(x, i) => i` gives undefined) be transpile errors? The reviewers suggested a card for each. I documented today's behaviour and did not create cards.

A parameterless entry (`function f()`) accepts any arguments, because its inputSchema has no additionalProperties:false. An entry with parameters refuses undeclared ones. Is that asymmetry intended? The chapter documents it as it stands.

Should `String(5)` / `Number('5')` / `Is(a,b)` get a transpiler message like 'String is not available; use a template' instead of "'String' takes named arguments"? The chapter quotes the current, confusing message.

findings.where: Line 2 / title + intro: "replace the JavaScript VM on the untrusted path for 1.0"
findings.problem: "The untrusted path" is never defined, but the whole page depends on it. Is it vm-ast, Eval/SafeFunction, the server, or all of them? Phase 3 later suggests it means all of them, client and server.
findings.fix: In the intro, add one sentence that names the APIs and contexts that count as the untrusted path, for example: vm.run on guest ASTs, Eval and SafeFunction.

findings.where: "What this means for you today": the single paragraph listing four things
findings.problem: Four separate actions are packed into one paragraph, so they are hard to scan. It also uses terms before the page explains them: `$ajs`, "the 0.14 membrane", "custom atoms", and "has no parser" (the reader is not told why having no parser matters). This is the most actionable section on the page, and it reads as a wall of text.
findings.fix: Turn it into a list of four items, one action per item. Gloss each term in a few words, e.g. "`$ajs` (the version stamp at the root of every AST)" and "the membrane (the copy-and-check step every value goes through between host and guest)". Link to the sections that explain them.

findings.where: "What this means for you today": "Custom atoms must return JSON data plus `Date`… an atom that works now will not break on the native VM"
findings.problem: The architecture section says the VM becomes a resumable step machine that returns `{ suspended, atom, args }` and waits for the host to call `resume`. An embedder will want to know whether `defineAtom` and today's async atom functions keep working, or whether the host loop changes. The page promises the return types survive but says nothing about the calling convention.
findings.fix: State what the host-side API for custom atoms will look like: whether defineAtom stays as it is, and whether the suspend/resume loop is hidden behind the same `vm.run` promise. If that is undecided, say so and add it to Open questions.

findings.where: "The ASTs you transpile and store are versioned (`$ajs`), and the native VM will run them"
findings.problem: The page doesn't say whether the native VM will run v1 ASTs (the builder output and every unversioned AST) or only v2. Constraint #5 also suggests a future AST version could change the rules. An embedder with stored ASTs cannot tell whether those ASTs are covered.
findings.fix: Say explicitly which AST versions the native VM commits to reading (v1 and v2, or v2 only).

findings.where: Status: "after 0.14 ships and Pattern lands"
findings.problem: "Pattern" is never explained. A first-time reader cannot tell whether it is a feature, a library, or a release.
findings.fix: Add a short gloss and a link: "Pattern (the planned regex replacement, docs/pattern.md)".

findings.where: Status → Why now: "Most 0.14.0-rc.2 blockers (thirty-one review rounds) were one class… find, bound and charge door by door… Each round closed a door; the next found a branch of the fix."
findings.problem: This is internal release history told in internal metaphors. "Door", "charge" and "bound" are never defined, and "rc.2" and the round count mean nothing to an embedder. The reader also meets "the 'structural to JS-in-JS' trigger below" before the triggers have been introduced.
findings.fix: Lead with the general point in plain words: in a JS-in-JS VM, every host builtin a guest can reach has to be found and metered one at a time, and reviews kept finding more. Move the rc.2 numbers to a footnote. Either define "door" once (a place where guest work runs in host code) or don't use the word.

findings.where: Status: "**Decided against:** a native TJS runtime (forking V8/JSC)."
findings.problem: For a reader of the AJS book this comes out of nowhere. Nothing on the page has proposed a native TJS runtime, so the reader has no idea why it is being ruled out.
findings.fix: Either cut it from this page, or open with the question it answers, e.g. "Why not also go native for TJS?"

findings.where: Thesis: "can serve as the client-side `Eval`/`SafeFunction` engine — so the end state is **one VM**, not two."
findings.problem: `Eval` and `SafeFunction` are not introduced. The "one VM" claim also conflicts with the CSP section, which keeps a JS fallback open ("which is two VMs again"), and with Phase 3 ("or kept strictly as CSP fallback").
findings.fix: Gloss Eval/SafeFunction in a few words. Qualify the thesis: "one VM, unless the CSP fallback is kept (see below)".

findings.where: What changes categorically: "The membrane becomes byte-copying by construction instead of descriptor-walking."
findings.problem: "Descriptor-walking" is jargon about how the membrane is implemented today, and the reader doesn't know that. The section never says what the byte format is (JSON? a custom encoding?).
findings.fix: Explain in one clause: today the membrane reads each property descriptor of a host object. Name or sketch the byte format at the boundary.

findings.where: "The 0.13.4 class of bug (transpile-time execution of untrusted source) cannot recur"
findings.problem: The bug is identified by version number alone, which the reader can't look up from here. The parenthesis helps, but the reader still can't tell how it happened or why removing the parser fixes it.
findings.fix: Add a short example of the bug (e.g. a `test` block in the source ran via `new Function` while the AST was being built), or link the CHANGELOG entry.

findings.where: "**JS-engine JIT bugs** (currently declared out of scope) no longer apply to guest execution."
findings.problem: The page doesn't say where JIT bugs are declared out of scope, or what that means for the embedder's threat model today.
findings.fix: Link the document that sets out the threat model, or add a sentence explaining what it means for embedders now.

findings.where: Known regression: CSP: "This is a milder version of the problem `Eval` exists to avoid."
findings.problem: The reader isn't told what problem `Eval` exists to avoid (presumably that native eval needs `'unsafe-eval'`), so the comparison tells them nothing. The section also mixes facts for embedders with an open decision ("Decide deliberately") that is addressed to the maintainers.
findings.fix: Spell the problem out: "Eval exists so you never have to grant 'unsafe-eval'; wasm needs the narrower 'wasm-unsafe-eval'." Move "Decide deliberately…" to Open questions, where it already appears again.

findings.where: Architecture sketch: "No JSPI/asyncify dependence… Fits the flight-recorder design."
findings.problem: JSPI, asyncify and "the flight-recorder design" are all undefined. The reader can't see why avoiding them is good, or how a serializable VM fits a flight recorder.
findings.fix: Gloss them: JSPI/asyncify are the wasm mechanisms that let wasm code await JS promises. Explain the flight recorder in one line or link it.

findings.where: Architecture sketch: "**Atoms:** core atoms remain host capabilities behind schemas."
findings.problem: This seems to contradict how the page itself treats atoms. Constraint #3 talks about `effects: 'io'` atoms crossing the membrane, which implies core atoms (arithmetic, seq, varSet…) are pure operations on guest data, not host capabilities. If core atoms really did cross the host boundary, the claim that "nothing live crosses" would be in question. A reader can't reconcile the two.
findings.fix: Separate the two kinds: core atoms are implemented inside the Rust VM, and only IO atoms (fetch, store, llm, custom) are host capabilities behind schemas. If that is wrong, explain which core atoms stay in the host.

findings.where: "Schemas embed AJS predicates, so the VM hosts the validator which hosts the VM."
findings.problem: The circularity is stated but not explained. The reader doesn't know what an AJS predicate is or why a schema contains one.
findings.fix: Add one sentence: schemas can carry a `$predicate` (AJS code that decides validity), so validating a value can mean running AJS. Link the predicate docs.

findings.where: "**String semantics:** with one VM we define them. UTF-16 `.length` quirks need not survive." vs "semantics must match the JS VM exactly" / The two-VM hazard
findings.problem: The page says parity with the JS VM is a security requirement while both exist, and also that string semantics can change. Those contradict each other unless the change happens only after the JS VM is retired, and the page doesn't say that. Constraint #1 also warns that documenting `.length` would turn it into an obligation.
findings.fix: Say when string semantics may change: only once the JS VM is retired from the untrusted path, or with a new AST version. Point to the matching open question.

findings.where: Estimates: "today… about 42 KB for `tjs-vm-ast.js`, 62 KB for `tjs-eval.js`, 95 KB for `tjs-vm.js`" vs Relationship to vm-ast: "about 137 KB of bundle against 324 KB for `tjs-lang/vm`"
findings.problem: The page gives two different size figures for the same bundles, both measured on the same date. One is gzipped and the other presumably isn't, but the second figure isn't labelled. A reader will think one of them is wrong.
findings.fix: Label each figure as gzipped or minified-uncompressed, and use the same measure in both places.

findings.where: Estimates: "**Binary:** 150–300 KB gzipped realistic"
findings.problem: The comparison is left for the reader to work out: the native VM would be about 3–7× larger than vm-ast today. Size matters to embedders, but the page doesn't say whether that growth is acceptable or what it buys.
findings.fix: State it directly: "roughly 3–7× the current vm-ast bundle", and say whether that is acceptable.

findings.where: The two-VM hazard: "a predicate accepted by one and enforced by the other is a hole"
findings.problem: As written this doesn't make sense, since "accepted" and "enforced" are not opposites. The intended meaning is probably "accepted by one VM and rejected by the other", or "validated under one VM's semantics and enforced under the other's". There is no concrete example of the hole.
findings.fix: Rewrite with a concrete case, e.g. a schema checked on the client by one VM and enforced on the server by the other, where the two disagree on string length, so one value passes on the client and is rejected on the server, or the reverse.

findings.where: Constraints on 1.0 table (rows 1, 2, 5, 6)
findings.problem: The table cells are paragraphs, and they lean on internal references: test filenames (`ast-version-producers.test.ts`), card numbers (#2788, #2789), "Tonio, 2026-10-02". Terms like "a `json` escape type", "lint-banned JS" and "typed slots instead of tagged values" are undefined. On a narrow screen this will be very hard to read.
findings.fix: Keep the table to three short columns (constraint, status word, link). Move each explanation into a short subsection underneath. Define "lint-banned" and the "json escape type".

findings.where: Constraint #2 vs "When #2 would have become expensive": "The root carries `$ajs` (`{"$ajs":2,…}`)… The transpiler writes 2, the builder 1" and "`$ajs: 1` landed comfortably inside it"
findings.problem: On a first read it's unclear what landed when. Was `$ajs: 1` stamped before v2? Do builder ASTs carry an explicit `$ajs: 1`, or no field at all? Elsewhere the page treats "absent means 1" as the rule.
findings.fix: Give a short timeline: the field was introduced as 1, then v2 shipped. State what the builder actually writes (an explicit 1, or nothing).

findings.where: "When #2 would have become expensive. An earlier draft of this note argued…"
findings.problem: Four paragraphs argue against an earlier draft the reader never saw. That is maintainer history, and it pushes the one actionable rule ("never change the AST format without bumping the version") to the very end.
findings.fix: Reduce it to the rule plus one sentence of reasoning. Move the self-correction to a footnote or the commit history.

findings.where: Phases: "Postgres via pgrx (logic travels to data, literally)"; "a short AST spec note as the format stabilises"
findings.problem: pgrx is undefined. The reader can't tell whether the AST spec note exists yet or where to find it, even though the native VM is supposed to implement it.
findings.fix: Gloss pgrx (the Rust framework for writing Postgres extensions). Say whether the AST spec exists and link it, or mark it as not written yet.

findings.where: Triggers: "Universal endpoints want predicates executed inside Postgres."
findings.problem: "Universal endpoints" is an undefined project term.
findings.fix: Gloss it or link docs/universal-endpoint.md.

findings.where: Open questions: errors-as-values bullet: "the guest checks it (`if (isError(r))`)"; "the grok REPAIR measure (#2809)"; "`ctx.error`"
findings.problem: This bullet runs to about 20 lines inside a list of one-liners, so it reads as a full proposal hidden in a list. `isError` is used without saying whether it would be a guest builtin; elsewhere in the project, isError is deprecated in favour of isMonadicError, which adds to the confusion. "Grok REPAIR measure" and `ctx.error` are internal terms.
findings.fix: Move it to its own subsection titled as a proposal. Define the grokkability measure in a clause, and say which guest function the check would use.

findings.where: Section "Relationship to `tjs-lang/vm-ast`" placed last
findings.problem: This section is the most practical connection between the plan and what an embedder can use today, and it is the last thing on the page. The opening section already tells the reader to prefer vm-ast, without this justification.
findings.fix: Move it directly after "What this means for you today", or merge it into that section.

findings.where: Line 2: `<!-- TODO review -->`; repeated "(Tonio, 2026-10-04)"
findings.problem: Named, dated decision credits read as an internal log rather than a design note written for readers. The TODO marker suggests the page is known to be unfinished.
findings.fix: Collect decision provenance in one "Decision log" line at the end, and resolve or remove the TODO marker.

findings.where: Brief: 'Add a one-line forward pointer in DOCS-AJS's error section'
findings.problem: DOCS-AJS.md's error section ('### Catchable, and run-ending', ~line 650) has no pointer to the errors-as-values proposal in this note. The language chapter still teaches try/catch with nothing to say a v3 proposal could change it. The note links to DOCS-AJS, but nothing links back.
findings.fix: In DOCS-AJS.md under 'Catchable, and run-ending', add one line, e.g. 'A proposal for a future AST version would replace try/catch with error values; nothing changes until it ships ([native VM note](/ajs-native-vm/), Open questions).' This is outside this file's scope, so whoever owns DOCS-AJS has to make the change.

findings.where: What changes categorically: 'The 0.13.4 class of bug (transpile-time execution of untrusted source)'
findings.problem: The transpile-time execution bug was not a 0.13.4 issue. CHANGELOG puts the fix in 0.13.7 ('SECURITY — a VM-target transpile no longer executes the code it is transpiling'; 0.13.8 shipped it to dist/), and the Known note says 'tjs-lang <= 0.13.8 all carry at least one transpile-time execution path'. The 0.13.4 entry covers asCompared, not this bug.
findings.evidence: grep -n 'transpile-time execution\|new Function(body)' CHANGELOG.md → line 2823 (0.13.10 Known: '<= 0.13.8'), line 2857 (0.13.7 SECURITY entry). The 0.13.4 section (line 3144) has no execution fix.
findings.fix: Say 'The 0.13.7 class of bug (transpile-time execution of untrusted source; `test` blocks run with `new Function`)', or drop the version.

findings.where: Open questions, errors-as-values: 'the guest checks it (`if (isError(r))`)'
findings.problem: `isError` is not an AJS guest builtin, and in TJS `isError()` is deprecated in favour of `isMonadicError()` (CLAUDE.md). A reader may take this as current API, or as reviving a deprecated name.
findings.fix: Mark it as hypothetical syntax ('e.g. a guest predicate such as `isError(r)`, name to be decided'), or use a name that does not clash with the deprecated TJS function.

findings.where: H1 'AJS Native VM (Rust → wasm): the planned 1.0 VM' vs guides/ajs.md toc entry 'AJS Native VM (Rust → wasm) — the 1.0 VM'
findings.problem: The brief's 'post-1.0 direction' wording is gone, so the main mismatch is fixed. The toc in guides/ajs.md still shows the old H1 text (em dash, no 'planned'). The site build regenerates the toc, but the committed guides/ajs.md is stale until then.
findings.fix: Leave it if the toc is always regenerated. Otherwise update the toc line in guides/ajs.md to match the new H1.

findings.where: Binary sizes: '42 KB … 62 KB … 95 KB' (gzip) vs Relationship to vm-ast: 'about 137 KB … against 324 KB'
findings.problem: I checked the figures and they are correct (gzip -9: tjs-vm-ast 43005 B, tjs-eval 63065 B, tjs-vm 97781 B; raw: 137459 B and 323877 B). The units are mixed, though: the gzip numbers are KiB (/1024) and the raw numbers are decimal KB (/1000). The section also never says which raw bundle numbers are being compared.
findings.evidence: for f in tjs-vm-ast tjs-eval tjs-vm; do gzip -9c dist/$f.js | wc -c; wc -c < dist/$f.js; done → 43005/137459, 63065/200700, 97781/323877
findings.fix: Use one unit throughout, and say '(unminified/raw bundle size of dist/tjs-vm-ast.js vs dist/tjs-vm.js)' in the vm-ast section so readers know the 137/324 figures are raw, not gzip.

findings.where: Constraints table rows 1–6
findings.problem: Row 2's stray extra cell is fixed and every row now has three cells. But the status cells are paragraph-length, so the table does not read well as raw markdown or at phone width. Rows 5 and 6 still carry dated attribution ('Tonio, 2026-10-02; card #2788'), the kind of dated audit language the brief asked to tidy.
findings.fix: Shorten each status cell to a one-line verdict (Partly satisfied / Done 0.14.0 / Satisfied / Started / Open). Move the explanations into a numbered list under the table, and move the card numbers to the end of those notes.

findings.where: Architecture sketch: 'Fuel / quotas / heap ceiling / depth cap / trace'
findings.problem: 'depth cap' is ambiguous. The JS VM has several depth limits: callDepth (helper recursion), runCodeDepth, MEMBRANE_MAX_DEPTH = 10_000 and GUEST_SCHEMA_MAX_DEPTH = 64 (src/vm/runtime.ts:368, 371, 613, 3159). A porter will not know which one is meant.
findings.fix: Write 'depth caps (call depth, membrane nesting, schema nesting)'.

rejected: The guides/ajs.md toc mismatch (polish): rejected. The toc line in guides/ajs.md already reads 'AJS Native VM (Rust → wasm): the planned 1.0 VM' and matches the H1, so nothing needed changing.

revised.summary:
I revised /Users/tonioloewald/tjs-lang/docs/ajs-native-vm.md. Only that file was edited, the metadata line and `<!-- TODO review -->` are kept, and nothing was committed. Of the 33 findings, I applied 31 and rejected 2.

**Changes for embedders**
- The intro now defines "the untrusted path": `vm.run` on guest ASTs (vm and vm-ast) and Eval/SafeFunction, on client and server.
- "What this means for you today" is now a list of four actions. It explains `$ajs` and the membrane in a few words, and says the native VM is planned to read both v1 and v2 ASTs.
- That section also says the host calling convention for atoms is not settled, and adds it to Open questions.
- The vm-ast section moved up to sit right after that list.

**Corrections, checked against the source**
- The transpile-time execution bug is now dated 0.13.7, not 0.13.4 (CHANGELOG line 2853), with a one-line description of how it happened.
- The "core atoms are host capabilities" claim now separates the two kinds: pure core atoms run inside the Rust VM, and IO atoms (`httpFetch`, store, LLM, custom) are host capabilities.
- String semantics may change only once the JS VM is retired from the untrusted path, or under a new AST version.
- The two-VM hazard now has a concrete example: client and server counting string length differently.
- Bundle sizes are now labelled. The gzip figures are given as 43/63/98 KB (they were 42/62/95 because they had been divided by 1024 rather than 1000), and the raw 137/324 KB figures name the dist files they come from. The page now says the native binary would be roughly 3–7× the size of vm-ast.

**Clarity**
- Explained or linked: Pattern, Eval/SafeFunction, the membrane's descriptor walk, JIT bugs, the CSP rationale (`'unsafe-eval'` vs `'wasm-unsafe-eval'`), JSPI/asyncify, the flight recorder, `$predicate`, pgrx, universal endpoints, the json escape type and "lint-banned" constructs.
- The thesis now says "one VM unless a CSP fallback is kept".
- "Depth cap" is now "depth caps (call depth, membrane nesting, schema nesting)".
- The page now says the AST spec note has not been written yet.
- I rewrote "Why now" in plain words, dropped the "door" metaphor, and moved the rc.2 numbers into a parenthesis rather than a footnote, since no other doc on the site uses footnotes.
- "Decided against" now starts from the question it answers: why not go native for TJS too.
- The CSP decision moved to Open questions.

**Structure**
- The constraints table is now three short columns, with a short subsection per row underneath.
- Constraint 2 now has a timeline: the field and v2 both shipped in 0.14.0, and the builder writes an explicit `$ajs: 1` (checked in `src/builder.ts:547`). The old four-paragraph argument with an earlier draft is cut down to the rule plus one sentence of reasoning.
- The errors-as-values bullet is now its own Proposal subsection. The guest check is a builtin "name to be decided, not TJS's deprecated isError", and the grokkability repair measure is explained.
- Named, dated credits are collected in a Decision log at the end.

The page has no tjs or ajs fences, so there were no examples to run. Every in-page anchor link points at a heading on the page, and other docs on the site already use in-page anchors.

findings.where: Intro: "wires it into a host with `getBatteries()`" / "The batteries speak plain OpenAI-compatible HTTP"
findings.problem: "batteries" and "host" are used before they are defined. A first-time reader can't tell whether "the batteries" means a module, a set of atoms, or a capabilities object. The page later uses the word for all three: "batteries module", "battery atoms", and `const batteries = await getBatteries()`.
findings.fix: Add one sentence near the top, something like: "`tjs-lang/batteries` is an optional module that finds a local model server and returns ready-made capabilities, plus a set of battery atoms (`llmPredictBattery`, `llmVision`, `storeVectorize`, …) that use them." Then use the words consistently.

findings.where: "Chat models serve `llmPredictBattery` and `llmVision`; the embedding model serves `storeVectorize` and vector search."
findings.problem: Four atom names show up in a requirements checklist with no word saying they are atoms or where they come from. The reader meets them before seeing any code.
findings.fix: Say "the battery atoms `llmPredictBattery` and `llmVision`" and point ahead to the host example, or move this explanation down to the table under "A host that uses it".

findings.where: A host that uses it (uses `llmPredictBattery`) followed by "Using it for `llmPredict`": "Most examples in this book, starting with LLM Chat, call the core atom `llmPredict`"
findings.problem: The ordering is backwards. The main example teaches an atom that most of the book does not use, and only afterwards says the book's examples need a different atom, a different capability (`llm`) and a hand-written adapter. The reader also isn't told when to pick `llmPredictBattery` over `llmPredict`, or why two exist.
findings.fix: Open with a short comparison: `llmPredict` is the core atom (takes a prompt, the host supplies `llm`, returns a string); `llmPredictBattery` is a battery atom (takes system/user, returns a chat message, supports tools/responseFormat/vision). Lead with whichever one the book's examples need, which is the `llmPredict` adapter.

findings.where: `const { ast } = transpile(source, { atoms: vm.atoms })` vs later `transpile(chat).ast`
findings.problem: The first example passes `{ atoms: vm.atoms }` and the second doesn't. The page never says the difference is that `llmPredict` is a core atom and `llmPredictBattery` is not. `vm.atoms` isn't explained either (what does it hold, is it core plus custom?).
findings.fix: Add a line: "core atoms such as `llmPredict` are always known to the transpiler; battery atoms are not, so pass the VM's atom table with `atoms: vm.atoms`."

findings.where: `{ fuel: 1000, capabilities: batteries, quotas: { llmPredictBattery: 1 } }`
findings.problem: `fuel` and `quotas` show up with no explanation. This book is about running untrusted, LLM-written code safely, so the quota is the most relevant line on the page: it caps how many model calls the agent can make. Nothing says so, or explains why fuel alone can't do that.
findings.fix: Add a sentence after the example: "`quotas` caps how many times an atom may run in one run — here one model call — because fuel measures VM work and cannot express 'at most N model calls'." Link the page that covers fuel and quotas.

findings.where: Import line: `import { AgentVM, batteryAtoms } from 'tjs-lang/vm-ast'`
findings.problem: `batteryAtoms` is imported from the VM entry point. A reader would expect it to come from `tjs-lang/batteries`, the module the page has just presented as the source of everything battery-related. If this is correct, the reason isn't obvious. If it's wrong, the example won't run.
findings.fix: Check the export. If `batteryAtoms` comes from `tjs-lang/batteries`, import it from there. If it really comes from `vm-ast`, add a comment saying why.

findings.where: Table row: `llmBattery` | `{ predict(system, user, tools?, responseFormat?), embed(text) }` and `models` | "the `LocalModels` object holding the audit"
findings.problem: The positional signature `predict(system, user, …)` sits next to an agent that calls `llmPredictBattery({ system, user })` with named inputs, and the reader can't tell which layer is which (host capability vs agent atom). `LocalModels` is never defined, and `tools` and `responseFormat` ("structured output") are never explained.
findings.fix: Label the table as the host-side capability shapes, as opposed to the atoms an agent calls. Define structured output / `responseFormat` in a clause. Either explain `LocalModels` or say only "the audit results, for inspection".

findings.where: "export TJS_LLM_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:1234/v1" right after "The default is `http://localhost:1234/v1`"
findings.problem: The example for "point anywhere else" sets what looks like the default again, with only the host changed. The reason (localhost resolving to IPv6) comes five sections later, so at this point the example reads as a mistake.

findings.where: "The variable is read once, when the batteries module loads, so set it before your host starts (`src/batteries/config.ts`)."
findings.problem: A repository source path in a page for embedders, who install from npm and have no `src/` to look at. "batteries module" also needs to be named as `tjs-lang/batteries`.

findings.where: Browser hosts: "`TJS_LLM_BASE_URL` is an environment variable, so a browser host always gets the default base URL."
findings.problem: The page stops at the problem. A browser host with its server on a different port or machine is left with no way to configure it, and the reader doesn't know whether there is an API option or whether it simply isn't possible.

findings.where: Intro: "On the doc site they print a message instead of running, because a static page has no model to call" vs Browser hosts: "This is why the doc site cannot run the LLM examples" (HTTPS)

findings.where: "Defaults are the first match, in sorted order"
findings.problem: "Sorted" by what? Alphabetical by model id? By size? The reader can't predict which model will be picked.
findings.fix: Say "sorted alphabetically by model id" (or whatever the actual order is) and suggest naming the models explicitly when the order matters.

findings.where: Model names: "`nomic-embed-text-v1.5` works" vs `export TJS_EMBEDDING_MODEL=text-embedding-nomic-embed-text-v1.5-embedding`
findings.problem: These look like the same model under two different ids, and the reader can't tell which one to type.

findings.where: "With both set, the audit is skipped entirely and nothing is probed"
findings.problem: With the audit skipped, the page doesn't say what happens to structured-output and vision support. Are `responseFormat` calls and `llmVision` assumed to work, refused, or sent to the named chat model?

findings.where: "To force a fresh audit, delete the cache file: rm -f ~/Library/Caches/tjs-lang/.models.cache.json   # macOS; adjust for your platform" and "In a browser it is kept in `localStorage` instead."
findings.problem: The command is given for macOS only, even though the paragraph just above lists Linux and Windows paths. The contributors section later uses a different form (`${TJS_CACHE_DIR:-…}`). No localStorage key is given, so a browser host can't clear the cache.
findings.fix: Give one command that respects `TJS_CACHE_DIR`, plus the Linux and Windows paths. Name the localStorage key and how to clear it.

findings.where: When there is no server: "the call fails with `No local LLM server reachable at http://localhost:1234/v1. …`"
findings.problem: Two failure messages for nearly the same situation (server down before the audit vs after a cached audit) make the reader work out which state they're in. The second message shows `localhost`, which the page has just told them to avoid. "a `try`/`catch` in the agent can handle" has no example.
findings.fix: Present the two cases as a two-row table: state → message → fix. Optionally add a three-line AJS `try`/`catch` snippet.

findings.where: Troubleshooting "No LLM available": "The audit found no usable model, and if the server listed models that failed their probes, that result is cached for 24 hours."
findings.problem: This implies some results are cached and others aren't (no models listed vs models that failed their probes) without stating the rule. Elsewhere the page says only "The result is cached for 24 hours".
findings.fix: State the rule once in the cache bullet (for example, "an audit that reached the server is cached even if every probe failed") and refer to it here.

findings.where: "LM Studio also has a command-line tool, `lms`. Run `lms bootstrap` once from the app's install to put it on your `PATH`"
findings.problem: This reads as circular: `lms` isn't on the PATH yet, so how do you run `lms bootstrap`? The binary paths that answer the question come only after the instruction.

findings.where: "// → { answer: 'The sky is typically blue during the daytime.' }" and "// → { response: 'Bonjour' }"
findings.problem: The model output is shown as if it were deterministic, so a reader may think their run is broken when the wording differs.

findings.where: Line 2: `<!-- TODO review -->`
findings.problem: A working note left in a published page. It is invisible when rendered, but it signals the page isn't finished.

findings.where: Check the server from a terminal: curl -s http://127.0.0.1:1234/v1/models | grep -oE '"id":"[^"]*"'
findings.problem: LM Studio pretty-prints /v1/models with a space after the colon ("id": "google/gemma-4-e2b"), so this grep matches nothing and the check prints nothing even when the server is up and models are listed. A reader will conclude the server is broken.
findings.evidence: curl -s http://127.0.0.1:1234/v1/models | grep -oE '"id":"[^"]*"' printed nothing (exit 0); the same with '"id": *"[^"]*"' printed "id": "mistral-small-3.2-24b-instruct-2506-mlx", "id": "google/gemma-4-e2b", "id": "text-embedding-nomic-embed-text-v1.5-embedding". (LM Studio was running locally.)
findings.fix: Use grep -oE '"id": *"[^"]*"' (works with or without the space), or curl ... | jq -r '.data[].id' if jq can be assumed.

findings.where: <!--{"parent": "ajs.md", "order": 9}-->
findings.problem: The brief asked for the order collision to be fixed. The page moved from 7 to 9, but 9 now collides with two other pages in the AJS book: docs/pattern.md and docs/universal-endpoint.md, both at order 9 in the working tree (other agents moved them too). findings.where: `TJS_LLM_BASE_URL` is an environment variable, so a browser host always gets the default base URL.
findings.problem: This is true of getBatteries() only. tjs-lang/batteries also exports LocalModels and getLLMCapability, and both take a base URL (LocalModels constructor(baseUrl = DEFAULT_BASE_URL); getLLMCapability(models, baseUrl = DEFAULT_BASE_URL)). A browser host can therefore point at another server. As written, a reader with a server on a different port thinks a browser host cannot use it.
findings.evidence: src/batteries/models.ts:29 `constructor(private baseUrl = DEFAULT_BASE_URL) {}`; src/batteries/llm.ts:109-111 `export function getLLMCapability(models, baseUrl = DEFAULT_BASE_URL)`; src/batteries/index.ts exports { LocalModels, getLLMCapability }.
findings.fix: Say that getBatteries() uses the default in a browser, and that a host needing a different URL can build the capability itself: const models = new LocalModels(url); await models.audit(); const llmBattery = getLLMCapability(models, url). Say too that the TJS_LLM_MODEL / TJS_EMBEDDING_MODEL overrides likewise do not apply in a browser.

findings.where: The result is cached for 24 hours, keyed by the base URL and the list of model ids.
findings.problem: The cache is also invalidated by a PROBE_VERSION change, so upgrading tjs-lang can re-run the audit. Not wrong, but a reader seeing an unexpected re-audit after an upgrade has no explanation.
findings.evidence: src/batteries/audit.ts readCache: `if (data.baseUrl !== baseUrl) return null; if (data.probeVersion !== PROBE_VERSION) return null; if (Date.now() - data.timestamp > CACHE_TTL_MS) return null`, then the model-id list is compared in auditModels.
findings.fix: Add: 'and by the version of the audit probes, so a tjs-lang upgrade that changes them re-runs the audit.'

findings.where: the run then fails at the first model call with `No LLM available.` in `run.error`, which a `try`/`catch` in the agent can handle like any other error.
findings.problem: Verified true, but a reader who writes the obvious catch (e.message) gets undefined: in AJS the caught value is the message string, not an Error object.
findings.evidence: A test agent with `catch (e) { return { answer: 'caught: ' + e.message } }` returned { answer: 'caught: undefined' } with no server; `return { answer: e }` returned the full message string ('No local LLM server reachable at http://127.0.0.1:1299/v1. Start your backend ...').
findings.fix: Optionally add a short clause or a link to the DOCS-AJS error-handling section: 'the catch binding is the message string'.

findings.where: getBatteries() returns four things: table, `vector` row
findings.problem: When no LLM capability was built (HTTPS page, or initialization threw), `vector` is undefined and `llmBattery` is null. The table does not say this; the HTTPS section mentions only llmBattery. storeVectorize then fails with "Capability 'vector' missing. Ensure vector battery is loaded."
findings.evidence: src/batteries/index.ts getBatteries: `vector: llm ? { embed: llm.embed } : undefined, ... llmBattery: llm`; src/vm/atoms/batteries.ts:55-57 the storeVectorize error.
findings.fix: Add 'undefined when llmBattery is null' to the vector row, or mention both keys in the HTTPS bullet.

rejected: Partly rejected: the doc-site finding's suggested reason (HTTPS) is not the real one. site/entry.ts injects no LLM at all and reports NEEDS_LLM for any llm op. The page now gives that as the reason and mentions HTTPS only as a second point: the site could not reach a local server even if it wanted to. The finding that the page gave two inconsistent reasons was applied.

Partly rejected: the import of batteryAtoms from 'tjs-lang/vm-ast' is correct. src/vm/ast.ts re-exports ./atoms, and tjs-lang/batteries exports only capabilities, LocalModels and getLLMCapability. I kept the import and added a comment saying why.

Partly rejected: the premise that the transpiler needs `atoms: vm.atoms` in order to accept battery-atom calls is false. transpile(source) without it compiles llmPredictBattery fine. What the table actually does is let the transpiler check the call's inputs ('sytem' is refused with it and passes without it). The page now says that.

No collapsed <details> section for the hardware notes. I moved them into a dated 'Hardware notes (Linux and NVIDIA, as of June 2026)' subsection instead, because I wasn't sure the doc site renders raw HTML.

revised.summary:
I revised /Users/tonioloewald/tjs-lang/docs/lm-studio-setup.md and kept `<!-- TODO review -->` on line 2. I changed the metadata order from 9 to 6.6 to fix the collision.

Changes:
- **Definitions up front.** "The batteries" (tjs-lang/batteries) and "battery atoms" are now defined at the top, and the doc-site reason is stated once.
- **Model-call comparison.** A new table compares the core atom llmPredict with the battery atom llmPredictBattery. The page now leads with the llmPredict adapter, which is what the book's examples use.
- **Host example notes.** The battery-atom host example now explains `atoms: vm.atoms`, which lets the transpiler check the call's inputs (verified: 'sytem' is refused with it and compiles without it). It also explains `quotas`: a second call fails with `Quota exceeded for 'llmPredictBattery': 1 call allowed`, and the page says why fuel cannot express a cap on model calls, with a link to /ajs-host/#run-options.
- **Capability table.** It is now labelled host-side. `llmBattery` is shown as possibly null and `vector` as undefined in that case, and LocalModels is replaced with "the audit results".
- **Curl check fixed.** The grep is now `'"id": *"[^"]*"'`, which matches LM Studio's pretty-printed output (verified). A note explains that the reported ids differ from download names.
- **Base URL example.** It is now a different machine (192.168.1.20) instead of what looked like the default. The env-var note no longer cites a `src/` path; that path moved to the contributors section.
- **Browser hosts.** I added the LocalModels(url) plus getLLMCapability(models, url) recipe (verified), and noted that the model env vars do not apply in a browser.
- **Model selection.** Default order is now described as plain string order of model ids. I added what named models imply: they are assumed to support structured output, and llmVision calls go to the named chat model untested.
- **Cache.** I added the cache rule (an audit that reached the server is cached whatever it found; a failed connection caches nothing) and PROBE_VERSION invalidation. There are per-platform delete commands that respect TJS_CACHE_DIR and XDG_CACHE_HOME, plus the localStorage key `.models.cache.json`.
- **No-server failures.** These are now a two-row table, followed by an AJS try/catch snippet showing that the catch binding is the message string (verified: `{ failed: 'No LLM available.' }`).
- **lms bootstrap.** Reordered so the binary path comes before the instruction.
- **Smaller fixes.** I added a Windows bullet, marked model outputs as varying, and said the audit logs go to the console and cannot be silenced. Hardware-specific notes moved into a dated subsection.

I verified all JavaScript host examples against the live local LM Studio. Both hosts returned the expected shapes ({ response: 'Bonjour' } and { answer: '...' }). The quota and the no-server catch behave as the page states.

findings.problem: This invites the obvious question: can I point `TJS_LLM_BASE_URL` at a hosted OpenAI-compatible API? The page never says whether that works, how an API key would be passed (no key variable appears in the env table), or why a local model is preferred. It also never says why someone embedding the VM would want a local model at all (cost, privacy, offline development?).
findings.fix: Add a short motivation paragraph and one line on hosted endpoints and authentication: supported or not, and how.

findings.where: Env var section: "When **both** ... are set, the batteries use them as given and skip the model audit. When only one is set, the batteries audit `/v1/models`..."
findings.problem: "Model audit" is used here before it is explained; the explanation only arrives in gotcha 1. The "only one is set" case is also never followed through for MLX: the audit returns an empty list, so the variable you did not set gives you nothing. Which battery is then null? The reader has to work that out alone.
findings.fix: Define the audit when it first appears ("at startup the batteries ask the server's /v1/models which models it has, and pick a chat and an embedding model"). Say plainly that on mlx-omni-server you must set both.

findings.where: Env table row: `TJS_LLM_MODEL` ... "chat model id; also used for structured output"
findings.problem: "Structured output" is not defined, and no atom or example on the page uses it.
findings.fix: Name the atom or feature that uses structured output, or drop the clause.

findings.where: Server table: "chat, embeddings, images, speech, STT" / "chat, limited completions"
findings.problem: "STT" is not expanded, and "limited completions" is vague. The `mlx_lm.server` row exists only to be ruled out, which adds a choice the reader then has to discard.
findings.fix: Expand STT to speech-to-text, or drop the column detail. Either drop the mlx_lm.server row or say in one line why someone might reach for it and why not to.

findings.where: Setup step 3/4: "# 3. Run the server. mlx-omni-server --port 10240 / # 4. In the shell that runs your host..."
findings.problem: Step 3 runs in the foreground and blocks that terminal. Step 4 hints at a different shell without saying so, and the `curl` check after the block also needs a second terminal. A reader pasting the whole block into one shell will hang at step 3.
findings.fix: Say explicitly: leave the server running in one terminal and run step 4 and the curl check in another (or background the server).

findings.where: Gotcha 1: "A named model is trusted rather than probed (a probe would load the whole model to ask about it), so its embedding dimension is unknown until the first call. That is expected."
findings.problem: The reader cannot tell why this matters. What would they see, and what code would care about the embedding dimension? The paragraph is already a wall of text (cause, symptom, exact console string, fix, caveat and upstream link in one block), and this tail adds a caveat with no consequence attached.
findings.fix: Split gotcha 1 into Symptom / Cause / Fix. Either state the visible consequence of the unknown dimension (for example, a vector collection cannot be sized ahead of time) or cut the sentence.

findings.where: "`getBatteries()` audits the server (or takes the named models) and returns the capabilities"
findings.problem: `getBatteries` appears here with no import path; the reader only finds out it comes from 'tjs-lang' in the next code block. The page also never says whether it is safe to call more than once or whether it caches (the env table mentions an audit cache).
findings.fix: Give the import in the prose, and say in one line whether it caches and when the cache is reused.

findings.where: "`llmBattery` and `vector` are `null`/`undefined` when no model was found."
findings.problem: The page never says what an agent then sees when it calls `llmPredictBattery`: a catchable error, the run ending, or something else, and with what message. "null/undefined" (which one?) is also imprecise. For a book about running untrusted agents, the failure mode is the point.
findings.fix: State the result of calling a battery atom when its capability is missing, quoting the error, and whether the agent can catch it.

findings.where: Store row: "`storeSearch`, `storeVectorAdd`, and others" / "an in-memory key-value + vector store"
findings.problem: "And others" leaves the reader guessing which atoms read `store`. "In-memory" implies the data is lost when the process exits, which the page does not say. The store also has nothing to do with MLX, so it is unclear why it is in this chapter.
findings.fix: List the atoms or link to where they are listed, add "(not persisted)", and say the store comes with getBatteries regardless of the model server.

findings.where: `const { ast } = transpile(source, { atoms: vm.atoms })` and "(`source` is the agent's text)"
findings.problem: The page does not say why `{ atoms: vm.atoms }` is passed. A reader would guess it is so the transpiler accepts the battery atom names, but the page does not say what happens without it. Defining `source` in a parenthetical also leaves the reader to stitch the two blocks together. The agent block is fenced as `javascript` even though it is AJS source meant to go into a string.
findings.fix: Show `const source = `...`` in the host block, or say "the agent above, as a string". Add one clause explaining that `atoms` lets the transpiler check calls to non-core atoms. Label the agent block as AJS.

findings.where: `vm.run(ast, {}, { fuel: 500, capabilities: batteries })`
findings.problem: The page gives no reason for 500 fuel, and does not say whether fuel or the run timeout covers time spent waiting on a slow local model. mlx-omni-server loads models on demand, so the first call can be slow. A first-time reader will wonder whether the first run times out.
findings.fix: Say what fuel and timeout a model call needs, and whether the first, model-loading call needs a larger `timeoutMs`.

findings.where: "### The core `llmPredict` atom" ... `llmBattery.predict('You are a concise assistant.', prompt)`
findings.problem: There is no motivation for why two LLM atoms exist or which one an agent author should use. The adapter calls `llmBattery.predict` with two positional arguments, while the atom took `{ system, user }`, and that signature is never described. The `run` in this block uses an `ast` for an agent calling `llmPredict` that is never shown.
findings.fix: Open with a sentence on when to use `llmPredict` and when `llmPredictBattery`. Document `llmBattery.predict(system, user)`. Show or name the agent the `ast` comes from.

findings.where: "Neither block above is a live example on this site: both need a model server on your machine."
findings.problem: "Neither" implies two blocks, but there are three code blocks above it (agent, host, adapter), so it is unclear which are meant. The note also comes after the reader may already have tried to run them.
findings.fix: Move the note to the top of "Wiring it into a VM" and say "None of the code in this section runs on the site".

findings.where: "## Running the live LLM tests" / `bun run test:llm`, `src/batteries/llm-transport.test.ts`, `UPSTREAM.md`
findings.problem: This section and parts of the Vision section are for tjs-lang contributors working in the repo. A developer embedding the published package has no `test:llm` script, no `src/` and no `UPSTREAM.md`. "The advisory AJS-grokkability lane ... also runs here" is unclear: does it run as part of test:llm, or against this server? "Advisory" and "lane" are not defined. The intro's "for the live LLM tests" has the same audience mismatch.
findings.fix: Mark the section as for contributors, or move it to a contributor doc. Rewrite the grok sentence as "`bun run test:grok` can also target this server; set GROK_MODEL to an MLX model id".

findings.where: Vision: "the 4-bit gemma-4 build tried here failed to load its weights on two different servers"
findings.problem: "Tried here" and "two different servers" are lab notes with no referent: which build, which servers? "Without a vision model they skip themselves" refers to repo tests again.
findings.fix: Name the model and the servers, or reduce it to "no MLX vision model has worked yet; use LM Studio".

findings.where: Whole page (browser hosts)
findings.problem: Nothing tells a reader whose host runs in a browser whether these local HTTP calls work there: mixed content from an HTTPS page, CORS against localhost:10240. A host embedding the VM in a web page has no way to know whether this setup applies to them.
findings.fix: Add one line on browser hosts: what happens from an HTTPS page, and whether mlx-omni-server needs CORS configured.

findings.where: Line 2: `<!-- TODO review -->`
findings.problem: A leftover working note in a published page's source. It is invisible when rendered, but it signals the page is unreviewed.
findings.fix: Remove it once the edit pass is done.

findings.where: Wiring it into a VM: "`llmBattery` and `vector` are `null`/`undefined` when no model was found."
findings.problem: They are not. `ensureInitialized()` builds `llm = getLLMCapability(localModels)` whenever the audit returns, even with zero models, so `llmBattery` and `vector` are live objects. They are null/undefined only on an HTTPS page, or if the audit itself throws. A host that checks `if (!batteries.llmBattery)` to detect 'no model' never sees the null, and every call fails at run time with `No LLM available.` instead.
findings.evidence: With TJS_LLM_BASE_URL=http://localhost:59999/v1 (nothing listening), `getBatteries()` printed `llmBattery object vector object` and the agent's run.error was `No LLM available.` Source: src/batteries/index.ts, ensureInitialized() and getBatteries().
findings.fix: Say: `llmBattery` and `vector` are null/undefined only when local endpoints are disabled (an HTTPS page). When no model is found they still exist, and each call fails with `No LLM available.` / `No embedding model available.`

findings.where: Running the live LLM tests: "The advisory AJS-grokkability lane (`bun run test:grok`) also runs here; set `GROK_MODEL` to an MLX model id."
findings.problem: Setting GROK_MODEL is not enough on mlx-omni-server. The grok test calls `models.getModels().some(m => m.id === PIN_MODEL)` and skips unless the pin is in the model list. On MLX that list holds only the env-declared models, so GROK_MODEL must equal TJS_LLM_MODEL. If it differs, the lane prints 'pin model … is not loaded in LM Studio' and skips.
findings.evidence: src/use-cases/ajs-grokkability.test.ts beforeAll: `pinAvailable = models.getModels().some((m) => m.id === PIN_MODEL)`; src/batteries/models.ts audit(): when both env vars are set, models = [declared LLM_MODEL, declared EMBEDDING_MODEL].
findings.fix: Say: set GROK_MODEL and TJS_LLM_MODEL to the same MLX model id (the default pin, google/gemma-4-e2b, is an LM Studio id).

The reader only learns this in gotcha 2, after the command has already failed with 'command not found'. findings.where: Gotcha 1: "every call fails with `No LLM available.` and the console shows `⚠️ No LLM found. …`"
findings.problem: There are three console warnings, not one: `No embedding model found.`, `No LLM found.` and `No LLM with structured output support found.`, plus `❌ Failed to connect…` when nothing is listening. An embed call fails with `No embedding model available.`, not `No LLM available.`.

findings.evidence: Run with TJS_LLM_MODEL=a TJS_EMBEDDING_MODEL=b and a dead port: run.error was 'No local LLM server reachable at http://localhost:59999/v1. …'. Source: src/batteries/llm.ts isConnectionRefused branch.

findings.where: The environment variables: "The batteries read these once, when `tjs-lang/batteries` is first imported"
findings.problem: This is true for TJS_LLM_BASE_URL, TJS_LLM_MODEL, TJS_EMBEDDING_MODEL and TJS_VISION_MODEL (module-level consts in config.ts). TJS_CACHE_DIR is different: resolveCacheDir reads it at each audit (audit.ts cacheDir()). Also, TJS_VISION_MODEL is read only by the vision tests (demo/examples.test.ts), not by the batteries.

findings.where: Opening: "Regex in AJS is on its way out. This page says what that means..."
findings.problem: The page never says up front why regex is leaving or what Pattern is. A reader has to get through about 200 lines, past 'Design history', to reach 'Why replace regex' and 'The goal: cost it accurately, for free'. Until then the deprecation looks arbitrary.
findings.fix: Add two or three sentences after the first paragraph: regex is a second language whose cost is hard to meter and whose mistakes go unnoticed; Pattern is a grammar built as data whose every step is charged as fuel. Link down to the history for the long version.

findings.where: "Today (0.14.0-rc.10), nothing." and the plan table, compared with "### Sequencing" (0.14: "the transpiler warns... `Pattern` ships if the design settles"; 0.14.x: "`Pattern` | `tjs-lang/regex`")

The Sequencing table says 0.14 warns, 0.14.x ships Pattern and regexAtoms, and 0.15 removes regex. Nothing in the Sequencing section says it is out of date, so a reader can't tell which timeline is current.
findings.fix: Label the Sequencing table as the plan as of 2026-10-04, superseded by the table at the top, or delete it and keep only the current table.

findings.where: "A regex that only works because the engine backtracks (`\w+\d`, where `\w+` would have to give a digit back)"

The real point is about regex semantics (characters being given back), not about how any engine is built.
findings.fix: Reword it: "A regex whose match depends on a repetition giving characters back (`\w+\d`: `\w+` must leave the last digit for `\d`) will not translate..."

findings.where: Terms used before or without definition: "charged as fuel", "`regexMatch` atom", "registered like `batteryAtoms`", "the membrane", "`effects: 'io'`", "pinned small model", "`bun run test:grok`", "board #2771"

findings.fix: Add a one-line gloss or a link to the AJS book's chapter for each of fuel, atom, membrane and effects. Replace board numbers with public links, or drop them from the reader-facing part of the page.

findings.where: `import { pattern } from 'tosijs-pattern'` with the status note "tosijs-pattern 0.1.0 exists as a library, not yet on npm"

written.changes:
Rewrote /Users/tonioloewald/tjs-lang/docs/universal-endpoint.md and kept its role as the "why" chapter for embedders.

- Metadata: the order moves from 5 to 9, as the brief asked, so it sits after the capabilities chapter. `<!-- TODO review -->` is added on line 2.
- Production claim: "In production we ran…" is now written as a pattern, since I could not name the product.
- Replaced the pseudo-code pair (`findLoaded`, `…`, `storeOf(ctx).query`) with one complete example that runs in Bun:
  - The client and server VMs come from `tjs-lang/vm-ast`, with `defineAtom` and schemas from `tjs-lang/schema`.
  - The agent is transpiled once against `clientVM.atoms`. On a miss the client atom POSTs the AST, not source, to the server.
  - The client atom reads the reply with `.then((response) => response.json())` and returns plain data.
  - The server takes `user` from the session and passes it to the atom through `ctx.capabilities`, so the agent cannot read it.
  - One `canRead` rule, built from `tjs-lang/rbac` (`buildRuleContext` and `evaluateAccessShortcut`), runs on both sides.
  - It shows three cases: a local hit makes no request, a miss makes one, and a record owned by another user is filtered out by the server.
- New "details that carry the safety" section, which covers:
  - Both atoms default to `effects: 'io'`, so input is a checked copy of `In` and the return is copied and checked against `Out`. That default is why the pair is safe.
  - Returning a `Response` is refused and ends the run. I confirmed the exact refusal.
  - The AST is the wire format, so the server holds no parser.
  - The server treats the agent as untrusted.
  - Per-request identity reaches atoms through capabilities.
- RBAC: the paragraph now points at the published `tjs-lang/rbac` entry point instead of `src/rbac/`. It has a second runnable example: an agent written as a rule, with its result passed through `interpretRuleResult`.
- Accuracy fix: "one security model" now says plainly that the client's copy of a rule does not protect data, because a hostile client can skip it. The server applying the same rule to every request does. The client copy keeps the page and the server consistent.
- Cut the `src/vm/vm.ts` constructor quote. It is now an inline `{ ...coreAtoms, ...customAtoms }` mention plus the fact that `transpile(source, { atoms })` checks each call against the atom's contract.
- "See also" now links to book pages: `/ajs-capabilities/`, `/ajs-host/`, `/patterns/` and `/vm-budgets/`. The links to CLAUDE.md, CONTEXT.md and source paths are gone.

Both examples use ```javascript fences, not ```ajs, because they need host atoms and so cannot run live on the page. All scratch scripts are in /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-tonioloewald-tjs-lang/ceca4d7c-a13f-43be-92e8-1e916ca662c7/scratchpad/docs-swarm/universal-endpoint/.
questions: The old text said 'In production we ran…'. Which product was this, and may the chapter name it? I've written it as a pattern for now.

Because `interpretRuleResult` denies an out-of-fuel run, the deny is safe. But the reason it reports ('rule returned an object whose `allow` is not a boolean') hides that the rule never finished. Should `rules.tjs` report run errors separately? That is a code change, so I didn't make it.

findings.where: "The local-first lookup and the fallback live in the atom, not in the program, so you write them once and every agent that reads records gets them."
findings.problem: The example contradicts this. The client atom does not fetch records. It re-sends one specific program (the module-level `ast` of `lookup`) with `args: { ids: missing }` and reads `reply.records`, which is that agent's return shape. Any other agent that calls `getRecords` would send the wrong program, or the wrong args, to the server, or would get back a reply with no `.records`. So as written, the atom is tied to exactly one agent.
findings.evidence: Lines 107, 120 and 124: `let ast // the client atom sends it on a miss` … `body: JSON.stringify({ ast, args: { ids: missing } })` … `return [...hits, ...reply.records]`
findings.fix: Either have the client atom send a fixed, server-owned 'fetch records' agent (or a plain records request) that does not depend on which agent made the call, or narrow the claim and say so plainly: on a miss, the whole calling agent is re-run on the server. Then explain what that requires of the agent (its args must be just `{ ids }`, and it must return `{ records }`).

findings.where: "If some are missing, it sends the agent to the server for just those."
findings.problem: The reader is never told that 'sending the agent' means re-running the entire program from the start on the server. For any agent that does more than one call, this means work is duplicated. If the agent has side effects (writes, LLM calls, counters), they happen twice, and a quota is counted separately on each side. 'When to reach for it' never says when not to use the pattern.
findings.fix: State outright that a miss re-executes the whole agent remotely. Add a 'When not to' note: agents with side effects before the read, or whose args are not just the ids. Alternatively, restructure the example so that only the read crosses the wire.

findings.where: Title: "The universal endpoint: isomorphic atoms, one security model" and "An agent endpoint exists in two places at once"
findings.problem: The page never defines 'universal endpoint', 'agent endpoint' or 'isomorphic', and 'isomorphic' never appears again. A reader embedding the VM does not know whether an 'endpoint' is an HTTP route, a VM, or the pair.
findings.fix: Add one defining sentence early, e.g. 'An agent endpoint is a VM plus a set of atoms that agents run against; "universal" means the same agent AST runs against a client endpoint and a server endpoint whose atoms share names and schemas (isomorphic atoms).'

findings.where: "return evaluateAccessShortcut('owner:ownerId', context).allowed" and buildRuleContext({ uid, roles, method: 'read', collection: 'notes', docId, doc })
findings.problem: Nothing explains the shortcut string syntax `'owner:ownerId'` (that it presumably grants when `doc.ownerId === uid`), what other shortcuts exist, or why `roles`, `method` and `collection` are required. Yet the whole safety argument rests on this function.
findings.fix: Add a sentence explaining that `'owner:ownerId'` means 'allowed if the doc's `ownerId` field equals the user's uid', and link to where shortcuts and the rule context are documented.

findings.where: console.log(await check({ published: true })) // { allowed: true, reason: null }
findings.problem: The rule returns `{ allow: true, reason: '' }`, but the output shows `reason: null` and a different key (`allowed`, not `allow`). A reader cannot tell whether this is a typo or `interpretRuleResult` normalizing the result. The fuel-exhausted and truthy-string cases that the prose stresses are not shown either.
findings.fix: Say that `interpretRuleResult` turns the rule's `{ allow, reason }` into `{ allowed, reason }` and that an empty reason becomes null. Add one line showing a rule that runs out of fuel (or returns 'yes') being denied.

findings.where: "A rule that a shortcut such as 'owner:ownerId' cannot express can be an agent itself. Run it in the VM on either side"
findings.problem: The page never shows how an agent-rule plugs into the `getRecords` pair: which VM runs it, and whether the server atom runs a nested `vm.run` inside its implementation. It also does not say how the rule's AST reaches the client while staying the 'same code'.
findings.fix: Show `canRead` rewritten to call `check(doc)` (or describe it in a sentence). Note whether running it inside an atom's implementation means a nested run with its own fuel and quota counter.

findings.where: "1. **One security model.** The same capability, fuel and authorization rules run in the browser and on the server, because they are the same code."
findings.problem: This overclaims until the caveat near the end ('The client's copy of a rule is not what protects the data'). A reader skimming the benefits list comes away thinking the client-side check provides security.
findings.fix: Put the caveat in the benefit itself, e.g. 'One security model: the same rules run on both sides; the server's copy enforces, the client's copy keeps the UI consistent with it.' Or move the 'Be precise' paragraph up next to the list.

findings.where: const hits = ids.filter((id) => loaded.has(id) && canRead(user, loaded.get(id))) … const missing = ids.filter((id) => !loaded.has(id))
findings.problem: A record that is loaded but unreadable is silently dropped: it is neither a hit nor missing. Why does the client re-check records the page already holds? The answer only comes much later. Results also come back hits-first rather than in `ids` order, and nothing says so.
findings.fix: Add an inline comment: 'loaded but not readable: dropped, same as the server would'. Say once that the order is not preserved, or preserve it.

findings.problem: The page opens by saying errors are values, not exceptions, and later explains that a non-JSON return ends the run rather than being catchable. It never says what happens when an atom implementation throws: is the error catchable by the agent, does it end the run, and what does `run.error` contain? The reader cannot predict how this line behaves.
findings.fix: Add one sentence after the example: a thrown error in an atom becomes an `AgentError` on the run, catchable or not (whichever is true), and show what the second `run` would print if the server refused.

findings.where: let ast // the client atom sends it on a miss … ast = transpile(source, { atoms: clientVM.atoms }).ast
findings.problem: There is a forward reference: the atom closes over a variable that is assigned only after the VM is built, because the transpiler needs the VM's atoms. The comment does not explain this ordering. The page also does not say why the server can run an AST that was checked against the client's atoms (it depends on the schemas being identical).
findings.fix: Comment: 'assigned below: transpile needs clientVM.atoms to check calls; the server accepts it because its getRecords has the same name and schemas'.

findings.where: console.log((await run(['n1', 'n2', 'n3'])).result.records) // n1 local, n2 from the server
findings.problem: The output comments describe the result instead of showing it, so the reader cannot check that `title` comes back and `ownerId` is stripped, which the `view` function exists for.
findings.fix: Show the literal printed value, e.g. `// [{ id: 'n1', title: 'Shopping' }, { id: 'n2', title: 'Talk notes' }]`.

findings.where: "**The server treats the agent as untrusted.** It sets its own fuel, it decides which atoms exist"
findings.problem: The server VM still includes the core atom set. The reader is not told what an arbitrary client-supplied AST could do with core atoms (e.g. whether `httpFetch` is usable when the server passes only `{ user }` as capabilities). This is the obvious next question for someone exposing `/agent` publicly.
findings.fix: Add a sentence: core atoms that touch IO need a capability, and the server passes only `{ user }`, so a hostile AST can reach only `getRecords` and pure computation bounded by fuel. Mention quotas/timeouts for a public route.

findings.where: "**Atoms are the seam.** `new AgentVM(customAtoms)` merges your atoms over the core set, `{ ...coreAtoms, ...customAtoms }`."
findings.problem: `coreAtoms` is introduced without definition. 'Merges over' implies a custom atom can shadow a core one, but the page does not say whether that is relevant or safe here.
findings.fix: Define it in a short clause ('the built-in atoms every VM has') or drop the spread notation.

findings.where: "Code travels to data" becomes a deployment option rather than a slogan.
findings.problem: It quotes a slogan the reader has not seen on this page.
findings.fix: Attribute it ('AJS's motto, "code travels to data", …') or drop the quote marks.

findings.where: "Several details carry the safety of this arrangement, and each is worth reading twice."

findings.where: "in a browser it would be `window.fetch`" (intro) and `// In the browser this is window.fetch.` (example)
findings.problem: If a reader takes this literally and passes `capabilities: { fetch: window.fetch }`, the atom calls `ctx.capabilities.fetch(...)` with `this` set to the capabilities object, and browsers throw 'TypeError: Illegal invocation'. The example works in Bun only because its `fetch` is a plain arrow function.
findings.fix: Say 'a wrapper around window.fetch', and show `fetch: (url, init) => window.fetch(url, init)` (or `window.fetch.bind(window)`).

findings.where: `const view = ({ id, title }) => ({ id, title })` / "Records as the agent sees them: no ownerId."
findings.problem: `view` reads like a cosmetic choice, but it is required. The Out schema is closed, so an atom that returns the raw record (with ownerId) fails output validation. I tested it: returning [{id,title,ownerId}] produced a catchable 'Output validation failed for 'getRecords''. This is a point in the chapter's favour (the declared output schema stops a field leaking) and it is not stated.
findings.fix: Add one sentence: the Out schema admits only id and title, so a record that still carried ownerId would be refused at the boundary rather than leaking to the agent.
findings.evidence: scratch c.mjs: an atom returning [{id:'a',title:'t',ownerId:'x'}] gave result {"caught":"Output validation failed for 'getRecords'"}

findings.problem: guides/patterns.md (line ~469) notes that the built-in httpFetch checks (allowlist, methods, the X-Agent-Depth header) do not apply to an atom you write that calls the fetch capability directly. This chapter's client atom does exactly that, and its server endpoint receives agent traffic, but the chapter does not mention it. The pair is safe as written: the server passes no fetch capability, so the agent cannot recurse. Readers extending it may not see that.
findings.fix: Add a short note: the custom atom bypasses httpFetch's checks, so the fetch capability it is given should be scoped to the endpoint, and a server whose atoms make further agent calls should forward requestDepth (link /patterns/).

findings.where: "Anything else denies, including a rule that ran out of fuel or returned a truthy string"
