findings.where: "The smallest complete agent: named input in, an object out."
findings.problem: Neither 'agent' nor 'AJS' is defined, and 'named input' is opaque. This is order 0, the first page a newcomer sees, so they get no sentence saying what an agent is (a function the VM runs) or who calls it.
findings.fix: Open with one sentence: 'An AJS agent is a JavaScript-like function that a host runs inside the sandboxed AJS VM; the host passes it one object of inputs and gets back one object.'

findings.where: "because agents are meant to be chained, and one agent's output becomes the next one's input"
findings.problem: The motivation rests on chaining, which a first-time reader has never heard of and which this page never shows. It also only explains the object OUT, not the destructured object IN.
findings.fix: Drop the chaining clause or make it a forward reference ('see Multi-agent pipeline'). Give a reason that fits this page, e.g. named fields can be validated and documented.

findings.where: ```ajs:inline function greet(...) ...```
findings.problem: The page never says how the example is run, who 'the caller' is, or what output to expect. Later bullets refer to 'the result line' and say 'This page runs every example with no arguments', but nothing shows the result. A reader of a static or printed copy cannot see `{ message: 'Hello, World!' }` or `fuelUsed`.
findings.fix: After each example, state the expected result, e.g. `→ { message: 'Hello, World!' }  fuelUsed: …`. Add one line on how a host runs it (transpile, then `vm.run(ast, { name: 'Ada' })`), or link to where that is shown.

findings.where: "`template` is an atom, and atoms take named inputs."
findings.problem: 'atom' is used without being defined. The reader can't tell whether `template` is a built-in, an import, or something the host supplies, or how it differs from an ordinary function.
findings.fix: Define it on first use: 'an atom is a built-in VM operation (the only things an agent can call); each declares named inputs.' Link to the atom list.

findings.where: "A positional call, `template('Hello, {{name}}!', { name })` (refused), is a transpile error that tells you what the atom takes, so it never reaches the VM."
findings.problem: 'transpile' and 'the VM' come in here without explanation, and so does the two-stage model (source is compiled first, then the VM runs it). The parenthetical '(refused)' in the middle of the sentence is awkward and repeats 'is a transpile error'.
findings.fix: Remove '(refused)'. Explain the pipeline once near the top: 'AJS source is transpiled to a JSON AST, which the VM executes.'

findings.where: "It cost fuel. The result line shows `fuelUsed`. ... a budget the host sets is what stops a runaway agent."
findings.problem: 'fuel' and 'the host' are not defined. The reader learns that fuel exists but not its units, a typical cost, or how a host sets the budget, so the point stays abstract.
findings.fix: Say 'fuel is the VM's unit of work; the host passes a `fuel` budget to `vm.run`, and the run stops when it is used up.' Show the fuelUsed this example produced, and link to the Fuel limits example.

findings.where: "`template` is an atom ..." vs "A template literal does the same job without an atom."
findings.problem: The page teaches `template` first, then says a template literal does the same job without one. That leaves the reader asking why they would ever use the atom. The page gives no reason for the atom, so it reads as a detour.
findings.fix: Say when `template` is preferable (e.g. the template string is data from an input or a model), or lead with the template literal and present the atom as the option for data-driven templates.

findings.where: "The entry function must return an object."
findings.problem: 'Entry function' implies a file can contain several functions, but the page never says which one is the entry (the first, the only one, a named export?).
findings.fix: Add a clause: 'the entry function is <rule>; helpers may also be declared in the file.' Or say each example is a single function.

findings.where: "AJS refuses to convert an array or object to a string behind your back, because that conversion is work (and memory) the VM could not budget."
findings.problem: 'Could not budget' is a jump: the reader has just learned that every step is metered, so they will ask why this one can't be. The error message is also quoted only in part, so the reader doesn't know what the full error looks like or whether it can be caught.
findings.fix: Add a half-sentence, e.g. 'the size of an implicit conversion isn't known until it has already happened, so the VM can't charge for it in advance'. Show the full error text as it appears in the result.

findings.where: ## The gotcha
findings.problem: The gotcha describes a failing variant, `${names}`, but never shows it as code next to the working version, so the reader can't compare the two.
findings.fix: Add a short paired snippet: the wrong line marked as refused, the right line, and the resulting error.

findings.where: "`name = 'World'` is the value used when the caller does not supply one"
findings.problem: A reader who knows the AJS/TJS colon syntax (`name: 'World'`) may wonder whether `=` here means something different, for example whether the input is optional.
findings.fix: Add 'so `name` is optional' and, if relevant, a pointer to the required-input form.

findings.where: <!-- TODO review -->
findings.problem: A TODO marker is left in the published source. It is harmless when rendered, but it signals that the page has not been reviewed.
findings.fix: Remove it once the page has been reviewed.

findings.where: "A positional call, `template('Hello, {{name}}!', { name })` (refused), is a transpile error that tells you what the atom takes"
findings.problem: The transpile error does not name template's inputs (tmpl, vars). It gives the generic named-call shape. It is a transpile error and never reaches the VM, which is correct.
findings.evidence: transpile of `template('Hello, {{name}}!', { name })` throws: "'template' takes named arguments: write template({ name: value, … }), not template(a, b). Positional arguments are for local functions. at <source>:2:16" (src/lang/emitters/ast.ts:1563)
findings.fix: Say "is a transpile error that tells you to write template({ name: value, … })" or quote the message. Do not claim it lists what the atom takes.

findings.where: "`name = 'World'` is the value used when the caller does not supply one"
findings.problem: The default is also an example that sets the input contract. A caller passing { name: 42 } or an extra key is refused before the agent runs. Readers who embed the VM need to know this, and the brief's book audience includes hosts.
findings.evidence: vm.run(ast, { name: 42 }) and vm.run(ast, { name: 'Ada', extra: 1 }) both return {"$error":true,"message":"Input validation failed: args do not match expected schema","op":"vm.run"}; { name: 'Ada' } returns {"message":"Hello, Ada!"}
findings.fix: Add a sentence: the default doubles as an example, so `name` must be a string, and a call with { name: 42 } or an unknown key fails input validation.

findings.where: "The run stops with an error that names the fix (`convert it explicitly (e.g. arr.join(','), JSON.stringify(obj))`)"
findings.problem: The quote is accurate, but the full message begins "'+' needs a string, number, boolean or null, not an array" (op expr.concat). A reader who wrote a template literal and no '+' may not see why. Also, 'stops' could be read as a thrown exception, but the run returns an error value (monadic).
findings.evidence: `Hello, ${names}!` run gives error "'+' needs a string, number, boolean or null, not an array — convert it explicitly (e.g. arr.join(','), JSON.stringify(obj))", op "expr.concat"
findings.fix: Note that a template literal compiles to string concatenation, so the error talks about '+'. Or quote the whole message.

I revised /Users/tonioloewald/tjs-lang/guides/examples/ajs/hello-world.md and kept the metadata line and the `<!-- TODO review -->` marker on line 2.

What changed:
- **Opening:** the page now starts by saying what an agent is (a function the host runs in the sandboxed VM, one object in and one object out). The chaining explanation is gone.
- **Order of examples:** the template literal comes first. The `template` atom comes second, framed as the choice when the template itself is data (an input, a stored setting, or model output). That gives the reader a reason to use the atom.
- **Expected results:** every example is followed by its result, so a printed copy shows it too.
- **New "How a host runs it" section:** shows `transpile`, then `vm.run(ast, args, { fuel })` from tjs-lang/vm-ast, and says the page plays the host and runs each example with no arguments.
- **Inputs:** `=` makes an input optional and `:` makes it required. The default doubles as the input contract: `{ name: 42 }` or an extra key fails with `Input validation failed: args do not match expected schema`. Links to DOCS-AJS Input/Output Contract.

  - `name: 'World'` makes the input required: calling with `{}` is refused.

written.changes:
Rewrote /Users/tonioloewald/tjs-lang/guides/examples/ajs/itunes-search.md (only that file). Metadata line unchanged; `<!-- TODO review -->` now sits directly after it, and the other four scattered TODO markers are gone. Removed the subtitle line ("Search Apple iTunes catalog").

Checked against the source:
- The error text 'map: items is not an array' is still exact. It comes from runtime.ts:6366, and I reproduced it on the current VM both with a literal object and by dropping responseType on the live call. The brief worried that v2 might have changed it; it hasn't.
- Fixed the responseType explanation. httpFetch parses JSON on its own only when Content-Type contains 'application/json' (runtime.ts:7281). Without the hint the body comes back as a string and the `map` fails.

Wording changes in the existing sections:
- "The gotcha" no longer says "if the request fails". httpFetch returns the body, not the status, and a rejected iTunes request (HTTP 400) still returns JSON, in the shape { errorMessage, queryParameters } with no `results`. I checked this with curl and through the VM.

New content:
- One sentence on why the parentheses in `(x) => ({ … })` matter.
- A bullet that the domain works only because the host allowlists it, pointing to the Weather API chapter instead of repeating it.
- A line on passing `resultCount` through.
- A third runnable ajs:inline example: a guarded search that checks `errorMessage` and uses `results ?? []`. Its default `entity = 'bogus'` makes it show the error path live. It returns { tracks: [], error: 'Invalid value(s) for key(s): [resultEntity]' }, and with entity: 'song' it returns tracks.
- The error message now has its own ```text fence.
questions: The guarded example's default `entity = 'bogus'` is there so the page shows the error path when it runs live, but a reader might copy it as a working search. Should it stay that way, or default to 'song' with the bad entity described in prose only?

`httpFetch` (the built-in client) drops the HTTP status, so an agent cannot tell a 400 from a 200 except by the body's shape. Is that intended? If not, it may deserve a card (e.g. a `{ status, body }` responseType); for now the chapter documents the current behaviour.

findings.where: Opening paragraph: "take a query, ask a catalog, and return a short, clean list"
findings.problem: The page never says what `httpFetch` is: a built-in, something the host provides, or a capability. It also never says what its argument object accepts besides `url` and `responseType`, or what it returns on success. A first-time reader meets it in the code with no introduction. "Ask a catalog" is vague, and the reader only learns from the code that it means the public iTunes Search API.
findings.fix: Add one sentence before the first example: "`httpFetch({ url, responseType })` is AJS's HTTP call. It works only when the host allows the domain, and it returns the parsed response body." Also name the iTunes Search API in the intro.

findings.where: "A raw iTunes track record has around thirty fields; this agent keeps three."
findings.problem: This claim is what motivates the whole page, but the page never shows it. There is no sample of the raw record and no sample of what the first agent returns. The reader can't see the trimming that the intro calls "most of the job".
findings.fix: Show a shortened raw `results[0]` (a handful of fields, then "…") next to the agent's output `{ tracks: [{ artist, track, album }, …] }`, so the before and after are visible.

findings.where: `function searchMusic({ query = 'Beatles', limit = 5 })` and "With `entity: 'song'` it returns the tracks."
findings.problem: The page never says how an agent receives its arguments: who calls it, and with what object. It also doesn't say whether the defaults are AJS-specific or plain JS destructuring defaults. "With `entity: 'song'`" assumes the reader knows how to pass that value, either in this inline example or from a host.
findings.fix: Add one line: "The host calls the agent with an arguments object; any field left out takes the default shown." If the inline runner lets you edit the arguments, say how.

findings.where: "Encode it, or `rock & roll` becomes a search for `rock`." vs. the gotcha example `'&entity=' + entity`
findings.problem: The page tells the reader to encode user text. Then the gotcha example takes `entity` (and every example takes `limit`) as an input and concatenates it into the URL without encoding. A careful reader will ask whether this is a mistake, or whether only some inputs need encoding.
findings.fix: Encode `entity` too (`encodeURIComponent(entity)`), or explain the rule: encode anything a caller supplies; `limit` is a number. Also consider `encodeURIComponent(String(limit))` for consistency.

findings.where: "The domain is allowed by the host. ... the page running this example put it on the run's fetch allowlist (see the Weather API example)."
findings.problem: The reader is never told what a "fetch allowlist" is, or how a host sets one. This book's audience includes developers embedding the VM, and for them this is the most important line on the page. It is a single sentence that sends them to another example. "The page running this example" also mixes up the doc site with the host, which is the concept the embedder actually needs.
findings.fix: Say in a sentence or two what the host does: it gives the run a fetch capability limited to named domains, so the agent cannot reach any other URL. Include or link the exact host-side option. Keep the pointer to Weather API for the full details.

findings.where: "`undefined.map(…)` fails with `map: items is not an array`. The message names the method's input (`items`), not your variable"
findings.problem: The reader wrote `response.results.map(...)`, an array method. Saying that `map` has an "input" called `items` suggests it is something other than the JS method, and the page never explains what. That leaves the reader unsure whether AJS `map` is JavaScript's `Array.prototype.map`.
findings.fix: Add a clause explaining it: "In AJS, `map` is implemented by the VM, and its error refers to the receiver as `items`." Or rephrase so the reader doesn't need that model: "the message doesn't say which `map` failed."

findings.where: "The failure ends the run unless you catch it."
findings.problem: The page doesn't show how to catch it in AJS (try/catch? something else?), and doesn't say what the host sees when the run ends: a thrown error, a returned error object, or something else. A reader who wants to catch rather than pre-check has nowhere to go.
findings.fix: Link the AJS error-handling example. Add one line on what the caller receives when the run fails (for example, "the run returns an error instead of a result").

findings.where: "`httpFetch` returns the response body, not the status."
findings.problem: This raises an obvious question the page never answers: how do I get the status, if I need it? It also doesn't say whether a 4xx or 5xx response is an error or just returns the body. That matters for knowing whether the `errorMessage` check is enough.
findings.fix: Add one sentence: what happens on a non-2xx status, and whether (and how) an agent can see the status code.

findings.where: Variation: `year: x.releaseDate.slice(0, 4)`
findings.problem: The gotcha section warns that calling a method on a missing field ends the run. Yet the variation calls `.slice` on `x.releaseDate` without a check, and the page doesn't comment on it. The reader is also never told the format of `releaseDate` (an ISO string such as `1959-08-17T07:00:00Z`), so it isn't clear why `slice(0, 4)` gives the year.
findings.fix: Show a sample `releaseDate` value. Either guard it (`x.releaseDate ? x.releaseDate.slice(0, 4) : null`), or say that iTunes always includes it for albums.

findings.where: "`resultCount` is part of the iTunes response, so the agent passes it through rather than counting the list itself."
findings.problem: The page doesn't explain why passing it through is better than `albums.length`: whether counting is costly in AJS, whether the two could differ, or whether this is just convenience. As written, it reads as a reason that isn't a reason.
findings.fix: Give the reason, or drop the sentence. If `albums.length` works equally well, say so.

findings.where: Gotcha example: `function searchMusic({ query = 'Beatles', entity = 'bogus', limit = 5 })`
findings.problem: The example reuses the name `searchMusic` but changes its shape: it adds `entity`, drops `album` from the output, and drops `&media=music`. None of these changes is mentioned. The default `entity = 'bogus'` is also a trap for anyone who copies the function as a template.
findings.fix: Give it its own name (for example, `searchMusicSafely`), keep the same output fields as the first example, and either make `'song'` the default with "pass `entity: 'bogus'` to see the error branch", or label the bogus default as a demonstration value.

findings.where: `if (response.errorMessage) { ... }` followed by `let results = response.results ?? []`
findings.problem: After the explicit error check, the `?? []` fallback looks redundant, and the page doesn't say why both are there: is there a third response shape? `??` also appears without comment, while AJS behaviour that differs from JS is pointed out elsewhere on the page.
findings.fix: Add a short comment, for example "belt and braces: a response with neither field still maps safely", or remove one of the two checks.

findings.where: Ordering: the first example, then "A variation", then "The gotcha"
findings.problem: The first two examples both contain the bug the gotcha describes (unguarded `response.results.map`), and nothing warns about it until the end of the page. A reader who copies the first example and stops reading gets the fragile version.
findings.fix: Add a one-line forward reference after the first example, for example "(this version trusts the response shape; see The gotcha)". Alternatively, move the gotcha before the variation.

findings.where: First bullet of "What to notice" and the code comment "iTunes serves JSON as `text/javascript`, so ask for JSON explicitly."
findings.problem: The bullet repeats the code comment almost word for word. It does add new information (that a missing hint gives you a string and the `map` fails), but that sentence is buried at the end.
findings.fix: Shorten the code comment, or lead the bullet with the consequence: "Without it, `response` is a string and `response.results` is undefined."

findings.where: The page as a whole, read by an embedder
findings.problem: The AJS book is partly for developers who embed the VM. This page shows only the agent side. It never shows a host running this agent with a fetch capability, so an embedder can't learn from it how the domain restriction or the return value reaches them.
findings.fix: Add a short host-side snippet or link: run the agent with fetch limited to `itunes.apple.com`, and show the result object the host gets back.

findings.where: The gotcha: "The failure ends the run unless you catch it."
findings.problem: Accurate, and I checked it (try/catch around the map catches it), but a reader who writes the obvious `catch (e) { return { error: e.message } }` gets `{}`, because in AJS the caught error is a string, not an Error object. I made exactly that mistake while checking the claim.
findings.fix: Add a clause such as: "In a `catch (err)`, `err` is the message string itself (`'map: items is not an array'`), not an object with `.message`." Or link the DOCS-AJS 'Raising and catching' section.
findings.evidence: In the scratch dir: tc.ajs with `catch (e) { return { caught: e.message } }` returned result `{}`. tc3.ajs with `return { caught: e }` returned `{ caught: 'map: items is not an array' }`.

findings.where: The gotcha: "When iTunes rejects a request, it still answers with JSON, just a different shape"
findings.problem: The real reason this catches people is that the response is HTTP 400 and httpFetch still returns the parsed body with no status attached. The opening sentence says the body is returned, not the status, but it never says the rejection is a 4xx. Saying so makes it concrete.
findings.fix: Say "answers with HTTP 400 and a JSON body of a different shape".
findings.evidence: `curl -s --compressed -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' 'https://itunes.apple.com/search?term=Beatles&entity=bogus'` gives 400. The body is `{"errorMessage":"Invalid value(s) for key(s): [resultEntity]","queryParameters":{...}}`. runtime.ts ~7270-7280 parses and returns the body with no res.ok check.

rejected: Finding 4, partly: I agree that `entity` must be encoded and now encode it. I did not encode `limit`, and the suggested `encodeURIComponent(String(limit))` does not work. AJS has no `String` (the run fails with 'Unknown function: String'), and `encodeURIComponent` refuses a number ('argument 1 must be a string'). Encoding `limit` also isn't needed: a destructuring default's value is its type, so a run with `{ limit: '5&x=y' }` is refused before the agent starts ('Input validation failed: args do not match expected schema'). I checked both behaviours, and the page now gives that as the reason.
questions: I didn't find out how a reader passes run arguments to an inline example on the doc site. site/entry.ts reads `options.args`, but I couldn't tell what UI sets it. The page says "pass `{ entity: 'bogus' }` as the run's arguments", the same wording as the Weather API page. If the runner has no argument editor, both pages should say to edit the default instead.

I revised /Users/tonioloewald/tjs-lang/guides/examples/ajs/itunes-search.md. The metadata comment and `<!-- TODO review -->` are unchanged.

**Changes:**
- **Intro:** names the iTunes Search API, says what `httpFetch` is (an atom, works only for domains the host allows, returns the parsed body), and says how arguments and defaults arrive.
- **Before and after:** shows part of a real 31-field record next to the trimmed `{ tracks }` output, then a forward pointer to the gotcha section.
- **"What to notice" bullets:**
  - The `responseType` bullet now leads with what goes wrong without it.
  - The encoding bullet now explains why `limit` needs no encoding.
  - The allowlist bullet now says what the host does and which three domains the doc site allows.
- **Album variation:** shows a sample `releaseDate`, guards `.slice` and explains why. It now counts with `albums.length` instead of `resultCount`.
- **Gotcha section:**
  - Says the rejection is an HTTP 400 that the built-in client never shows the agent, and that a host's own `fetch` capability can include the status.
  - Explains that the VM implements `map` itself, which is why its error says `items`.

I did not run the host snippet itself: it imports `tjs-lang/lang` and `tjs-lang/vm-ast`, while the test ran the same agent and arguments through the source-path `transpile` and `AgentVM`.

written.changes: Rewrote /Users/tonioloewald/tjs-lang/guides/examples/ajs/json-processing.md (only that file). Metadata line unchanged; `<!-- TODO review -->` is now the line right after it, and the four in-body TODO markers are gone. Removed the "Parse and stringify JSON" subtitle. Kept the round-trip example and the try/catch example, and quoted the real error text in the `'data: ' + data` note. Folded "The gotcha" (err is a string) into the parse-failure section. Added a new section, "When it is JSON but not the shape you expected", covering `filter(data, schema)` with a `Schema.object({ name: Schema.string, score: Schema.number })` example. It shows that fields the shape doesn't name (`token`) are dropped, and has a table of the verified errors for other inputs: missing field, wrong type, an array, and text that isn't JSON. It also says every named field is required (use `{ type: ['string','null'] }` for an optional one), that `filter` accepts an example in place of a schema, and that in the example form `0` means integer and `0.0` cannot express a float, so `Schema.number` is the way to accept any number. It ends with a short paragraph on why to filter untrusted model or API output.
questions: In AJS, `filter(data, { age: 0.0 })` still rejects 41.5 with 'age: Expected integer'. The source spelling `0.0` is lost before `filter` sees the example, which is not how TJS reads `0.0` (there it means a float). The chapter documents this and points readers to `Schema.number`. Is this intended, or should the AJS transpiler keep the float meaning of an example literal passed to `filter` (and `Schema.fromExample`)?

The text of a JSON.parse failure comes from the host engine (in Bun: "JSON Parse error: Expected '}'"), so it will read differently in another engine or in the browser. The chapter calls it 'the parser's message' and doesn't quote it. Is that acceptable, or should the VM give one message whatever the host?

findings.where: Table rows: `'{"name":"Ann"}'` -> `{ error: 'root: Missing score' }` vs `'{"name":"Ann","score":"high"}'` -> `{ error: 'score: Expected number' }`
findings.problem: The prefix means different things in the two rows: a missing field is reported against `root`, a wrong type against the field itself. Someone writing code to pick out the offending field from the message will be surprised, and the page never says what the prefix is (a path to the object that failed?).
findings.fix: Add one sentence explaining that the prefix is the path to the value that failed, so a missing key is reported against its parent object (`root`), while a wrong-typed key is reported against itself.

findings.where: "Every field `Schema.object` names is required. For a field that may be absent or null, give it a nullable type: `nick: { type: ['string', 'null'] }`."
findings.problem: Two jumps. (1) Up to here every field was written as `Schema.string` / `Schema.number`. Now a raw JSON-Schema object literal appears with no word on whether it can be mixed inside `Schema.object({...})`. (2) 'Absent or null': a nullable type says the value may be null. Readers who know JSON Schema expect that a nullable field still has to be present, which contradicts the sentence just before it ('every field is required'). Is an absent `nick` accepted or not?
findings.fix: Show the full shape, e.g. `Schema.object({ name: Schema.string, nick: { type: ['string','null'] } })`, and give one row each for an absent `nick` and for `"nick": null`, with the results.

findings.where: "Writing `0.0` does not help here, because by the time `filter` sees the example it is a plain number."
findings.problem: This answers a question this reader never had. Nothing on the page says `0.0` means 'float' anywhere else. The sentence only makes sense if you already know TJS's example-value rules, and to a first-time AJS reader it is noise that suggests a hidden rule they have missed.
findings.fix: Say it outright: 'In TJS signatures `0.0` means a float example. That does not carry over here, because `filter` receives the runtime value 0.' Or drop the sentence and keep only 'for any number, use `Schema.number`'.

findings.where: "`filter(data, schema)` checks the parsed value against a shape and returns a copy that holds only the fields the shape names."
findings.problem: The page never says what `filter` is: a global, an atom, a built-in? It is called bare while its partner is namespaced (`Schema.object`), so the reader cannot guess where it lives or whether `Schema.filter` is the real name. It also never says whether stripping unnamed fields reaches into nested objects and arrays or only the top level. That matters for the security claim in the closing paragraph.
findings.fix: Name what `filter` is (and its relation to `Schema`) in one clause. State whether extra fields are stripped at every depth, or add a nested example showing it.

findings.where: "Change `raw` to `'{oops'` and run it again: you get the parser's message instead of a result." and the table row `'nope'` -> "the parser's message"
findings.problem: The one error the reader is most likely to hit is the one the page never shows. Every other table row gives an exact string. 'The parser's message' leaves me unable to recognise it, or tell it apart from a filter failure, when it reaches my host code.
findings.fix: Show the actual output, e.g. `{ error: 'not JSON: <message>' }` with a representative message, or say outright that the text comes from the host engine and varies.

findings.where: "A failed `JSON.parse` is an error you can catch"
findings.problem: The page doesn't say what happens if I *don't* catch it: does the agent stop, return an error value to the host, keep going? For the embedder half of the audience that is the question that matters (what does `vm.run` hand back?). For agent writers it decides whether `try` is required or optional.
findings.fix: Add one sentence on the uncaught case: what the run returns to the host and whether later statements run. Link to the error-handling example.

findings.where: "In a `catch`, `err` is the error's **message**, a string. It is not an `Error` object, so `err.message` is `undefined`."
findings.problem: This is a real break from JavaScript, but it comes with no reason, and it appears after the example that relies on it (`'not JSON: ' + err`). A reader who is surprised by it is left wondering whether it is a bug or a design decision, and whether other error details (an op or code) can be read anywhere.
findings.fix: Move it to just before the first `try` example, and add a short reason (errors cross into the agent as plain strings, for safety). Say whether any other error field can be read.

findings.where: `catch (err) { return { error: 'not JSON: ' + err } }` followed later by "If the value does not fit, it fails with a message naming the field, and the same `catch` handles it"
findings.problem: The first catch labels *every* failure 'not JSON'. The next section then says the 'same `catch`' handles shape failures as well. A reader who merges the two examples ends up reporting 'not JSON' for valid JSON with the wrong shape. The page also never says that one `catch` cannot tell a parse error from a filter error.
findings.fix: Drop the 'not JSON: ' prefix in the first example, or say explicitly that one `try` catches both kinds and that the message text (the `field:` prefix) is how to tell them apart.

findings.where: "`JSON.parse` and `JSON.stringify` work as in JavaScript." / first example `jsonRoundTrip`
findings.problem: The first example shows no output, so the reader cannot check the claim that it works 'as in JavaScript'. The parameter form `({ data = { name: 'Alice', age: 30 } })` also goes unexplained: is `data` the agent's input from the host, and is the default what runs on the page? The second and third examples tell you to 'change `raw`', which implies an interactive editor the page never mentions.
findings.fix: State the result of the first example (as the third does: 'The result is ...'). Add one line saying an agent's inputs are destructured parameters, the defaults are what the live example runs with, and you can edit them and run again.

findings.where: "**Reading a missing field is safe.** Member access is null-safe: `parsed.address.city` is `undefined` when there is no `address`"
findings.problem: No example on the page shows this; `jsonRoundTrip` never reads a missing field. `readConfig` uses `config.user.roles ?? []`, but the reader is not told this relies on null-safety, so the connection is lost.
findings.fix: Add `let city = parsed.address.city` to the first example and include it in the return, or point to the `?? []` line in `readConfig` as the null-safe read in action.

findings.where: "`'data: ' + data` is an error in AJS (`'+' needs a string, number, boolean or null, not an object`)"
findings.problem: No motivation, and no 'when'. The reader cannot tell whether this fails at transpile time or at run time, or why AJS departs from JavaScript here. Without a reason it looks arbitrary, and the reader cannot generalise it (does template interpolation of an object fail too?).
findings.fix: Say whether it is a transpile-time or run-time error, give a one-clause reason (implicit object-to-string conversion is refused, so building text stays explicit and budgeted), and note that `${data}` in a template is refused the same way.

findings.where: "Filtering is worth doing on anything a model or a remote service gave you before your agent acts on it or returns it..." (final paragraph)
findings.problem: The reason for the whole third section comes last. While reading the `filter` section I had no reason to care about dropping `token`. For this book's audience, people running untrusted, LLM-written agents, that reason is the headline.
findings.fix: Move this paragraph, or a one-sentence version of it, to the top of 'When it is JSON but not the shape you expected', ahead of the mechanics.

findings.where: "The keywords a schema may use are listed under Schema in the AJS reference."
findings.problem: A pointer with no link. 'The AJS reference' is not a page name the reader can click or search for.
findings.fix: Make it a link to the Schema section of the AJS reference.

findings.where: `Schema.object({ name: Schema.string, score: Schema.number })`
findings.problem: `Schema.object` is called as a function while `Schema.string` and `Schema.number` are bare properties. The reader cannot tell whether `Schema.string()` would also work or is an error, and because they will copy this pattern, it matters.
findings.fix: Add a parenthetical: 'scalar types are values (`Schema.string`), containers are calls (`Schema.object({...})`, `Schema.array(...)`)'.

findings.where: "`filter` also accepts an **example** in place of a schema: `filter(data, { name: '', age: 0 })`."
findings.problem: The page leaves it unclear when to choose an example over a schema. It mostly lists the example form's pitfall (integer-only numbers), and the reader is left unsure whether the example form also strips extra fields and also requires every field.
findings.fix: Add one line: 'The example form strips and requires fields exactly as a schema does; use it for quick shapes with strings, booleans and integers.'

findings.where: "JSON is the agent's native format: APIs return it, models are asked to produce it, and an agent's result is JSON data."
findings.problem: 'An agent's result is JSON data' reads as a hard rule, but the page never says what happens if an agent returns something else (a Date? a function?). The embedder will want to know.
findings.fix: Either soften it to a motivation, or add a short clause on what a non-JSON return does, with a link.

findings.where: Line 2: `<!-- TODO review -->`
findings.problem: A leftover working note in the source. It doesn't render, but it shows the page is unreviewed.
findings.fix: Remove it once the page has had its edit pass.

findings.where: table row `'nope'` -> "the parser's message" and "you get the parser's message instead of a result"
findings.problem: Correct as written, but the message text comes from the host's JSON.parse, so it differs between engines. Under Bun it is `JSON Parse error: Unexpected identifier "nope"` (and `not JSON: JSON Parse error: Expected '}'` for '{oops'). On the doc site in Chrome it will read something like `Unexpected token 'o'...`. A reader comparing against a quoted message could be confused, so the prose is right to stay vague.
findings.fix: Optional: add a few words such as "(the wording depends on the JavaScript engine)" so nobody treats the text as stable or matches on it.

findings.where:
"`'data: ' +
  JSON.stringify(data)` says what you mean."
findings.problem: An inline code span is split across a line break. It renders, but the source is awkward to read and edit, and it puts a `+` at the end of a wrapped line, close to the column-one `+` hazard named in the house style.
findings.fix: Rewrap the line so the code span `'data: ' + JSON.stringify(data)` sits whole on one line.

rejected: Finding 17 (remove the `<!-- TODO review -->` line): the brief says that line must stay so the owner can find every chapter during his edit pass. Kept.
questions: Link anchors: I linked [Schema](/DOCS-AJS/#schema) on the assumption that the doc site slugs headings in lowercase. For Input/Output Contract I used a plain /DOCS-AJS/ link, because I could not confirm how tosijs-ui slugs a heading with a '/' in it. Worth a check on preview:site.
revised.summary:
I revised /Users/tonioloewald/tjs-lang/guides/examples/ajs/json-processing.md and applied every finding except removing the TODO line. I ran all four ajs:inline fences, plus every documented alternative input, through transpile and AgentVM (vm/ast). Every result matches the prose. Scripts are in the scratchpad at docs-swarm/json-processing/.

Changes:
- **First example:** it now reads a missing field (`parsed.address.city ?? 'unknown'`) and states its result. The page also explains that inputs are destructured parameters, that the defaults are what the example runs with, and that you can edit them and run again.
- **`'+'` and templates on objects:** the page now says these fail at run time, not at transpile time, and that the error is catchable. The template form gets the same error (verified). It gives the reason: the conversion has no size bound and the VM only does work it can charge for.
- **`err` is a string:** this now sits before the first try example, with the reason (errors reach the agent only as plain text) and the fact that the message is all there is to read.
- **First catch:** I dropped the 'not JSON: ' prefix. The parse-error text is described as engine-dependent (Bun's wording is quoted as an example).
- **Uncaught parse error:** a new paragraph says it ends the run and that vm.run returns the error as a value, with fuel spent. It links to /ajs-error-handling/.
- **Security reason:** this moved to the top of the shape section.
- **`filter`:** the page names it as a global builtin. It states that stripping applies at every depth (verified: nested objects and array elements are stripped).
- **Error prefix:** explained as the path to the value that failed, with deeper paths shown (`address: Missing city`, `tags.0.id: Expected number`).
- **One `try`, two kinds of error:** the page says one catch gets both parse and shape errors, and how to tell them apart.
- **`Schema.string` vs `Schema.string()`:** scalars are values and containers are calls. `Schema.string()` ends the run with 'not callable' (verified).
- **Optional fields:** a new runnable example and table. A nullable field may be absent or null (verified, and it matches the DOCS-AJS note 'a nullable field is optional').
- **Example form:** it strips and requires fields like a schema, and the 0.0 sentence is rewritten so it no longer assumes TJS knowledge. Verified that `{ age: 0.0 }` still demands an integer.
- **Smaller fixes:** the Schema keyword pointer is now a link, the claim about agent results is softened to motivation with a pointer to the I/O contract, and the split code span is rewrapped. No prose line starts with '+'.

As the rules require, I edited only this file, ran no build or format, and made no commit.

written.changes: Rewrote /Users/tonioloewald/tjs-lang/guides/examples/ajs/llm-api-data.md. Removed the subtitle line. The file now has one `<!-- TODO review -->`, on the line right after the unchanged metadata comment, and the section-level markers are gone. In the main example, a track with no `collectionName` now reads "(single)"; before, it printed "(undefined)" in the prompt, which I saw on a live iTunes run. I replaced the "much cleaner!" comment with a plain one. "What to notice" now explains what `Schema.response(name, example)` produces (a strict OpenAI-style response_format). It also says that `llmPredict` returns a string even when a format is set, and that a non-JSON reply makes `JSON.parse` end the run with an error. I added a "Running it locally" section. It reuses the llm capability from LLM Chat and adds `context: { allowedFetchDomains: ['itunes.apple.com'] }`, because without it the built-in client refuses with "Fetch blocked: no allowedFetchDomains configured" (verified). It also sets a quota, and the section gives the measured fuel (about 123). The variation now says why it searches the song alone, and notes that the `includes` filter is case-sensitive and literal. The gotcha is reframed as "what happens if you forget responseType": the body arrives as a string, `.results` is undefined, and the model gets an empty list. It shows the empty prompt the model actually receives and gives a guard snippet to put after `let results`.
questions: How I verified: each example was transpiled and run on the AST VM against live iTunes, with a stub LLM in place of a real model. The stub stood in for: the main `ajs:inline` agent, the variation, the agent without `responseType` (to reproduce the gotcha), and the guarded version. The host snippet was checked through the same harness, with the same options. No real model was called, so the quality of a real model's covers answer is unverified.

The variation and the gotcha fix are `javascript` fences, not `ajs`, because both need an LLM and cannot run on the site. Should they become `ajs:inline` like the main example (the site would print its 'needs an LLM' message), so readers can see they are AJS?

findings.where: "**Two capabilities.** The network (limited to the domains the host allows) and `llm`." vs the run snippet `capabilities: { llm }, ... context: { allowedFetchDomains: ['itunes.apple.com'] }`
findings.problem: The prose says the agent gets two capabilities, but the host code passes only one (`llm`). The network appears as a `context` option, which is a different mechanism and is never explained. A reader can't tell whether the network counts as a capability, what `context` is, or how `fetch` as a capability differs from the allowlist.
findings.fix: Say plainly that `httpFetch` uses a built-in client gated by `context.allowedFetchDomains`, unless the host injects its own `fetch` capability. Then reword the bullet so it matches the snippet, e.g. "Two powers: the network (the built-in client, limited to allowedFetchDomains) and the `llm` capability."

findings.where: `capabilities: { llm }, // the llm object from LLM Chat` and "Use the `llm` capability from [LLM Chat](/llm-chat/)"
findings.problem: The one snippet you need to run the page uses an undefined variable. A reader who lands here can't run it without leaving the page, and isn't even told what shape `llm` has (an object with `predict`? an async function?).
findings.fix: Inline a minimal `llm` object (e.g. `const llm = { predict: async (prompt, options) => ... }` against an OpenAI-compatible endpoint), or at least state its shape in one line before linking out.

findings.where: `fuel: 1000,` ... "The run uses a little over 120 units of fuel: 100 for the model call, 5 for the fetch"; also "cheap, deterministic, and metered"
findings.problem: 'Fuel' and 'metered' are never defined on the page. The reader doesn't learn that fuel is the VM's work budget, what happens when it runs out, why 1000 was chosen when the run needs about 120, or where the '120' comes from (no field on `run` is shown).
findings.fix: Add one sentence defining fuel (the VM's budget for work; the run stops when it is used up) and show how to read the amount used from `run` (e.g. `run.fuelUsed`, or whatever the real field is). Also say why the budget leaves headroom.

findings.where: `quotas: { llmPredict: 1 },`
findings.problem: The option is never mentioned in the prose. Since fuel already caps the model call at 100 units, a reader can't see why a separate cap on the number of calls is needed.
findings.fix: Add a sentence: fuel counts VM work and can't express 'at most N model calls', so `quotas` caps calls per atom. Here it guarantees exactly one paid model call.

findings.where: `let response = httpFetch({ url, responseType: 'json' })`, `Schema.response(...)`, `llmPredict({ prompt, options: { responseFormat: schema } })`
findings.problem: The page uses `httpFetch`, `llmPredict` and `Schema` with no imports and no word on where they come from. A newcomer can't tell whether they are globals, atoms or host functions, or why they take one object argument instead of positional arguments.
findings.fix: After the first code block, add a short line: these are AJS atoms the VM provides, called with named inputs in a single object, and no import is needed.

findings.where: "and `JSON.parse` turns the reply into an object the host can use without reading prose."
findings.problem: In the example it is the agent that parses and uses the object (`parsed.covers`), not the host. Saying 'the host' muddles who does what, on a page that is all about the line between agent and host.
findings.fix: Change it to "an object the agent (and whoever receives its result) can use without reading prose."

findings.where: "run it locally with the host below" and "the built-in client refuses every request"
findings.problem: 'Host' and 'built-in client' are used as known terms but never defined. A reader new to the AJS model doesn't know that the host is the JavaScript program embedding the VM, or which client is 'built-in'.
findings.fix: Define each in place: "the host (the JavaScript program that runs the VM, shown below)" and "the VM's built-in fetch client".

findings.where: The variation and the gotcha guard are fenced as ```javascript; the main agent is fenced as ```ajs:inline
findings.problem: `findCoversCheaply` and the `if (results.length == 0)` guard are AJS agent code, but they are labelled as the same language as the host snippet. A reader may think they are host-side JavaScript, or that they run unchanged as plain JS (they call `httpFetch`/`llmPredict`, which only exist inside the VM).
findings.fix: Fence both as `ajs` (or ajs:inline if it should be live), so agent code and host code are visibly different.

findings.where: "Reading `.results` on a string gives `undefined` (AJS member access is null-safe)"
findings.problem: The reason given doesn't fit the claim. Null-safe access is about null/undefined receivers, but here the receiver is a string, and reading a missing property on a string is `undefined` in plain JS too. The reader is left wondering what null-safety has to do with it.
findings.fix: Say "a string has no `.results` property, so it reads as `undefined`". Drop the null-safe aside, or keep it only for the case where `response` itself is null.

findings.where: "Put that guard right after `let results = ...` and an empty or misread response returns honestly, without a model call."
findings.problem: The page's last section tells the reader the main example is missing a guard it needs, so the 'shape of a real agent' at the top has a known hole that is only admitted at the end. A reader who copies the first block and stops reading ships the bug. (The variation already has an equivalent check.)
findings.fix: Put the guard in the main example and turn the gotcha section into an explanation of why the guard is there (what happens without `responseType`, and without the check).

findings.where: Variation: `let answer = llmPredict({ prompt })` / `return { song, candidates: others.length, answer }` vs the early return `{ song, covers: [], note: ... }`
findings.problem: The variation quietly drops the structured-output lesson the page just taught: no schema, the reply stays a raw string, and the two branches return different shapes (`covers` vs `candidates` + `answer`). The reader can't tell whether this was a deliberate simplification or a regression.
findings.fix: Either keep `responseFormat` + `JSON.parse` so both branches return `{ song, covers }`, or say outright that the schema is left out for brevity and the return shapes differ.

findings.where: "The filter alone answers the easy cases." ... "it removes \"The Beatles\" but keeps \"Paul McCartney\", and a search for \"Yesterday\" also returns unrelated songs"
findings.problem: The variation is framed as a cost-saving win, but the next sentences show the filter is case-sensitive and keeps false candidates, so the model is asked almost every time. What it saves in practice is unclear.
findings.fix: State the realistic saving (it skips the call only when every result is by the original artist), or choose an example where the pre-check often skips the call.

findings.where: The prompt and URL construction: `'Search results for "' + song + '" by ' + artist + ':\n\n' + trackList + ...` (and the `tracks` map)
findings.problem: Heavy `+` concatenation spread over many lines is hard to read, and it raises an unspoken question: why not template literals? A reader may infer that AJS lacks them.
findings.fix: Use template literals if AJS supports them on strings. If it doesn't, or if the concatenation is deliberate, add a one-line note saying why.

findings.where: "If the model ignores the format and the reply is not JSON, `JSON.parse` fails and the run ends with that error"
findings.problem: The page doesn't cover the case where the reply is valid JSON but has no `covers` key. Then `parsed.covers` is `undefined` and the agent returns a half-answer, which is exactly what this sentence says can't happen.
findings.fix: Soften the claim ("if the reply is not JSON..."), or add a check that `parsed.covers` is an array before returning.

findings.where: Line 2: `<!-- TODO review -->`
findings.problem: A working note left in a published page. It isn't rendered, but it shows up for anyone reading the source and suggests the page hasn't been reviewed.
findings.fix: Remove it once the page has been reviewed, or track it on the board instead.

findings.where: **Two capabilities.** The network (limited to the domains the host allows) and `llm`.
findings.problem: The run snippet injects only one capability (`capabilities: { llm }`). The network is not a capability here. It is the VM's built-in fetch client, enabled by the `context.allowedFetchDomains` policy (runtime.ts:7170-7180; a host `fetch` capability is the alternative). A reader who checks the snippet against this bullet sees one capability where the bullet promises two.
findings.fix: Reword the bullet as 'Two grants: the `llm` capability, and network access limited to the domains in `allowedFetchDomains` (or a `fetch` capability of the host's own). The agent cannot reach anything else.'
findings.evidence: Snippet line 90: `capabilities: { llm }`; line 91: `context: { allowedFetchDomains: ['itunes.apple.com'] }`. runtime.ts:7178 reads ctx.context?.allowedFetchDomains and only uses ctx.capabilities.fetch if the host supplied one.

findings.where: A variation: 'The filter alone answers the easy cases.'
findings.problem: For the default input the early return never fires. A search for 'Yesterday' alone returned 22 non-Beatles tracks (Boyz II Men, Leona Lewis, Toni Braxton...), so the model was still asked and the run used about 123 fuel, the same as the main example. Popular titles will almost never leave zero results, so 'the easy cases' oversells the saving.
findings.fix: Say when the guard actually helps, for example 'When nobody else recorded the title, the filter answers on its own and the model is never asked', and keep the existing note that a common title also brings back unrelated songs.
findings.evidence: bun run.ts cheap.ajs → RESULT {"song":"Yesterday","candidates":22,...} FUEL 122.7

findings.where: A variation: `let answer = llmPredict({ prompt })` / `return { song, candidates: others.length, answer }`
findings.problem: Unlike the main example, the variation returns the model's free-text reply as an unparsed string. The page does not say so, and it undercuts the page's own point that 'the model sees text, the program gets data'.
findings.fix: Add one sentence saying the variation returns the model's prose to keep it short, and that it would take the same `Schema.response` plus `JSON.parse` to get data back. Or give it the same responseFormat.

rejected: Finding 15 (remove `<!-- TODO review -->`): rejected. The ground rules require that line right after the metadata, so the owner can find every chapter for his edit pass. It stays until his review.
revised.summary:
I revised /Users/tonioloewald/tjs-lang/guides/examples/ajs/llm-api-data.md and applied every finding except the one asking to remove the TODO line (rejected above). The review had a few duplicates: the capabilities/grants finding appeared twice, and so did the two about the variation. I checked their evidence against runtime.ts and against real runs.

What changed:
- **The guard now lives in the main example.** The `results.length == 0` check sits in the main agent, so the snippet at the top is safe to copy. The gotcha section now explains why the check is there. Its reason is corrected to "a string has no `.results` property"; the null-safe aside is gone.
- **Checking the model's reply.** Added an `Array.isArray(parsed.covers)` check, and softened the claim about replies that are not JSON.
- **Template literals.** All string building now uses template literals; AJS supports them.
- **Where the built-in names come from.** Added a short line after the first block: `httpFetch`, `llmPredict` and `Schema` are built in, and atoms take named inputs in one object.
- **Wording fixes.** "Host" and "built-in fetch client" are now defined where they first appear. The JSON.parse sentence now says "the agent (and whoever receives its result)" instead of "the host".
- **Two grants.** The bullet now says: the `llm` capability, plus network access limited to `allowedFetchDomains`. The running section explains that the network is the VM's built-in client gated by `context.allowedFetchDomains`, not a capability, unless the host injects its own `fetch` (runtime.ts ~7178).
- **Runnable host.** The host snippet now defines a minimal OpenAI-compatible `llm` object inline, so the page runs without leaving it. The `predict` shape is stated before the code.

Host atoms default to 'io', so they are counted. Then a test run with no capabilities. The section says plainly what the walk cannot do: it over-reports (a data literal like `{ op: 'storeSet' }` counts as a call) and it cannot see into `runCode`, so the real control is the capabilities you grant. findings.where: Code comment "// Strip Markdown fences, and undo newlines the model escaped twice" vs the final gotcha "The unescape is a trade-off... If your model's structured output is clean, delete those two lines."
findings.problem: The risk of the `\\n`/`\\t` replacements (they corrupt `\n` inside string literals of the generated code) is explained about 100 lines below the code it applies to, so a reader copying the agent misses it.
findings.fix: Put a short warning in the code comment ("also rewrites \n inside string literals; delete these two lines if your model's output is clean"), and keep the gotcha as the longer explanation.

findings.where: `let result = JSON.parse(response)` / `let code = result.code`
findings.problem: Nothing says what happens if the model returns malformed JSON or omits `code`. A reader running untrusted model output will want to know whether this throws, returns an error, or produces `undefined`.
findings.fix: Add one line to "What to notice" on how a parse failure surfaces in the run result, or guard it in the agent.

findings.where: `Schema.response('generated_code', { code: '', description: '' })`
findings.problem: The first argument (`'generated_code'`) is not explained: is it a schema name the model sees, or an id?
findings.fix: Add a brief comment: `// a name for the response format; the object is the shape by example`.

findings.where: "Types by example" bullet: "`n = 10` would make it optional, with a default."
findings.problem: The agent itself uses this very form (`{ task = 'Calculate the factorial of n' }`), but the page does not point to it, so a good concrete example goes unused.
findings.fix: Add: "This agent's own `task` input uses `=`, so it can be called with no arguments."

findings.where: "run it locally with the host from [LLM Chat](/llm-chat/)"
findings.problem: "The host" is undefined for a first-time reader. The reader cannot tell whether it means a server, a script, or the embedding app.
findings.fix: Say "with the host script (the JavaScript that creates the VM and passes it an LLM capability) shown in LLM Chat".

findings.where: For the factorial task this prints `io atoms: []` and `{ result: 120 }`. A program that calls `httpFetch` lists it, and the capability-free run fails with `Fetch blocked: no allowedFetchDomains configured`.
findings.problem: The snippet always runs with args `{ n: 5 }`. A generated program that calls httpFetch will normally declare different inputs (e.g. `url`), so the test run fails first with `Input validation failed: args do not match expected schema`, not with the Fetch-blocked message. The Fetch-blocked message only appears when the args match the program's inputs. The next paragraph mentions inputSchema, but only after the claim has been made.
findings.fix: Put the inputSchema paragraph before the claim, or say 'given args matching its inputs, the capability-free run fails with ...'. The snippet could also build its args from `ast.inputSchema` rather than hardcoding `{ n: 5 }`.
findings.evidence: Generated `function f({ url: "https://x.com" }) { let r = httpFetch({ url }) ... }`, ran with `{ n: 5 }` → `Input validation failed: args do not match expected schema`; ran with `{ url: 'https://example.com' }` → `Fetch blocked: no allowedFetchDomains configured. Set ctx.context.allowedFetchDomains or provide a custom fetch capability.` (src/vm/runtime.ts:7092, src/vm/vm.ts:487)

findings.where: Run it with the least you can grant. Capabilities are the real control: an atom whose capability you did not pass fails, whatever the walk said.
findings.problem: httpFetch does not fail only because no `fetch` capability was passed: its default path is blocked by an empty allowedFetchDomains allowlist (the error suggests setting allowedFetchDomains OR passing a fetch capability). The claim is right in effect but names a slightly different mechanism.
findings.fix: Optionally add: 'httpFetch with no fetch capability is refused unless the run allowlists domains (allowedFetchDomains)'.
findings.evidence: Fetch blocked: no allowedFetchDomains configured. Set ctx.context.allowedFetchDomains or provide a custom fetch capability.

findings.where: The transpiler names each one as it refuses it (`AJS has no 'for' loops. Use 'while' with a counter`).
findings.problem: The real message uses backticks, not single quotes, and starts with 'Unsupported statement type: ForStatement.' The ajs-llm-prompt table quotes it exactly; this chapter paraphrases while presenting it as a quote.
findings.fix: Quote it exactly, e.g. ``Unsupported statement type: ForStatement. AJS has no `for` loops. Use `while` with a counter``, or drop the code formatting so it reads as a paraphrase.
findings.evidence: src/lang/emitters/ast.ts:597; running the check snippet on a for-loop program printed `Rejected: Unsupported statement type: ForStatement. AJS has no `for` loops. Use `while` with a counter:`

questions: Should the agent's prompt name the input explicitly (e.g. 'take one input named n')? The default task already says 'of n', but naming it in the prompt would make the host's input check fail less often.

The section defines the `effects` tag (`'pure'`/`'io'`) and host atoms (`new AgentVM(customAtoms)`), says what the walk is for (it tells a reviewer which capabilities the program wants), and notes the `httpFetch`/allowedFetchDomains behaviour. written.changes:
Rewrote /Users/tonioloewald/tjs-lang/guides/examples/ajs/llm-code-solver.md (the only file touched). The metadata line is unchanged. The subtitle line is gone, a single `<!-- TODO review -->` now sits on line 2, and the four inline TODO markers are cleared.

The agent example:
- The inline system text now allows `for (const x of list)` and `while`, and forbids only the C-style `for (;;)`. It matches the corrected ajs-llm-prompt.md that is in the working tree.
- Fence stripping is now one regex instead of two.
- The escape fix (`\n` → newline) now runs only on one-line replies. Before, it ran on every reply and broke any generated string literal such as `'a\nb'`.
- `runCode` is wrapped in try/catch, and the catch returns `error: err`. In AJS the catch receives a string, so `err.message` would be undefined.
- The result now returns the whole `output` instead of `output.result`, which was undefined whenever the model returned another key.
- A reply with no `solve` function returns `error` plus the raw reply.

New sections:
- **Expected result:** the output object the default problem produces.
- **Passing data in:** a `runCode` call with `args`. It shows the fresh scope: the generated code cannot see the caller's variables. This fence is plain javascript, because the doc site has no `code` capability and a live fence would fail there.
- **Running it locally:** the full host, with imports, the `code` capability, `{ atoms: vm.atoms }`, and an `llmPredict` quota of 1. It explains the exact "capability missing" error and the 8KB generated-source cap; `maxSourceBytes` can only lower that cap.
- **The prompt:** points to the maintained prompt page.
- **The gotchas:**
  - A transpile error is catchable, and the message is meant to be sent back to the model.
  - Running out of fuel ends the whole run and cannot be caught; it is not a separate budget for the generated code.
  - `runCode` nests at most 10 deep, and the page quotes the error.
  - Running the program makes the arithmetic right, not the program, so return the code with the output.
  - `transpileCode` and the LLM Code Generator page cover keeping a program instead of running it.

The old gotcha "the prompt forbids for loops" is gone now that the prompt is fixed.

Not done: no atom-reference or capabilities chapter exists yet to link to. Those links need adding once those chapters land.

Problem found in another file, not edited: DOCS-AJS.md around line 279, in "What's Allowed", shows `catch (e) { return { error: e.message } }`. In AJS that returns undefined, because `e` is the message string. The error-handling chapter says so correctly.
questions: DOCS-AJS.md shows `catch (e) { return { error: e.message } }` in "What's Allowed". In AJS that returns undefined, because `e` is a string. Should someone fix it there, and should AJS give the caught value a `.message` so JavaScript habits work?

The doc site has no `code` capability, so no runCode example can run live in the page. Should site/entry.ts grant a `code` capability (transpile with the site's atoms) so the args example could be a live ajs fence?
Should this page link to the new atom-reference and capabilities chapters once they exist? Their slugs are not known yet.

findings.where: "under the same fuel budget and with the same capabilities" (intro) and later "calls atoms through the same capabilities", "live-heap ceiling and call quotas"
findings.problem: The page's central safety argument rests on fuel, capabilities, atoms, the live-heap ceiling and call quotas, and it defines none of them or links to where they are defined. A first-time reader can't judge the claim "It cannot do anything the agent could not already do" without knowing what bounds the agent in the first place.
findings.fix: Add one sentence per term on first use, or link once to the AJS guide's sections on fuel, capabilities, atoms and quotas (for example: "fuel: the VM's work budget; capabilities: the IO functions the host injects").

findings.where: "**The fence has four backticks** because the code contains three: it strips Markdown fences from the model's reply."
findings.problem: On the rendered page the reader never sees the fence, so this bullet explains something invisible to them. It is a note to whoever maintains the source, and it takes the top spot in "What to notice".
findings.fix: Remove it, or turn it into an HTML comment in the source. Lead the section with the sandboxing or runCode bullet.

findings.where: `let response = llmPredict({ prompt })` followed by `response.replace(...)`
findings.problem: The page never says what llmPredict returns. The code treats it as a plain string. A reader who knows OpenAI-style APIs will expect a message object ({ role, content }) and won't know whether `.replace` works here.
findings.fix: Add a comment, for example `// llmPredict returns the reply text as a string`, or link to the llmPredict atom's documentation.

findings.where: Running it locally snippet: `capabilities: { llm, code }` and `transpile(agentSource, ...)`
findings.problem: Neither `llm` nor `agentSource` is defined. The snippet is only half a host: the reader has to go to the LLM Chat page and merge two snippets in their head. "the agent above" in a comment does not say how the agent's source gets into a variable.
findings.fix: Make the snippet self-contained: build `llm` in a line or two (or `import { llm } from './llm-host'` with a pointer to the page that defines it), and show `const agentSource = \`function solveWithCode(...) {...}\`` or a read from a file.

findings.where: "Size the budget for the model call (100 fuel) plus the work you expect the generated program to do." vs `fuel: 2000` in the host snippet
findings.problem: The 100-fuel cost of a model call first appears in the gotchas, after the snippet that picks 2000. Nothing says where 2000 comes from or what a Fibonacci loop costs, so the reader can't size a budget themselves.
findings.fix: State the llmPredict cost next to the snippet, and give a rough figure for the generated program's share (for example "~100 for the call, plus a few fuel per loop iteration").

findings.where: `quotas: { llmPredict: 1 }`
findings.problem: Quotas appear in the snippet without explanation. A reader won't know they cap calls per run, or that the cap also binds code generated through runCode, which is the interesting part here.
findings.fix: Add a sentence: "quotas caps how many times an atom may run in this run; generated code counts against the same cap, so it cannot call the model again."

findings.where: "The `maxSourceBytes` run option can lower that cap for generated code, never raise it."
findings.problem: The option is named but not shown, and the snippet above doesn't use it. Readers won't know whether it goes in vm.run's options or in transpile's.
findings.fix: Show it in context, for example `vm.run(ast, args, { ..., maxSourceBytes: 4096 })`.

findings.where: "Transpiling runs on the host, synchronously, before fuel can stop it. So the VM refuses generated source over 8KB..."
findings.problem: This jumps a step: the reader isn't told why synchronous pre-fuel transpiling is dangerous (a large or hostile source can stall the host process, and parse cost is unbudgeted). The link between "fuel can't stop it" and "cap the size" is left implicit.
findings.fix: Add the missing link: "so a huge or pathological source could tie up your process before any budget applies; the VM therefore refuses..."

findings.where: "`args` ... holds them by reference, the way a function holds its arguments, and sees nothing else"
findings.problem: "By reference" raises a question the page doesn't answer: can the generated program mutate the agent's objects? For readers focused on sandboxing, that matters. It also sits awkwardly with the isolation story.
findings.fix: Say plainly whether mutations made by the generated code are visible to the agent afterwards. If "by reference" only means "not copied", say so.

findings.where: Prompt rule "- Loops: for (const x of list) and while. NO for (let i = 0; i < n; i++)"
findings.problem: A reader new to AJS will find C-style for loops being banned surprising, and the page only explains it near the end (the ForStatement transpile error). Without the reason, the rule reads as arbitrary prompt superstition.
findings.fix: Add a comment at the rule or in What to notice: "AJS has no C-style for loop; the transpiler rejects it (see gotchas)."

findings.where: "`runCode` and its sibling `transpileCode` need the `code` capability" (Running it locally)
findings.problem: transpileCode is named here before the page says what it is; that only comes in the last gotcha. The reader stops to wonder what the sibling does.
findings.fix: Add a short gloss here ("transpileCode, which returns the AST without running it"), or don't mention it until the last gotcha.

findings.where: "The agent needs a model, so on this site it prints a message instead of running." and "This example is not live on the page, because the site provides no `code` capability"
findings.problem: "this site" is ambiguous, and the reader isn't told what the printed message says or whether the first example is live at all. The two notes give different reasons (no model vs no code capability) for similar behaviour, so the reader can't predict what they'll see.
findings.fix: Say exactly what the reader will see on the page, for example "Running it here prints: <message>", and give both reasons in one place: no model, and no code capability.

findings.where: "not the agent's variables, not its local helpers, not its arguments"
findings.problem: "local helpers" is undefined. A reader can't tell whether AJS agents can declare helper functions, or what this refers to.
findings.fix: Use a concrete term (for example "functions declared in the agent"), or drop it.

findings.where: "`replace`, `includes` and `match` run on the VM's own regex engine and are charged as fuel like everything else, so no pattern can hang the run."
findings.problem: The idea of the VM having its own regex engine, as opposed to JavaScript's, comes with no context, and the reason it matters (catastrophic backtracking or ReDoS) is only implied. A reader may also wonder whether every JavaScript regex feature works.
findings.fix: Add a clause: "not the host's RegExp, so patterns that backtrack catastrophically in JavaScript just spend fuel". Also mention the limits (no backreferences or lookaround) or link to them.

findings.where: `let found = code.match(/function\s+solve\s*\([^)]*\)\s*\{[\s\S]*\}/)` with comment "Keep only the function, dropping any explanation around it"
findings.problem: The greedy `[\s\S]*\}` runs to the last closing brace in the reply. A trailing explanation that contains braces is kept, so the comment overstates what the line does.
findings.fix: Qualify the comment ("up to the last closing brace") or mention the limitation in What to notice.

findings.where: "With a model that answers the default problem with a working loop, the result is:" followed by a block containing `...`
findings.problem: The block is labelled as the result, but it is elided pseudo-output, and the `javascript` label invites the reader to treat it as code.
findings.fix: Say it is abbreviated ("the result looks like this, with the code shortened").

findings.where: "Running out of fuel ends the whole run... the agent's `catch` never runs" vs earlier "Generated code fails like any code ... an error the agent can catch"
findings.problem: The reader learns piecemeal which failures are catchable (transpile errors, missing capability) and which aren't (fuel), across three sections.
findings.fix: Gather them into one short list in the gotchas: catchable (transpile failure, missing capability, generated runtime errors) and not catchable (out of fuel, ...).

findings.where: Running it locally / What to notice (runCode, `code` capability)
findings.problem: The brief asks for runCode and the `code` capability to be linked to the new atom reference and capabilities chapters. Both chapters now exist (guides/ajs-atoms.md has a runCode row and section; guides/ajs-capabilities.md has a `### code` section), but this page links to neither.
findings.fix: Link `runCode`/`transpileCode` to [the atom reference](/ajs-atoms/) and the `code` capability to [Capabilities](/ajs-capabilities/#code), for example in the first sentence of 'Running it locally'.

findings.where: "The escape fix runs only on one-line replies. Turning every `\n` into a newline would also break a generated string literal such as `'a\nb'`"
findings.problem: The one-line path still breaks string literals. A one-line reply that contains an escaped literal (`\\n` inside a string) has its `\n` turned into a real newline, leaving a backslash before it, which reads as a line continuation. As written, the text suggests only multi-line replies are at risk.
findings.fix: Say it is a heuristic: it repairs a fully escaped reply, but a string literal inside that reply can still be corrupted. That is acceptable here because a reply with real newlines is never touched.

findings.where: "Cleanup is ordinary string work. `replace`, `includes` and `match` run on the VM's own regex engine"
findings.problem: `includes` takes no regex. Only `replace` and `match` (here) go through the VM regex engine.
findings.fix: "`replace` and `match` run on the VM's own regex engine, and every string method is charged as fuel..."

findings.where: "with the host below. It returns `{ output: { result: 42 } }`, and the code it runs could not have read `apiKey`"
findings.problem: This prose line is much longer than the rest of the page (it looks like an edit left it unwrapped). Separately, the claim is true but does not say what happens: a reference to `apiKey` in the generated code reads as undefined. It does not raise an error.
findings.evidence: Generated `return { k: apiKey }` with `args: {}` returned `{"output":{}}` and no error.
findings.fix: Rewrap the paragraph. Optionally add: "a reference to `apiKey` there is simply undefined".

findings.where: Gotchas: "Running out of fuel ends the whole run... Size the budget for the model call (100 fuel)"
findings.problem: Verified correct (llmPredict cost 100; an infinite-loop program ended the run with `Out of Fuel` and the catch did not run). Worth noting for cross-chapter consistency: guides/ajs-atoms.md line 75 says runCode running generated code that takes longer than a second fails with a timeout. In practice, a generated infinite loop with fuel 1e7 ran 36 s and ended with Out of Fuel, not a timeout. If a reader trusts the atoms page, they will expect a 1 s timeout here.
findings.evidence: run2.ts `bigfuel`: 35894 ms, result `{"$error":true,"message":"Out of Fuel","op":"catch"}`.
findings.fix: No change needed on this page. Flag the ajs-atoms.md timeout claim to that chapter's reviewer. Optionally add here that the run's timeout (default fuel × 10 ms) is the only wall-clock bound on generated code.

rejected: Finding 13 ("local helpers" undefined) was only partly right. AJS does have local helper functions: they are top-level functions declared before the entry (DOCS-AJS.md, 'Local helper functions'), so I did not drop the term. I kept it, linked it, and stated the behaviour I verified: generated code that calls one gets `Unknown function: twice`.

Finding 22 (runCode 1 s timeout vs Out of Fuel) needs no change on this page, as the finding itself says. I did not add the optional 'fuel × 10 ms' timeout line. guides/ajs-host.md says the default run timeout is twice the slowest atom's timeout and at least 60 s, which contradicts that figure. The ajs-atoms.md claim that runCode times out after 1 s also disagrees with the reviewer's 36 s measurement. Both should go to the reviewers of those chapters.
questions: guides/ajs-atoms.md (around line 75) says runCode running generated code fails with a timeout after 1 s. The reviewer measured a generated infinite loop that ran 36 s and ended with Out of Fuel, not a timeout. Can the atoms-chapter owner check this?
