findings.problem: The page is only an intro paragraph and a link list. A reader who lands here gets no sense of what each of the six examples teaches, how hard it is, or which capabilities and models it needs. The toc holds bare titles only, so 'LLM Code Solver' and 'LLM Code Generator' look like the same thing.
findings.fix: Give each toc entry a one-line gloss: what it shows, which capability it needs (llmBattery, a vision model), and what is new compared with the previous example. Or group the six entries under subheadings: Tools, Pipelines, Vision, Models writing AJS.

findings.where: "and models that write AJS: one agent returns the code, the other runs it in the same sandbox"
findings.problem: 'One agent ... the other' has nothing to refer back to. The sentence has not introduced two agents, and it does not say which example does which. It reads as if one example contains both agents. Yet the toc has two entries, Code Solver and Code Generator, and the reader can't tell whether the solver/generator split is the returns/runs split. 'The same sandbox' is also undefined: the same as what?
findings.fix: Spell it out, for example: "LLM Code Generator asks a model to write AJS and returns the source. LLM Code Solver goes one step further: it transpiles that source and runs it in the same VM, under the same fuel and capability limits as the agent that asked for it."

findings.where: "All of them need a model, so here they print a message instead of running."
findings.problem: 'Here' is unclear: this page, the doc site, or the live examples? A first-time reader doesn't know what 'print a message' means, why the docs can't supply a model, or what they would have to do to run an example for real (start a local LLM server? pass capabilities?). It also leaves open whether the code is still correct and runnable elsewhere.
findings.fix: Say what the reader will see and how to run it for real, for example: "The live editors on this site have no model attached, so each example reports that and stops. To run one, connect a model capability (see LLMs) and run it in your own VM." Link to the setup instructions.

findings.where: "a model that plans while code computes"
findings.problem: 'Plans while code computes' suggests the two run concurrently. The later phrase 'the model decides and code does the work' suggests turn-taking. A reader can't tell which pattern is meant.
findings.fix: Use one precise description of the pattern in both places, for example: "the model chooses which tool to call and with what arguments; ordinary AJS code executes the call and feeds the result back."

findings.where: Intro paragraph (lines 6-8)
findings.problem: Nothing motivates the page for its two audiences. An embedder wants to know why these patterns matter for safety, for example that model-written code runs under the same fuel limits and capability limits. An agent author wants to know when to reach for a pipeline instead of a single call. The page lists what exists but not why or when.
findings.fix: Add one or two sentences on why: what these patterns buy you, and the safety property that makes 'a model writes code and we run it' acceptable in AJS when it would not be with eval.

findings.where: "a pipeline of roles"
findings.problem: 'Roles' is undefined here. It could mean system-prompt personas, separate agents, or separate VM runs.
findings.fix: Say "a pipeline of agents, each with its own prompt and role (e.g. researcher → writer → critic)", or whatever the Multi-Agent Pipeline example actually does.

findings.where: "Read [Basics](/ajs-basics/) and [LLMs](/ajs-llm/) first."
findings.problem: The prerequisite is good, but the reader isn't told which concepts from those pages they need (atoms, capabilities, llmPredict, fuel). A reader who skims Basics won't know whether they are ready.
findings.fix: Name the concepts they need, for example: "You should be comfortable calling atoms, passing capabilities, and reading an llmPredict result."

findings.where: Run-on sentence at lines 6-8
findings.problem: A single sentence carries four items, a colon, and a nested clause about two agents, so the list is hard to parse.
findings.fix: Break it into a short bulleted list of the four kinds of example, or into two sentences.

findings.where: "its pattern, where the model decides and code does the work, recurs in all the others."
findings.problem: This overstates it. In Multi-Agent Pipeline each llmPredict call does the work itself (summarize, critique, rewrite) with no tool code involved. In Vision OCR and Vision Classification the vision model reads the image and the code only fetches it. LLM Code Generator returns code without running it. Only LLM Code Solver repeats the pattern closely (the model writes the code, runCode does the work).
findings.fix: Make the claim smaller, e.g. "its pattern, where the model decides and code does the work, comes back in LLM Code Solver", or "recurs in most of the others".

findings.where: "Read [Basics](/ajs-basics/) and [LLMs](/ajs-llm/) first."
findings.problem: Both vision examples call httpFetch to get the image (checked by transpiling them: ops include httpFetch, then llmVision). The API section is where fetch is taught, and this prerequisite list leaves it out.
findings.fix: Add the API section to the list: "Read Basics, API and LLMs first."

questions: The toc block is regenerated by the site build, so I left it as bare titles. Each example's one-line gloss is in prose above it under '## The examples'. If you want the descriptions inside the toc list itself, the toc generator needs to support that.
revised.summary:
I rewrote /Users/tonioloewald/tjs-lang/guides/sections/ajs-advanced.md and applied all 10 findings. I checked each one against the six example pages first, and all held up.

What changed:
- **Why the page matters:** a new intro says why these patterns are safe for an embedder. Model-written code runs in the same VM under the same fuel, heap and quota limits, with only the capabilities the host passed, which `eval` cannot offer.
- **Prerequisites:** the page now names the concepts the reader needs: named atom inputs, capabilities, fuel, `httpFetch`, and `llmPredict` returning a string. It also adds the APIs section to the reading list, since both vision examples fetch the image with `httpFetch`.
- **Running the examples:** a "What you will see here" section explains that the live editors on this site have no model attached, so each example reports that and stops. It says how to run one for real: LM Studio or MLX setup, the host from LLM Chat, plus the extra capability each example's page names. It also mentions the scripted-model test in Multi-Agent Pipeline.
- **Per-example glosses:** each example now has a short description: what it shows, what it adds over the one before, and which capability it needs. Every example needs `llm`, except that the vision examples need the batteries (`batteryAtoms`, `llmBattery`) and a vision model, and Code Solver also needs `code`.
- **Wording fixes:**
  - "Plans while code computes" is replaced with an exact description of the turn-taking.
  - "Roles" is now defined as researcher → writer → editor: prompts inside one agent, not separate programs. The example page says this itself.
  - The claim that the pattern "recurs in all the others" now says it recurs in LLM Code Solver only.
  - The confusing "one agent … the other" sentence is now two bullets that separate Code Solver (runs the code with `runCode`) from Code Generator (returns the source unrun, and shows how to check it before running).
  - The run-on intro sentence is split up.

The metadata line, the `<!-- TODO review -->` marker and the toc block are unchanged. I added no executable fences, so there was nothing to run.

written.changes:
Rewrote /Users/tonioloewald/tjs-lang/guides/sections/ajs-api.md, a section overview page. I kept it short to match the sibling section pages (ajs-basics.md, ajs-llm.md).
- Moved `<!-- TODO review -->` to the line right after the metadata comment, where the other sections have it. The metadata comment is unchanged.

- Added a line for readers embedding the VM: in your own host nothing is allowed by default. I quoted the exact refusal message, `Fetch blocked: no allowedFetchDomains configured`.
- Replaced the vague "you will see how..." paragraph with one sentence per chapter on what it teaches:
  - Weather API: the capability, and why an HTTP error status is not an AJS error.
  - iTunes Search: encoding queries, a server that mislabels its JSON, trimming the response.

questions: There is no ajs-host.md page in the repo yet. DOCS-AJS.md, guides/patterns.md and guides/examples/ajs/weather-api.md (its #fetch-policy anchor) all link to /ajs-host/. I didn't add a link to it on this page. Is another agent writing that chapter, or should those links point somewhere else?
This page has no live example. Should section overview pages stay prose-only, as they are now across the AJS book, or should each one carry a small runnable teaser?

findings.where: "AJS has no `fetch`; the network is a capability the host grants" (para 2) vs. "Each one calls a public API with `httpFetch`" (para 1)
findings.problem: As a first-time reader this looks like a contradiction: the agents fetch things, but AJS 'has no fetch'. The page never says that `httpFetch` is an atom (a built-in operation) that does no I/O itself and sends each request to whatever the host provides. Without that sentence the reader can't tell how `httpFetch`, the allowlist and the `fetch` capability relate.
findings.fix: Add one bridging sentence, for example: "`httpFetch` is an atom: it has no network access of its own and sends every request through what the host grants, either an allowlist of domains for the built-in fetcher or a `fetch` function the host supplies."

findings.where: "a run with no allowlist and no `fetch` capability refuses every URL with `Fetch blocked: no allowedFetchDomains configured`"
findings.problem: This names two separate mechanisms (an allowlist, and a `fetch` capability) but never says how they combine. Does supplying a `fetch` capability bypass the allowlist? Does the allowlist also apply to a custom fetch? The error names `allowedFetchDomains`, but the page never says that this is the option's name or where it is set (an option to `vm.run`? a capability?). Later, "an API token belongs: in the host's `fetch` capability" relies on the reader already knowing the answer.
findings.fix: Say in one or two sentences: the allowlist is `allowedFetchDomains` (and where it goes); a host-supplied `fetch` capability replaces the default fetcher (and whether the allowlist still applies to it). A three-line host snippet showing where each one is passed would settle it.

findings.where: Whole page: there is no code
findings.problem: The page claims "the allowlist is the first lesson" and that the network is granted "one run at a time", but it shows nothing: no `vm.run(ast, args, { ... })` call with the allowlist and no `httpFetch` call. An embedding developer finishes the overview without seeing what granting a domain looks like, and the most important lesson is only promised for a later page.
findings.fix: Add one short host-side snippet (a `vm.run` call that grants `api.open-meteo.com`), or point to the exact section of Weather API where it is shown.

findings.where: "why an HTTP error status is not an AJS error"
findings.problem: "AJS error" is never defined. A newcomer doesn't know AJS has monadic errors (an error value that makes later steps skip, and that `try` can catch) as opposed to a thrown exception. So the point, that a 404 or 500 comes back as ordinary data and the agent must inspect it, only makes sense to someone who already knows the error model.
findings.fix: Spell it out: "a 404 or 500 does not stop the agent or become an error it can catch; `httpFetch` returns the response body as ordinary data, so the agent has to check it." Optionally link to the error-handling page.

findings.where: "They run live here: the page gives every run a fetch allowlist of three domains"
findings.problem: "the page" and "a run" are ambiguous. Which page: this overview or each example page? Is the doc site acting as the host? "run" (one `vm.run` invocation) is used as a technical unit here and in "one run at a time" without being introduced.
findings.fix: Say "The example pages below run live: the doc site acts as the host and passes each `vm.run` an allowlist of three domains", and use "run" consistently after that.

findings.where: "a server that mislabels its JSON"
findings.problem: Vague. Mislabeled how: wrong Content-Type, JSONP, text/javascript? The reader can't tell whether this is a lesson about AJS behaviour (does `httpFetch` parse based on Content-Type?) or a quirk of iTunes, so it doesn't motivate reading on.
findings.fix: Be concrete: "a server that sends JSON labeled `text/javascript`, so `httpFetch` hands back a string you must `JSON.parse`" (if that is the actual lesson).

findings.where: "returns a result small enough to hand to a model" / "the few fields a caller or a model needs"
findings.problem: The reason for trimming (model context or token limits, the membrane size cap, fuel cost) is assumed, not stated. A developer embedding the VM may not see why a large result is a problem for the host rather than just untidy.
findings.fix: Add a clause on why size matters: model context cost, `membraneMaxBytes` on values crossing the boundary, and/or fuel.

findings.where: "the network is a capability the host grants, one run at a time"
findings.problem: "capability" is used as a term of art without a definition or a link. Readers who arrive here directly (the section is a child of the examples page) may not have met capability-based security in this book yet.
findings.fix: Gloss it inline ("a capability: an I/O function the host passes in; the agent has none by default") or link to the security or capabilities chapter.

findings.where: "# APIs" plus the prose links followed by the toc list
findings.problem: The title "APIs" doesn't tell a reader that this is a group of runnable example agents. The same three links appear twice in a row (in the prose and then in the toc), which reads as redundant on a very short page.
findings.fix: Retitle as something like "Calling APIs" or "Agents that call APIs". Either keep the toc as the only list and trim the prose links, or accept the duplication on purpose.

findings.where: "<!-- TODO review -->" (line 2)
findings.problem: An internal working marker in a published page. It probably doesn't render, but it shows the page hasn't been reviewed.
findings.fix: Remove it once this review pass is done.

findings.where: "a run with no allowlist and no `fetch` capability refuses every URL with `Fetch blocked: no allowedFetchDomains configured`"
findings.problem: Close, but not every refusal reads that way. A private or internal address (localhost, 10.x and so on) gets a different message first: `Blocked URL: private/internal addresses not allowed in default fetch`. A non-http(s) scheme gets `Blocked URL: only http: or https: URLs may be fetched`. The quoted message is also only the start of the real text, which goes on: `Set ctx.context.allowedFetchDomains or provide a custom fetch capability.` A reader who greps for the exact string, or who tests with localhost, will see something else.
findings.fix: Say 'refuses public URLs with `Fetch blocked: no allowedFetchDomains configured. Set ctx.context.allowedFetchDomains or provide a custom fetch capability.`' and add that private addresses and non-http(s) schemes are refused with their own messages. Alternatively quote the message as a prefix ('an error beginning `Fetch blocked: no allowedFetchDomains configured`').
findings.evidence: src/vm/runtime.ts admitFetchUrl (~7083-7094). Scratch run of httpFetch with no context: open-meteo URL => 'Fetch blocked: no allowedFetchDomains configured. Set ctx.context.allowedFetchDomains or provide a custom fetch capability.'; http://localhost/ => 'Blocked URL: private/internal addresses not allowed in default fetch'

findings.where: "That allowlist is the first lesson. AJS has no `fetch`; the network is a capability the host grants"
findings.problem: The overview says what the allowlist is but not how exact it is, and that changes what a host has to write. An entry matches one exact hostname on the scheme's default port only. Subdomains need a `*.example.com` wildcard, and another port must be named (`api.example.com:8443`). Relative URLs are refused whenever an allowlist is set. Someone embedding the VM will reasonably expect `example.com` to cover `api.example.com`, and it does not.
findings.fix: Add one sentence, here or in Weather API where the grant is shown: entries are exact hostnames on the default port; use `*.example.com` for subdomains and `host:port` for another port.
findings.evidence: src/vm/runtime.ts isDomainAllowed (~6870-6900): port compared against the entry's named port; wildcard branch `p.startsWith('*.')`; otherwise `host === p`.

findings.where: "handles the answers that are not the data you asked for" (closing paragraph)
findings.problem: The built-in client returns two other kinds of answer that the chapter, and as far as grep shows the three example pages, never mention. (1) Redirects are not followed: a 301/302/303/307/308 comes back as data, `{ redirect: true, status, location }`, and the agent has to fetch `location` itself. (2) A body over `membraneMaxBytes` (default 4MB) is an error (`httpFetch: response too large ...`), not a truncated result. Both are part of 'answers that are not the data you asked for'.
findings.fix: Add a short sentence to the overview, or make sure Weather API / iTunes Search covers both: redirects arrive as `{ redirect: true, status, location }`, and oversized responses are refused.
findings.evidence: src/vm/runtime.ts httpFetch default path (~7225-7255): `redirect: 'manual'` ... `return { redirect: true, status: res.status, location: absolute }`; readBounded throws 'httpFetch: response too large'.

findings.where: "the page gives every run a fetch allowlist of three domains, `api.open-meteo.com`, `itunes.apple.com` and `api.github.com`, and any other URL is refused."
findings.problem: No problem with this claim; the brief asked for it to be checked. site/entry.ts's ALLOWED_FETCH_DOMAINS is exactly ['api.github.com','itunes.apple.com','api.open-meteo.com'], passed as `context: { allowedFetchDomains }` on every ajs run with no `fetch` capability. Example.com is refused with 'Fetch blocked: domain not in allowlist. Allowed: api.github.com, itunes.apple.com, api.open-meteo.com'. All three APIs send `access-control-allow-origin: *` (checked with curl), so they really do run live in the browser. The chapter's other claims also hold: the HTTP-error-body behaviour (open-meteo latitude=999 returns `{error:true, reason:...}` as data), iTunes' `text/javascript`, and GitHub's rate limits and where the token goes are each covered by the linked pages.
findings.fix: None needed. The edit pass can drop the brief's verification note.
findings.evidence: site/entry.ts lines 96-100 and 133-137; scratch run results; curl -H 'Origin: https://tjs.tosijs.net' on all three APIs shows access-control-allow-origin: *

rejected: Remove `<!-- TODO review -->`: rejected. The ground rules require that marker on line 2 so the owner can find every chapter during his edit pass.
Final finding (allowlist domains verified): no change needed. It confirms the claim. The verification note it mentions is not in the page.

findings.where: # Basics / "The language itself, one idea per page"
findings.problem: The page never says what AJS is or what an "agent" is. A first-time reader who arrives here (the book is aimed both at embedders and at people writing agents) gets no one-sentence definition: a JavaScript subset that compiles to a JSON AST and runs in a sandboxed, fuel-metered VM. "The language itself" assumes the reader already knows which language.
findings.fix: Open with one or two sentences: what AJS is (a JavaScript subset for agent code), what an agent is (a function the host runs in the VM with arguments, getting a result back), and why the reader should care (it runs untrusted or LLM-written code safely).

findings.where: "the shape of an agent, arithmetic, decisions, lists, text, JSON and errors"
findings.problem: This list doesn't line up with the TOC titles. "The shape of an agent" is "Hello World", "decisions" is "Conditional Logic", and "lists" is "Loop & Filter". The reader has to work out the mapping, and "the shape of an agent" never says what that shape is.
findings.fix: Either use the TOC titles in the sentence, or turn the TOC into a short annotated list (e.g. "Hello World: the shape of an agent, which is a function with typed inputs that returns an object").

findings.where: "Every example in these pages runs live"
findings.problem: "Runs live" isn't explained. Runs where: in the browser, in the real VM, against real network APIs? Can the reader edit it? Do the examples cost anything or need an LLM? An embedder will want to know whether these run on the real VM with real fuel limits.
findings.fix: Say what live means: e.g. "each example is editable and runs in the AJS VM in your browser; edit it and press run to see the result", and mention whether any of the examples need network or an LLM.

findings.where: "every page ends with the place where AJS differs from the JavaScript you know"
findings.problem: This assumes the reader knows JavaScript and expects AJS to behave like it, but the page never says that AJS is a JavaScript subset. It also doesn't say whether the differences are restrictions (things you can't write) or changed semantics (things that behave differently), which is the key thing to know before reading on.
findings.fix: Add a sentence such as "AJS looks like JavaScript and is mostly a subset of it, but a few things behave differently (for example, reading a member of null returns undefined instead of throwing) or are refused. Each page ends with the difference that matters for its topic." A single concrete example sets expectations.

findings.where: "returns a result a host can use"
findings.problem: "Host" is undefined. It's a key term for the embedder audience (the JavaScript program that runs the VM and injects capabilities), but a first-time reader can't tell whether the host is a server, the browser page, or something else.
findings.fix: Define it inline: "the host (the program that runs your agent in the VM and hands it capabilities like fetch)", or link to the page that introduces it.

findings.where: "handles bad data without crashing"
findings.problem: This hints at a distinctive feature (errors are values, not thrown exceptions, and the VM halts on fuel exhaustion) without naming it, so the promise is vague. It also leaves unclear whether "crashing" means the agent, the VM, or the host.
findings.fix: Be concrete: "handles bad input by returning an error value instead of throwing", and point to the Error Handling page as the place this is explained.

findings.where: Whole page (who is it for)
findings.problem: The book serves two audiences (embedders and agent authors), but this section addresses only agent authors. An embedder doesn't know whether to read Basics or skip to embedding and VM setup. There's also no mention of what's NOT here (calling atoms or capabilities such as fetch or LLMs, fuel and budgets), so the reader can't tell where those live.
findings.fix: Add a line on who should read this section and where to go next: e.g. "If you are embedding the VM, read this to learn what your agents will look like, then see <embedding section>. Calling the outside world (fetch, LLMs, store) comes in <next section>."

findings.where: Frontmatter `"parent": "ajs-examples.md"`
findings.problem: The section is filed under an "examples" parent but presents itself as the language tutorial ("The language itself... Read them in order"). A reader navigating the book may be unsure whether these are reference examples or the tutorial path, and whether a separate language reference exists.
findings.fix: Make the intent explicit on the page, e.g. "These examples are the tutorial: there is no separate prose chapter on syntax", or link the language reference (DOCS-AJS) for readers who want it.

findings.where: "Read them in order. After the last one you can write an agent that takes input, computes, loops, handles bad data..."
findings.problem: There's no sense of size or time (seven short pages? each a few minutes?), and no prerequisite stated (does the reader need to know JavaScript?). A reader can't judge the commitment involved.
findings.fix: Add a short note: "Seven short pages; assumes you know basic JavaScript."

findings.where: <!-- TODO review -->
findings.problem: An internal TODO marker sits in the published source. It's invisible in rendered output, but it signals the page hasn't been reviewed yet.
findings.fix: Remove it once the edit pass is done.

findings.where: "every page ends with the place where AJS differs from the JavaScript you know"
findings.problem: This doesn't hold for every child page. math-operations.md ends with "## The gotchas", which covers floating point and `a / 0` being Infinity. Both are explicitly "as in JavaScript". The page's real AJS difference (an array is refused by `+`; write `xs.join(',')`) is in "What to notice", near the top. json-processing.md ends on advice about `filter` and has no gotcha section. Its JS differences (`err` in a catch is a string, so `err.message` is undefined; `'data: ' + data` is refused) are in the middle. loop-filter.md has a closing difference (a helper called inside an expression is refused), but its main list of differences is the earlier "What is not there" section. So the brief's premise ("holds for every child") is false for at least math-operations.
findings.evidence: guides/examples/ajs/math-operations.md lines 78-99: '## The gotchas ... `a / 0` is `Infinity`, as in JavaScript.' Running `ratio({a:10,b:0})` on AgentVM returned { ratio: Infinity }, the same as JS. Line 34: "Between primitives JavaScript's rules still apply" (the AJS difference sits in the middle of the page).
findings.fix: Make the claim weaker, e.g. "every page says where AJS differs from the JavaScript you know" (dropping "ends with"). Or ask the owner to end math-operations with the array-coercion refusal and json-processing with the err-is-a-string note.

findings.where: "Every example in these pages runs live"
findings.problem: ajs-error-handling.md has a plain ```javascript fence (host-side code under "What the host sees", line 146) that does not run on the page. Every AJS example is live, but not every example is.
findings.evidence: grep: guides/examples/ajs/ajs-error-handling.md:146:```javascript
findings.fix: "Every agent in these pages runs live".

revised.summary:
I rewrote /Users/tonioloewald/tjs-lang/guides/sections/ajs-basics.md. The metadata line, the <!-- TODO review --> marker and the toc block are unchanged.

What changed on the page:
- **Opening:** it now says what AJS is (a JavaScript subset for agent code written by people or models), what an agent is (one function), and what a host is (the program that embeds the VM, calls the agent with inputs, sets the fuel budget and grants capabilities such as fetch).
- **Scope:** it says these are seven short pages, that they assume basic JavaScript, and that they are the tutorial. DOCS-AJS is linked as the full reference.
- **Chapter list:** an annotated list now uses the real TOC titles, so the reader no longer has to map "decisions" to Conditional Logic and so on.
- **Differences from JavaScript:** I stated AJS is a JavaScript subset, gave two concrete differences (reading a member of null returns undefined; `'total: ' + [1, 2]` is refused), and changed the claim to "each page says where AJS differs". I checked the "wrong" finding before accepting it: math-operations does end on JavaScript-identical gotchas, and its real AJS difference is in "What to notice".
- **"Runs live":** this now says each agent is editable and runs on the same sandboxed VM you would embed, with no arguments and 10,000 fuel. It links AJS Examples for the details and says none of these agents needs a network or a model. The httpFetch call in Error Handling is refused before any request goes out.

findings.fix: Add one sentence: "Each example has two parts: the agent (AJS, which could be written by a model or a stranger) and the host (your JavaScript, which creates the VM and hands it a model to call). The agent can't reach a model unless the host passes one in."

findings.where: Whole page (motivation)
findings.problem: Nothing says why an agent calling an LLM deserves its own section, or what is safe about it. The book is for people running untrusted or LLM-written code, and the obvious question is "can the agent run up my model bill, or call the model as often as it likes?" The page never addresses it, apart from the vague "cap what it may cost".
findings.fix: Add a short paragraph: the model is a capability the host injects; the VM has no IO by default; and each model call can be limited (per-call quotas, fuel, timeouts). Name the knob the examples use, e.g. `quotas: { llmPredict: 3 }`.

findings.where: "After these you can prompt a model from an agent, cap what it may cost, and get JSON back instead of prose."
findings.problem: It isn't clear what "cost" means here. It could be fuel, wall-clock time, a number of model calls, tokens, or money. A first-time reader will probably guess money or tokens, and that may be wrong.
findings.fix: Say which one, e.g. "cap how many model calls it may make (a quota) and how much work it may do (fuel)". Link the term to wherever fuel and quotas are defined.

findings.where: "Start with [LLM Chat](/llm-chat/), which sets up the host the others reuse."
findings.problem: "Reuse" is unclear. The reader can't tell whether the later examples import a shared module, expect them to copy code, or just assume the same server is running. A reader who opens Summarizer first won't know what they're missing.
findings.fix: Spell it out: "LLM Chat shows the host code once (creating the VM, connecting a model, passing it as a capability). The other two examples assume that same host and show only the agent." If a reader has to copy something, say what.

findings.where: "To get one running on your machine, see [LM Studio setup](/lm-studio-setup/) or [MLX setup](/mlx-setup/)."
findings.problem: The reader gets two options and no way to choose between them. They don't know which one the examples were tested against or what each one needs (MLX is Apple Silicon only). Also, "one" here means a server, and that only becomes clear on a second read.
findings.fix: Add a choice rule: "On Apple Silicon, MLX is the recommended backend; otherwise use LM Studio. Either works because the examples speak the OpenAI-compatible HTTP API." Also mention the config the host reads (e.g. `TJS_LLM_BASE_URL`) so a reader with an existing server knows how to point at it.

findings.where: "each page shows how to run it locally with a model server such as LM Studio"
findings.problem: The page lists prerequisites only by implication. The reader doesn't learn that they need a chat model loaded, whether the summarizer or structured-output examples need a particular model or an embedding model, or roughly what hardware is involved. They will only find out when an example fails.
findings.fix: Add a one-line "You'll need" list: a running OpenAI-compatible server, a chat model loaded, plus any extras a specific example needs (e.g. an embedding model).

findings.where: TOC: LLM Chat / LLM Summarizer / LLM Structured Output
findings.problem: From this page alone I can't tell what each example teaches beyond its title, especially how Structured Output differs from Chat. The intro also promises "get JSON back instead of prose" without a code snippet showing what that looks like in AJS. The repo also seems to have more LLM examples (llm-with-tool, llm-code-generator, llm-code-solver, llm-api-data, vision-*) that aren't listed here. This is a possible completeness gap; I didn't open them to check.
findings.fix: Give each TOC entry a few words saying what it teaches (e.g. "Structured Output: pass a schema and get validated JSON back"). Consider a three-to-five-line AJS snippet of a model call so the section shows something concrete. Either list the other LLM examples or say where they live (another section or a later chapter).

findings.where: "<!-- TODO review -->" (line 2)
findings.problem: A working note left in the source. It doesn't show in the rendered page, but it marks the page as unreviewed and should be removed once the edit pass is done.
findings.fix: Remove the note after the edit pass.

findings.where: "Agents that call a language model: a chat, a summarizer, and structured extraction."
findings.problem: The opening is a sentence fragment that lists contents before saying what the section is for. "Structured extraction" in the intro and "Structured Output" in the TOC name the same example two different ways.
findings.fix: Open with the purpose ("These examples show an agent asking a model for text or JSON, with the host deciding which model it gets and how often it may ask"), and use one name for the third example throughout.

findings.where: "each page shows how to run it locally with a model server such as LM Studio" (lines 7-8), then "The host code on each page talks to any OpenAI-compatible server. To get one running ... see [LM Studio setup] or [MLX setup]" (lines 10-11)
findings.problem: The line the brief asked for (a pointer to the local-model setup chapters) is already there, and both targets exist with unique basenames (docs/lm-studio-setup.md, docs/mlx-setup.md). But the two paragraphs say the same thing twice, and the first names only LM Studio, while CLAUDE.md calls MLX the intended backend from now on. Also, "each page shows how to run it" is slightly loose: llm-structured-output has no host of its own. It points to LLM Chat's host and adds a mock-model test host.
findings.fix: Merge the two sentences into one. For example: "A static page has no model to call, so these examples print a message here instead of running. Each runs locally against any OpenAI-compatible server: see MLX setup or LM Studio setup to get one running." Name MLX first, or keep the two neutral.

findings.where: "Agents that call a language model: a chat, a summarizer, and structured extraction."
findings.problem: Other LLM examples in the book sit in other sections and get no mention here: llm-with-tool, llm-code-generator, llm-code-solver, vision-ocr and vision-classification (parent ajs-advanced.md), and llm-api-data (parent ajs-featured.md). A reader who wants tool calls or vision from this LLM section has no route to them.
findings.fix: Add one closing line, e.g. "Tool calls, vision and code generation are in Advanced; LLM API Data is in Featured", linking /llm-with-tool/, /vision-ocr/ and /llm-api-data/.

findings.where: "these examples print a message here instead of running"
findings.problem: This is accurate only for fences that call an LLM atom. site/entry.ts line 126 skips a run only when the AST contains "op":"llm. Fences on these pages that make no model call, such as priceSchemas in llm-structured-output, run normally. The claim is broadly right but could make a reader skip an example that does run.
findings.fix: Optional: change it to "the examples that call a model print a message here instead of running", the wording llm-structured-output already uses.

findings.where: "After these you can prompt a model from an agent, cap what it may cost, and get JSON back instead of prose."
findings.problem: The chapters cap the NUMBER of model calls (quotas: { llmPredict: 1 }) and charge flat fuel. The pages themselves stress that fuel does not track what a call costs you. "Cap what it may cost" slightly overstates this.
findings.fix: Write "cap how many model calls it may make".

rejected: Part of finding 6 (mention TJS_LLM_BASE_URL so a reader with an existing server knows how to point at it): rejected because it is wrong for these pages. TJS_LLM_BASE_URL is read by tjs-lang/batteries (src/batteries/config.ts). The example host in llm-chat.md is a hand-written fetch to http://localhost:1234/v1/chat/completions, so the page now tells the reader to change that URL for MLX or another server. The rest of finding 6 (a rule for choosing MLX or LM Studio, and making clear that 'one' means a server) was applied.
revised.summary:

What changed on the page:

- **Agent and host:** it defines the agent (untrusted AJS) and the host (your JavaScript), and says the model is the `llm` capability the host passes in. The VM has no IO of its own.
- **New code example:** a short live ```ajs fence with an `ask` agent that calls `llmPredict`.
- **New section, "What an agent may spend":** a quota limits the number of model calls (`quotas: { llmPredict: 3 }`, with the exact error text). Fuel is a flat 100 per call and does not measure tokens or money (links to /fuel-limits/). Timeout is two minutes by default, changed with `timeoutOverrides`. I did not remove `<!-- TODO review -->`: the ground rules require it, and the finding itself says to remove it after the edit pass.

Checks I ran:
