- **Quota error text:** four calls under a quota of 3 fail with `Quota exceeded for 'llmPredict': 3 calls allowed`, exactly as the page quotes it.
- **Links:** every link target exists, and I matched the link text to each page's actual title ("Embedding the AJS VM", "Vision: OCR", "LLM + API Data").

Scratch scripts are in /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-tonioloewald-tjs-lang/ceca4d7c-a13f-43be-92e8-1e916ca662c7/scratchpad/docs-swarm/ajs-llm/. I edited no other file and did not run `bun run docs`.

written.changes:
I rewrote /Users/tonioloewald/tjs-lang/CONTEXT.md as "The AJS VM: Technical Context". It is now the architecture and internals chapter of the AJS book, for people embedding or reviewing the VM.

Metadata: I changed `parent` from `the-tjs-language.md` to `ajs.md`, as the brief asked, and left the other fields alone. `<!-- TODO review -->` is on line 2. The filename stays the same, because doc-site-structure.test.ts and the old playground look the page up by the name CONTEXT.md.

Fixes to what was wrong:
- **Numbering:** sections now run 1 to 8 with no jump.
- **Bundle size:** I removed the "~17KB gzipped" claim. In its place are figures I measured on the 2026-11-05 dist/ build, with tosijs-schema external: vm-ast is 137KB minified (43KB gzipped) and vm is 324KB (98KB gzipped). They carry that date in the text.
- **Dependencies:** the old "tosijs-schema 1.2.0 Coverage" section is gone. The new table shows tosijs-schema ^1.12.0 and why 1.12 is the floor. It now lists acorn-walk and acorn-loose as runtime dependencies (they were wrongly listed as dev-only). It names the optional peers (@codemirror/*, typescript) and drops the dev-dependency table and the "what we don't depend on" table.
- **How to run an agent:** every example now uses `transpile` from tjs-lang/lang and runs on tjs-lang/vm-ast. The text says `vm.run(source)` is deprecated, that vm-ast refuses source, and to pass `maxSourceBytes` when transpiling source you didn't write.
- **Run timeout:** the default was documented as fuel × 10ms. It is actually twice the slowest registered atom's timeout, with a 60s floor. I checked this in src/vm/vm.ts and by running it.
- **Sub-agent fuel:** the old text said fuel is never shared. In fact a sub-agent given an AST or a token runs on the caller's fuel and quotas; I confirmed a looping child runs the caller out of fuel. Only a named sub-agent goes to the host's `agent.run`.
- **Stored-procedure costs:** `releaseProcedure` costs 0.1, not 0.5. `clearExpiredProcedures` is a flat 0.5, not "plus 0.01 per procedure".
- **Expressions:** I removed the stale claim that expressions can't read state except through `vars`. The table of expression node types now matches the `ExprNode` type in the source; the old one left out logical, array, object, call, methodCall and regex.
- **Builder conditions:** the old "chained `a > b > c` unsupported" claim was false, so it's gone. I also corrected the "use `computed: true`" advice: a builder condition must be a string, so the workaround is to compute the value with `varSet` first and test that variable. I checked that workaround.
- **Broken examples removed:** an object literal with a duplicate `llmPredict` key, an atom returning a raw fetch `Response` (the membrane refuses it), an agent using a C-style for loop (AJS refuses it), and a try/catch example that called methods in a condition string (the builder refuses that).

Cut because other chapters already cover it: the detail on run options, timeouts, cost overrides and Express integration (now links to /ajs-host/), and the dated January 2025 test-coverage section. New material: a table of the pieces, the eight steps of a `vm.run`, a security table with links to where each guarantee is explained, request context (an authorization atom the agent cannot see, plus a streaming atom), the stored-procedure store's behaviour, whose budget a sub-agent spends, and a runnable example showing that runs are not transactions.

All 6 examples are `typescript` fences of whole programs, with no fragments. Each one runs (its output matches the comments) and compiles under `tjs()`, as src/doc-snippets.test.ts requires. doc-site-structure and repo-hygiene pass.

I found these problems outside my file and did not change them:
1. guides/ajs.md (Quickstart) says "`timeoutMs` defaults to fuel × 10 ms", and so do CLAUDE.md and a comment in vm.ts. That is wrong.
2. **Possible transpiler bug:** `total += lookupPrice({ sku })`, an atom call inside an expression, passes `transpile()` but fails at runtime with "Atom calls in expressions not yet supported". Under the "transpiler prevents bad code" rule, the transpiler should refuse it.
3. The `storeProcedure` size error ends with "Consider … using a shorter TTL", but TTL has nothing to do with size.
4. The size comments in src/vm/vm.ts and src/vm/ast.ts (56KB / 221KB) are stale; the current build is 137KB / 324KB minified.
5. src/doc-snippets.test.ts currently fails for TJS-FOR-TS.md, not CONTEXT.md: its fragment ratio improved to 44%, so the ALLOWED entry needs lowering.
questions: `vm.run(token)` THROWS `Procedure not found` / `Procedure expired` into the host for a missing or expired token, while the same token inside `agentRun` gives a catchable AgentError. The chapter documents the throw as it behaves today. Is that intended, or should `vm.run` return it as `error` like every other failure?

The chapter is nav-ordered 14 under ajs.md, last after vm-budgets (5.5) and ajs-capabilities (6), so it reads as the internals appendix. Keep it there, or move it earlier as an overview before the hosting chapters?

The chapter now leans on the new guides/ajs-host.md (Embedding the AJS VM) for run options, quotas and fetch policy, and links to its anchors. If that chapter is not kept, those links break and the timeout and cost-override material would need to come back here.
The title is now 'The AJS VM: Technical Context' (navTitle 'Technical Context' is unchanged). Is that acceptable, or do you want a different name now that it lives in the AJS book?

findings.where: Page as a whole / front matter: section "ajs", heading "# The AJS VM: Technical Context"
findings.problem: The page never says what an "agent" is, what AJS is for, or why anyone would run code inside a VM rather than calling a function. It opens with "how agents compose" and "embedding the VM" as if all of that were known. A reader coming from the TJS book, and certainly one from the learn-to-program chapters, has no way in. The file is named CONTEXT.md, the nav title is "Technical Context" and the H1 is "The AJS VM", so the reader can't even tell what kind of page this is.
findings.fix: Open with two or three sentences of motivation, for example: "AJS lets you run code you did not write (from a user, another service or an LLM) safely: it cannot touch anything you did not hand it, and it always stops." Add a prerequisites line ("read AJS: The Agent Language first"). Say in the intro who the page is not for.

findings.where: "what happens when the host calls `vm.run`"; "front ends"; "guest" (security table)
findings.problem: "host", "front end" and "guest" are used as terms of art and never defined. "Guest" first shows up inside a table cell ("No host code from the guest"), and by then the page has been calling the same thing "the agent".
findings.fix: Define host (your program that creates the VM and passes capabilities), agent or guest (the untrusted program the VM runs), and front end (anything that produces an AST: transpiler, builder) once, early. Then pick either "agent" or "guest" and use only that one.

findings.where: Pieces table, VM row: "All atom implementations, fuel, timeouts, the heap ceiling and the membrane live here."
findings.problem: The first table uses four undefined concepts (fuel, heap ceiling, membrane, atom). Fuel is first quantified much later ("Each node costs 0.01 fuel"), "membrane" is never defined anywhere on the page (it only reappears in "copied through the membrane" in section 2), and "heap ceiling" is only explained by the maxHeapBytes row in section 3.
findings.fix: Add a short glossary right after the table, or a one-line gloss in each cell: "fuel (a work budget; every step spends some, and the run stops at zero)", "membrane (the copy-and-check layer every value passes through when it enters or leaves the VM)".

findings.where: "so a hostile payload cannot reach a parser defect inside the sandbox" / "Parsing is the one step that runs before any budget exists."
findings.problem: The reasoning skips steps. The reader isn't told why a parser could be dangerous, what a "budget" is at this point, or why 64 KB is the suggested cap. Both sentences read as conclusions with the argument cut out.
findings.fix: Spell it out: "Parsing cost is decided by the source text, and it happens before fuel or timeouts apply, so a crafted input can make it slow or memory-hungry. Do it outside the sandbox, and cap the size if the source is untrusted."

findings.where: First example: `function total({ price: 0.0, taxRate: 0.0 })` and `{ fuel: 100 }`
findings.problem: Nothing explains the colon values (`0.0` as an example value that also means "float"), and the destructured-object signature differs from the `function f(x: 0)` form a TJS reader has seen elsewhere. The reader also gets no idea whether `fuel: 100` is generous or tight.
findings.fix: Add a comment: `// AJS parameters are examples: 0.0 means 'a number'; see DOCS-AJS`. Give a scale for fuel, for example "this run uses about N fuel; 100 is plenty", or print `run.fuelUsed`.

findings.where: Builder example: `.varsImport(['n'])` and `.if('n > 10', { n: 'n' }, ...)`
findings.problem: `varsImport` is never explained. The second argument `{ n: 'n' }` looks redundant and isn't explained until two paragraphs later. A first-time reader can't tell what the map is for or why the condition can't just read `n`.
findings.fix: Annotate inline: `.varsImport(['n']) // copy input field n into agent state` and `{ n: 'n' } // condition name -> state variable`. Or move the explanatory paragraph above the example.

findings.where: "The builder writes a version-1 AST (`"$ajs": 1`)... a bare string that names a variable in scope is read as that variable."
findings.problem: This hazard bites the example just above it: `varSet({ key: 'size', value: 'big' })` would silently read a variable if one named `big` existed. The page states the rule but never connects it to the code the reader just saw, and it doesn't say how to write a literal string that is guaranteed to stay a string in v1.
findings.fix: Point it out directly: "In the example above, 'big' is a string only because no variable called big exists." Then show how to force a literal, or recommend the transpiler for anything handwritten.

findings.where: "To test one, compute it first with a `varSet` whose value is an expression node, then test that variable."
findings.problem: This is a workaround without a code example, and the reader hasn't yet seen what an expression node looks like (the table comes in the next subsection). The paragraph is also a wall of text that mixes grammar, an error message, a workaround and the warning behaviour.
findings.fix: Split it into a short list (what conditions support / what is refused / the workaround), give the workaround a 3-line example, and say where the "builder warns" warning actually shows up (console? thrown? returned?).

findings.where: Expressions table: `call` "a builtin (`Math.max`) or a local helper"; `methodCall` "(`s.trim()`)"; `regex` "the VM's own linear engine"; `member` "computed?"
findings.problem: "Local helper" is undefined: can an agent declare functions? `s` in `s.trim()` reads like the `s` schema import used in every other example. "Linear engine" means nothing to a reader who doesn't know about ReDoS. `computed?` is unexplained.
findings.fix: Use `name.trim()` instead of `s.trim()`. Gloss "linear engine" as "a regex engine whose running time cannot blow up on crafted input". Say what a local helper is, and that `computed` means `obj[key]` rather than `obj.key`.

findings.where: "Each node costs 0.01 fuel."
findings.problem: There is no scale: the reader can't tell how this compares with an atom's cost or with the `fuel: 100` used earlier. It is also the first number given for fuel at all, and it arrives after fuel has already been used in two examples.
findings.fix: Introduce fuel once, with a scale (for example "an atom call costs about 1; an expression node 0.01; 100 fuel runs a small agent"), before the first example that sets it.

findings.where: Run steps: "2. Resolve the AST  a stored-procedure token (proc_…) is looked up here"; "6. Execute  the root seq"; "5. Check the input  the arguments against the AST's inputSchema"
findings.problem: Stored procedures are a forward reference to section 5 with no link. "seq" is never defined. The page never says where inputSchema and outputSchema come from (presumably the function signature or the builder's `.take` and `.return`), so steps 5 and 7 look like magic.
findings.fix: Link step 2 to section 5. Gloss `seq` ("the AST's top-level list of steps"). Add one sentence: "The transpiler derives inputSchema from the function's parameter examples and outputSchema from its return; the builder takes them from .take() and .return()."

findings.where: "A failure at any step comes back as the run's `error`... The one exception is a host mistake in step 2"
findings.problem: The reader is left wondering what happens with a bad option in step 1, or a malformed AST in step 3: is that also a host mistake that throws? "Any step" followed by a single exception doesn't settle it. `AgentError` is also used without saying where it's exported or how to recognise one.
findings.fix: Say explicitly which failures throw and which return, perhaps as a two-column table. Mention how to test for an AgentError.

findings.where: Security table, "Bounded time" row: "default: twice the slowest registered atom's timeout, at least 60 s"; "Errors are values" row: "Bugs at the capability boundary end the run; failures of the world are catchable."
findings.problem: The timeout rule is hard to parse. Twice the slowest atom's timeout, or 60 s, whichever is larger? And does it apply per run or per call? The errors row is cryptic: "failures of the world" and "bugs at the capability boundary" are undefined categories, and "catchable" assumes the reader knows AJS has try/catch. `ctx.signal` in the paragraph above is also undefined.
findings.fix: Rephrase: "the larger of 60 s and twice the longest per-atom timeout". For errors, give one example of each kind: a capability returning a class instance ends the run; a fetch returning 500 or an oversized body can be caught with try/catch. Gloss ctx.signal as an AbortSignal.

findings.where: Security table layout
findings.problem: Several cells are full sentences or paragraphs inside a three-column table, which becomes a wall of text and is unreadable at phone width.
findings.fix: Turn it into a definition list (guarantee as heading, one short paragraph, a link), or cut each How cell to a single clause.

findings.where: Section 4 example: `async ({ id }, ctx) => { ... throw new Error('not allowed to read records') ... }`
findings.problem: Section 3 has just insisted that errors are values and never thrown, and now the atom throws. The reader isn't told that a throw inside an atom is fine and becomes the run's AgentError. `defineAtom`'s four positional arguments (name, input schema, output schema, implementation) and the `ctx` parameter are also introduced without explanation, and the explanation of `{ atoms: vm.atoms }` comes after the code.
findings.fix: Add a comment or sentence: "An atom may throw; the VM turns that into the run's error, and the agent sees it as a failed step." Label defineAtom's arguments inline. Mention that ctx is the per-call context the VM passes to every atom.

findings.where: Streaming example: `emit({ data: { n } })` in the agent, `await ctx.context?.onChunk?.(data)` in the atom
findings.problem: The agent calls `emit` as if it were synchronous while the atom is async. A reader will wonder whether the agent waits and whether chunks come out in order. "The atom's input is a copy, so the callback receives plain data" relies on the undefined membrane concept and doesn't say why that matters.
findings.fix: State that atom calls in AJS are awaited implicitly, so chunks arrive in order. Explain the copy ("the callback can't be handed a live object from inside the agent").

findings.where: Section 5 example: `function register({ handler })` vs `function dispatch({ handler: 'proc_', value: 0 })`
findings.problem: `register`'s parameter has no example value while every other example has one, and the page doesn't say whether that's allowed or what type it implies. In `dispatch`, `'proc_'` as an example value is clever (a string that looks like a token) but unexplained. Passing an AST as a run argument (`{ handler: double }`) is also surprising after the membrane rules, and nothing confirms it's legal.
findings.fix: Comment both: "handler: an AST object, passed as plain JSON" and "'proc_' is just an example string; any token matches".

findings.where: "`procedureStore` (exported from the VM) is a module-level `Map`." / "An AST over `maxSize` bytes" / "Anything without an `op` is refused"
findings.problem: There are three undefined specifics. Why would the reader care that it's a Map, and should they touch it? Where is `maxSize` set (a storeProcedure input, or a VM option)? What is `op`? The reader has never been shown an AST's raw shape.
findings.fix: Say whether procedureStore is for hosts to inspect or clear. Show maxSize as `storeProcedure({ ast, ttl, maxSize })` if that's where it goes. Say "an AST's root must have an op field (every transpiler or builder AST does)".

findings.where: Stored-procedure fuel table: "Base fuel 1 / 0.1 / 0.5"
findings.problem: Without a fuel scale these numbers mean nothing, and "a charge that grows with AST size" gives no rate.
findings.fix: Once fuel has a scale earlier on the page, link back to it. Give the size rate or link to VM budgets.

findings.where: Section 6: "An AST or a stored-procedure token runs inside the caller's run... Anything else (usually a name) goes to the host's `agent.run`"
findings.problem: A token and a name are both strings, and the page doesn't say how the VM tells them apart (the `proc_` prefix? a lookup?). A name that happens to start with `proc_` is an obvious question. The `agent` capability's shape is also never shown.
findings.fix: State the rule ("a string starting with proc_ is treated as a token") and show the minimal `capabilities: { agent: { run: async (id, input) => ... } }` shape.

findings.where: Section 7 example: `if (amount > 100) { Error('limit exceeded') }`
findings.problem: Calling `Error(...)` as a statement without `throw` would do nothing in JavaScript. A JS developer will think this is a bug in the example. Nothing explains that this AJS idiom fails the run. The `store` capability shape (`get`/`set` async) is also shown here for the first time with no explanation.
findings.fix: Add a comment: `// in AJS, Error(...) fails the run (there is no throw); see Errors`. Note that this is the store capability's minimum interface.

findings.where: Section 8 "Dependencies"
findings.problem: This doesn't belong in a VM chapter. acorn-loose (editor scope extraction), the codemirror peers and typescript have nothing to do with embedding or reviewing the VM. "Relies on its branded builders" is unexplained jargon, and the dated bundle sizes will go stale.
findings.fix: Keep only what matters to a VM embedder (vm-ast depends on tosijs-schema only, plus its size). Move the full dependency table to an install or packaging page. Drop or explain "branded builders".

findings.where: Book placement (TJS Programming Language)
findings.problem: Nothing on the page tells a reader who arrived from the TJS chapters whether they need this page at all, or how AJS relates to TJS (subset? separate language?). For a learn-to-program reader the page is wholly unreachable, and nothing marks it as advanced material.
findings.fix: Add a lead-in: "Advanced: for people running untrusted code. AJS is a safe subset of TJS; you can skip this chapter unless you embed the VM."

findings.where: §2 What happens in a run: 'A failure at any step comes back as the run's error ... The one exception is a host mistake in step 2'
findings.problem: Several more failures throw into the host instead of returning `error`: the step-3 format gate, the root-op check (which the list leaves out), source passed to tjs-lang/vm-ast, and a failed transpile on tjs-lang/vm. These do come back as `error`: bad options, the argument membrane, and input/output schema failures.
findings.evidence: Scratch script review/throws.ts: vm.run({...ast, $ajs: 99}) THREW 'AgentVM.run: This AST declares format version 99, but this build of tjs-lang understands at most 2'; vm.run({ op: 'if' }, {}) THREW 'Root AST must be seq'; vm-ast vm.run(source) THREW 'This VM accepts an AST, not source'. In src/vm/vm.ts run(), checkAstVersion(ast,'AgentVM.run') and the op !== 'seq' check both throw, and so does 'AJS transpilation failed'. fuel: -1 RETURNED 'Invalid run option fuel: -1'.
findings.fix: Add a step between 3 and 4 ('the root must be seq'). Reword: failures from the agent, and from admitting its options, arguments and schemas, come back as `error`. A host mistake about WHAT is being run throws: a missing or expired token, a format version this build cannot read, a root that is not seq, source given to vm-ast, or source that fails to transpile.

findings.where: §8 Dependencies: 'None of the four has dependencies of its own.'
findings.problem: acorn-walk and acorn-loose both depend on acorn. What is true is that the four pull in nothing beyond themselves.
findings.evidence: node_modules/acorn-walk/package.json lists dependencies { acorn: '^8.11.0' }; acorn-loose lists { acorn: '^8.15.0' }; acorn and tosijs-schema list none.
findings.fix: 'Between them they pull in nothing else: acorn-walk and acorn-loose depend only on acorn, and acorn and tosijs-schema have no dependencies.'

findings.where: §4 Request context: link [Fetch policy](/ajs-host/#fetch-policy-the-context-keys)
findings.problem: Broken anchor. In guides/ajs-host.md the heading is '## Fetch policy', so its anchor is #fetch-policy.
findings.evidence: grep -n '^#' guides/ajs-host.md gives line 182 '## Fetch policy'
findings.fix: Link to /ajs-host/#fetch-policy.

findings.where: §6 Sub-agents: 'An AST or a stored-procedure token runs inside the caller's run'
findings.problem: A sub-agent run inline by agentRun has neither its inputSchema nor its declared result (outputSchema) checked. The chapter lists the checks in §2's steps 5 and 7, so readers will assume they apply to a sub-agent too, and they do not. This also looks like a sibling-site gap to #3834 ('a typed agent's declared result is enforced'), which only covers vm.run.
findings.evidence: Scratch script review/sub.ts stores double = `function double({ n: 0 }): { n: 0 } { return { n: 'str' + n } }` as token proc_x, then dispatches with input { n: 'x' }. Result: { out: { n: 'strx' } }, no error. Run directly, vm.run(double, { n: 'x' }) returns 'Input validation failed'. In src/vm/runtime.ts, agentRun only calls seqAtom.exec(ast, childCtx) and never validates against inputSchema or outputSchema.
findings.fix: Either state it ('an inline sub-agent's declared input and result types are not checked; only vm.run checks them'), or, better, file a card for agentRun to enforce both schemas, as vm.run does, and leave the chapter as is once that is fixed.

findings.where: §1 'The builder and the transpiler contain no execution logic; the VM contains no parser.'
findings.problem: Two sentences later the chapter says tjs-lang/vm is the same AgentVM with the transpiler (and acorn) wired in. So 'the VM contains no parser' is true only of vm-ast.
findings.fix: '...the VM's core contains no parser; tjs-lang/vm-ast ships it without one.'

findings.where: §1 table, Builder row: 'No checks: what you build is what runs.'
findings.problem: The next section says the builder refuses unsupported condition syntax at build time and warns about unmapped names. Both are checks.
findings.evidence: Scratch script review/b.ts: Agent.take().if('a ? 1 : 0', ...) throws 'Unsupported condition syntax near ? 1 : 0'; .if('a > b', { a: 'a' }) warns '[Agent99 Builder] Condition "a > b" references variables not in vars mapping: b'
findings.fix: 'Builds the same AST in code with a fluent API. It does not check atom calls or parameters, as the transpiler does.'

findings.where: §3 'When there is no store capability, the run gets a private in-memory store and a warning.'
findings.problem: The warning appears only once the agent actually reads or writes the store. A run that never touches it gets no warning.
findings.evidence: src/vm/vm.ts: defaultStore.get/set call warn(); a plain run returned warnings: undefined (review/throws.ts)
findings.fix: '...a private in-memory store, and a warning in `warnings` if the agent uses it.'

findings.where: §1 'Passing source to vm.run is deprecated as of 0.14.0 ... If you transpile source you did not write, cap it'
findings.problem: Not mentioned: tjs-lang/vm already caps source given to vm.run at 8 KB by default (the maxSourceBytes run option) and refuses anything longer with an error. Readers who stay on the deprecated path should know the limit exists.
findings.evidence: src/vm/vm.ts: admitted.maxSourceBytes ?? DEFAULT_MAX_SOURCE_BYTES; the doc comment says 'Source is capped at 8KB (maxSourceBytes) meanwhile'
findings.fix: Add one clause: 'vm.run(source) itself refuses source over maxSourceBytes (8 KB by default).'

findings.where: Coverage against the old CONTEXT.md
findings.problem: The rewrite drops the old 'Test Coverage', 'Isomorphic Deployment (Universal Endpoint)' and 'Error Handling Granularity' sections. The brief did not ask to keep them, but the old chapter had nothing else that pointed to docs/universal-endpoint.md, and the brief describes this chapter as including test coverage.
findings.fix: Optional: add a 'Further reading' line linking docs/universal-endpoint.md and the guardrail tests (or CLAUDE.md's guardrail list). Or confirm with the owner that test coverage is out of scope for a reader-facing chapter.

findings.where: Brief checklist
findings.problem: Verified as addressed: metadata now says section 'ajs' with parent 'ajs.md' (guides/ajs.md exists); sections run 1 to 8 with no gaps; tosijs-schema is shown as ^1.12.0 with the reason; vm.run(source) is shown as deprecated with vm-ast recommended. All six typescript examples run and print exactly what the comments say (scratchpad docs-swarm/context/review/ex1-6.ts). The bundle sizes are correct: dist/tjs-vm-ast.js is 137,459 B and 43,005 B with gzip -9; dist/tjs-vm.js is 323,877 B and 97,781 B; both import tosijs-schema externally, and acorn is in tjs-vm.js but not in tjs-vm-ast.js. Also confirmed in source: storeProcedure's proc_ plus UUID tokens, the 1 h TTL, the 100 KB maxSize, 'Invalid AST', fuel costs of 1, 0.1 and 0.5, the version gate both at store time and at resolve time, 'Capability agent.run missing', and the default timeout of max(60 s, 2 x the slowest atom).
findings.fix: None. Recorded so the edit pass knows these claims were checked. One related note: src/vm/vm.ts line ~370 and CLAUDE.md still say the default timeout is 'fuel x 10ms', which is stale. The chapter has it right.

rejected: The final 'polish' finding (the brief checklist) is a record that earlier claims were checked, not a defect, so there was nothing to apply. I kept the claims it confirmed: the sizes, the procedure-store constants and the default timeout.

I applied the 'Dependencies does not belong here' finding only in part. The section is now 'Dependencies and size' and leads with what a vm-ast embedder needs (tosijs-schema only) plus the measured sizes. I kept one short paragraph naming the other runtime packages instead of moving that content to another page, because the rules say I may edit only this file. The finding that 'none of the four has dependencies' is wrong is fixed: acorn-walk and acorn-loose depend only on acorn. 'Branded builders' is now explained.
questions: An inline sub-agent run through agentRun (an AST or a proc_ token) has neither its inputSchema nor its declared result checked. I ran it to confirm: a stored `double({ n: 0 }): { n: 0 }` given { n: 'x' } returned { n: 'strx' } with no error. The chapter now says so in section 6. Should agentRun enforce both schemas the way vm.run does (a sibling of #3834)? If so, it needs a card, and that paragraph should change once it is fixed.

Some host mistakes throw from vm.run and others come back as `error`. Throws: a missing or expired token, an unknown AST format version, a non-seq root, source passed to vm-ast, a failed transpile. Returns: bad options, refused arguments, input/output schema mismatches. Section 2 now documents this as a table and gives the rule ('a mistake about WHAT is being run throws'). Is that split intended, or should the throwing cases also come back as `error`?
Unchanged from the writer's earlier questions: should the chapter stay at nav order 14 (the internals appendix), and is the title 'The AJS VM: Technical Context' acceptable?
revised.summary:
I revised /Users/tonioloewald/tjs-lang/CONTEXT.md and applied every review finding; two I applied only in part, as listed under rejected.

**Clarity fixes**
- The chapter now opens by saying what AJS is for and that it is a subset of TJS. It marks itself as advanced, says who can skip it, and points to DOCS-AJS first.
- A new Terms list defines host, agent ("guest" is noted as a synonym), front end, atom, capability, fuel, membrane and heap ceiling. The fuel entry gives a scale (0.01 per expression node, 0.1 per variable set, 5 for storeSet, 100 for llmPredict, default budget 1000).
- The reason parsing is risky is now spelled out.
- First example: a comment says colon values are examples, and it prints `fuelUsed < 1` to show how much of the 100 fuel it uses.
- Builder example: comments explain `varsImport`, the name map, and the input and output schemas.
- The condition rules are now a list (supported / refused / name map, and the warning is a `console.warn` at build time). A new runnable example shows the varSet workaround. The v1 bare-string hazard is tied to the `'big'` example, with `{ $expr: 'literal', value: 'big' }` as the way to force a plain string.
- Expressions table: `name.trim()` replaces `s.trim()`, "local helper" links to DOCS-AJS helper functions, and the table says what `computed` and the regex engine mean.
- The security table is now one short paragraph per guarantee. The timeout rule now reads "the larger of 60 s and twice the longest atom timeout", the catchable vs run-ending row has an example of each, and `ctx.signal` is glossed as an AbortSignal.
- The `defineAtom` arguments are labelled, and the page says that an atom may throw and the agent can catch that (verified).
- Streaming: says the VM waits for each atom call, so chunks arrive in order, and explains why the callback gets a copy.
- Stored procedures: comments on the `handler` and `'proc_'` parameters; says an AST is legal JSON as a run argument; says `procedureStore` is a Map a host can inspect or clear; shows `maxSize` as a `storeProcedure` input; explains the `op` field; the size charge now links to VM budgets.
- Sub-agents: states the `proc_` prefix rule and shows the minimal `agent.run` capability shape.
- Transactions example: comments on `Error(...)` (AJS has no throw) and on the minimal store capability.
- A Further reading section links ajs-host, vm-budgets and universal-endpoint.

**Accuracy fixes**
- Section 2 adds the root-must-be-seq step (the list now runs 1 to 9). A table shows which failures throw into the host and which come back as `error`; I checked every case by running it. It also mentions `isAgentError`.
- Fixed the broken anchor to `/ajs-host/#fetch-policy`.
- "The VM contains no parser" now says this is true of the VM core and vm-ast, not tjs-lang/vm.
- The Builder row no longer says "no checks".
- The store warning appears only when the agent uses the store (verified).
- Added the 8 KB `maxSourceBytes` default on `vm.run(source)`.
- Documented that inline sub-agents' schemas are not checked (verified).

**Verification**
- All 7 typescript examples (6 kept, 1 new) run and print what their comments say. Scratch files are in /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-tonioloewald-tjs-lang/ceca4d7c-a13f-43be-92e8-1e916ca662c7/scratchpad/docs-swarm/context-md/.
- I ran four guard tests over the repo: doc-snippets, doc-site-structure, repo-hygiene and docs-tombstones. Six tests fail, all in other files that other agents are editing (local-extensions.md, a-calculator.md, dictionary-defaults.md, PRINCIPLES.md) plus the repo-wide fragments ratio. None of the failures is in CONTEXT.md.
- The metadata line is unchanged and line 2 is `<!-- TODO review -->`.

written.changes:
Edited only /Users/tonioloewald/tjs-lang/PRINCIPLES.md. These are clarity and accuracy fixes, since it is a design note.
- Added `<!-- TODO review -->` after the metadata line. The metadata line is unchanged.
- "You cannot lie to a worked example": added a failing `add(a: 2, b: 3): 0` example. It is marked `<!-- tjs-doc: expect-error -->` and uses a ```tjs:static fence, the same pattern guides/learn/functions.md uses. The prose quotes the real error message. After it comes a live ```tjs version with `: 5` that prints 5.
- Subset invariant 1: the `TjsCompat` directive restores JS semantics but still validates parameters at runtime. I measured this. `dialect: 'js'` turns both off.
- Signature-test coverage gap: "tracked in TODO.md" now points to the Virta board. I re-measured that class methods and arrow consts still get no signature test.
- Removed the "Routing all three dialects" recipe and its code block. A three-sentence summary of the rule replaces it (send .ts through fromTS from its own subpath; there is no one-call helper, so the TS compiler stays out of tjs-lang/lang).
- Rewrote the loop section as a general principle: when a lower layer takes on a duty, the layers above stop paying for it. The AJS facts are corrected: AJS keeps `for…of` (bounded) and `while` (unbounded) because fuel guarantees termination, and bans C-style `for(;;)` for legibility. I measured all three. The Starlark contrast is restated to match.
- Ugliness table: `LegacyEquals` is now `DangerousLegacyEquals`.
- Conversion contract: replaced "per-mode directives (TjsCompat, then one mode at a time)" with per-construct migration and a pointer to TJS-SYNTAX. "Enforcement (open)" is now "(partial)" and mentions `test:compat`, which runs six real projects' own test suites against the converted code.
- Shortened "The formal AST contract is AJS's" to two paragraphs. Dropped the "~16 transforms" count. Replaced the stale "unversioned today" node list with the `$ajs` v2/v1 facts and a pointer to DOCS-AJS.md.
- North-star section is now a short pointer to docs/type-system-north-star.md. The earlier "north star below" reference is reworded to match.
- Unchanged: the type-system section, on-ramp/off-ramp with the two confession tests, the subset invariants, "more, never illegal" with signature tests, "make stupid stuff stand out", and the dialect table.
questions: The brief said to move the AJS loop rationale, the AST-contract section and the three-dialect routing recipe out of this chapter. None of them has a home yet: DOCS-AJS.md and the AJS book don't carry the rationale, and the running-tjs chapter doesn't exist. Rather than deleting them, I kept short, corrected versions here. Should they move into the AJS book and a running-tjs or integrations chapter? The full original text is in git history.

TJS-SYNTAX.md line 525 says `TjsCompat // ... JS semantics, safety none`. I measured that this is wrong: a bare `TjsCompat` directive still validates parameters (calling f('x') on `f(n: 0)` returns a MonadicError). Please fix TJS-SYNTAX, or decide whether TjsCompat is supposed to turn validation off.
Only the bare `TjsCompat` statement works as the directive. A `/* TjsCompat */` comment does nothing. Is that intended? Some readers will expect the comment form to work.

findings.where: Conversion contract, obligation 3: "**say so at the site**: `// TJS: \`= 5\` narrows to an integer, \`= +5\` to unsigned`"
findings.problem: Backslash escapes do not work inside a CommonMark code span. The span closes at the first backtick after `\`, so this renders as broken fragments with stray backslashes, and the one concrete example of "guidance at the site" can't be read.
findings.evidence: PRINCIPLES.md line 416: `**say so at the site**: \`// TJS: \\\`= 5\\\` narrows to an integer, \\\`= +5\\\` to unsigned\``
findings.fix: Use a double-backtick code span (`` // TJS: `= 5` narrows to an integer, `= +5` to unsigned ``) or show it as a small fenced code block.

findings.where: "`var` has `let`/`const`; `eval()` has `Eval()`; both are refused outright" (The consequence…) vs. "every legal JavaScript program is legal TJS _with the same meaning_" (Language subset relationships)
findings.problem: Read in order, these contradict each other. First the page says var and eval are refused outright. Two sections later it says every legal JS program is legal TJS. Nothing yet tells the reader that 'refused' applies only to native .tjs files, not to dialect 'js'.
findings.fix: Qualify the first passage at the point it appears ("refused in native `.tjs`; plain JS keeps them via the on-ramp"), or move the subset/dialect sections before the on-ramp/craters section.

findings.where: "`unsafe`, `!`, `:!`, `DangerousLegacyEquals`, `LegacyDefault`, `/* @tjs-unsafe */`: each is named, greppable…" vs. "`unsafe` gated three unrelated things behind one vague marker and could not be removed in one step… two of the three came to be refused and one kept"
findings.problem: First `unsafe` is held up as a model confession. Later it is described as a vague marker that had to be split up. The reader can't tell whether `unsafe` still exists, what its 'three unrelated things' were, or which one was kept.
findings.fix: Name the three things and say what each became (refused, or which named confession replaced it). Also make the first list match the current state of the language.

findings.where: Opening: "Foundational, non-negotiable invariants for the tjs-lang language stack."
findings.problem: This is page 2 of the book, and the page leans on many terms it never defines: AJS, fromTS, modes, dialect, graduation, provenance annotation, atom, fuel, membrane, inline stub, signature test, `:!`, `$predicate`, Timestamp, Eval, observe mode. A first-time reader has met almost none of them yet.
findings.fix: Add a short 'terms used here' box at the top, each with a one-line gloss and a link. Or move this page later in the book, after the syntax and AJS chapters.

findings.where: "**A TJS type is an example: a real value that exists at runtime.**" (line 23), with the first code at line 78
findings.problem: The central idea is stated in the abstract and argued for about 55 lines before the reader sees one example of the syntax. Until then a JS developer has no picture of what `name: 'Alice'` looks like or does.
findings.fix: Put a two-line example (`function greet(name: 'Alice')` plus the `add(a: 2, b: 3): 5` pair) right after that sentence, then give the argument.

findings.where: "That is the same defect this project already knows in another costume: **a gate that alters the thing it measures.** `tosijs-ui` changed its semver policy after finding versions were being chosen to dodge a review…"
findings.problem: This is an internal anecdote about a different project. A reader of a language book doesn't know tosijs-ui, its review process or its semver policy, so the analogy explains nothing.
findings.fix: Replace it with a general example (Goodhart's law, or teaching to the test), or cut it. The `as`/`any`/`@ts-ignore` sentence carries the point by itself.

findings.where: "The uncomfortable corollary… **`fromTS` preserves the lies rather than laundering them.** A TypeScript `: string` becomes `:!`…" / "And it is why `fromTS` degrades the way it does… `:!` records that loss explicitly" / "`:!` exists to say _'I have only a claim here…'_ — which is also what `fromTS` must emit"
findings.problem: The same point (fromTS turns `: string` into `:!`) is made three times in one section. `:!` is never explained in plain terms: is it syntax on the return? what does it do at runtime?
findings.fix: Make the point once, with a before/after code pair (TS `function f(): string` → TJS `function f():! ''`), and say in one sentence what `:!` does.

findings.where: "- **A predicate is code.** `predicate(x) { return typeof x === 'number' && x > 0 }`"
findings.problem: The reader can't tell whether this is real TJS syntax (a declaration form?) or pseudocode. Nothing on the page shows where a predicate is declared or used.
findings.fix: Show the real declaration form (e.g. a `Type` with a predicate) and link to where predicates are taught.

findings.where: "### It adjudicates…": "**Where the inline stub and the real `Type` disagree, the stub is right.**… CLAUDE.md's instruction — _'the stubs are the contract for emitted code; fix them'_"; also the file citations `src/lang/features.test.ts`, `src/lang/equality-invariants.test.ts`, and the word 'canary'
findings.problem: This is contributor-facing material. A book reader doesn't know what the inline stub or the real Type are, what CLAUDE.md is, or what a 'canary' or a 'known-disagreement list' means. The whole subsection reads as internal policy.
findings.fix: Move contributor rules to a contributor doc. Or explain 'emitted code carries a small built-in runtime; that copy is what actually runs' and drop the CLAUDE.md and test-file references.

findings.where: "### Applied to our own documentation" and "Guardable. These are testable properties: keep a fixture of representative AJS/JS snippets…"
findings.problem: Both are about how the maintainers test the project, not something the reader can use. They break the flow of a principles chapter.
findings.fix: Cut them, or collapse them into a single 'how we keep ourselves honest' sidebar with no file paths.

findings.where: "This is what `docs/ambient-contracts.md` is for: TypeScript's `e.target.value` pessimism is a claim…"
findings.problem: 'e.target.value pessimism' is a reference the reader has to already know. Nothing explains what TypeScript does wrong with it.
findings.fix: Add one sentence: TS types `e.target` as `EventTarget`, so `.value` doesn't type-check without a cast, even when the element is plainly an input.

findings.where: "## An on-ramp and an off-ramp… **The on-ramp** — `fromTS` / `dialect: 'js'`. Converted source keeps JavaScript semantics _wholesale_, marked by the provenance annotation… **The off-ramp** — graduation. Remove the annotation… (`src/lang/graduate.ts`)."
findings.problem: 'Provenance annotation', 'graduation' and `dialect` are used before they are defined (dialect is defined three sections later). The annotation's actual text isn't shown. A source path is not an explanation.
findings.fix: Show the annotation as it appears at the top of a converted file, say what graduation does to it, and either move the Dialect section before this one or add a forward link.

findings.where: "Measured, `\"use strict\"` still permits `var` and `eval` — so the lesson is not _which_ constructs were removed…" and "measured, zero occurrences in real `.tjs` source"
findings.problem: 'Measured' sounds like an internal lab note: measured how, and on what corpus? For strict mode it is a well-known fact that needs no measuring, so the word adds noise.
findings.fix: Drop 'Measured,' for strict mode. For the eval count, name the corpus ("in this repo's .tjs sources") or cut it.

findings.where: "`LegacyDate` passes both. A `Date` INSTANCE cannot be produced any other way — `Timestamp` is epoch-ms"
findings.problem: Timestamp has never been introduced. The reader isn't told that TJS refuses `new Date()`, which is why a confession is needed in the first place.
findings.fix: Add one sentence first: 'Native TJS replaces `Date` with `Timestamp` (epoch milliseconds); `LegacyDate()` is how you get a real Date object when an API demands one.'

findings.where: Subset diagram: "JavaScript ⊆ TJS (no modes on) ⊆ TJS (modes on)" and "TJS's footgun-removal rules… are gated on the **dialect**"
findings.problem: 'Modes' is never defined, and the page then moves to 'dialect' for what seems to be the same switch. The reader can't tell whether modes and dialect are one thing or two. The `TjsCompat` paragraph adds 'validation' as a third, independent axis.
findings.fix: Define once: dialect picks the language; in the tjs dialect the footgun rules ('modes') are on; validation is separate. A small 3-column table (dialect / footgun rules / validation) for `.js`, `.tjs`, `TjsCompat` and fromTS would settle it.

findings.where: "TJS may enforce `:` contracts, run signature tests, treat `:` like `->`, etc."
findings.problem: 'Treat `:` like `->`' means nothing to a JS developer. JS has no `->`, and the page never defines it.
findings.fix: Explain it, or remove it from the list.

findings.where: "Measured 2026-09-05, because this list previously also said 'the harness can't execute the module (e.g. multiple top-level functions)' and **that is not true**…"
findings.problem: This is changelog history in a principles chapter. The reader is told about a claim they never saw being withdrawn, which interrupts the worked example.
findings.fix: State the current behaviour plainly and move the correction history to the changelog.

findings.where: "This is a Very Good Thing™"
findings.problem: A jokey aside in a section otherwise about hard rules. Small, but it undercuts the 'non-negotiable' framing.
findings.fix: Cut it.

findings.where: "## When a lower layer takes on a duty…": "Starlark keeps `for`… AJS's guarantee lives in **fuel**… (`S1`/`S4` in ASSUMPTIONS.md)… what a 4B model write correctly?… the capability membrane absorbs host-reference safety, so atom authors…"
findings.problem: Starlark, fuel, the S1/S4 IDs, '4B model', capability membrane, atom authors and verified predicates all arrive at once with no definitions. A TJS reader who hasn't met AJS can't follow the argument.
findings.fix: Spend one sentence each on fuel ('every step costs budget; the run stops when it runs out') and Starlark, replace '4B model' with 'a small language model', and link to the AJS chapter for the rest.

findings.where: Table in "Make stupid stuff stand out": "`Timestamp.now()` | `LegacyDate()`" and "a validated function | `function f(! x: 0)`"
findings.problem: The rows aren't parallel. `Timestamp.now()` returns a number and `LegacyDate()` returns an object, so it is unclear what is being swapped for what. The `!` row shows only the escape and never the 'good' syntax, and the reader hasn't been told that `!` turns off validation.
findings.fix: Use parallel cells (`Timestamp.now()` ↔ `LegacyDate()` as 'the current time', `function f(x: 0)` ↔ `function f(! x: 0)`) and add a third column saying what the escape gives up.

findings.where: Conversion contract, obligation 1: "`n = 5` (TypeScript `number`) converts to `n = 5.0`, which accepts floats and still defaults to `5`"
findings.problem: The example works only if you know that in TJS `5` means 'integer' and `5.0` means 'float'. The page never says so.
findings.fix: Add a clause: 'because in TJS an example of `5` means integer-only, while `5.0` means any number'.

findings.where: "The value still gets delivered, but through **observe mode** — check, record, return the original value"
findings.problem: Observe mode appears in bold as if it were a known feature, but the reader isn't told how to turn it on or where the 'record' goes.
findings.fix: Link to where observe mode is documented, or name the switch and say that records go to the error flight recorder (`__tjs.errors()`).

findings.where: "## The formal AST contract is AJS's…": "it rewrites TJS source to JavaScript text with a set of source transforms and hands that to acorn — and the ecosystem does not need a fifth JavaScript AST"

written.changes:
I rewrote /Users/tonioloewald/tjs-lang/TJS-SYNTAX.md. The first-line metadata is unchanged, `<!-- TODO review -->` is on line 2, and I touched no other file.

**New order** (the order the brief asked for):
1. Parameters: examples, type names, defaults and typed defaults, null defaults, object shapes, dictionary defaults, arrays and rest, literal unions.
2. Return annotations (`:` / `:!` / `:?`).
3. Safety markers, plus the `safety` directive.
4. The rules of `.tjs`: the named escapes, the deprecated `unsafe` prefix, what converted TypeScript gets, and the two dialect directives.
5. Declarations, cut down to one runnable overview that points to /declarations/.
6. Equality, `typeof` and truthiness.
7. `given` (new section).
8. Test blocks (new section).
9. Errors (new section): MonadicError, `isMonadicError`, `.path`/`.expected`/`.actual`, `try` without `catch`, bang access.
10. Classes, then polymorphic constructors.
11. Polymorphic functions.
12. `extend`.
13. `const!`.
14. Bare assignments.
15. Doc comments.
16. Modules and imports (new section).
17. Async functions (new section).
18. WASM, now short and pointing to /DOCS-WASM/.
19. `@tjs` annotations.

Each section links to its chapter, using `/slug/` links like the section page does.

**Accuracy fixes:**
- **Opening section:** the TypeScript-style `constructor(public x: number…)` is gone. Classes now use TJS examples, with a live example of a class called without `new`, and a separate example that is supposed to fail showing that `new` is an error.
- **Intro link:** it now points to Hello TJS instead of DOCS-TJS.
- **TjsCompat:** the old line said "JS semantics, safety none". It is corrected: parameters are still validated, and you add `safety none` to stop that. TjsStrict is described from the parser code, including that it turns unverifiable predicates into errors.
- **`safety`:** `safety all` is described as adding nothing in emitted code, and `?` as having no effect. The section also says why `safety` survived the removal of modes: modes changed what the code means, while `safety` only sets how much is checked at runtime.
- **`extend`:** the runtime-fallback (`registerExtension`) claim is gone. The text now says only literal receivers are rewritten, and that a call on a variable throws `xs.last is not a function`.
- **WASM:** the "no imports/exports" limitation is replaced by `export wasm function` libraries.
- **FunctionPredicate `returnContract`:** settled from `src/types/Type.ts` and the inline stub. It is metadata only: it defaults to `'assertReturns'` and can be set in the block. Nothing throws or wraps a result because of it.
- **`@tjs-unsafe`:** measured with `fromTS`. It still converts to the deprecated `unsafe` prefix, while a plain `new Date` converts to `LegacyDate`. The section says so. It also says that `example`/`predicate`/`declaration`/`skip` apply only to the interface or type alias that follows (I measured this).
- **Equality example:** it now uses `Is(a, b)`, and the limits of the infix spelling are moved into prose.
- **`const!`:** corrected to shallow. I measured that a nested write, a second binding, and a function argument can all still change the value.
- **Fences:** every `typescript` fence is now `tjs:inline` (runs live) or `tjs:static`. The `@tjs` listing uses `javascript`.

**Verification:**
- **Live examples (27):** each one extracted, run through `tjs check` (all pass), then `tjs run`, with the output compared to the comments.
- **Examples that must fail (3):** confirmed they fail `check`.
- **Fragments (5, of 35 blocks):** the module example was run separately as two files under the Bun plugin.
- **Tests:** `bun test src/doc-snippets.test.ts`, filtered to TJS-SYNTAX, passes 31 of 31. `docs-tombstones`, `doc-site-structure` and `repo-hygiene` pass.

findings.where: ## Control flow: `given` — "TJS accepts every JavaScript program, so it cannot change what `switch` means." (also ## Dialect: "or TJS would stop accepting every JavaScript program")
findings.problem: Earlier on the same page, the rules table says a `.tjs` file rejects `var`, `eval()`, `new Date` and `new` on a local class. To a first-time reader, "TJS accepts every JavaScript program" flatly contradicts that table. The page never explains that the superset claim covers JS-dialect input (`.js`, `TjsCompat`, converted TS) and not `.tjs` files. As written, the reader is left wondering why `switch` must be preserved when `var` was not.
findings.fix: State the invariant once, early (at 'The rules of .tjs'): 'JavaScript source, in its own dialect, is always accepted; a `.tjs` file opts into stricter rules.' Then rephrase the `switch` sentence: because `switch` is legal JavaScript that the strict rules do not ban, TJS keeps its meaning and steers you to `given` with a warning instead.

findings.where: Named escapes table: "JavaScript's `===` / `!==` | `LegacyExactly(a, b)`" and example "LegacyExactly(NaN, NaN) // false, as NaN === NaN is"; vs the Equality table: "`===` | identity, as in JavaScript"
findings.problem: If `===` in TJS is 'as in JavaScript', there is no reason for an escape named 'JavaScript's ===' to exist. The NaN comment hints that TJS `===` differs from JS (maybe NaN equals NaN?), but the page never says so. The reader cannot tell what TJS `===` actually does.
findings.fix: In the Equality section, say exactly how TJS `===` differs from JS (e.g. NaN, ±0), with an inline example. Otherwise remove LegacyExactly from the escapes table.

findings.where: Rules table: "statements | a newline ends a statement"
findings.problem: This is a big change for a JS developer and gets one table cell. It leaves open: how to continue an expression across lines (leading-dot method chains, a long `&&` condition, an arrow function returning an object), whether a trailing operator continues the line, and whether semicolons are still allowed. Several examples on the page contain multi-line constructs, and the reader cannot tell why those are fine.
findings.fix: Add a short subsection with an example: what continues a line (open bracket, trailing operator?), what does not (leading `.`?), and what the error looks like.

findings.where: ## Parameters, first example: "it returns a `MonadicError` (see [Errors](#errors))" and `isMonadicError(greet(42))`
findings.problem: The first example on the page relies on `isMonadicError` and MonadicError, but these are only explained around 500 lines later. A reader sees `console.log(isMonadicError(...)) // true` everywhere without knowing that it is a global, what the error object holds, or why it is not thrown.
findings.fix: Add one or two sentences after the first example: 'A refused call returns an error value instead of throwing; `isMonadicError(x)` (always in scope) tells you whether you got one. More under Errors.'

findings.where: "function scale(rate: 3.14) ... // a number (has a decimal point)" then `scale(2) // 4`; later "`rate: float`", "`n: number`", "`number[]` ... rewritten to [0.0]", "`number` keeps meaning 'any number'"
findings.problem: The comment suggests the argument must have a decimal point, yet `scale(2)` is accepted. The page then uses 'float', 'number', `3.14` and `0.0` without saying whether they are all the same check. 'int[] narrows where number[] does not' suggests float == number == any number, but this is never stated outright.
findings.fix: State directly: 'A decimal example (`3.14`, `0.0`), `float` and `number` all accept any number, integers included; `42`/`int` accept only integers; `+0`/`unsigned` only non-negative integers.' Rewrite the comment as 'any number'.

findings.where: ### Literal unions — "This is the one place the examples model bends. Read as examples, `'on' | 'off'` would widen to `string | string`, which says nothing, so it is read the way a reader reads it. A union that does say something as examples (`0 | ''`) keeps the example rule."
findings.problem: The rule for when a union is a closed set and when it is a union of types is hard to work out. 'Read the way a reader reads it' is vague. The reader still doesn't know whether `0 | 1` accepts only 0 and 1 (the next paragraph implies yes) or any integer, or what `0 | null` (used earlier as 'an integer or null') means under this rule. 'All literals of the same type' is the actual rule, but only the heading sentence says it.
findings.fix: Give the rule as a table: `'on' | 'off'` → only those values; `0 | 1` → only 0 and 1; `0 | ''` → any integer or any string; `0 | null` → any integer or null. Drop the 'reader reads it' phrasing.

findings.where: "function grant(mode: 'grant' | 'deny' = 'grant') { return mode } // a type AND a default" and "It is how you give a literal union a default."
findings.problem: The page's central idea is that 'the value after a colon is an example, not a type', yet here the colon value is called a type. The reader also hasn't seen literal unions yet (they come later), so it is unclear why `mode = 'grant'` alone would not do.
findings.fix: Move the `name: Type = default` paragraph after Literal unions, or add a forward note: '`mode = 'grant'` would accept any string; the union restricts it.' Use one term consistently ('example/type annotation') or define when the page says 'type'.

findings.where: "function opt(name?: '') { return name } // the same as name = ''" with `opt()` → `""`
findings.problem: TypeScript developers read `name?:` as 'may be undefined'. Here it silently becomes a default of `''`. This difference from TS is a major gotcha and is stated only in a code comment.
findings.fix: Add a prose sentence: 'Unlike TypeScript, `x?: ''` does not leave `x` undefined; it defaults to the example.'

findings.where: ## Return annotations — "When the file is transpiled, the function is called with its parameter examples and the result must equal the annotation"
findings.problem: Running user code at build time is surprising, and the page doesn't address the obvious worries: what if the function does IO, has side effects, or is slow? The 'inconclusive' rule that partly answers this appears only much later, under Test blocks.
findings.fix: Add a sentence here: what runs, in what environment, and that a call that throws or needs an import is 'inconclusive' rather than failing (link to Test blocks). Say that `:!` is the opt-out for functions with side effects.

findings.where: Terminology: 'worked example', 'signature example', 'signature test', 'transpiled', 'built', 'compile error', 'fails the build'
findings.problem: The same concepts get several names across sections. A reader wonders whether a 'signature example' (Test blocks) is the same as a 'worked example' (Return annotations), and whether 'compile error' differs from 'fails the build'.
findings.fix: Pick one name each (e.g. 'worked example' and 'transpile error'), define it once, and use it throughout.

findings.where: ## Safety markers — "under `safety none` a `?` does not switch the checks back on" (before `### The safety directive` is introduced); and "There is no `unsafe { }` block."
findings.problem: `safety none` is used before it is defined. Denying an `unsafe { }` block the reader never heard of raises more questions than it answers. Later the page adds the deprecated `unsafe <expression>` and a `/* unsafe */` marker (in the doc-comment example). That makes three 'unsafe' forms, none clearly explained.
findings.fix: Introduce the `safety` directive before markers, or link forward. Remove the `unsafe { }` denial, or put it in a short 'Removed syntax' note. Explain or remove the `/* unsafe */` marker in the doc-comment example.

findings.where: ### The safety directive — "`safety` is not one of the abolished modes. A mode changed what the source _means_..."
findings.problem: 'The abolished modes' is used before the page says that modes ever existed (that comes in the next section, 'nine mode directives that used to provide one were removed'). A reader new to TJS has no idea what this is defending against. The parenthetical about `wrap()` and hosts using a global `safety: 'all'` is internal detail in a syntax reference.
findings.fix: Move the history to one short note in 'The rules of .tjs' (or cut it). Drop or footnote the `wrap()` parenthetical. Since `safety all` does nothing today, say so plainly in a single line.

findings.where: ### Converted TypeScript and ### Dialect — "a converted file keeps its behaviour when it graduates to native `.tjs` (`graduate()`)" / "TjsStrict // full TJS, for TS-originated source (where the default is JavaScript semantics)"
findings.problem: The reader can't picture what a 'converted file' physically is: which extension, what the `/* tjs <- … */` annotation looks like, and what 'graduate' does. It is also confusing that conversion writes named escapes so the code works under TJS rules, while converted code still defaults to JavaScript semantics. Why would it need both?

findings.where: ## Async functions: "The return example describes the resolved value and is not run as a test, and the resolved value is not checked at runtime"
findings.problem: This holds for `:` and `:!`, but not for `:?`. With `:?` on an async function the resolved value is checked at runtime, and a wrong result resolves to a MonadicError. The doc states it with no exception, and the Return annotations section sends readers here.
findings.evidence: async function f(a: 1):? 1 { return 'str' }; const r = await f(1).catch(e => 'REJECTED'); console.log(isMonadicError(r)) -> `true MonadicError: Expected integer for 'asyncres2.tjs:1:f:return', got string` (it resolved, it did not reject). The same function with `: 999` and a wrong value passes `tjs check` and prints 1, which confirms the return example is not run.
findings.fix: Write: "The return example is not run as a test. With `:` or `:!` the resolved value is not checked; with `:?` it is, and a wrong result resolves to a MonadicError." Make the matching sentence under Return annotations agree.

findings.where: ## Equality: "`Is` also has an infix spelling ... only recognises simple operands (a name, a dotted path, a literal) in a statement of its own. Inside an argument list, or with an object literal or a call as an operand, it is misread or fails to parse."
findings.problem: The listed failure cases mostly work. An infix `Is` inside an argument list, with an object-literal operand, or with `Math.max(1, 2)` as the left operand all give the right answer. What actually fails is a bare call on the left (`f() Is a`), which fails to build.
findings.evidence: `console.log(a Is {x:1})` -> true; `console.log(Math.max(1, 2) Is 2, a Is [1])` -> true true; `console.log(1, a Is b)` -> 1 true; `console.log(a Is 1 ? 'y' : 'n')` -> y. `console.log(f() Is a)` -> `Runtime error: 2 errors building ...`, and `const r = f() Is a` -> `Expected ";" but found "const"`.
findings.fix: Narrow the caveat to what was measured: "the infix form is a source rewrite and some operands, such as a call on the left (`f() Is a`), do not parse. Prefer `Is(a, b)`." Or drop the specifics and keep only the recommendation.

findings.where: ## Bare assignments: "A later `Settings = …` in the same file is a const reassignment and throws"
findings.problem: The second assignment is not a runtime throw. The file fails to compile, because the second bare assignment is also turned into a declaration.
findings.evidence: `Settings = { debug: true }` followed by `Settings = 2` -> tjs check: `✗ ... > 2 | Settings = 2  ^ Identifier 'Settings' has already been declared` (a syntax error at transpile time).
findings.fix: "A second `Settings = …` in the same file does not compile ('Identifier has already been declared'), so declare `let Settings` yourself if it needs to change."

findings.where: ## extend: "only when the receiver is a literal (a string or template literal, an array literal, a number)"
findings.problem: "a number" is too broad. Only a number literal with a decimal point is rewritten. Integer and parenthesised numbers are not, and the call fails at runtime. local-extensions.md has a table that says exactly this, so the two pages disagree.
findings.evidence: `extend Number { dbl() { return this * 2 } }; console.log((3).dbl())` -> `Runtime error: 3 .dbl is not a function`; `console.log(3.5.dbl())` -> 7. guides/examples/tjs/local-extensions.md:137-140: "a number with a decimal point: `7.5`, `12.0` | yes ... an integer or parenthesised number: `(7)`, `7..clamp` | no".
findings.fix: Change to "a number literal with a decimal point (`7.5`)" and add a pointer to the receiver table in Local Class Extensions.

findings.where: ## Equality: "`==` stays fast because it is not structural ... Objects can define their own equality: a `[tjsEquals]` method ... is used first, then an `.Equals` method, then the structural comparison."
findings.problem: The paragraph opens with `==`, so a reader can take the hooks to apply to `==`. They apply only to `Is`/`IsNot`; `==` ignores both hooks. A comment in src/lang/runtime.ts:94 says the opposite ("control how `==` / `Is()`"), which is a source-comment drift worth reporting separately.
findings.evidence: An object with `[Symbol.for('tjs.equals')]` returning true: `a == b` -> false, `Is(a, b)` -> true. A class with `Equals(o) { return true }`: `A(1) == A(2)` -> false, `Is(A(1), A(2))` -> true.
findings.fix: Say "`Is` lets objects define their own equality: ... `==` never calls these hooks." Separately, flag the runtime.ts:94 comment to its owner.

findings.where: ## WASM: "today a wasm function returns `f64` or nothing"
findings.problem: This is accurate (DOCS-WASM:123, 402), but `: i32` is accepted without a warning and quietly returns an f64. A reader who writes `: i32` will think it is honoured.
findings.evidence: `wasm function f(a: i32): i32 { return a * 2 }` passes check, and `f(3)` -> `6 number`. DOCS-WASM.md:402: "`i32`, `f32`, `v128` returns are parsed but not yet emitted as the bytecode return type."
findings.fix: Add: "`: i32` and other return types are accepted but the result is still returned as `f64`."

findings.where: ## Test blocks: "A test that needs something the transpiler cannot load (an import, a host object), is reported as inconclusive"
findings.problem: Accurate, and verified: a test importing a missing module, and a signature example that throws, both pass `tjs check`. The section does not say where inconclusive results are visible (`testResults.inconclusive` / the `'report'` mode), so a reader cannot find out that a test was skipped.
findings.evidence: src/lang/tests.ts:372-374 returns `{ passed, failed, results, inconclusive }`. `tjs check` on `import { x } from './nope.tjs'; test 'imp' { expect(x).toBe(1) }` -> ✓ with nothing reported.
findings.fix: Add one clause: inconclusive results are listed in `testResults.inconclusive` when you pass `runTests: 'report'`.

findings.where: ### Converted TypeScript: "makes `graduate()` refuse, naming the site"
findings.problem: `graduate()` does not throw. It returns a result with a `refused` field that holds the eval message; the measured message did not include a line number. "Refuse, naming the site" overstates this a little.
findings.evidence: graduate(fromTS('function e(s: string) { return eval(s) }').code) -> `{ code: ..., notes: [], upgraded: 0, refused: "`eval()` is not allowed in TJS. Use `Eval()`..." }`
findings.fix: "graduate() refuses: its result's `refused` field says why, and the code is returned unchanged."

revised.summary:
I revised /Users/tonioloewald/tjs-lang/TJS-SYNTAX.md and edited no other file. The metadata line and the `<!-- TODO review -->` line are unchanged.

**The three wrong-severity findings, each checked by running it first:**
- An async `:?` function's result is checked at runtime. The Async section and the Return annotations section now say so, and the async example shows it.
- A second bare assignment does not transpile ("Identifier has already been declared"); the page used to say it throws at runtime.
- `extend` rewrites only number literals with a decimal point. `(3).dbl()` fails at runtime and `3.5.dbl()` works. The page now links to the receiver table.

**Smaller accuracy fixes:**
- `Is`/`.Equals` hooks: `==` never calls them.
- A wasm `: i32` return still comes back as an f64.
- `graduate()` reports a refusal in its `refused` field rather than throwing.
- With `runTests: 'report'`, inconclusive results appear in `testResults` marked `inconclusive: true`.
- TJS `===` is unchanged from JavaScript (NaN === NaN is false). So `LegacyExactly` is the same as `===`; it moved out of the escapes table into a note.
- The redundant `x !== null` in the Generic example is gone, and the page says why: `typeof null` is `'null'` in TJS.

**Clarity fixes:**
- The superset rule is stated at the start of 'The rules of .tjs': JavaScript in its own dialect is always accepted, and `.tjs` opts into stricter rules. The `switch` sentence now follows from that.
- New subsection 'Statements and newlines', written from insertAsiProtection: lines starting with `(`, `[` or a backtick begin a new statement; a leading `.` or a trailing operator continues the line; semicolons are allowed.
- `isMonadicError` is explained right after the first example.
- Plain rules for the numeric examples and for literal unions, written as lists.
- The `x?:` difference from TypeScript is now stated in prose.
- `name: Type = default` is motivated, with a forward link to literal unions.
- The Return annotations section now covers inconclusive signature tests and `:!` as the opt-out for side effects, and uses one set of terms (worked example, signature test, "does not transpile").
- The `unsafe { }` denial is removed, the doc-comment example no longer mentions `/* unsafe */`, and the modes history moved into the rules section.
- Converted TypeScript gets a before/after example (verified with fromTS) and an explanation of why the annotation and the escapes coexist.
- Declarations: added notes on descriptions, the `Even` shorthand, Type<T> vs Generic, and fuel. The FunctionPredicate paragraph is shorter.
- The truthiness escape sentence is fixed.
- The bang-access path is explained, and `__tjs` and 'metadata' are defined.
- A runnable mock example is added.
- API and CLI names are written out in full.
- The `extend` limitation now comes first.
- The WASM note explains why `Float32Array` is needed and that `!` also drops the `len` check.
- Added the tuple note, links for Timestamp/Eval/AJS/Learn to Program, clearer comments in the `repeat` example, the word 'sound' dropped, and a real `assert` message.

**Verification:** I extracted all 29 live tjs:inline examples; each one passes `tjs check` with no warnings, and `tjs run` output matches the comments. The modules fragment ran as two real files under the Bun plugin. `bun test src/doc-snippets.test.ts` filtered to TJS-SYNTAX passes 32 of 32. Two tests in docs-tombstones currently fail, both in other files (docs/dictionary-defaults.md and PRINCIPLES.md).

findings.where: Title: "Ambient Contracts — probe reality, derive verified predicate contracts"
findings.problem: The title uses three terms the page never defines: 'ambient', 'contract' and 'verified predicate'. 'Ambient' gets a parenthetical list in the first paragraph ('the DOM, Node globals, `window`, host objects') but never a definition. 'Contract' is first used as 'predicate contracts' at line 58 and only explained much later, in the 'Contract vs. shim' section. 'Predicate' and 'verified' are assumed throughout ('That predicate is exactly what the verifier accepts').
findings.fix: Add a short glossary-style opening paragraph. Ambient = objects the environment hands your code that you didn't create (the browser's `document`, an event, Node's `process`). Predicate = a function that answers true/false about a value. Verified = TJS has checked it is pure (it only reads, never changes anything, and never throws). Contract = a predicate that describes what an object must look like. Link to the chapter where predicates and `verifyPredicate` are taught.

revised.summary:
I revised /Users/tonioloewald/tjs-lang/docs/ambient-contracts.md, keeping it to clarity and accuracy fixes because it is a design note. The metadata line and the TODO review marker are unchanged.

What changed:
- **Opening.** The status block now opens with 'a direction, not a feature you can use today' and points to what you can use now: verifyPredicate and tjs-lang/css. A short paragraph after it defines ambient, predicate, verified and contract.
- **TypeScript example.** The prose now explains the TypeScript error for JS-only readers and shows the instanceof form. The bold claim now says a runtime check tells you whether the value is there, and the cast tells you nothing.
- **Smaller fixes.**
  - Defined pure and total.
  - Added the missing paragraph break and a sentence on why hand-writing predicates is a problem.
  - Glossed .d.ts/lib.dom, happy-dom, suggest() (with a red/blue example) and realm.

  - Explained the AJS VM's capabilities.

written.changes:
Edited only /Users/tonioloewald/tjs-lang/docs/case-study-switch.md. It is a design note, so I fixed clarity and accuracy and did not expand it. Changes:
- Metadata: changed to {"parent": "the-tjs-language.md", "order": 10}, the shape its sibling design notes use. I dropped the legacy `section: home` and `navTitle`, and added `<!-- TODO review -->` on line 2.
- §3: the note now names the probe's path, the model (qwen3.8-27b) and N=5. The "one-line comment took it to 5/5" claim was overstated. Per switch-probe-results.md and FINDINGS.md, that only happened on the 27B model; gemma-4-e4b scored 0/5 on every TJS arm, comment or not. The prose now says so.
- §4: the table now names the model and says that the "new keyword" arm was `match`.
- §5: one claim was wrong. `match (x) { }` written on one line is a SyntaxError in node. It is only valid JS when the brace is on the next line, where automatic semicolon insertion makes it a call followed by a block. I rewrote it to say that, and to say that `match x {` is never valid JS.
- §7 "What survives": the eleven arms were replicated on the 27B model. Only the first two findings also hold on the 4B. The inline-comment finding is now limited to models large enough to use it.
- §9/§10: the `else if` extension appeared in both sections. I removed it from §9 and kept it in §10, marked as considered and not taken.
- §10: "Still open" is dated 2026-11-06 and says that neither item has a card on the Virta board. I checked with `virta ls`/`virta similar`; the only related cards are #1792 and #1797, both in review.
- §1 keeps four problems. guides/examples/tjs/given-dispatch.md already says four and no longer cites the 4/5 figure, so the critic's alignment concerns are already met in that file. I did not touch it.

Examples: the note's only code fence is an illustrative `js` sketch containing `…`, and it has no tjs/ajs fences. I checked the note's claims against the code in my scratch dir:

findings.where: Opening (lines 6-14), before section 1

findings.where: §2: "It also needed `Exactly(…)` underneath, because a discriminant is a literal and the example rule widens `kind: 'circle'` to "a string", which is why `Circle` and `Rect` looked identical to the dispatcher."
