The phrase "says 'an object'" fits `{}` but not the detailed one.
findings.fix: Lay out the three return forms side by side (`:` = test only, `:!` = declaration only with no test and no check, used for docs and types, `:?` = test plus a check on every call). Say what the `processUserData` shape is used for, if not checking.

findings.where: "A wrapper declared `:? ['']` around `map(users, 'age')` returns a `MonadicError` on its first call: ... Expected array of string for '…names:return', got array of number"
findings.problem: This example refers to code that isn't on the page. There is no `map` import and no function called `names`, and the reader has to piece together a wrapper from fragments. It is also the only illustration of `:?`, the form the page recommends for distrusted libraries, and it can't be seen running.
findings.fix: Show the full function (e.g. `function names(users: [{ name: '', age: 0 }]):? [''] { return map(users, 'age') }`), add `map` to the import or to a second snippet, and say what call produces the error.

findings.where: `expect(sortByAge('not an array') instanceof Error).toBe(true)` vs prose "comes back as a `MonadicError` naming the parameter"
findings.problem: The prose says the result is a `MonadicError` but never defines the term. The test checks `instanceof Error`, so the reader has to guess that a MonadicError is an Error subclass. It is also not said that the error is *returned* rather than thrown. A JS developer would expect a throw and a try/catch.
findings.fix: Define it the first time it appears: "a `MonadicError`, an Error object that is returned instead of thrown". Either test with the documented check (`isMonadicError`) or say why `instanceof Error` works.

findings.where: "The last line prints the wrapper's refusal: `Expected array of object for '…sortByAge.users', got string`."
findings.problem: The `…` in the message isn't explained. Is it literal output, or did the doc cut something out? Also, only the last line of output is described. The reader isn't told what the other three `console.log` lines print, so they can't check their understanding against the run.
findings.fix: Show the full expected console output in a text block (e.g. `Unique users: 3`, `Departments: ['Engineering', 'Sales']`, `Engineering team: ['Alice', 'Carol']`, then the error). Either show the full error path or say that the module/file prefix has been shortened.

findings.where: Ordering: code block, then "The boundary is the signature", then "Worked returns and type-only returns"
findings.problem: The reader meets the most surprising behaviour (a return annotation is a test that runs lodash at check time) inside the code, explained only by terse comments like "A worked example: called with the two users shown, it must return them youngest first". The full explanation comes two sections after the code. While reading the code, the reader has no model for `:!` or for why `uniqueByEmail` has two records with the same email.
findings.fix: Move the "Worked returns and type-only returns" explanation, or a short version of it, above the code block. Or split the code: show `sortByAge` alone with its explanation first, then the others.

findings.where: "Array examples nest: `[['a', 'b'], ['c']]` is an array of arrays of strings."
findings.problem: This sentence repeats the code comment on `paginate` and is left on its own at the end of the `:?` section, where it has nothing to do with the surrounding text.
findings.fix: Delete it, or move it next to the `paginate` bullet in the worked-returns list.

findings.where: "With the `tjs` CLI, `tjs check` and `tjs test` run the tests at transpile time, beside the module's text, where a package import is not loaded."
findings.problem: "beside the module's text" is vague. The reader can't picture what environment the tests run in, or why imports are not loaded there. "On this page ... the tests and worked examples run beside it" uses "beside" in a different sense, which makes it more confusing.
findings.fix: Say it concretely: at transpile time TJS runs the tests in an isolated sandbox that has the module's own code but does not resolve `import` statements. On this page the tests run in the browser after the import has loaded.

findings.where: "so on the CLI the whole module cannot execute and even `the wrapper refuses what lodash would accept`, which never reaches lodash, comes out inconclusive."
findings.problem: This contradicts the previous paragraph, which says the transpile-time run never loads imports. If imports never load, every test that uses an imported name fails, whatever the top level does. So why blame `processUserData({ users })` at the bottom? The advice "keep demo calls out of the module you test" then reads as if it would make the CLI tests pass, which the previous paragraph says they cannot.
findings.fix: Separate the two effects. (1) Tests that call lodash are always inconclusive on the CLI. (2) Top-level code that calls lodash also makes the tests that don't touch lodash inconclusive. Say what moving the demo calls out actually buys you: the non-lodash tests run.

findings.where: "(see _Date Formatting (with import)_ and _CDN Hints_)"
findings.problem: These are italic names, not links. The reader doesn't know where those pages are, or whether _CDN Hints_ is a page or a section.
findings.fix: Make them real links.

findings.where: Gotchas: "A rule like that belongs in the function body, or in a `Type` with a predicate."
findings.problem: `Type` and "predicate" appear here for the first time with no explanation or link, so the suggested fix is out of reach for this reader.
findings.fix: Link to the Type/predicate docs, or show a two-line `Type` that checks `key` is one of the allowed field names.

findings.where: Intro: "lodash is untyped JavaScript. This example wraps four of its functions"
findings.problem: The page assumes the reader knows lodash and what `groupBy`, `sortBy`, `uniqBy` and `chunk` do. The page also covers five functions (`processUserData` is a fifth, combining the others), which makes "four" slightly confusing.
findings.fix: Add a one-clause gloss for each lodash function, or a link to lodash's docs. Say "four wrappers plus a pipeline that combines them".

findings.where: "Gotchas: **`age: 40` is an integer.** ... Write `age: 40.0` if fractional ages are valid."
findings.problem: This affects the main example, but it only appears in the last bullet. A reader who tries `age: 25.5` in the playground gets refused without knowing why, and the same rule silently applies to `id: 0` and `count: 0`.
findings.fix: Mention the integer reading where `sortByAge` is first explained, or add a code comment on `age: 40`.

findings.where: ## Where the tests run… — "With the `tjs` CLI, `tjs check` and `tjs test` run the tests at transpile time… Every test that reaches lodash is reported _inconclusive_ (`?`)"
findings.problem: Only `tjs test` prints the `?` inconclusive lines. `tjs check` runs the tests too, but says nothing about inconclusive ones. It prints a tick and the signatures, then exits 0, so a reader using `check` sees no sign that the tests did not run.
findings.evidence: `bun src/cli/tjs.ts check ex.tjs` prints `✓ …/ex.tjs` plus 5 signature lines and exits 0, with no `?` lines. `bun src/cli/tjs.ts test ex.tjs` prints 6 lines of `? … inconclusive: Module could not be executed for testing: uniqBy is not defined` and `0 passed, 0 failed, 6 inconclusive`, exit 0. src/cli/commands/check.ts never reports inconclusive results.
findings.fix: Say that `tjs test` lists every lodash-dependent test and worked example as `?` (inconclusive) and exits 0, while `tjs check` stays silent about them and also exits 0. A green `check` here means the tests did not run, not that they passed.

findings.where: Gotchas — "Excess keys pass… which is how `processUserData` accepts full user records."
findings.problem: The behaviour is real, but the example given is wrong. processUserData's parameter example lists all four fields (`id, name, email, dept`), and the users passed to it have exactly those fields, so no excess key is involved. The function that does accept extra fields is `groupUsers`, whose example has only `name` and `dept`.
findings.evidence: `groupUsers([{ id: 1, name: 'a', dept: 'eng', email: 'x' }], 'dept')` run with `tjs run` returns `[ "eng" ]`, so excess keys are accepted. processUserData's signature at lines 46-48 of the chapter declares `{ id: 0, name: '', email: '', dept: '' }`.
findings.fix: Use groupUsers: "so `groupUsers` accepts the full user records (with `id` and `email`) even though its example names only `name` and `dept`." Or have the Try-it section pass full records to groupUsers.

findings.where: "`tjs run` does load it from `node_modules`, so the console output is real."
findings.problem: `tjs run` resolves the import the way Bun does. lodash-es is not in this repo's node_modules, yet the example runs. With no node_modules directory, Bun auto-installs the package from its cache. Saying "from node_modules" suggests the reader must install lodash-es first, and leaves them unable to explain why it works when they have not.
findings.evidence: `bun -e "require.resolve('lodash-es')"` in the repo root gives `Cannot find package 'lodash-es'`. Even so, `tjs run` on the example copied to /private/tmp/claude-501/lodtest/ (no node_modules anywhere above it) prints `Unique users: 3 / Departments: [Engineering, Sales] / Engineering team: [Alice, Carol] / Expected array of object for 'ex.tjs:11:sortByAge.users', got string`.
findings.fix: Write "`tjs run` loads the package the way Bun resolves any import (your node_modules, or Bun's auto-install), so the console output is real."

findings.where: "A wrapper declared `:? ['']` around `map(users, 'age')` returns a `MonadicError` on its first call"
findings.problem: The prose says `:?` runs the worked example as well as checking every result. That means this wrapper's worked example would fail first: the ages map to `[0]`, which does not deep-equal `['']`. On the page the reader would see a failed signature test before any call. The wrapper is not shown, so the reader cannot work this out.
findings.evidence: Probe: `function names(users: [{ name: '', age: 0 }]):? [''] { return map(users, 'age') }`. Calling it under `tjs run` returns `Expected array of string for 'probe.tjs:8:names:return', got array of number` (matches the chapter). Its signature example compares `[0]` with `['']`, which fails whenever lodash is available, as on the page.
findings.fix: Show the wrapper in a fence, and say that both checks would catch it: the worked example fails on the page, and a real call returns the MonadicError shown.

findings.where: Brief: "Use the canonical form (or, if both are legal, say so once in TJS-SYNTAX)"
findings.problem: The chapter now uses the canonical `test 'name' { }` and no longer imports `debounce`, as the brief asked. But the parenthesised form `test('name') { }` is also legal, and TJS-SYNTAX.md does not mention it. guides/examples/tjs/local-module-imports.md:127 also uses `test('calculate', () => {`. The brief's "say so once in TJS-SYNTAX" is still open (that file is outside this chapter).
findings.evidence: A file containing `test('paren form') { expect(f(2)).toBe(2) }` gives `✓ 'paren form':2` under `bun src/cli/tjs.ts test`. `grep "test(" TJS-SYNTAX.md` finds nothing.
findings.fix: Hand this to whoever owns TJS-SYNTAX.md: add one sentence there saying `test('name') { }` is also accepted and `test 'name' { }` is the house form. Nothing to change in this chapter.

findings.where: "If the CDN is unreachable, the import fails, so the example stops at its first line with an error instead of printing, and its tests cannot run."
findings.problem: This matches the code but I did not see it in a browser. tosijs-ui rewrites the import to `const { … } = await import('<prefix>lodash-es')` (tosijs-ui src/live-example/code-transform.ts, rewriteBareImportsToDynamic), and the test runner is appended after the code, so a rejected import aborts before any output and before any test. The prose does not say what the error looks like, and the brief asks for what the reader sees.
findings.evidence: tjs-site.config.ts:150 `importResolver: true`. code-transform.ts:146 `await import(${q}${urlFor(spec)}${q})`. component.ts:2070 `${whole.code}\n${api.testUtils}\nreturn ${whole.testRunner}`.
findings.fix: Load the page offline in `bun run preview:site`, or block jsDelivr in devtools, and quote the actual message. It is likely to be the browser's "Failed to fetch dynamically imported module …", or whatever the import-resolver service worker returns. Also note that a copy the service worker cached on an earlier visit may still load.

findings.where: Brief item: "Verify that `sortByAge`'s worked example really runs lodash"
findings.problem: Verified, and the chapter is right. With real lodash supplied, all three test blocks and all three worked examples pass. Replacing sortBy with a reversed sort makes the sortByAge worked example fail. On the doc site, signature examples go into tjs-lang's `testRunner` (src/lang/emitters/js.ts:3461, runnerSigInfos) and run beside the imported module, so the claim that they pass in the page is sound. No change needed. This entry records the evidence.
findings.evidence: A bun script that put lodash's groupBy, sortBy, uniqBy and chunk on globalThis and transpiled the chapter's code without its import line got PASS for all 6 results. With the reversed sortBy it threw `Expected [{name: "Bo", age: 25}, {name: "Ann", age: 40}] at 'sortByAge', got [{name: "Ann", age: 40}, {name: "Bo", age: 25}]`.
findings.fix: None.

rejected: Part of the '/# ... #/ unexplained' finding: its suggestion to check whether the delimiter should be `/*# ... */` was wrong. TJS-SYNTAX.md ('Doc comments: `/# … #/`') makes `/# … #/` the canonical TJS form, and `/*# */` is the .ts convention. I kept the delimiter and added a sentence plus a link explaining it.

TJS-SYNTAX parenthesised `test('name') { }` form: correct, but it needs an edit to TJS-SYNTAX.md, which is outside this chapter. The chapter already uses the canonical `test 'name' { }`. Nothing changed here.

Partly rejected: 'quote the actual offline error message'. I couldn't load the site offline from this agent. The CDN-unreachable bullet stays hedged and quotes no message. I added that a copy the service worker cached earlier may still load.
Verified, no change needed: 'sortByAge worked example really runs lodash'. I put real lodash on globalThis and transpiled: all 3 tests and 3 worked examples passed.
questions: Should TJS-SYNTAX.md get one sentence saying `test('name') { }` also parses and `test 'name' { }` is the house form? guides/examples/tjs/local-module-imports.md:127 uses the parenthesised form.
Please confirm in a browser what the doc site shows when the CDN is unreachable, so the chapter can quote the real error text.
The error line in the output block uses `<file>:12:` (the line number comes from `tjs run`; the file name differs per environment). Confirm the live site reports line 12 too.

written.changes:
Rewrote /Users/tonioloewald/tjs-lang/guides/examples/tjs/object-types.md (only file touched). Metadata line unchanged; moved `<!-- TODO review -->` to line 2, where the ground rules put it. The ground rules require that marker, so I did not follow the critic's "strip TODO". Changes:
- Replaced `getFullName(...): ' '` with `fullName(person: { first: 'Ada', last: 'Lovelace' }): 'Ada Lovelace'`, a real worked example. Added a bullet on why realistic examples make the signature test worth having.
- `distance` now has the worked example `p2: { x: 3, y: 4 }): 5.0`, so its return example is a real tested value, not a bare `0.0`. Its usage now calls it with non-example points, and the first fence also prints a missing-member error.
- Split the bullet on structural comparison of returned objects out of the worked-example bullet.
- Added a sentence after the nested-shapes example explaining that the last line fails on `size.w`, not on the empty `tags` array.
- Turned the optional-member trip-up into its own short "Optional members" section with a runnable `greet` example (`nick: 'Countess' | undefined`): absent, present and wrong-type cases.
- Kept the dictionary-default and named-Type trip-ups. I checked that the links (/dictionary-defaults-example/, /declarations/) match existing pages.
questions: The critic's brief said to strip the TODO marker, but the swarm ground rules require `<!-- TODO review -->` on line 2. I followed the ground rules. Remove the marker after your edit pass if you want the critic's version.

findings.where: Code block 1, the `/# ... #/` block: "An object example describes a shape: `{ first: 'Ada', last: 'Lovelace' }` means an object whose `first` and `last` are strings."
findings.problem: The opening comment and the first paragraph of "What to notice" say nearly the same thing, so the reader meets the same idea twice in a few lines. The `/# ... #/` delimiter is never explained either, so I can't tell whether it is prose, a comment, or part of the program.
findings.fix: Keep one statement of the shape idea, either in the code-block header or in "What to notice". If the `/# #/` block stays, say in one line that it is rendered documentation and not code.

findings.where: `test 'createPoint returns correct structure' { ... }` placed before the functions
findings.problem: The first runnable thing on the page is a `test` block for `createPoint`, which hasn't been defined yet. The prose just above it is about `fullName`. `test`, `expect` and `toBe` are never introduced, and the page doesn't say when this block runs or where its result appears.
findings.fix: Move the test after `createPoint`, or drop it, since the prose relies on return examples and not on test blocks. If it stays, add one sentence: "`test` blocks run when the file is checked; `expect(a).toBe(b)` fails the test unless a equals b."

findings.where: "it is tested at transpile time" (code comment) vs "If the function returned anything else, `tjs check` would fail" (What to notice)
findings.problem: Two different triggers are named for the same test, "transpile time" and "`tjs check`", and neither term is defined on the page. On a live page I can't tell where a failing return example would show up: in the output, as an error, or nowhere.
findings.fix: Pick one wording and say what the reader would actually see on this page if the example were wrong, e.g. "change `'Ada Lovelace'` to `'Ada'` and the example reports a failed signature test".

findings.where: `console.log(fullName({ first: 'Grace' }).message) // last is missing` and the later bullet "returns a `MonadicError` whose path names the member"
findings.problem: The code reads `.message` on what is supposedly a string-returning function before the page has said that a bad argument returns an error object instead of throwing. `MonadicError` appears later in the prose and is never defined. The comment `// last is missing` paraphrases the message, so I can't check the real output against it, and the path `fullName.person.last` that the prose promises doesn't appear in any comment.
findings.fix: Before or beside the first `.message` line, say: "A wrong argument doesn't throw. The call returns an error value (a MonadicError), and `.message` says what was wrong." Show the actual message text, including the path, in the comment.

findings.where: "**Number members follow the number rules.** `{ x: 0, y: 0 }` is a point with *integer* coordinates, so `createPoint(1.5, 2)` is rejected."
findings.problem: The bullet is about object members, but `createPoint(1.5, 2)` passes plain numbers to scalar parameters `x: 0, y: 0`, so the example doesn't show the claim. That call isn't in the code block either. "the number rules" points to rules this page never states (that `0` means integer and `0.0` means float).
findings.fix: Use a call that shows the member rule, e.g. `distance({ x: 1.5, y: 1 }, { x: 4, y: 5 }).message`, and add it to the code with its output. Spell the rule out in one clause: "`0` means integer, `0.0` means any number".

findings.where: `function distance(...): 5.0` with `console.log('Distance:', distance({ x: 1, y: 1 }, { x: 4, y: 5 })) // 5`, and `area({ width: 2, height: 1.5 })` where `width: 0.0`
findings.problem: The prose stresses that `5.0` is a float and `0` is an integer, then shows output `5` with no `.0`, and passes the integer `2` where a float `0.0` is declared. A careful reader will ask whether a float slot accepts integers and whether the output really is a float. The page never says that integers are valid where a float is expected, though every example depends on it.
findings.fix: Add one sentence: "An integer is a valid float, so `width: 2` is fine and `5` satisfies `5.0`. The reverse is not true."

findings.where: "a `'' + ' ' + ''` example would only prove the function returns a single space"
findings.problem: The expression `'' + ' ' + ''` isn't the form of any example on the page. It takes a moment to work out that it means "if the parameter examples were `{ first: '', last: '' }` the return example would have to be `' '`".
findings.fix: Write it out: "With `person: { first: '', last: '' }` the return example would have to be `' '`, and that only proves the function adds a space."

findings.where: "It builds a new object, and that passes because the contents match; identity does not matter here."
findings.problem: "identity" isn't defined, and "here" suggests identity matters somewhere else, but the page doesn't say where. A reader coming from JS knows `{x:0} !== {x:0}`, but a learner won't know what is being contrasted.
findings.fix: Say it concretely: "Two separately built objects with the same contents count as equal for a return example, even though `===` would call them different."

findings.where: "Every listed member is required, and checked. Leaving `last` out, or passing a number for it..." and "Extra members are allowed. `{ first: 'Grace', last: 'Hopper', born: 1906 }`"
findings.problem: Neither the wrong-type case nor the extra-member case for `fullName` appears in the first code block, so the bullets describe calls the reader can't see run. Extras are only shown later, with `area`.
findings.fix: Add `fullName({ first: 'Grace', last: 7 }).message` and `fullName({ first: 'Grace', last: 'Hopper', born: 1906 })` to the first block, with their real outputs.

findings.where: `function label(item: { name: '', tags: [''], size: { w: 0, h: 0 } })`
findings.problem: `label` is the only function on the page without a return example, and the page never says that a return example is optional or why it was left out. "an array member uses an array example" also never explains that `['']` means "array of strings", i.e. that the single element gives the element type.
findings.fix: Say: "`['']` means an array whose items are strings; one sample item is enough." Mention that the return example is optional and that `label` leaves it out.

findings.where: Lines 86–88: three `label(...)` calls with no output comments, followed by "The last line fails on `size.w`..."
findings.problem: Every other block puts the expected output in a comment, but here the reader has to guess what each line prints. The explanation comes after the block and covers only the last line. Line 87 (`tags: ['a', 2]`) has no explanation at all, even though it's the one that shows an error path into an array.
findings.fix: Add output comments to all three lines (e.g. `// box [a, b] 3x4`, `// path: label.item.tags[1]`, `// path: label.item.size.w`), so the full-path claim can be seen.

findings.where: "To let one be absent, give it a union with `undefined`: ... `nick: 'Countess' | undefined`"
findings.problem: "union" and the `|` syntax aren't introduced; this page uses them for the first time. It also doesn't say whether `nick: null`, or an explicit `nick: undefined`, is accepted.
findings.fix: Add a clause: "`A | B` means either A or B, so `'Countess' | undefined` is a string that may be left out." State what happens with `null`.

findings.where: "Name a shape you use twice. ... works but drifts. `Type Point { example: { x: 0, y: 0 } }` gives it a name"
findings.problem: "drifts" is jargon, meaning the copies can get out of step when one is edited. The `Type` declaration syntax is shown, but not how to use it in a signature (`p: Point`?), so I couldn't apply the tip from this page.
findings.fix: Say "if you change one copy, the others silently disagree", and show a single usage line, e.g. `function distance(p1: Point, p2: Point): 5.0`.

findings.where: "`p: { x: 0, y: 0 }` (colon) requires a whole point."
findings.problem: "requires a whole point" sounds like it contradicts "Extra members are allowed", because it reads as "exactly a point". The colon-vs-equals contrast is the most useful sentence on the page, but it sits at the very end.
findings.fix: Say "requires every listed member" in place of "a whole point". Consider moving the colon-vs-equals contrast up to the first "What to notice" bullet, where readers first meet the colon form.

findings.where: Subtitle "Typed object parameters and returns"
findings.problem: A sentence fragment that adds nothing to the H1, and it uses "typed" while the rest of the page carefully talks about examples and shapes.
findings.fix: Replace it with a one-line motivation, e.g. "Give a parameter a sample object and TJS checks every call has the same shape."

findings.where: Use of `??`, template literals `${...}` and `.join(', ')` in `label` and `greet`
findings.problem: This page is in the "basics" group, and if a learn-to-program reader lands here these JS features are unexplained and unrelated to the topic. A JS developer will be fine.
findings.fix: Either use `+` concatenation and an `if` to keep the topic-free noise down, or state at the top that the page assumes working JavaScript.

findings.where: What to notice: "That is why `distance` returns `5.0`, a float: the distance between two integer points is usually not an integer."
findings.problem: This reads as if an integer return example (`: 5`) would make non-integer results fail. It doesn't: return values are not checked at runtime by default. I tested `function d(p1: Point, p2: { x: 3, y: 4 }): 5 { return Math.sqrt(...) }`, and `tjs check` passes (the signature shows `-> integer`) and `tjs run` prints `1.4142135623730951 undefined` with no error. Choosing `5.0` only changes the documented and inferred type (`-> number` instead of `-> integer`).
findings.fix: Say what 5.0 actually does, for example: "so the signature documents a float; `5` would declare an integer return, which is wrong for most inputs". Optionally add that return values are only checked at runtime with `:?`.
findings.evidence: scratchpad/docs-swarm/object-types/m5.tjs: check -> `d(p1: declared, p2: object) -> integer`; run -> `1.4142135623730951 undefined`

findings.where: Things that trip people up: "Name a shape you use twice ... `Type Point { example: { x: 0, y: 0 } }` gives it a name"
findings.problem: The tip leaves out a cost the chapter's own theme makes relevant. The chapter says errors name the member path (`fullName.person.last`, `label.item.size.w`), but a value that fails a named Type reports only the type. `d({x:0.5,y:0}, ...)` with `p1: Point` gives `Expected Point for 'm5.tjs:2:d.p1', got object`, which does not say that `x` was the problem.
findings.fix: Add a short clause: a named Type's error names the type (`Expected Point ... got object`), not the failing member, so inline shapes give more precise errors.
findings.evidence: bun src/cli/tjs.ts run m5.tjs -> `Expected Point for 'm5.tjs:2:d.p1', got object`

findings.where: "returns a `MonadicError` whose path names the member: `fullName.person.last`"
findings.problem: This is accurate, but the actual message is `Expected string for '<file>:17:fullName.person.last', got undefined`, with a file:line prefix and an 'Expected X ... got Y' form. A reader comparing the live output with the prose may wonder why they differ.
findings.fix: Quote the real message once, e.g. "`.message` reads `Expected string for '…:fullName.person.last', got undefined`".
findings.evidence: ex1 run output: `Expected string for 'ex1.tjs:17:fullName.person.last', got undefined`

findings.where: First fence's doc block `/# ## Object Types ... #/`
findings.problem: The `/#` block's H2 "Object Types" repeats the page's H1 "Object Types" and the subtitle line. On the doc site the same heading appears twice in a row.
findings.fix: Drop the H2 from the doc block, or retitle it (e.g. "Shapes by example").

findings.where: Inline comments `// last is missing`, `// height is missing`, `// not an object`, `// nick must be a string if present`
findings.problem: These are paraphrases. The page prints `Expected number for '…area.rect.height', got undefined`, etc. That's acceptable, but readers who check the comment against the output see different words.

- **Dispatch order, as the source does it:**
  - Argument count must match exactly.
  - Then the narrowest type wins: `+0` before `0` before `0.0`, and any declared type before an untyped parameter.
  - Then declaration order.
  - A new inline example declares the widest variant first, to show that writing order does not change which variant runs.
- **No match:** returns a `MonadicError` (no throw, no "closest" fallback). If an argument is already a MonadicError, that error passes through unchanged. Inline example.
- **New section, telling objects apart:** every object-literal example has the same type, "object", so two of them are rejected as ambiguous. Named `Type`s (Circle/Rect) do dispatch. Inline example.
- **New section, metadata and docs:** `tjs check` shows the dispatcher as `name(__args?: array)` and lists the variants separately under their numbered names. - **Gotchas:**
  - Kept: the ambiguity rule (still a static `expect-error` block, reformatted) and types-not-values with the link to `given`.
  - New: a defaulted parameter still has to be passed, because the count must match exactly.

findings.where: ## The order variants are tried in: "The order you write them in does not matter; the narrower type is always tried first"
findings.problem: This holds only when every variant of the name has the same arity. The dispatcher's sort comparator (src/lang/parser-transforms.ts ~4505) returns 0 for variants of different arity, which makes it inconsistent, so a variant with a different parameter count declared between them stops the narrower one moving ahead of the wider one. The integer then goes to the float variant.
findings.evidence: t7.tjs: `function g(n: 0.0){return 'float'}` / `function g(a: 0, b: 0){return 'two'}` / `function g(n: 0){return 'int'}`; `console.log(g(42), g(1.5), g(1, 2))` prints `float float two` (expected `int float two`). The emitted dispatcher tests g$1 (number) before g$3 (integer).
findings.fix: Fix the comparator in the source (sort by arity first, or sort within each arity group) and file a card with this repro. Until that lands, qualify the sentence ("among variants with the same number of parameters, declared next to each other...") or drop the absolute claim. A row in the chapter's tests that mixes arities would pin the fix.

findings.where: ## What the metadata and docs show: "read it from a test or after the file has loaded, not from a top-level statement above it"
findings.problem: The sentence implies a top-level statement BELOW the declarations can read the metadata. It cannot: `__tjs` is still undefined at that point, and only a test block (or code that runs after the module finishes) sees it.
findings.evidence: t9.tjs: the two `show` variants, then `console.log(show.__tjs.polymorphic)` on the next line → `Runtime error: undefined is not an object (evaluating 'show.__tjs.polymorphic')`.
findings.fix: Say "not from a top-level statement anywhere in the same file; read it from a test block or from another module after this one has loaded".

findings.where: Step 2, "How specific the types are... the one with narrower types is tried first"
findings.problem: Specificity is a summed score for each variant (+3 for a non-negative integer, +2 for an integer, +1 for any other declared type, 0 for untyped), not a comparison of each position. With several parameters, a variant whose types are not narrower can still win.
findings.evidence: t8.tjs: `function h(a: +0, b)` (score 3) and `function h(a: 0, b: 0)` (score 4); `h(1, 2)` prints `second`, although the first variant's `a` is narrower. Source: parser-transforms.ts lines ~4509-4527.
findings.fix: Describe the rule as it is ("variants whose parameters are more specific overall, counted across all parameters"), or keep the single-parameter wording and add that for several parameters the narrowness is counted across all of them.

written.changes:
I rewrote /Users/tonioloewald/tjs-lang/guides/examples/tjs/predicate-types.md and touched no other file. The metadata line is unchanged. A single `<!-- TODO review -->` now sits on line 2, and the three TODO markers that were scattered through the body are gone.

Changes:
- **First example's doc block:** tightened. It now lists what the verifier rejects (no IO, clock, randomness, loops, `await` or `new`) and says what a hostile input does: the check answers false instead of hanging. The old claim that a predicate "serialises into JSON Schema as `$predicate`" now reads "its source can be carried in JSON Schema", because a Type does not do this automatically.
- **"Writing your own" section:** the `HexColor` example is kept. I added the real warning text TJS prints when a predicate uses a `for` loop (taken from a run), to show that an unverifiable predicate still works, with a warning.
- **New section, "Regular expressions: two different paths":** this resolves the apparent contradiction with Declarations.
  - In a `.tjs` `Type` predicate, a regex makes the predicate unverifiable, because the emitted guard is self-contained native JS and cannot carry the linear engine. The section quotes the real warning text and links to Declarations' rule and its `Email` example.
  - In `compilePredicate` and all the `$predicate` evaluators, a regex literal runs on the metered linear engine. A live example shows `/^(a+)+$/` answering at once on a hostile input.
  - It states that backreferences and lookaround are refused; I tested both.
- **New section, "Predicates in JSON Schema: `$predicate`":** shows a real `$predicate` schema from `cssColorSchema()`, checked two ways with `compilePredicateSchema`: predicate-aware, and with `ignorePredicates`, as a validator that doesn't know `$predicate` would. It introduces `tjs-lang/schema` (its `validate` runs `$predicate` with no setup) with a live example, and points to the Zod chapter for `trustPredicate` on your own source.
- **Limits:** the trust bullet now says exactly what failing closed means: `compilePredicateSchema` throws and `validate` returns false. A new bullet covers running out of fuel: a `Type` check and `tjs-lang/schema` `validate` answer false, while `compilePredicate` and `compilePredicateSchema` throw `PredicateFuelExhausted`. The note about which examples need package imports is updated.

**One thing I couldn't do as briefed.** The brief asked for a `$predicate` schema produced from a Type. No such thing exists: `HexColor.toJSONSchema()` returns `{}`, as a run shows. The chapter now says so plainly instead of implying otherwise, and shows a `$predicate` schema built from predicate source.
questions: Should a Type with a verified predicate export it in its JSON Schema (`toJSONSchema()` emitting `$predicate` with the predicate's source)? Today it returns `{}`, a gap ts-from-zod.md already flags as a possible defect. If that is the intended direction, the brief's 'show a $predicate produced from a Type' becomes possible and the chapter's 'does not carry its predicate today' paragraph should change.

Running out of fuel behaves differently by path: a Type check and `tjs-lang/schema` `validate` return false, while `compilePredicate` and `compilePredicateSchema` throw `PredicateFuelExhausted`. The chapter documents this as it is. Is the split intended, or should the library paths also fail closed with false?
Should this chapter use plain `/* */` for its doc block rather than the `/# ... #/` form it inherited? `tjs check` accepts `/# ... #/`, but CLAUDE.md documents the `/*#` form.

findings.where: "It compiles to native JavaScript with a fuel bound, so validation costs a function call and a hostile input makes it answer `false`"
findings.problem: 'Fuel' is never defined on the page, but the whole safety argument rests on it. It comes back later as 'fuel-bounded', 'metered engine', 'charges each step to the predicate's fuel' and 'runs out of fuel'. A JS developer arriving here doesn't know what fuel is, how much there is, or who sets it.
findings.fix: Add one or two sentences the first time it appears: fuel is a step budget, every operation spends some, and when it runs out the predicate stops. Say who picks the budget, or give the default, or link to where that's explained.

findings.where: Opening paragraph: "When the toolchain can prove the function is safe..." and "checked to be pure, synchronous and composable"
findings.problem: 'Safe' and 'composable' are used before they're defined. 'Safe' gets a meaning only later (no IO, no clock...), and 'composable' never gets one. The reader also isn't told when the proving happens (at compile time? on import?) or how they'd find out it succeeded.
findings.fix: Define 'safe' in the first paragraph (it can't hang, has no side effects and is deterministic). Either drop 'composable' or explain it (predicates may call each other). Say when verification runs and what success looks like (no warning).

findings.where: First tjs:inline block: the long `/# ... #/` comment ("The gap this fills" / "What verification buys" / "tjs-lang/css is built this way")
findings.problem: The reader gets three subsections of abstract claims (JSON Schema's gap, three benefits, the CSS library) before seeing a single line of code. It reads as a wall of text, and the `/# ... #/` delimiter is never explained, so a first-time reader can't tell whether it's prose or code.
findings.fix: Lead with the four isColor calls and their output, then explain. Or move the 'What verification buys' list below the example as 'what you just saw'. If the `/#` comment syntax is new to this book, mention it in a line or link to where it's introduced.

findings.where: `forRe.every((s) => s.kind !== 'value' || isColor(s.value))` and the test 'completions come from the predicate, and are all valid'
findings.problem: Suggestions have a `kind` field, and the check skips everything whose kind isn't 'value'. The page never says what the other kinds are or why they're exempt. So the example doesn't show the prose's claim that 'suggestColor never offers anything isColor would reject'. It only shows it for some suggestions, and the line printed above (`forRe.map(s => s.value)`) mixes the kinds together.
findings.fix: Describe the suggestion shape (`{ kind: 'value' | 'stub', value }`). Explain that a stub is an open-ended prefix like `rgb(` that can't be validated until the user finishes typing, and soften 'never offers anything' to 'never offers a complete value'.

findings.where: "Each suggestion is run through the compiled predicate before it is offered." (prose) followed by the code re-checking every suggestion
findings.problem: The prose says the library already does this filtering, and then the example does it again by hand. A reader may wonder whether they're expected to filter suggestions themselves.
findings.fix: Add a comment saying the check is a demonstration of the guarantee, not a step the caller needs, e.g. `// we re-check here only to show it; you don't need to`.

findings.where: "What to notice": "a predicate is a test you can hand to `filter`, `every`, a parameter, or a `Type`."
findings.problem: The example never uses isColor with filter, as a parameter type, or inside a Type, so the claim has nothing to back it. The bullet about `verifyCss()` names a function that's never shown, and the reader isn't told why they would call it.
findings.fix: Add one line such as `['red','nope'].filter(isColor)`, or cut the list down to what the example actually shows. Either show `verifyCss()` returning something or drop the mention.

findings.where: `Type HexColor { description: ... example: ... predicate(x) { ... } }` and `HexColor.check(v)`
findings.problem: The Type block syntax (what description, example and predicate each do, and whether example is checked against the predicate) and the `.check` method are used without explanation. The link to Declarations only appears in the last line of the page. The reader also can't tell from the output whether this predicate passed verification.
findings.fix: Before the block, add a sentence that names the three fields and the `.check(value)` method and links to Declarations there. After it, add a line like 'This compiles with no warning, which means it was verified.'

findings.where: "The return annotation is a worked example: swatch('#ff0000') must return exactly this string."
findings.problem: This is a detour on a page about predicates. A JS or TS reader will see `: 'swatch #ff0000'` as a literal return type, then watch `swatch('#0af')` return `'swatch #0af'` and conclude the annotation is broken. One sentence isn't enough to undo that reading.
findings.fix: Use a plain return example the reader won't stumble on, or link to where return examples are explained ("see Declarations: return examples are tests, not types").

findings.where: `bad instanceof Error ? 'MonadicError: ' + bad.message : bad`
findings.problem: MonadicError is never introduced: the page doesn't say that a failed parameter check returns an error value instead of throwing. Testing it with `instanceof Error` also leaves the reader unsure whether that is the recommended check.
findings.fix: Add a sentence such as 'A failed parameter check returns a MonadicError instead of throwing (see Error handling)', and use the recommended check (`isMonadicError`) if that's the idiom.

findings.where: "Write the same check with a `for` loop and it still works... It compiles it as a plain function and warns:" followed by the warning about `Type 'Digits'`
findings.problem: The warning names a Type `Digits` that never appears on the page. The for-loop version the prose describes isn't shown, so the reader can't connect the warning to any code.
findings.fix: Show the loop version of HexColor, or the `Digits` Type that produces the warning, right before the warning text, and make sure the names match.

findings.where: "Loops are outside what the verifier certifies, because their work is not fuel-bounded."
findings.problem: This skips a step. `every`, `split` and `slice` also iterate, so why are they fuel-bounded when a `for` loop isn't? It looks arbitrary unless you already know how metering is attached to built-in methods but not to loop bodies.
findings.fix: Add one sentence explaining why array methods are metered (each call is charged by input length) and why a hand-written loop can't be bounded the same way.

findings.where: Regex section: "emitted guard", "that output cannot carry tjs-lang's own regex engine", "metered engine", "linear regex engine"
findings.problem: The reader has to grasp three different execution paths: a verified predicate compiled into a .tjs file, compilePredicate, and $predicate evaluators. Each is named with new jargon ('emitted guard', 'library paths', 'metered engine') and none of the terms is defined. It's also unclear why the emitted output can't just include the engine.
findings.fix: Put a small table near the top of this section: path → where it runs → regex allowed? → which engine. Define 'linear engine' once (time grows with input length, no catastrophic backtracking).

findings.where: `compilePredicate(source, ['isRun'])` returning `{ isRun }`

findings.where: `console.log(isRun('a'.repeat(100000) + '!'))    // false`  vs Limits: "a function from `compilePredicate` ... throws `PredicateFuelExhausted`"

findings.where: "The linear engine has no backreferences and no lookaround; a pattern that uses them is refused."
findings.problem: 'Refused' isn't specific. Does compilePredicate throw, return a value, or warn, and when: at compile time or at call time?

written.changes:
Rewrote /Users/tonioloewald/tjs-lang/guides/examples/tjs/safety-validation.md. I kept the metadata line and put `<!-- TODO review -->` directly after it. The other stray TODO markers are gone.

- **Framing:** removed the "three levels" opening and the two-row table. The new intro says what gets checked and when. The "problem" example moved out of the `/# #/` block into prose with a plain javascript fence.
- **Main example:** no longer starts with `safety inputs`. It covers input checks, `+0` narrowing and a single propagation example, which links to /error-handling/ for the full treatment. The console lines now print `.message`, so the page shows readable errors rather than raw error objects and stack traces. There is also a link to /declarations/ for how other examples narrow (`0` is any integer, `0.0` is any number), which I checked.
- **New section "Turning the checks off":** has two parts. "`!` on one function" has its own small runnable example, and says that the metadata and the transpile-time signature test remain. "`safety none` for a whole file" is one paragraph: `inputs` is the default, so you never write it; `none` turns off runtime checks for the file; `all` is accepted but currently checks the same as `inputs`. It has a runnable example that shows `greet(42)` → "Hello, 42!".
- **Checking returns with `:?`:** now has a three-row table comparing `:`, `:!` and `:?` (what each checks at transpile time and at runtime). The class constructors/methods section is unchanged apart from a link to /better-classes/ about calling without `new`.
- **"`try` without `catch`":** now has its own heading. The new example, `readPort`, parses JSON. The section notes that the message wording comes from the JavaScript engine, and that try/catch and try/finally behave as in JavaScript (I checked both).

questions: Should the `safety` directive be taught at all? I kept it as one paragraph plus a `safety none` example because `safety none` really does turn off checks (verified) and TJS-SYNTAX already documents it under 'Module Safety Directive'. That reference section still carries its own `<!-- TODO review -->`, and it sits next to the 'there are no mode directives' section, which a reader may find contradictory. If you would rather retire `safety`, delete the `safety none` subsection.

`safety all` and the `?` parameter marker are documented in TJS-SYNTAX but add no checks in emitted code (verified: `?` under `safety none` is ignored). Should they be fixed, removed from the language, or stay documented as no-ops? The Gotchas section currently says they are no-ops.

`try` without `catch` is not documented anywhere else: TJS-SYNTAX and DOCS-TJS have no mention of it. It now has its own heading here, but Error Handling would be the better long-term home, and it needs a reference entry in TJS-SYNTAX. I could not edit those files under this task's rules.

findings.where: First example: `function sayHello(name: 'World'): 'Hello, World!'`

The page also never says that `'Hello, World!'` is checked by calling `sayHello('World')` when the code is transpiled. That only appears, abstractly, in the table near the end.

findings.where: Gotchas: "The exported schema is stricter than the type about extra keys." ... "`toJSONSchema()` writes the example's shape exactly, with `additionalProperties: false`, the same closed form `strip` works from."
findings.problem: The gotcha presents the closed schema as intended behaviour. It is a known inconsistency between the two implementations. The inline stub in emitted .tjs code writes `additionalProperties: false`. The real runtime (`Type(...)` from tjs-lang, the form CLAUDE.md documents) re-opens inferred shapes and writes `additionalProperties: true`. docs/type-identity.md lists it under 'Surface, not decisions' as 'not yet consistent', not as a design choice. The brief asked for the reason it differs; the chapter gives a reason that isn't the real one.
findings.evidence: In the scratch dir, real.ts runs `Type('pt',{x:1,y:1}).toJSONSchema()` via src/index and prints `{...,"additionalProperties":true} true`. ex2.tjs (the chapter's Address example) under `tjs run` prints `"additionalProperties": false`. docs/type-identity.md:201 has the table row (real runtime: true, re-opened by `openInferredShapes`; inline stub: false). Line 126 says "`toJSONSchema()` is not yet consistent with this in emitted code".
findings.fix: Keep the warning, but say why: in a .tjs file `toJSONSchema()` comes from the inline runtime, which still closes object shapes. The library's `Type(...)` re-opens them. findings.where: Gotchas: "If the consumer should accept them, set `additionalProperties` to `true` on the schema before handing it over."
findings.problem: The emitted schema closes every nested object too, including objects inside array items. Setting the flag at the top level still leaves a validator rejecting extra keys in nested objects. So this advice is incomplete for any nested shape.
findings.evidence: Scratch file s.tjs, `Type Order { example: { id: '', customer: { name: '' }, items: [{ sku: '' }] } }`. `Order.toJSONSchema()` prints `additionalProperties:false` at the top level, inside `customer`, and inside `items.items`.

findings.where: "A whole function as JSON Schema": the output comment shows `additionalProperties: false`, and the input comment has none
findings.problem: The example shows the input schema open and the output schema closed, with no comment. Readers who have just read the Gotcha will wonder about the output schema. It has the same closed-shape behaviour (src/lang/json-schema.ts:81,136).
findings.evidence: meta.ts output: input `{type:'object',properties:{...},required:[...]}` with no additionalProperties; output has `"additionalProperties":false`. This matches the comment in the chapter.
findings.fix: Add one sentence: the output schema closes the return shape the same way `toJSONSchema()` does (see Gotchas), and the input schema leaves extra keys allowed.

findings.where: Type Address { description: 'a postal address' ... } followed by JSON.stringify(Address.toJSONSchema())

findings.where: "`strip` returns a new object holding only the example's keys"
findings.problem: This is accurate for object values. For a non-object value (or a Type whose example is not an object), `strip` returns the input unchanged. Also, `.strip` exists on a type in emitted code only when the file's source contains `.strip(` (js.ts:2544). So a host module can't call `.strip` on a type imported from a .tjs file that never calls it.
findings.evidence: src/lang/emitters/js.ts:2920: `t.strip=v=>{...if(!ex||typeof ex!=='object'||!v||typeof v!=='object')return v;...}`. Line 2544: the toJSONSchema/strip helpers are inlined only when `/\.(toJSONSchema|strip)\(/` matches the code. A careful reader sees the demo do that risky step for unauthenticated callers, while the prose says nothing runs.
findings.fix: Move the `storeFor` / Unauthorized check above the parse step, and renumber the comments (1. authorize, 2. parse, 3. run). Then the prose is true and the demo models the advice in "Making it real".
findings.evidence: the-universal-endpoint.md lines 51-62: the `transpile(...)` try block (line 55) comes before `const store = storeFor(...)` / `if (!store) return … 'Unauthorized'` (lines 61-62)

findings.where: "Making it real" sketch: `capabilities: { store: storeFor(req.headers.authorization) }`
findings.problem: The production sketch drops the authorization check the demo had. `storeFor` returns `undefined` for an unknown token, and the sketch passes that straight into `vm.run`, so an unauthenticated caller still gets a run, just without a store. The client half also sends no `authorization` header at all, so as written every real request would be unauthenticated. This is the part readers will copy.
findings.fix: In the sketch, reject when `storeFor` returns undefined, as the demo does, and add `headers: { authorization: token }` to the client `fetch`. Also say where `storeFor` comes from ("as defined above").

findings.where: "It is safe to point at code you did not write because of three properties of the AJS VM, which the demo shows one at a time."
findings.problem: The opening paragraph uses "AJS", "AJS VM", "fuel" and "capabilities" with no definition. This page sits in the TJS book, and the AJS book is linked only in the very last line. A JS developer arriving here doesn't know what AJS is, how it relates to TJS, or why its source is a string inside a TJS file.
findings.fix: Add one or two sentences up front: AJS is a sandboxed JavaScript subset that compiles to a JSON AST and runs on a metered VM; fuel is its work budget; capabilities are the IO functions the host chooses to hand in. Link the AJS book there, not only at the end.

findings.where: "three properties … which the demo shows one at a time" / "Three properties of the VM make this safe" list
findings.problem: The demo has four numbered tests, but the page promises three properties shown one at a time. The mapping is uneven. Fuel maps to test 2 and no-ambient-authority to test 3. "Errors are values" has no test of its own and points back at test 2. Test 4 (parse error) maps to no property, and its failure is actually a thrown exception caught with try/catch, the opposite of "errors are values". So the reader can't line the claims up with the demos.
findings.fix: Either say "four cases, three properties" and give each property its test number, or make test 4 explicitly the contrast: the transpiler throws, which is why `post` wraps it in try/catch, while the VM never throws, which is the property.

findings.where: "**Errors are values.** A failed run returns `{ error }` rather than throwing" alongside `try { ast = transpile(...) } catch (e) { ... }`
findings.problem: The handler's first act is a try/catch around a call that throws. The page never says that the transpiler throws and only the VM returns errors as values. A reader takes "errors are values" as a property of the whole toolchain and is confused by the catch block.
findings.fix: Add a sentence in the code comment or the prose: transpile is ordinary host code and throws on bad source; vm.run never throws, so the run itself needs no try/catch.

findings.where: `let greeting = storeGet({ key: 'greeting' })` and "the VM hands that call to whatever `store` the host passed in `capabilities`"
findings.problem: Three things are unexplained. (1) How `storeGet` in the agent connects to the `get` method on the host's store object: who decided the names `get`/`set`, and is that a required interface? (2) Why there is no `await` when `store.get` is async. (3) What `storeGet` even is (a built-in? a global?). "Atom" is only defined in the final Limits section.
findings.fix: After the demo, add: "`storeGet` is a built-in AJS atom; the VM implements it by calling `capabilities.store.get(key)`, so your store must expose async `get`/`set`. Atom calls are awaited implicitly." Define "atom" where it first appears.

findings.where: `async function post(req: { body: { agent: '', args: {}, fuel: 1000 }, headers: { authorization: '' } })` and `function storeFor(token: '')`
findings.problem: These are TJS example-value annotations, but nothing on the page says so. A JS developer reading `fuel: 1000` will likely take it as a default value, or as a literal type. The page also never says what happens when a request doesn't match this shape (does `post` return a type error instead of the `{ status }` envelope?). That matters for the claim "Whatever the agent does, `post` returns a value."
findings.fix: Add a short comment: "the colon values are examples: `req.body.fuel` must be a number, `1000` is just a sample". Say that a malformed request gets a TJS type error back rather than reaching the VM.

findings.where: `fuel: Math.min(req.body.fuel, 10_000)` and "reports the fuel it used, well under one unit"
findings.problem: The server-side cap on the client's requested fuel is a key part of the design, but the prose never mentions it. The reader also gets no sense of scale: the computation used "well under one unit" of a 100-unit budget, and an infinite loop burned 50. How much work is one unit, and how would someone pick 1000 or 10,000?
findings.fix: In the item 1 or item 2 prose, say that the client asks for a budget and the server clamps it. Give a rough scale ("each expression node costs 0.01 fuel; an atom call costs more") so the numbers mean something.

findings.where: "Fuel is the *time* budget: by default a run also gets a wall-clock timeout of fuel × 10ms, and `timeoutMs` overrides it, which covers time spent waiting on a capability rather than computing."
findings.problem: This is one long sentence with an ambiguous "which": does the default timeout cover capability wait time, or does `timeoutMs`? It also calls fuel "the time budget" and then introduces a separate time budget. Readers will stall here.
findings.fix: Split it: "Fuel bounds computation. Waiting on a capability (a slow fetch) costs no fuel, so runs also have a wall-clock timeout: fuel × 10ms by default, or `timeoutMs` if set. Here it is 5000ms."

findings.where: `const tenants = { token_alice: …, token_bob: … }` / `const data = tenants[token]; if (!data) return undefined`
findings.problem: In a page about safe authorization, the lookup indexes a plain object with a caller-supplied string. A token such as `constructor` or `toString` resolves to an inherited function, which passes the `!data` check, so the request is not treated as unauthorized. That teaches a pattern a security-minded reader would flag, and a copier might keep.
findings.fix: Make `tenants` a `Map` and use `tenants.get(token)`, or use `Object.hasOwn(tenants, token)`. Optionally add a one-line comment saying why.

findings.where: "An agent that needs more asks the host for an atom (a named capability)" (Limits) vs. `capabilities: { store }`
findings.problem: Atoms are first defined in the last section, as "a named capability". Yet the page has used "capability" all along for the host object (`store`), and `storeGet` is clearly not itself a capability. The two terms blur together. "Expensive atom" in Making it real (item 3) also appears before that definition.
findings.fix: Define both early and distinctly. An atom is an operation the agent can call (`storeGet`, `httpFetch`, `llmPredict`). A capability is the host-supplied implementation that some atoms need (`store`, `fetch`, `llm`).

findings.where: `quotas: { llmPredict: 3, httpFetch: 10 }` in the sketch
findings.problem: `llmPredict` and `httpFetch` show up out of nowhere. The sketch's VM is `new AgentVM()` with only a `store` capability, so the reader can't tell whether these atoms exist by default, need extra atoms registered, or need `llm`/`fetch` capabilities. A quota on an atom that can't run is confusing.
findings.fix: Add a comment such as "if you also grant `fetch`/`llm` capabilities", or include them in the capabilities object.

findings.where: "A production endpoint needs three more decisions." item 3: "`maxHeapBytes` (default 64MB) bounds how much memory a run may hold at once"
findings.problem: `maxHeapBytes` is named as a decision but is missing from the sketch right above it. The sketch also returns `vm.run(...)` raw, unlike the demo's `{ status, error, fuelUsed }` envelope, and doesn't say whether exposing the raw run object (error internals, fuel) to clients is fine.
findings.fix: Add `maxHeapBytes` to the sketch's options and reuse the demo's response shaping, or say why the sketch returns the raw result.

findings.where: Opening paragraph: "a single endpoint that accepts the client's *logic* as data"
findings.problem: The motivation covers only the server's side (no per-route deploys). It never asks the questions a reader will have: how does the client know which atoms and store keys exist? What stops a tenant from doing expensive but legal things within its own data? How do you version or observe what clients are running? Without at least a nod to these, the closing claim "no deployment when the client wants a new query" reads as too good to be true.
findings.fix: Add a short "When to use this / what you give up" paragraph, or fold these points into Limits: discoverability means documenting the atom surface, cost is fuel plus quotas, observability means tracing runs.

findings.where: `/#` … `#/` at the top of the code block
findings.problem: Nothing explains the comment-doc delimiters. To a JS reader, `/#` is not a comment at all and looks like a syntax error at the top of the example.
findings.fix: Use the form the rest of the TJS docs teach for markdown doc comments (`/*# … */`), or add a one-line note that this block renders as prose above the code.

findings.where: `function spin({ })` / `function read({ })` / `function broken({ })`
findings.problem: The empty destructured parameter is unusual and unexplained. Readers will wonder whether AJS requires it.
findings.fix: Add one sentence: "An agent is a function taking one object of named arguments; `{ }` means it takes none."

findings.where: `const fuelUsed = Math.round(run.fuelUsed * 100) / 100`
findings.problem: The rounding is unexplained. Readers may wonder whether fuel is fractional or whether this hides something.
findings.fix: Add a comment: "fuel is fractional (expression nodes cost 0.01); round for display".

findings.where: "A quota is per run. … pass the same `quotaUsed` object to both"
findings.problem: `quotaUsed` is introduced in the very last bullet with no indication of its shape or where it goes (a `vm.run` option?).
findings.fix: Say "pass the same `quotaUsed: {}` object in the run options of both runs", or link to where it is documented.

findings.where: Line 2: `<!-- TODO review -->`
findings.problem: A leftover working marker in a published chapter.
findings.fix: Remove it after the edit pass.

findings.where: What the output shows, item 2: "by default a run also gets a wall-clock timeout of fuel × 10ms, and `timeoutMs` overrides it"
findings.problem: The default run timeout is not fuel × 10ms. In the source it is the slowest registered atom's timeout × 2, with a floor of 60s, and it does not depend on fuel. A plain `new AgentVM()` reports 240000ms. (CLAUDE.md and a comment at vm.ts:370 still say fuel × 10ms, so those are stale as well.)
findings.evidence: src/vm/vm.ts:149-167 `defaultRunTimeout` = Math.max(MIN_DEFAULT_RUN_TIMEOUT_MS /*60_000*/, slowest * 2); vm.ts:322 `const timeoutMs = admitted.timeoutMs ?? this.defaultRunTimeout`. Running `new AgentVM().defaultRunTimeout` printed `240000`.
findings.fix: Say: "if you don't pass `timeoutMs`, the run gets a default wall-clock limit (at least 60 seconds, set from the slowest registered atom); pass `timeoutMs`, as `post` does, to bound time spent waiting on a capability." Report the stale CLAUDE.md line and the vm.ts:370 comment separately.

findings.where: Making it real sketch: `capabilities: { store: storeFor(req.headers.authorization) }` with no token check
findings.problem: The live demo turns away a bad token before running. The production sketch drops that check. `storeFor` returns undefined for an unknown token, and the VM then falls back to a per-run default in-memory store, so an unauthorized caller's agent runs anyway: storeGet/storeSet work against a scratch store and only add a warning. That contradicts point 2 of the section ("Build them from the request's credentials").
findings.evidence: src/vm/runtime.ts:7315 `return ctx.capabilities.store ?? ctx.defaultStore`; vm.ts:338-360 builds a default memoryStore. Running with `capabilities: { store: undefined }` returned `{"result":{},"warnings":["Using default in-memory store (not suitable for production)", ...]}` and no error.
findings.fix: Add `const store = storeFor(req.headers.authorization); if (!store) return { status: 401 }` before `vm.run` in the sketch. Add a sentence saying that an absent `store` capability falls back to a scratch in-memory store; it is not refused.

findings.where: post(): step 1 (transpile) comes before step 2 (`storeFor` / Unauthorized); prose: "A caller with no valid token is turned away before anything runs."
findings.problem: The handler parses the source before it checks the token. The chapter itself says parsing is the one step that runs before any fuel is charged and whose cost the sender controls. So an unauthenticated caller still gets the pre-budget parse. That is the opposite of the lesson the page teaches. "Before anything runs" is true of the agent, but not of the parser.
findings.evidence: Lines 51-62 of the chapter: transpile at line 55, the auth check at lines 61-62. Output: token_mallory gets `Unauthorized`, fuelUsed 0, but only after transpile has run.
findings.fix: Move the `storeFor` / Unauthorized check above the transpile step and say why in a comment ("authenticate before doing any work the caller controls"). The output does not change.

findings.where: What the output shows, item 1: "reports the fuel it used, well under one unit"
findings.problem: The output is accurate (fuelUsed: 0.5), but the reader isn't told the actual numbers to compare against. Verified output: test 1 fuelUsed 0.5; test 2 'Out of Fuel', fuelUsed 50.06; test 3 alice and bob 5.22 each, mallory 'Unauthorized' 0; test 4 'Parse error: Unexpected token at <source>:1:32', 0. All of these match the prose, and the brief's 'Charged 50 fuel units' claim is gone.
findings.fix: You could quote the figures ("about 0.5", "50.06") so a reader can check the page against its own output. Not required.

revised.summary: I revised /Users/tonioloewald/tjs-lang/guides/examples/tjs/the-universal-endpoint.md. The metadata line and the `<!-- TODO review -->` line are unchanged. I checked both 'wrong' findings against the source and both were right. First, `post` now checks the token before it parses. The comments are renumbered: 1 authorize, 2 parse, 3 run. Second, the default timeout is not fuel × 10ms. The prose now says that without `timeoutMs` the default is at least 60s, set from the slowest registered atom. The production sketch now refuses a request when `storeFor` returns undefined. A new note explains that a missing store falls back to a scratch in-memory store; I verified that it does. The client `fetch` now sends an authorization header. The sketch adds `maxHeapBytes`, gives the response the same shape the demo uses, and notes that `httpFetch`/`llmPredict` need `fetch`/`llm` capabilities. A new opening section defines AJS, fuel, atom and capability as separate terms and links the AJS book. The demo is now framed as four cases for three properties. Test 4 is the contrast: `transpile` throws, `vm.run` does not, and code comments say why. Other changes: a code comment says the colon values are TJS examples, and a malformed request returns a MonadicError (verified: `fuel: 'lots'` gives 'Expected integer'); the prose says `storeGet` calls `store.get` and atom calls are awaited implicitly; the clamp on the client's fuel request is mentioned, with a sense of scale (0.01 per node, 5 per storeGet) and the measured figures 0.5, 50.06 and 5.22; the timeout sentence is split in two; `tenants` is now a Map (a 'constructor' token now returns Unauthorized; verified); there are notes on `{ }` and on why fuel is rounded; `quotaUsed` says where it goes; and a new 'What you give up' section covers discoverability, cost and observability (tracing). I also checked httpFetch: it is blocked unless the host supplies a fetch capability or an allowlist, so the 'no ambient authority' wording holds as 'unless the host grants it'. The extracted example passes `tjs check`, and `tjs run` prints output that matches the prose for all four tests.
