findings.problem: The Building blocks example only asks for `h1` and `p` (`const { h1, p } = elements`). A beginner who follows the instruction literally writes `h2(...)` and `strong(...)` and gets an error, because neither name was requested. The page did say "When an example needs a different building block, it asks for it by name in the same way", but the exercise never connects that sentence to this step.
findings.fix: Say explicitly: "first add `h2` and `strong` to the list in `const { h1, p } = elements`". Or point the exercise at the Blocks inside blocks example, which already brings in `h2` and `strong`.

A reader expecting each `append` to start a new line will be surprised. The page also never says why `' She said'` begins with a space (so it doesn't run into the previous sentence).
findings.fix: Say that the program's lines run in order from top to bottom, and that each `append` puts its text right after the previous text on the same line, not on a new one. Point out the leading space in `' She said'` as the first instance of the 'computers don't add spaces' lesson.

findings.where: "This book teaches one such language, **TJS**" (opening paragraph)
findings.problem: TJS is named with no context. A true beginner doesn't know whether it's a real language people use, how it relates to the 'JavaScript' they may have heard of, or why they should learn this one rather than another. There is no motivation for the choice.
findings.fix: Add one or two sentences: TJS is a version of JavaScript, the language every web browser runs, with extra help for catching mistakes; what you learn here carries over to JavaScript.

findings.where: "Here is a complete program. It puts a greeting on the page:" / "`preview` is the box the program draws in"
findings.problem: The output is first called 'the page', then 'the box', and later (Console section) 'a picture'. Three names for one thing make a beginner wonder whether they are three different things.
findings.fix: Pick one name (e.g. 'the preview box') and use it everywhere, including in the console section's 'instead of a picture'.

findings.where: `preview.append('Hello, world!')` and "`preview` is the box the program draws in, and `append` adds something to it."
findings.problem: Only the two words are explained. The dot, the parentheses, and above all the quote marks around Hello, world! are not. A beginner can't tell which parts are free to change. The text then has them delete a quote (Breaking things) and contrasts quoted and unquoted text (the test example) before saying what quotes mean. The 'Quote marks must be plain' note doesn't come until near the end.
findings.fix: Add a sentence right after the first example: the quote marks mark the text to display, the parentheses hold what you give to `append`, and the dot connects `append` to `preview`. Say that later chapters explain these properly.

findings.where: "Swap the first and last lines and run it in your head before you look: what will the page say? Then look."
findings.problem: The page runs your code as you type, so the moment you swap the lines the answer is already on screen. You can't predict 'before you look' in the order the sentence gives.
findings.fix: Put the prediction first: 'Before you touch anything, predict what the page will say if the first and last lines swap places. Then swap them and check.'

findings.where: "Delete the closing quote after `this, ` on the second line."
findings.problem: 'Closing quote' assumes the reader knows quotes come in opening/closing pairs, which nothing has taught. `this, ` also appears on line 1, and its trailing space is invisible in code font. A beginner may delete the wrong mark.
findings.fix: Be explicit, e.g. 'On the second line, delete the ' that comes just before the closing parenthesis, so the line reads preview.append('then this, ).'

findings.where: "The message says that `Preview` is not defined. The exact words depend on your browser"
findings.problem: 'Defined' is never explained. The reader also doesn't know why the browser is involved: the page has only talked about TJS sending messages, so it is surprising that a browser chooses the wording.
findings.fix: Explain 'not defined' in plain words ('the computer has never heard of anything called Preview'). Add a clause saying that TJS programs run inside your web browser, which is why the browser picks the exact wording.

findings.where: "Every mistake you will meet is one of two kinds ... TJS is good at telling you about both"
findings.problem: The 'runs but does the wrong thing' kind isn't shown here, and the reader can't see how TJS would know that a program which runs is doing the wrong thing. The answer (tests) comes two sections later with no pointer to it.
findings.fix: Add a forward reference: 'For the second kind you tell TJS what should happen, using tests, which you'll meet below.'

findings.where: "use the example's **undo** button, or its menu, which can put the original back"
findings.problem: The reader is never told where the undo button or the menu is, or what they look like. A panicking beginner who needs this sentence can't act on it.
findings.fix: Describe where they are (e.g. 'the ↶ button at the top right of each example; the ⋯ menu has Reset'), or show a small screenshot or callout.

findings.where: Console section: the example shows `console.log('The console shows what a program tells it.')`, followed by "Try typing `2 + 3` at the prompt"
findings.problem: Two different ways of using the console appear together: a program writing to it with console.log, and you typing at a prompt. console.log is explained only at the end of the section. A reader may think they have to wrap everything in console.log, or may not know where 'the prompt' is in the example. 'It shows you the value' also uses 'value', which hasn't been defined.
findings.fix: Start with typing at the prompt (and say where the prompt is and what it looks like). Explain console.log right next to the example that uses it. Replace 'value' with 'the answer' or define it.

findings.where: `const greeting = 'Hello, world!'` / `preview.append(greeting)` in "Checking your answers"
findings.problem: This is the reader's first variable. `const` and naming a value are never explained; the disclaimer covers only 'how a test works'. Worse, `preview.append(greeting)` has no quotes, while every earlier example needed them, and the Reading code section stresses that every quote mark matters. A careful beginner will think it's a typo, or 'fix' it to `'greeting'` and get the wrong output.
findings.fix: Add one sentence: '`const greeting = …` gives the text a name, greeting, so later lines can use the name instead of repeating the text. Without quotes, greeting means the name; with quotes it would be the word greeting itself.' Alternatively, use an example with no variable.

findings.where: "The line under the result says how the tests did: when they pass, how many passed. Change the greeting and the test fails: the line turns red"
findings.problem: 'The result' is ambiguous: is it the preview, or the program? The phrase 'when they pass, how many passed' is hard to parse. 'Change the greeting' could mean either of the two places the greeting text appears (the const or the toBe), and only one of them makes the test fail. Signalling by red alone also fails colour-blind readers.
findings.fix: Say exactly where the status line is and what it reads when tests pass (e.g. '✓ 1 passed'). Say 'change the text on the first line'. Mention the symbol or wording that changes on failure, not only the colour.

findings.where: "## Reading code" section (capital letters, plain quotes)
findings.problem: This advice comes after the reader has already been asked to type and edit code, and after a capital-P mistake has already been demonstrated, so most of it is repetition that arrives late. A beginner copying from a document would hit the curly-quote problem on the very first example.
findings.fix: Move 'Reading code' to just before or just after 'Running an example', and cut the duplicated capital-letter explanation from 'Breaking things on purpose' (or point back to it).

findings.where: Try it #1: "make the program say hello to two people, with two separate `preview.append(…)` lines"
findings.problem: Following this literally produces 'Hello, AliceHello, Bob!' run together, with no space or line break. A beginner will think they did it wrong. The earlier example hid this by putting trailing spaces inside the quotes, and never pointed it out.
findings.fix: Either warn ('notice the two greetings run together; how could you add a space?') to turn it into a deliberate lesson, or point back to the trailing spaces in the 'One step after another' example.

findings.where: "Now change it. Replace `world` with your own name. The page runs your new version as you type"
findings.problem: The page never says whether edits are kept if you reload or leave, or whether each example is independent. Readers who do the exercises across sessions will wonder whether their work is lost, or why an example reset itself.
findings.fix: Add one line: 'Your changes last until you reload the page' (or whatever is actually true).

findings.where: "## How each chapter works" — "It starts with a **problem**"
findings.problem: This chapter doesn't follow the pattern it describes. It opens with no problem and has no 'common mistake' section in that form, so a reader checking the claim against the page just read sees a mismatch.
findings.fix: Add 'This first chapter is the exception: it only shows you around.'

findings.where: "You cannot break anything" (Running an example) vs heading "Breaking things on purpose"
findings.problem: The page reassures the reader that nothing can be broken, then asks them to break things. That's a slight mixed message for an anxious beginner.
findings.fix: Rephrase the reassurance as 'Nothing you do here can harm your computer or the page; mistakes just produce a message', so the later 'breaking' clearly means breaking the program.

findings.where: Line 2: `<!-- TODO review -->`
findings.problem: A leftover working note in the source. It is harmless if hidden, but it signals the page isn't finished.
findings.fix: Remove it before publishing.

findings.where: Breaking things on purpose: "If a change goes badly and you cannot see how to fix it, use the example's **undo** button, or its menu, which can put the original back."
findings.problem: In the inline code view these examples use (`tjs:inline {"view": "code"}`), the live example hides its undo and redo buttons. A reader who looks for an undo button will not find one. Undo is in the example's menu (and on Cmd/Ctrl-Z), and the menu also has 'Revert to original'.
findings.evidence: node_modules/tosijs-ui/dist/live-example/styles.js:79-80 — `':host.-inline-code:not(.-maximize) [part="undo"], ... [part="redo"]': { display: 'none' }`, with the comment "undo/redo (which are also in the example menu, and on the keyboard) give up their place". component.js:2682 menu item `caption: 'Undo', shortcut: '⌘Z'`; component.js:2746 `caption: 'Revert to original'`.
findings.fix: Say: "open the example's menu and choose **Undo** (or press Ctrl-Z, ⌘Z on a Mac), or **Revert to original** to put the example back the way it was."

findings.where: "Every mistake you will meet is one of two kinds: the program does not make sense, so it cannot run at all, or it runs and does the wrong thing."
findings.problem: The `Preview` mistake from step 3, right above, fits neither kind well. The program runs, then stops with an error; it does not quietly 'do the wrong thing'. The later chapter When Things Go Wrong also says "Three kinds of wrong" and has a section "Mistakes that stop the program", so this chapter's 'every mistake... two kinds' is contradicted later in the same book.
findings.evidence: In my scratch copy (a stub `preview` on line 1, `Preview.append` on line 3), `tjs check` passes and `tjs run` prints `APPEND First this,` then `Runtime error: Preview is not defined`. guides/learn/when-things-go-wrong.md:16 says '## Three kinds of wrong', and lines 108-113 cover mistakes that stop the program.
findings.fix: Hedge it and match chapter 10. For example: "Mistakes come in two broad kinds: the program does not make sense, so it cannot run at all, or it runs and goes wrong, either stopping with a message (like `Preview`) or quietly giving the wrong answer. When Things Go Wrong sorts them more finely."

findings.where: "TJS is good at telling you about both"
findings.problem: This overclaims for the quietly-wrong-answer case. Chapter 10 says that only a test can catch this case: "Nothing in the computer can know that 51% is not what you meant."
findings.fix: Say "TJS tells you about the first kind, and about many of the second. Tests, below, catch the rest."

findings.where: "On a narrow device, such as a phone, what it did appears above the program instead."
findings.problem: The stacked layout depends on how wide the example is, not on the device. It also happens in a narrow desktop window.
findings.evidence: component.js:2807 `this.classList.toggle('-vertical', this.offsetWidth > 0 && this.offsetWidth < LiveExample.INLINE_STACK_WIDTH)`
findings.fix: "When the page is narrow, as on a phone, what it did appears above the program instead."

findings.where: Blank lines before several headings (after the only-block, before '## One step after another', '## Breaking things on purpose', the console paragraph, the test paragraph, '## Try it')
findings.problem: Some sections have two blank lines between paragraphs or before a heading, and others have one. It does no harm when rendered, but the source is inconsistent.

findings.evidence: Changed `expect(squares(4)).toEqual([1, 4, 9, 16])` to `.toBe(...)` (m5.tjs) and ran `bun src/cli/tjs.ts test m5.tjs`: output `✓ 'the first squares':12 ... 1 passed, 0 failed`. Drop the 'change toEqual to toBe and read the failure' experiment. The other option is to make the harness's toBe use identity, but that is a language/harness change (and checking-your-work.md:60-61 makes the same claim), so raise it with the owner rather than fixing it in the doc.

findings.where: "`startsWith` checks how it begins, and `includes` checks that the last line is in it somewhere"
findings.problem: This is the first use of dot-method calls on a string (`timesTable(7).startsWith(...)`), and the dot syntax is not explained. A beginner may not see that `.startsWith` is something you ask of a string.
findings.fix: Add: 'A string can answer questions about itself: write a dot, then the question.' Or point forward to the chapter that covers methods.

findings.where: Drawing many things: `display: 'inline-block'`, `` `${i * 10}px` ``

findings.fix: Add: '`inline-block` lets the boxes sit side by side like words; `px` means pixels, the dots on your screen.'

findings.where: `evens = evens + `${i} `` vs `fromZero += 1` vs `total = total + i`

findings.where: Exercise 3: "Test it with 1, 2 and 1,000."

findings.where: ## Counting with `for`: "Try changing `let` to `const` in the loop: the first round runs and shows `1`, then the loop stops with an error the first time `i++` tries to change a constant."
findings.problem: The claim holds on the page, but not if a reader or editor checks it with the CLI. Run through `new Function` (which is how the page runs it), the emitted code prints `1 ` and then throws, in node (`TypeError Assignment to constant variable.`) and in Bun/JSC (`TypeError Attempted to assign to readonly property.`). `tjs run` on the same file prints nothing and stops with `Runtime error: This assignment will throw because "i" is a constant`, because Bun's transpiler rejects it before anything runs. So the prose is right for the browser. The wording of the error differs by browser, and the chapter rightly doesn't quote it.
findings.fix: Keep the sentence as it is. During the edit pass, check it on the page (preview:site) rather than with `tjs run`, and do not quote the error text, since it differs between Chrome and Safari.
findings.evidence: scratchpad/docs-swarm/repetition/e_const.tjs: `tjs check` passes; `tjs run` gives `Runtime error: This assignment will throw because "i" is a constant` with no output; `node -e new Function(emitted)()` prints `1 ` then `ERR TypeError Assignment to constant variable.`

written.changes:
I edited only /Users/tonioloewald/tjs-lang/guides/learn/responding-to-the-reader.md. The brief said the chapter was already strong, so the changes are small (15 lines added, 17 removed):
- **Markers:** removed all eight scattered `<!-- TODO review -->` markers. One remains, on line 2 right after the metadata comment, followed by a blank line. The metadata line is unchanged.
- **Numbers from a text box:** the opening now says what happens (the reader types `37`, the program gets `'37'`) and points back to Values and Names, which already covers `+` joining text and `Number(...)`. That replaces "That catches everyone".
- **Plain-JavaScript aside:** kept, shortened to three lines, and now gives the reason behind it: `*` converts text to a number, `+` joins it.
- **NaN paragraph:** dropped the second definition of NaN (Values and Names already defines it). It now says what the page shows: `NaN °F`.
- **Traffic light:** added one sentence saying a part of the model can be handed to a function like any other value (`nextLight` sees `'red'`). The calculator chapter relies on this.
- **Ending:** added the pointer the brief asked for: not every event is a click; a timer or an answer from the network is one too, and Things That Take Time shows how to wait for them.
- `event.target.value` is left as it was, with no TypeScript discussion.

**How I verified the examples:** all 8 `tjs:inline` fences run in real headless Chrome. I transpiled each with `tjs()`, loaded it against the real tosijs 1.10.9 bundle, clicked every button and typed `37`, `abc` and `Grace` into each input. The output matched the prose every time:
- the wave button adds a wave per click;
- the counter goes 0, 1, 2, then 0 after Reset;
- the tally goes 1, 2, 7 … 132;
- `bindValue` updates the heading as you type;
- `'37'` gives 98.6 °F;
- the converter starts at 68 (20 °C), gives 98.6 for 37, and shows `NaN °F` for `abc`;
- the light cycles red, green, amber.

The fences without tosijs also pass their tests and signature examples at transpile time. I also checked the deliberate mistake the chapter asks for (changing `fahrenheit(Number(text))` to `fahrenheit(text)`): the transpile-time check fails, and the error names `fahrenheit.celsius`, expected number, got string, as the prose says.

**Brief item, checked in Chrome:** a `press`-style function with an object-shaped parameter (`{ x: 0.0, y: 0.0, op: '', fresh: true }`) accepts a tosi proxy. It returns the proxy, not an error, and updates the model. Passing a proxied string to `nextLight` and a proxied number to a `0.0` parameter also works, with no type errors recorded.

**Two things that could mislead the next checker:**
- `tjs check` on a fence that uses `preview` shows a ✓ even though its tests never ran: they are skipped as inconclusive because `preview` is not defined in the CLI. The step in CLAUDE.md ("check exits 1 on a bad signature example") does not hold for these doc-page fences.
- happy-dom, used for headless testing, displays 0 and NaN as blank, while Chrome shows "0" and "NaN". Use Chrome to judge.

findings.where: First example: `import { elements } from 'tosijs'` / `const { button } = elements`
findings.problem: The page never says what tosijs is, why it has to be imported, or what `elements` is. Someone who has never programmed meets a library name, an import, and a destructuring line all in the first three lines of the chapter's first program. Whether the `const { button } = elements` shape was taught earlier is not stated here.
findings.fix: Before the first example, add one or two sentences: tosijs is a library (code someone else wrote) that makes page pieces; `elements` holds one function per kind of page piece; `const { button } = elements` picks the button maker out of it. If destructuring was covered in an earlier chapter, name that chapter, as the page does for Lists and Things with Parts.

findings.where: `button(...)`, `div`, `span`, `strong`, `h2`, `label`, `input` ("An `input` element makes a box")
findings.problem: The word "element" and the idea that each of these functions makes a piece of the page are never explained. The reader gets div/span/strong/h2/label with no hint of what each one looks like or why you would pick one over another, and the call shape (an optional settings object, then contents) is only implied.
findings.fix: Add a short note: each function makes one HTML element (a box, a heading, a bold word, a text box). If the first argument is an object, it holds settings; everything after it is what goes inside. One line per new tag (strong = bold, h2 = heading, label = text attached to a box) is enough.

findings.where: "`preview.append(...)`"
findings.problem: `preview` is used throughout and never introduced on this page. A reader who arrives here, or has forgotten, cannot tell that it is the area below the code where output appears.
findings.fix: Add a half-sentence reminder the first time it is used: "(`preview` is the area under the code, as in earlier chapters)".

findings.where: "This chapter adds buttons, and a way of keeping the page in step with your program that needs almost no code."
findings.problem: "Keeping the page in step with your program" means nothing yet to a beginner, who does not know the page can fall out of step. The motivation only arrives much later ("Why is this better…").
findings.fix: Make the intro concrete ("…and a way to make the page update by itself whenever a number in your program changes"), or bring a short version of the score-in-many-places motivation up into the model section's opening.

findings.where: `const { counter } = tosi({ counter: { count: 0 } })`
findings.problem: The name `counter` appears twice, once as a key inside the object and once as the variable taken out of it, and nothing explains why the facts are nested inside an outer object. "A stand-in for it that notices changes" is vague: a stand-in for what, the whole model or just `{ count: 0 }`? The name `tosi` is never explained either.
findings.fix: Explain the shape step by step: the outer object is the whole model; `counter` is one named part of it; the destructuring takes that part back out as a watched version. Use a different name for the part, or say plainly why the two names must match.

findings.where: "`span(counter.count)` … It is not a copy of the number: the span keeps showing whatever `counter.count` is." vs `counter.count = counter.count + 1`, and later "you can hand it to a function like any other value: `nextLight` sees `'red'`"
findings.problem: The page says `counter.count` is not a plain number, then does `+ 1` on it as if it were one. Much later it says passing `light.colour` to a function gives the plain `'red'`. A beginner is left asking when it is a live link and when it is a value. That is the central idea of the chapter, and it is never reconciled.
findings.fix: In the model section, say it outright: given to an element, `counter.count` stays linked; used in arithmetic or handed to a function, it acts as its current value. Move the "`nextLight` sees `'red'`" remark up to that point.

findings.where: `() => preview.append(' 👋')` vs `() => { counter.count = counter.count + 1 }`
findings.problem: The first arrow has no curly braces; the later ones do. The difference is never mentioned, so a beginner may think braces are optional decoration, or copy the wrong form.
findings.fix: Add one sentence at the counter example: an assignment is a statement, so the arrow's body needs `{ }`. Or use braces in every handler in the chapter for consistency.

findings.problem: The `...` spread is new syntax and is never explained. The prose only says the row is made with `map` "the way the planets were in Lists", so a beginner cannot tell what the three dots do or whether they matter.
findings.fix: Explain it in a sentence: `map` gives back a list, and `...` spreads the list out so `div` receives each button as a separate argument. If Lists already taught it, say so explicitly.

findings.where: `function add(amount: 1)`
findings.problem: The colon example value `1` is not remarked on. A beginner who remembers TJS signatures less well might think `amount` is always 1, especially since the buttons pass 5, 10 and 50.
findings.fix: Add a short reminder: "`amount: 1` is an example, so `amount` is any whole number."

findings.where: "## Typing" … then "Now the converter itself. When the reader types, an `onInput` handler reads the box"
findings.problem: The page has just taught that `bindValue` removes the need for a handler, then the converter switches to `onInput` without saying why. The reader cannot tell when to use each one.
findings.fix: Add one sentence: `bindValue` copies the text as it is, and here the text has to be converted first, so we read it in a handler ourselves.

findings.where: `input({ value: '20', … })` with `tosi({ weather: { fahrenheit: 68 } })`
findings.problem: 68 is typed in by hand to match the starting '20' (20 °C is 68 °F), and the page never says so. It also undercuts the chapter's own lesson: the same fact sits in two places, and change one and the page contradicts itself before the first keystroke.
findings.fix: Use `fahrenheit: convert('20')` in the model and explain it. Or keep the 68, point out the duplication, and say why it is acceptable here.

findings.where: "Now make the classic mistake… `convert`'s own example fails at once… It gives an error from `fahrenheit`, saying it expected a number and got a string."
findings.problem: The reader is not told where or when the failure shows up (as they type? in a test panel? in the preview?) or what it looks like, so they cannot tell whether they reproduced it. "At once" is also unclear without knowing when signature examples run.
findings.fix: Say where the failure message appears in the live example and quote roughly what it says. Remind the reader that signature examples run every time the code changes.

findings.where: "`Number('abc')` is `NaN`, and NaN goes through the arithmetic and comes out as NaN"
findings.problem: NaN is never defined. A beginner does not know it stands for "Not a Number", or why a non-number counts as a kind of number. The line is also over-long and reads as a run-on.
findings.fix: Add a definition: "NaN ("not a number") is JavaScript's special number meaning the answer makes no sense." Split the sentence.

findings.where: Traffic light: "`light.colour` is a part of the model, and you can hand it to a function like any other value: `nextLight` sees `'red'`."
findings.problem: This sentence comes after the first traffic-light example, which has no model, and before the code it describes. As the reader takes it in, there is no `light` anywhere in view. Bad ordering.
findings.fix: Move the sentence below the second traffic-light example, or begin it with "In the next example…".

findings.where: `given colour { 'red' {…} 'green' {…} } else { return 'red' }`
findings.problem: Amber is handled only by the `else`, and nothing in the prose says so. A beginner looking for the amber→red step will not find it. Also, `given` is used with no pointer to where it was taught.
findings.fix: Add: "anything else, including amber, goes back to red." Name the chapter that introduced `given` (Decisions?).

findings.where: Try it: "Then add a line that shows `'You win!'` when the score reaches 100. (Hint: a second, computed part of the model, set alongside the score.)"
findings.problem: The chapter never shows how to display text that depends on a condition, or how to keep a computed part in step. "Set alongside the score" is too cryptic for a beginner: set by whom, where? The NaN 'please type a number' exercise depends on the same untaught step.
findings.fix: Spell the hint out: give the model `message: ''`, and in each button's handler, after changing the score, set `message` to `'You win!'` or `''` with an `if`. Or show a tiny worked example of a second model part set in a handler.

findings.where: "Write `celsius(fahrenheit: 212.0): 100.0` first"
findings.problem: The parameter is named `fahrenheit`, the same as the existing `fahrenheit` function in the same program. Inside `celsius` that name would hide the function, which is exactly the kind of thing that trips up a beginner.
findings.fix: Rename the parameter, e.g. `celsius(degreesF: 212.0): 100.0`.

findings.where: "With a model, a button only has to get the **fact** right. Showing it is someone else's job, done once."
findings.problem: "Someone else" is vague: is it tosijs, or the line that puts the span on the page?
findings.fix: Say "Showing it is the job of the line that put it on the page, written once; tosijs keeps it up to date."

findings.where: "`event` describes what happened, and `event.target` is the box itself"
findings.problem: `(event) =>` is the first handler with a parameter, and the reader is not told who passes `event` in or that every handler receives one.
findings.fix: Add: "the browser passes every handler an event object; earlier handlers just ignored it."

findings.where: `light.colour` is a part of the model, and you can hand it to a function like any other value: `nextLight` sees `'red'`.
findings.problem: nextLight does not receive the string 'red'; it receives a tosi proxy that TJS treats as 'red' in some places and not others. The signature check unwraps it (`__tjs_rt.__tv(colour)`) and so does `given` (`switch (__tjs.swKey(colour))`), which is why the example works. Inside the function, `typeof colour` is 'object' and `colour === 'red'` is false. TJS `==` does unwrap it. A learner who tries `===` or `typeof` (the chapter's own exercise asks for more `nextLight` logic) gets a surprising false. The brief's question has an answer: object-shaped params accept tosi proxies too (press(calculator, '7') on a proxy mutates it, x=73, no type errors).
findings.evidence: seen2.tjs: `const { light } = tosi({ light: { colour: 'red' } }); function show(colour: 'red'): '' { return `${colour == 'red'} ${colour === 'red'} ${typeof colour}` }; preview.append(show(light.colour))` printed `true false object` (happy-dom with the real tosijs dist). Emitted nextLight: `const __cv_colour = __tjs_rt.__tv(colour); ... switch (__tjs.swKey(colour))`.
findings.fix: Say what is actually handed over: 'nextLight gets the model's part, not a copy; TJS checks and compares it by the value it holds, so given and == treat it as the text red.' Or pass a plain value explicitly (`String(light.colour)`) and say why. At the least, drop the claim that it 'sees' the bare string.

findings.where: button({ onClick: () => { counter.count = counter.count + 1 } }, 'Click me')
findings.problem: This is the first arrow function in the learn chapters with a braced body. Lists and the Wave example only show the expression form (`() => preview.append(...)`, `(price) => price * 1.5`). The braces appear here with no explanation of what they mean or why this handler uses them while the Wave one does not.
findings.evidence: grep -n "=> {" guides/learn/*.md: the only other matches are in things-that-take-time.md (lines 46, 91), which comes after this chapter.
findings.fix: Add one sentence after the counter example: braces after `=>` hold statements, the same as a function body. A handler that changes something, rather than giving back an answer, is written this way.

findings.where: input({ value: '20', onInput: ... }) ... tosi({ weather: { fahrenheit: 68 } })
findings.problem: The converter writes the same fact down twice by hand. The box starts at '20' and the model starts at 68, which is 20 °C worked out in your head. This is the mistake the chapter warned about a few sections earlier ('the same fact turns up in many places... sooner or later one would be forgotten'). A reader who changes '20' to '30' sees '30 °C is 68 °F' until they type. The output is right as written (initial ' °C is 68 °F', typing 37 gives 98.6, in headless Chrome), but the example works against the lesson.
findings.evidence: Headless Chrome: `ex7 INITIAL:  °C is 68 °F`, `typed 37 :  °C is 98.6 °F`.
findings.fix: Start the model from the rule: `tosi({ weather: { fahrenheit: convert('20') } })`. Or keep the celsius text in the model as well and bind the box to it. Or add a sentence saying the two starting values must agree and why that is fragile.

findings.where: `() => preview.append(' 👋')` is a function with no parameters, written with an arrow as in Lists.
findings.problem: Lists shows arrows that have one parameter (`(price) => ...`, `(planet) => li(planet)`), never the empty `()` form. 'As in Lists' slightly overstates what the reader has already seen.
findings.evidence: guides/learn/lists.md:186 `prices.map((price) => price * 1.5)`; :288 `planets.map((planet) => li(planet))`.
findings.fix: 'written with an arrow as in Lists, but with empty brackets because it needs no input.'

findings.where: Converter and traffic-light fences (tosi import plus signature examples)
findings.problem: Outside the doc site, the signature examples in the two fences that import tosijs do not run. `tjs check` passes them, but transpile-time testing reports INCONCLUSIVE ('Module could not be executed for testing: tosi is not defined'), and the fences that use `preview` report 'preview is not defined'. On the live site this is fine: a-calculator's preview-plus-tests example shows '4/4 passed', so tests get `preview` there. The claim that convert's example 'fails at once' is true: with `preview` removed, `tjs check` exits 1 with 'Function signature example is inconsistent: Expected 212 at convert, got MonadicError ... expected number, actual string'. Nothing in the chapter needs to change; this note is for whoever checks these fences with the CLI.
findings.evidence: runner on ex7/ex9: TESTS [["fahrenheit signature example",false,"INCONCLUSIVE","...tosi is not defined"]]; m3.tjs (the mistake, with no preview line): `✗ ... convert signature example ... got MonadicError`, rc=1.
findings.fix: No chapter change needed. Optionally, the converter fence could leave out the duplicated fahrenheit/convert examples, or say they were tested above.

div/span/strong/h2 never explained (missing): partly rejected. Hello, Screen teaches elements, strong and h2, and Repetition uses div. I added only the tags that are new here (label, plus input as before).
`...` spread never explained (missing): partly rejected. Lists (line 248) teaches `...`. I still added a one-line reminder of what it does in this call.

I created /Users/tonioloewald/tjs-lang/guides/learn/things-that-take-time.md, the only file I touched. Its first line is the metadata comment given in the brief, `<!-- TODO review -->` comes right after it, and A Calculator was already at order 12.

The chapter has these sections:
- **Later, not now.** `setTimeout` in the console, showing that lines run out of order, then a reminder button that drives a tosi model. It links the timer back to "the handler runs later" and to the earlier mistake of calling a handler too early.
- **A countdown.** A pure `tick(seconds: 10): 9` rule with a test, `setInterval`/`clearInterval`, timer ids, and a `running` guard. A suggested experiment removes the guard; I confirmed that two clicks then make the number drop by two each second. There is also an honest note that an old timer keeps running if you edit the example.
- **Waiting in order.** The `wait()` recipe (a promise explained as a ticket at a counter), and a breakfast sequence using `async`/`await`.
- **An answer that takes time.** `slowDouble`, with a test that uses `await`. I checked the in-page harness first: it runs each test body in an async wrapper and waits for it. The section explains why async functions get no `: 42` return example.
- **Common mistakes.** Using a value before it has arrived (`[object Promise]`, and `ticket + 1` giving `[object Promise]1`), and forgetting `await`. A typed async function given a wrong value resolves to an error; this ties back to When Things Go Wrong with the same `instanceof Error` habit, and a test checks `received`.
- **Asking another computer.** A real `fetch` from Open-Meteo, which I confirmed sends `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`. It also introduces `try`/`catch` for the first time in the book, used only to turn a thrown network failure into an error value. It covers `response.ok`/`status` and tells readers how to break it on purpose: a wrong host gives "could not be reached", and a wrong path gives "answered 404".
- **Testing the parts that wait.** Test the pure `weatherReport`, not the network call.
- **Try it.** The stopwatch with start/stop/reset and a `showTime` rule written test first. A "random saying" button using `api.github.com/zen` (CORS confirmed), with a friendly message on failure; the 403 GitHub sends when you go over the rate limit is a natural way to try that. Three more exercises: add a second city, start the countdown from a typed number, and a traffic light that changes by itself using `await` in a `while` loop with a Stop button.

To match how the page works, every timer and fetch starts from a button. Tests run the example's top-level code once before the real run, so a timer started at the top level would run twice. Examples that have no tests never contain the word "test", which keeps them on the faster path.

How I verified: I ran `tjs check` on every fence and all pass. I also wrote a simulator of the doc site (scratchpad sim.ts and drive.ts). It uses happy-dom, installs the real runtime, transpiles with `tjs(src, { runTests: false })` as tosijs-ui does, and runs code plus testUtils plus testRunner in an AsyncFunction. A driver clicks the buttons and waits real time. All console output, page states over time and test results match the prose, including a live fetch that returned the real Berlin temperature, and both failure cases.

The simulator has two quirks that are not chapter bugs. happy-dom shows the number 0 as empty text where a real browser shows "0". Its fetch also fails to decompress the Open-Meteo reply, so the simulator uses Bun's own fetch; I checked CORS separately with curl.

I did not run `bun run docs`, and I did not check the chapter in a real browser.
questions: The command-line test runner cannot run a test that contains `await`. `tjs check`, `tjs test` and `tjs()` mark such a test inconclusive with 'Module could not be executed for testing: Unexpected identifier …', and `tjs check` still exits 0. The page's test runner handles the same test correctly, so the chapter's async tests pass on the site but show as inconclusive from the CLI. Is this a bug to put on the board? It looks like the transpile-time runner executes test bodies synchronously.

When `tjs test` / `tjs()` checks an async function's return example, it reports it as passed even when it is wrong (`async function f(n: 2): 999` shows '✓ signature example'). guides/examples/tjs/async-functions.md says the example is 'not run', which is true in the page but not what the CLI prints. Should the CLI report it as not checked instead? The chapter tells readers to leave return examples off async functions.

On the doc site, an example's timers are not stopped when it re-runs: after an edit, or the run of its tests that comes before the real run. The chapter works around this by starting every timer from a button, and includes a 'reload the page' note. Do you want a tosijs-ui card so that a re-run clears its own timers, so the note can go?

This chapter is the first place the book teaches `try`/`catch`, kept narrow: only to turn a fetch that throws into an error value. Is this the right place, or should it be introduced in When Things Go Wrong?

The Try it uses https://api.github.com/zen (a random saying rather than a 'fact'; unauthenticated limit about 60 requests per hour) because it is CORS-friendly and already on the site's AJS fetch list. findings.where: "Many services answer in **JSON**, a way of writing data that looks almost exactly like the objects in Things with Parts." / "In that object, the temperature is at `data.current.temperature_2m` (Open-Meteo's own documentation lists what is where)."
findings.problem: The reader never sees a JSON reply. They are told it 'looks almost exactly like' objects, then asked to accept that the number is at `data.current.temperature_2m` with no picture of the object. Without seeing the reply, the path `.current.temperature_2m` is a magic string, and the reader can't apply the idea to another service (e.g. the Paris exercise or their own API). Sending them to Open-Meteo's documentation is a big jump for a beginner.
findings.fix: Show a trimmed real reply as a static block, e.g. `{ "latitude": 52.52, ..., "current": { "time": "…", "temperature_2m": 8.3 } }`, and point at the two levels. Or add a `console.log(data)` step the reader can switch on. Say in one clause that `temperature_2m` means the temperature 2 metres above the ground.

findings.where: "When there is no reply at all, `fetch` does not give back an error value: it **throws** one. A thrown error stops the function right there, and keeps going up through every function that called it ... `try { … } catch { … }` is that something..."
findings.problem: Throwing and try/catch are a brand-new control-flow idea, the first time in the book a function can stop without returning, and they are introduced inside the second item of a bullet list under a subheading about failures. A beginner may skim right past it. The code that uses `try`/`catch` also appears about 50 lines before this explanation, so on first read the reader meets `try {`, `catch {` with nothing to go on. (The source line starting 'that throws, the program jumps to the `catch` block instead of stopping. Here the `catch` block gives back...' is also wrapped much longer than its neighbours.)
findings.fix: Give throwing its own short subsection, ideally with a tiny example before the weather code (a function that throws, called with and without try/catch, showing that the lines after the throw do not run). Then in the weather example, say 'the `try`/`catch` here is explained below' or move the explanation ahead of the example.

findings.where: "Click three times quickly and you get three reminders, each arriving three seconds after its own click."
findings.problem: The example can't show this. All three reminders write the same text to the same `div`, so the reader sees 'Waiting…' and then 'Time to stand up and stretch!' once. The second and third reminders change nothing on screen. The prose claims something the reader has no way to see.
findings.fix: Either make each reminder visible (count them: `reminder.message = `Reminder ${n}!``, or log to the console), or drop the claim. If you keep it, it's also a good setup for the `running` guard in the countdown section.

findings.where: "With only `setTimeout`, each step goes inside the function of the step before, and the code drifts further to the right with every step."
findings.problem: This is the whole motivation for async/await, and it is only described, never shown. A beginner can't picture 'goes inside the function of the step before', so the 'better way' that follows has nothing to be better than.
findings.fix: Show the nested-setTimeout version of the breakfast (three levels is enough) as a static block, then the async version. Seeing the two side by side is the motivation.

findings.where: "A typed async function checks what it is given ... The difference is when you see it: the error arrives where the answer would have, after the `await`."
findings.problem: It's unclear whether the error comes after the one-second wait or straight away. 'Arrives later' and 'after the await' suggest the wrong value is only noticed after `wait(1000)`. The reader also can't tell whether calling `slowDouble('ten')` without `await` gives an error or a promise. The 'when you see it' point is the heart of the section and stays vague.
findings.fix: Say exactly what happens: the check runs when the function is called, before the wait, and the error is handed back as the promised answer, so you only see it once you `await`. If the timing matters, a console line before and after would show it.

findings.where: `expect(wrong.received).toBe('ten')`
findings.problem: The test uses a `received` property on the error that the page never mentions. The reader only knows `.message` (used just above).
findings.fix: Add one sentence: TJS's type errors also carry the value that was received in `.received` (plus whatever else is relevant), or use `.message` in the test instead.

findings.where: "Instead, keep the network call small ... with examples and tests, as the calculator does with `press`."
findings.problem: A calculator and a `press` function are never mentioned on this page, and no chapter is named. A first-time reader has no idea what this refers to.
findings.fix: Name the chapter (e.g. 'as the calculator in <Chapter> does with `press`'), or drop the comparison. The weatherReport example already makes the point.

findings.where: "[Open-Meteo](https://open-meteo.com), a free weather service that answers any web page"
findings.problem: 'Answers any web page' suggests that some services don't, but never says why (cross-origin rules). A beginner who later tries some other API from their page and gets nothing has no idea this sentence was the warning.
findings.fix: Add one sentence: many services only answer requests from their own sites or with a key, so this book uses ones that answer anyone. A failed fetch to such a service looks like the 'could not be reached' case.

findings.where: `'https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast' + `?latitude=${latitude}&longitude=${longitude}&current=temperature_2m``
findings.problem: The query string (`?`, `name=value`, `&`) is new syntax for a beginner and is never explained. The reader is told 'the address is built from the latitude and longitude' but not how an address carries a question.
findings.fix: One short sentence: after `?`, an address can carry named values, `name=value`, separated by `&`. Here they are the place and what we want to know.

findings.where: "While `makeBreakfast` is paused, the rest of the page is not. The browser goes on responding to the reader..."
findings.problem: This is claimed but not shown, and the breakfast example has the problem the countdown section just warned about. Pressing 'Make breakfast' twice starts two breakfasts whose steps overwrite each other, and the page gives no hint that this is the same lesson as `running`. Separately, the key idea that a loop *without* await freezes the page only appears in the last exercise.
findings.fix: Invite the reader to press the button twice and watch the messages tangle, and connect it to the `running` guard. Consider moving the 'without the await, the page would freeze' point up from the traffic-light exercise into this section.

findings.where: Countdown bullets: "- `let timer = null` makes the name before there is a timer to put in it."
findings.problem: This bullet comes last, but `let timer = null` comes before `setInterval` in the code, and the first bullet already says 'The program keeps it in `timer`'. The page doesn't say why this is `let` and not `const`, or why `timer` lives outside `start`.
findings.fix: Move this bullet first. Say it's `let` because a value is put into it later, and that it's outside `start` so the function inside setInterval can still find it after `start` has finished.

findings.where: "Try it: delete the three lines starting `if (countdown.running)`, and click **Start** twice."
findings.problem: The result is worse than 'the number would fall twice a second'. `timer` is overwritten, so the first interval is never cleared and keeps running after zero. A curious reader who watches closely (or clicks Start again) sees behaviour the text didn't predict.
findings.fix: Either mention that the first timer can no longer be stopped because its id was lost (a good extra lesson on why the id matters), or soften the prediction.

findings.where: "Notice that `slowDouble` has no worked example of its answer, no `: 42` after the parentheses."
findings.problem: `wait` also has no return example, and it isn't async, so this explanation doesn't cover it. A reader trained to expect worked examples will wonder why. 'Comparing the answer at once' is also ambiguous ('immediately' or 'all together').
findings.fix: Add a clause: `wait` gives back a promise, and the same reasoning applies. Change 'at once' to 'straight away'.

findings.where: `function weatherReport(celsius: 21.5)` with test `weatherReport(-3)`
findings.problem: If earlier chapters taught that `42` means a whole number and `3.14` means a number with a fractional part, a reader may wonder whether `-3` is accepted where the example is `21.5`. Nothing here says so.
findings.fix: Add a short note that a decimal example accepts whole numbers too (temperatures can be either), or use an example whose type is obvious.

findings.where: "Change `api.open-meteo.com` to `api.open-meteo.co` ... Then put it back, and change `forecast` to `forcast`"
findings.problem: The reader isn't told what they should see. Without that they can't tell whether the experiment worked. A non-existent host may also leave 'Asking…' showing for a while before failing.
findings.fix: Give the expected messages ('Sorry, the weather service could not be reached…', 'Sorry, the weather service answered 404…'), and warn that the first may take a few seconds.

findings.where: `setTimeout(() => console.log('The kettle has boiled.'), 2000)`
findings.problem: This is the first code on the page, and it depends on arrow-function syntax (`() =>`), passing a function as a value. The page relies on the reader already knowing it from Responding to the Reader but never says so. If that chapter used named functions only, this is a sudden jump.
findings.fix: Add a half-sentence recalling that `() => …` is a function with no name, as in Responding to the Reader (or wherever it was introduced).

findings.where: "Here is a timer on the page, with a model (Responding to the Reader) to show its message"
findings.problem: 'Model', `tosi`, `elements` and `preview` are all relied on with only a chapter name as reference. That's fine for linear readers, but someone landing on this page sees jargon. 'Model' especially is easy to misread on a page about weather.
findings.fix: Add a one-line reminder: 'a model, the object made with `tosi` whose changes show on the page'.

findings.where: Line 2: `<!-- TODO review -->`
findings.problem: A leftover working note in the source. It's invisible when rendered, but it is the only marker that the page hasn't been reviewed.
findings.fix: Remove it after the edit pass.

findings.where: "TJS's own errors and the errors you give back are values, and only `fetch` and a few other built-in functions throw. That is why this book has not needed `try` before."
findings.problem: This contradicts When Things Go Wrong, "Mistakes that stop the program": `… is not defined` and `… is not a function` are thrown errors as well, and the reader has already met them. Reading a part of something that is not there also throws. If Open-Meteo's reply had no `current`, then `data.current.temperature_2m` would throw a TypeError. That one is inside the `try` here, so the example is safe, but the sentence makes it sound as if only built-in functions throw.
findings.fix: Tie the two together. For example: "The mistakes that stop the program, from When Things Go Wrong, are thrown errors too. Until now there was nothing to do about them except fix the typo. `fetch` is different: it throws because of the world, not because of a mistake in your code, so it is worth catching." Then drop the "only fetch and a few other built-in functions" wording.

findings.where: "Notice that `slowDouble` has no worked example of its answer… so the example would not be checked."
findings.problem: This is true, but it leaves out the part a learner would trip on. A wrong worked example on an async function is not just left unchecked: it is reported as passing. The emitter adds async signature examples to the results as `passed: true` (src/lang/emitters/js-tests.ts, the "Add skipped results for async signature tests" loop near line 1053). So a learner who adds one anyway sees green.
findings.evidence: as.tjs: `async function slowDouble(n: 21): 99 { return n * 2 }` → `bun src/cli/tjs.ts check as.tjs` prints `✓ as.tjs` and exits 0, although slowDouble(21) is 42.
findings.fix: Add one sentence: "If you write one anyway, TJS cannot check it and does not complain, even when it is wrong, so leave it off and write a test that awaits the answer."

findings.where: "Click three times quickly and you get three reminders, each arriving three seconds after its own click."
findings.problem: The reader cannot see this. All three timers set `reminder.message` to the same text, so the page changes once, about three seconds after the first click. The later two make no visible change. A learner who tries it will think the sentence is wrong.
findings.fix: Either make the timers visible, for example by counting reminders in the model (`reminder.count += 1` and showing the count), or say "each one sets the message again, three seconds after its own click; because the message is the same, you only see the first".

findings.where: "Try it: delete the three lines starting `if (countdown.running)`, and click **Start** twice."
findings.problem: This experiment leaves a timer running forever. The second click overwrites `timer` with the second timer's id, so `clearInterval(timer)` at zero stops only the second timer. The first one keeps calling `tick(0)` every second until the page is reloaded. This is a real lesson (a lost timer id cannot be stopped), and the later note about reloading half covers it, but the experiment does not say it.
findings.fix: Add a sentence after the experiment: "Notice that at zero only one timer stops: `timer` holds the second timer's id, the first id was lost, and a timer whose id is lost can never be stopped. Reload the page to clear it."

findings.where: "when you go over, `response.ok` is false and `response.status` is 403"
findings.problem: GitHub documents 403 or 429 for a rate-limited request. The exercise's advice to check `response.ok` is right either way, but a learner who tests for `status == 403` specifically may miss a 429. I confirmed that the endpoint is CORS-open (`access-control-allow-origin: *`, `x-ratelimit-limit: 60`, `content-type: text/plain`). I did not trigger the limit itself.
findings.evidence: curl -i -H 'Origin: https://tjs.tosijs.net' https://api.github.com/zen → HTTP/2 200, access-control-allow-origin: *, x-ratelimit-limit: 60
findings.fix: Say "`response.status` is 403 (sometimes 429)", or say only that `response.ok` is false, which is what the reader should check.

findings.where: "The test uses `await` too. A test can wait for an answer in the same way as the rest of the program, and it is checked when the answer arrives."
findings.problem: This is true on the doc site. There, tosijs-ui runs the code and `testRunner` in an AsyncFunction, and each test body is wrapped in `await (async () => {…})()` (src/lang/tests.ts:346). In a simulation of that path, both async tests pass. But the build-time and CLI test path runs the module synchronously with `new Function`. There, both async tests are reported inconclusive, so a reader who runs the chapter locally with `tjs test` will not see them pass. The chapter does not need to change for site readers. This is a note for the owner's edit pass, or for a card on the board.
findings.evidence: `bun src/cli/tjs.ts test f6.tjs` → "? 'slowDouble doubles, eventually' — inconclusive: Module could not be executed for testing: Unexpected identifier 'slowDouble'. Expected ')' to end an argument list." The same happens with the top-level await lines removed (f6b.tjs). The simulated page run gives TESTS: [["slowDouble doubles, eventually",true,""]].
findings.fix: No change to the chapter needed. Optionally file a board card noting that the transpile-time runner (src/lang/emitters/js-tests.ts) cannot run a test that awaits, so the CLI and build checks report these tests inconclusive.

rejected: Polish finding to remove `<!-- TODO review -->`: rejected. The ground rules require that line right after the metadata comment.

CLI/build-time runner reports the async tests as inconclusive: no change to the chapter. The finding says so itself. On the page both tests pass; I re-checked this with the page simulation (sim.ts). It belongs on the board, which I can't file under these rules.

findings.where: ## Going through the parts — `import { elements } from 'tosijs'` / `const { ul, li } = elements` / `preview.append(ul(...lines.map((line) => li(line))))`

findings.where: Lines 149-150: "Use `const` unless you need the name to change; then a reader knows at a glance that the value stays put."
findings.problem: "then" seems to refer to the nearest clause ("unless you need the name to change"). Read that way, the sentence says using `let` tells a reader the value stays put, which is the opposite of what it means.
findings.fix: Rewrite as: "Use `const` unless the name really needs to change. When a reader sees `const`, they know at a glance that the value stays put."

findings.where: Lines 96-98: "A name is not a formula that keeps updating; it is a label stuck on a value."
findings.problem: The example cannot show this, because `width` is a `const` and cannot be changed after `area` is computed. Editing the first line changes both, so the reader never sees `area` failing to update. The claim is stated but not shown.
findings.fix: Show it in the `let` section: `let width = 6; const area = width * 7; width = 10` and test that `area` is still 42. Or move the claim there.

findings.where: Exercise 4: "build the full name from them with a space in between"
findings.problem: The page never shows joining two strings with a space between them. String joining with `+` is only shown as a bug (`'5' + 3`), and no example puts a literal space between two names. A beginner may not realise they need `first + ' ' + last` or `${first} ${last}`.
findings.fix: Add one line to an example or to the `+` section, e.g. `'Ada' + ' ' + 'Lovelace'`, showing that `+` joining strings is useful as well as a source of bugs.

findings.where: 'Try it' exercises 1-4: "Write a program that names your age..."
findings.problem: The exercises do not say where to write the program: a fresh editor, one of the examples above, or somewhere else. They also do not say whether to write a `test` block, which is only implied by "Add a test".
findings.fix: Add a lead-in such as: "Edit any example above, or use the empty editor below, and write a `test` block like the ones in this chapter."

findings.where: Line 109: "A few words belong to the language itself, such as `const` and `let`"
findings.problem: `let` has not been introduced at this point; it appears at line 135. The reader also gets no idea which other words are reserved, or what happens if they use one.
findings.fix: Use `const` alone as the example, or add "(`let` is coming up)". Say what error to expect if a reserved word is used as a name.

findings.where: Lines 27-28: "you have the three kinds of value this chapter is about: numbers, strings and booleans" vs. 'Nothing at all' introducing `undefined`
findings.problem: The page says there are three kinds of value, then introduces a fourth, `undefined`, without saying whether it is a kind of value or what `typeof` reports for it. A reader who just learned `typeof` will want to try it.
findings.fix: Say in 'Nothing at all' that `undefined` is a value of its own, and invite the reader to try `typeof undefined`.

findings.where: Line 52: "Checking Your Work explains why" and line 211: "the tenth item of a list that has three"
findings.problem: 'Checking Your Work' reads as a phrase rather than a chapter title (no link, no quotes, no 'the chapter'). Lists have not been introduced, so the "tenth item" example relies on an idea the reader does not have yet.
findings.fix: Link it: "the chapter [Checking Your Work](...) explains why". Replace the list example or add "(lists come later)".

findings.where: Lines 9-12: room-carpeting motivation with `4.5`, then line 81: `const width = 6`, `const height = 7`
findings.problem: The opening motivation (one width used in area, cost and time) is never followed up. The naming example switches to a 6x7 rectangle, so the payoff, writing the value once and using it three times, is never shown.
findings.fix: Have the naming example use the room: `const width = 4.5`, then area, cost and time all computed from it, so changing one line updates all three.

findings.where: Line 180: "the answer is `NaN`, which stands for 'not a number'. Words do not convert."
findings.problem: A curious reader will run `typeof NaN` (the page just taught `typeof`) and get `number`. Nothing on the page prepares them for that.
findings.fix: Add a half-sentence: "(Oddly, `typeof NaN` is `number`: it is the number that means 'this did not work'.)"

findings.where: ## Nothing at all: "At a console, type `let later`, press Enter, then type `later`."
findings.problem: In the doc-site console, a `let` or `const` typed at the prompt lasts only for that one input. Typing `later` on its own as a second input shows a 'later is not defined' error, not `undefined`. So the one hands-on step in this section shows the beginner the wrong thing.
findings.evidence: node_modules/tosijs-ui/dist/live-example/component.js lines 175-177 (tosijs-ui 1.16.38): "Two differences from devtools: a `const` or `let` you declare lives only for that one input (use `var`, or one input, to keep a value)". In one program `let later` followed by `console.log(later)` does print `undefined` (scratch q.tjs, `tjs run`).
findings.fix: Have the reader type it as one input: "type `let later; later` and press Enter" (or use Shift+Enter for a second line). The console then shows `undefined`.

findings.where: ## Asking whether two values are the same: "the next chapter, on decisions, shows what TJS does about it."
findings.problem: Decisions is not the next chapter. By the metadata order, values-and-names is order 2, functions.md is order 3, checking-your-work.md is order 4 and decisions.md is order 5. The material on mixing up `=` and `==` (`if (n = 0)`) is in decisions.md.
findings.evidence: head -1 guides/learn/*.md: functions.md {"order": 3}, checking-your-work.md {"order": 4}, decisions.md {"order": 5}; grep finds `if (n = 0)` at guides/learn/decisions.md:141.
findings.fix: Write "a later chapter, Decisions, shows what TJS does about it".

findings.where: ## Naming a value: "move the `const area` line to the top, and TJS stops with an error, because on that line `width` and `height` do not exist yet."
findings.problem: The error the reader sees is "Cannot access 'width' before initialization", not the "is not defined" message this chapter teaches two sections later. A beginner told "they do not exist yet" and then shown different words may not connect the two.
findings.evidence: Scratch m4.tjs (area line moved first): `tjs run` gives "Runtime error: Cannot access 'width' before initialization." `tjs check` passes, so the error only shows up when the code runs.
findings.fix: Quote the message: "TJS stops with an error saying it cannot access `width` before initialization: on that line, `width` and `height` do not exist yet."

findings.where: ## Text that looks like a number: "Try `Number('five')` at a console"
findings.problem: This example uses the code view. It does not say which console to use or how to open one. The only example in the chapter that opens on the console is the first one, several sections up.
findings.fix: Say where to type it: "open this example's Console tab and type `Number('five')`" (the REPL is in each example's Console tab), or "at the console at the top of this chapter".

findings.where: ## When a name goes wrong: "an error about assigning to a constant"
findings.problem: This is accurate, but the exact words depend on the browser. Bun prints 'Cannot assign to "width" because it is a constant'; Chrome's V8 says 'Assignment to constant variable.' Keep the wording loose, as it is now. Do not quote either message.
findings.evidence: Scratch m3.tjs (`width = 8` added after line 1): `tjs run` gives 'Runtime error: Cannot assign to "width" because it is a constant'. `tjs check` passes.
findings.fix: No change needed. Just do not quote one engine's message if this sentence is edited.

findings.where: ## Try it (brief's optional typeof item)
findings.problem: The brief's optional `typeof null` item was not added. That is allowed. If it goes in, it is accurate: in TJS, `typeof null` is 'null'. The chapter says nothing more about `typeof` than it should.
findings.evidence: Scratch q.tjs: `console.log(typeof 42, typeof 'hi', typeof true, typeof '42', typeof Number('42'), typeof null)` prints `number string boolean string number null`.
findings.fix: Optional: add a sixth item, "Try `typeof null` and remember the answer; a later chapter uses it."

rejected: Polish: don't quote the const-reassignment message. Nothing to change: the wording stays loose ('an error about assigning to a constant'), because Bun and V8 word it differently.

Polish: optional `typeof null` item. Not added. No learn chapter has introduced `null` yet, so this item would have to introduce it with nothing to support it. The finding itself says the item is optional.
